stories.title: Scientists make possible breakthrough in hunt for dark matter
stories.summary: Dark Matter is invisible to the human eye and to telescopes, but scientists are confident it exists due to its gravitational effects at galactic scales
stories.author: Will Dunham
stories.content:
Scientists have made a possible breakthrough in the hunt for dark matter – observing hints of it during an experiment about a 1.6 kilometres underground in South Dakota – though they stopped short of saying they have finally detected this elusive cosmic component.

The researchers described a particle interaction documented at the Sanford Underground Research Facility – built in a former gold mine in the state’s Black Hills region – that May have involved a hypothesized particle called a Wimp, short for “weakly interacting massive particle.” This is one of the proposed candidates for being a dark matter particle.

Ordinary matter makes up stars, planets, people and everything else we can see. But it represents only about 15 per cent of all the matter in the universe. The rest is thought to be dark matter, which does not emit or reflect light, making it invisible to the human eye and to telescopes. But scientists are confident dark matter exists because of its gravitational effects at galactic scales.

Scientists produce most extensive map yet of dark matter in northern skies

Particle physicist Sam Eriksen of the University of Bristol in England, lead author of a study describing the work, said it “could be the first hint of a dark matter observation.”

Dark matter is thought to interact only extremely rarely with ordinary matter. The ongoing LUX-Zeplin, or LZ, experiment in which the observation occurred is designed to catch such interactions and is optimized to look for WIMPs.

It employs ten tonnes of the chemical element xenon in liquid form inside a detector device – a large cylindrical vessel – that is managed by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

The researchers are searching for dark matter scattering off xenon atoms. When a particle scatters, they would observe flashes of light, with the properties of these flashes revealing what type of particle interacted with the xenon.

In an announcement made on Tuesday at a scientific conference in Japan and described in the study submitted to the journal Physical Review Letters, they described the detection of an interaction between a xenon atom and another particle that appeared to unfold in a way hypothesized for a Wimp.

They said what they May have observed was a Wimp colliding with a xenon atom’s nucleus, transferring a small amount of energy that produced a faint flash of UV light that was detected in the experiment. And the collision caused the xenon atom’s nucleus to jolt forward in what is called a nuclear recoil.

While the researchers said the interaction acted as they would expect a Wimp to act, they cautioned that the observation does not yet meet the statistical threshold needed to claim a discovery of dark matter.

“Importantly, as it’s just a single event, we are not claiming that it is dark matter,” Eriksen said.

The researchers are working to rule out other explanations.

“We May be looking at something extraordinary, but we have to be exceptionally rigorous before drawing that conclusion,” Ucla astrophysicist and study co-author Alvine Kamaha said.

Scientists are unsure of the nature of dark matter, just as they are uncertain about the nature of the mysterious cosmic force called dark energy.

“There could be millions of dark matter particles passing through our bodies every second, and yet almost none of them will ever interact with an atom in our bodies,” Kamaha said.

A leading hypothesis is that dark matter is made of a type of particle produced in the early universe and still present today.

“When we observe galaxies and clusters of galaxies, we see that they behave as though they contain much more mass than the matter we can see. So although we cannot see dark matter itself, we can observe what its gravity does,” Kamaha said.

“You can think of dark matter as the cosmic glue that helped enable the formation of galaxies like our Milky Way. Without dark matter, the universe would have evolved very differently, and the structures that eventually led to our solar system May not have formed in the same way,” Kamaha said.

Scientists are searching for dark matter in several ways.

“We study its gravitational effects on galaxies and the universe. We try to produce dark matter particles in particle accelerators. And we perform direct detection using experiments buried deep underground, like LZ, to shield them from cosmic rays and other sources of background while we look for the extremely rare occasion when a dark matter particle interacts with ordinary matter,” Kamaha said.

The researchers described a particle interaction documented at the Sanford Underground Research Facility – built in a former gold mine in the state’s Black Hills region – that May have involved a hypothesized particle called a Wimp, short for “weakly interacting massive particle.” This is one of the proposed candidates for being a dark matter particle.

Ordinary matter makes up stars, planets, people and everything else we can see. But it represents only about 15 per cent of all the matter in the universe. The rest is thought to be dark matter, which does not emit or reflect light, making it invisible to the human eye and to telescopes. But scientists are confident dark matter exists because of its gravitational effects at galactic scales.
Scientists produce most extensive map yet of dark matter in northern skies
Particle physicist Sam Eriksen of the University of Bristol in England, lead author of a study describing the work, said it “could be the first hint of a dark matter observation.”

Dark matter is thought to interact only extremely rarely with ordinary matter. The ongoing LUX-Zeplin, or LZ, experiment in which the observation occurred is designed to catch such interactions and is optimized to look for WIMPs.

It employs ten tonnes of the chemical element xenon in liquid form inside a detector device – a large cylindrical vessel – that is managed by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

The researchers are searching for dark matter scattering off xenon atoms. When a particle scatters, they would observe flashes of light, with the properties of these flashes revealing what type of particle interacted with the xenon.

In an announcement made on Tuesday at a scientific conference in Japan and described in the study submitted to the journal Physical Review Letters, they described the detection of an interaction between a xenon atom and another particle that appeared to unfold in a way hypothesized for a Wimp.

They said what they May have observed was a Wimp colliding with a xenon atom’s nucleus, transferring a small amount of energy that produced a faint flash of UV light that was detected in the experiment. And the collision caused the xenon atom’s nucleus to jolt forward in what is called a nuclear recoil.

While the researchers said the interaction acted as they would expect a Wimp to act, they cautioned that the observation does not yet meet the statistical threshold needed to claim a discovery of dark matter.
“Importantly, as it’s just a single event, we are not claiming that it is dark matter,” Eriksen said.
The researchers are working to rule out other explanations.
“We May be looking at something extraordinary, but we have to be exceptionally rigorous before drawing that conclusion,” Ucla astrophysicist and study co-author Alvine Kamaha said.
Scientists are unsure of the nature of dark matter, just as they are uncertain about the nature of the mysterious cosmic force called dark energy.
“There could be millions of dark matter particles passing through our bodies every second, and yet almost none of them will ever interact with an atom in our bodies,” Kamaha said.

stories.title: Why buying Canadian makes us feel good
stories.summary: It’s not purely about patriotism – it’s also about agency
stories.author: Gary Mason
stories.content:
My wife was an early adopter of the Buy Canadian movement.

It began around the time U.S. President Donald Trump decided to start insulting us last year, referring to former prime minister Justin Trudeau as “ Governor ” and Canada as America’s “ 51st state .” Then there were the tariffs Mr. Trump was hitting Canada with that would hurt our economy.

It all boiled over – for her and many others - during the infamous ambush of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office on Feb. 28. It prompted us to cut short an American holiday by several weeks.

Things haven’t been the same since.

My wife became single-minded in her determination to not see a cent of our money spent on an American product. Some things have snuck past her detection techniques. But mostly she has been an unabashed patriot, determined to keep as much of our money in this country as she can, with travel dollars spent in destinations not marked with an American flag.

The Big Guide to Canadian Shopping

Then came last week when she went to our local grocery store to buy apples.

Our local Thrifty’s, it needs to be said, has done an admirable job sourcing fruits and vegetables, in particular, from countries other than the U.S. We have seen Asian pears from China, Valencia oranges from Egypt and tangerines from South Africa. It’s not uncommon to see food in the produce aisles from countries such as Vietnam, Ecuador and Brazil. And those are just some examples. But recently she went to buy apples and there were tons of them – almost entirely from Washington State.

The Okanagan region of B.C. used to be known for its apple crop. But years ago, many orchard growers decided there was more money to be made in wine than fruit, so the great conversion took place. Apples are still grown, but not nearly to the same extent. And today, much larger orchards in Washington State are squeezing out the much smaller Okanagan growers. Even when local apples soon arrive in B.C. stores they won’t be able to compete with the price of the Washington State apples. Therein lies the dilemma for many.

Demand for Canadian-made goods gives rise to more direct-to-consumer sales, less focus on U.S. market

For my wife, buying Canadian is as much about helping to protect Canadian jobs as it is punishing U.S. producers. She understands her choices May not be other people’s. She doesn’t believe in shaming those who don’t share her Buy Canadian enthusiasm. She also understands people have limits: many want to help workers in this country out, but not at any price.

And this would seem to describe a prevailing ethic in the country.

Abacus Data recently did a deep dive into people’s attitudes when it comes to Buy Canadian. Its research, conducted in late June and early July, found that buying Canadian has become a regular decision for many of us. And a majority said they go out of their way to choose a Canadian product over a non-Canadian one. But the findings revealed something else: this behaviour isn’t purely about patriotism.

It’s about agency.

“When asked how choosing Canadian makes them feel, the largest single response is that it makes them feel ‘more in control, like I have some say in what happens to the country.’” David Coletto, CEO of Abacus, wrote in a report last month.

Robyn Urback: Don’t bring back COVID-era shaming in this Buy Canadian moment

Here are some numbers I found interesting:

Fifty-three per cent of those surveyed said they go out of their way to choose a Canadian product often or almost always. Somewhat surprisingly – make that a lot surprisingly – that number shoots to 59 per cent in Quebec – the highest percentage of any region in the country on that question. The closest is Saskatchewan/Manitoba at 57 per cent. The lowest? Alberta at 42 per cent. (The province also has the highest share of those who say they “rarely or never go out of their way” to buy Canadian – 20 per cent.)

I agree with Mr. Coletto’s assessment that Buy Canadian does give people a sense they are having some input in this trade war. And that’s important, given the utter lack of control we have over any number of other things affecting our lives: inflation, housing costs, tariffs, climate change, war and the overwhelming feeling that the world seems to be spinning out of control.

Sure, putting down an orange you discover is from California and picking up one that says Mexico isn’t going to change the trajectory of trade talks with the U.S. But it’s something.

And let’s face it, it feels good to take a stand. Especially when you know you’re on the right side of the issue.

stories.title: Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet says he’ll donate $100K from defamation suit win
stories.summary: Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ruled on Monday that Paméla Groleau's accusations against Ouellet were unfounded and ordered her to pay him $100,000.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud
stories.content:
expressed his gratitude today after winning a civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit.

Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ruled on Monday that Paméla Groleau’s accusations against Ouellet were unfounded and ordered her to pay him $100,000.

Ouellet issued a brief written statement today from his residence in Rome, Italy.

In it, he expresses his gratitude to the civil justice system and thanks his lawyers and the witnesses who testified.

Groleau had accused Ouellet of touching her without consent on three occasions between 2008 and 2010, while she was training or working for the church.

Ouelette reiterated his plan to donate the $100,000 in damages to organizations fighting sexual abuse against Indigenous Peoples in Canada.

“I pledge to continue the fight within the Church and in society against every form of abuse, particularly sexual abuse, and I unreservedly support substantiated victims in their pursuit of restorative justice,” he writes.

Castonguay’s 52-page ruling, handed down Monday at the Montreal courthouse, is harsh on Groleau.

The judge concluded that her testimony “was neither credible nor reliable.” He noted that she changed her account of the facts several times and that the alleged incidents took place during public events attended by other people.

stories.title: London under heat warning, temperatures forecast to reach 32 C
stories.summary: Humidex values could approach 40 as the Middlesex-London Health Unit urges residents to take precautions.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Humidex values could approach 40 as the Middlesex-London Health Unit urges residents to take precautions.

Environment Canada has issued a yellow-level heat warning for London and the surrounding region for Tuesday and Wednesday, with the hot weather possibly lasting into Thursday.

At 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, the national weather agency issued the alert, warning of hazardous conditions that May pose health risks, with maximum temperatures expected to reach 30 to 32 C on Tuesday and Wednesday.

Minimum temperatures are expected to range from 20 to 23 C, with humidex values near 40.

For Tuesday, Environment Canada is calling for a high of 30 C, with a 30 per cent chance of showers this afternoon and a risk of a thunderstorm. Temperatures are expected to fall only to a low of 21 C overnight.

“The heat event May continue into Thursday, particularly for Windsor and Essex County, however, confidence is low,” officials wrote in the alert.

The Middlesex-London Health Unit also urged residents Tuesday afternoon to take precautions during the heat.

“Be safe and check in on family, friends and neighbours – especially those who May be more vulnerable to extreme heat,” health unit officials wrote.

The health unit recommends drinking plenty of water, even if you don’t feel thirsty; avoiding caffeinated and alcoholic beverages; and limiting time outdoors. Those who must be outside should seek shade and, where possible, plan activities for the early morning or evening.

Residents are also advised to keep drapes or blinds closed on the sunny side of their homes, take cool showers and use fans to draw in cooler air at night, but not rely on fans as a primary cooling device during prolonged heat.

The health unit also urged residents never to leave a child or pet in a parked car or sleeping outside in direct sunlight.

stories.title: Former Montreal priest convicted in 2019 of abusing boys facing new charges
stories.summary: Montreal - A former Montreal priest who was found guilty in 2019 of sexually abusing two boys is facing charges of possessing and accessing child sexual abuse material.
stories.author: Morgan Lowrie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A former Montreal priest who was found guilty in 2019 of sexually abusing two boys is facing charges of possessing and accessing child sexual abuse material.

Brian Boucher’s lawyer appeared in a Montreal courtroom today on his behalf, and the case was postponed to Sept. 8.

Court documents say the alleged offences occurred between April 7 and April 9.

The 64-year-old was sentenced in 2019 to eight years in prison for sexually assaulting two boys, after being found guilty in one case and pleading guilty in the other.

Boucher worked in 10 Montreal-area churches between 1985 and 2015. The abuse took place at two churches, between 1995 and 1999 in the case of one victim and between 2008 and 2011 in the other.

Boucher was granted statutory release in 2024 and was serving the remainder of his sentence in the community at an approved residential facility before his recent arrest.

In a 2024 report before his release, the Parole Board told Boucher that his case management team “mentions that there is a strong possibility that you have committed other sexual acts in the past.”

“In fact, a public inquiry report in September 2020 revealed that several complaints were made against you since the early 1980s concerning your unacceptable behaviour and interest in young boys,” it read. “In 2002, your name was included on an official list of potential pedophiliac priests, produced by a member of the clergy.”

stories.title: Alberta’s revised statement celebrating province’s birthday removes reference to Indigenous peoples
stories.summary: Updated version was ‘issued in error’ and the original ‘stands,’ government spokesperson says
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
The Alberta government released a statement celebrating the province’s birthday on Tuesday, but an hour later, a revised version was sent out that removed any reference to Indigenous peoples.

The misstep unfolded at a time when relations between the government and the First Nations in Alberta have been strained over the coming referendum on Oct. 19.

Several First Nations have said that any vote on whether Alberta should separate from Canada is a violation of treaty rights.

Shortly after 10 a.m. local time on Tuesday, the government published a statement on behalf of Premier Danielle Smith commemorating the day Alberta joined Confederation in 1905 and became a province of Canada.

The third paragraph of the first statement read: “We recognize the Indigenous Peoples whose enduring connection to and stewardship of this land continues to shape Alberta. Over generations, people from many backgrounds have strengthened our communities through hard work, innovation, entrepreneurship, and a shared belief in opportunity.”

But an hour after it came out, the province sent an edited, expanded statement that removed any reference to Indigenous peoples from the English-language statement.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Danielle Smith (@abdaniellesmith)

“Generations of Albertans from many backgrounds have helped build our province through hard work, innovation and a shared belief in freedom. Their legacy can be seen in the strong communities, thriving industries and quality of life we enjoy today,” Ms. Smith’s new statement read.

The original French-language statement mentioning Indigenous peoples was not revised in the second release.

Yonathan Sumamo, a government spokesperson, said the revised version was “issued in error” and the original, which mentioned First Nations, “stands.”

“We apologize for this error and any confusion that it May have caused,” Mr. Sumamo said in an e-mailed statement.

Ms. Smith, at an unrelated news conference, blamed Alberta’s public service for the revision.

“The public service posted one statement and then took it down and put up another one. I said, ‘Why didn’t you put up the original one?’ And so I’m not exactly sure what happened with that glitch,” Ms. Smith said, adding that Indigenous communities are one of many groups that have “helped build the province.”

Trevor Mercredi, the Grand Chief of Treaty 8 First Nations, called the change made to the Premier’s statement “deeply troubling.”

“Treaty 8 Sovereign First Nations and all First Nations across Alberta have always been part of the history, present and future of this province. Our Nations are not a footnote to Alberta’s story,” Mr. Mercredi said in a statement. “Treaty Nations were here long before Alberta existed, and our place in this land cannot be erased when it becomes politically inconvenient.”

He went on to say that the omission was concerning given the Oct. 19 referendum, which he says challenges “the constitutional status of Treaty rights and the duty to consult.”

“Respect for First Nations must be reflected in the government’s words, actions and relationships,” Mr. Mercredi said.

The revised statement remains on Ms. Smith’s social-media accounts on X and Instagram.

stories.title: Temperatures feeling close to 40 as heat warning continues
stories.summary: Temperatures in London and surrounding areas will feel close to 40 C as the heat warning persists.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Temperatures in London and surrounding areas will feel close to 40 C as the heat warning persists. “Intense heat and humidity. It will be brief, it’s not going to last through the weekend,” said CTV Meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“The risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms develop overnight and through the early morning hours. You will likely hear some rumbles of thunder, especially towards the Bruce Peninsula.” Storms could push through first thing in the morning.

Upwards of 20 millimetres is expected Wednesday, bringing a mix of sun and cloud by the afternoon. “Then, the risk of thunderstorms once again developing in parts of southern Ontario,” Atchison added. “Lots of instability over the next seven days at temperatures close to where we should be for this time of year.” Here’s a full look at your forecast: Tuesday night: A few clouds.

Increasing cloudiness this evening, then a 40 per cent chance of showers late this evening and overnight. Showers beginning before morning, risk of thunderstorms late in the evening and overnight. Low 21 C. Wednesday: Showers ending in the morning, then mainly cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers in the afternoon.

Showers or thunderstorms beginning late in the afternoon. High 31 C, humidex 41 C. Thursday: Cloudy with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 26 C. Friday: Cloudy with a 30 per cent chance of showers. High 26 C.

stories.title: A long lost rock opera from British band Squeeze finally sees the light of day in Toronto
stories.summary: Veteran new wave group played Trixies, a newly recorded album written in 1974, in its entirety during their concert in the city
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Four songs into its concert on Monday at Toronto’s RBC Amphitheatre, the veteran British new wave band Squeeze stopped what they were doing. Which was playing melodically perky pop-rock hits from the late 1970s and early 1980s: Pulling Mussels (From the Shell) , Up the Junction , Another Nail in My Heart and Is That Love .

Singer-guitarist Glenn Tilbrook then introduced the band’s first LP in nine years, Trixies . It’s a concept album released earlier this year based on music he and co-founder Chris Difford wrote as teenagers in 1974. When the songs failed to land them a record contract at the time, they were put away in a drawer as a time capsule of sorts.

“This,” Tilbrook said, “is what it sounds like.”

Squeeze played the album in its entirety, top to bottom. This was the Trixies segment of the band’s current Tried, Tested and Trixies tour. What did it sound like? Like a band reinventing itself.

The crowd, which had been on their feet, sat down en masse , as if instructed to do so. The mood had shifted; the air of nostalgia was gone. This was going to be a rock ’n’ roll recital, not a boomer dance party.

Olivia Rodrigo’s Lilith Fair was sanctuary in turbulent times between Canada and the U.S.

Difford, 71, and Tilbrook, 69, don’t talk much on stage to begin with. But for the Trixies concert centerpiece they clammed up like mussels in a shell. No banter. Musical segues between songs set in a fictional night club added to the dreamy vibe.

The music is moodier, more muscular and mostly without the pop hooks that mark the tuneful rock that made Squeeze legends in dorm rooms on both sides of the Atlantic. It should come to no one’s surprise that the teenaged lyrics of Trixies are not particularly sophisticated. From the album-opener What More Can I Say : “The tables have been cleared, the strangers have been feared, the lipstick has been smeared.”

And to think, Tilbrook and Difford would grow up to write cheeky lines about William Tell and earn comparisons to John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Speaking of which, the Trixies song Don’t Go Out in the Dark is reminiscent of McCartney’s Let Me Roll It from 1973. A line from Hell on Earth (“the bouncer’s name is Eddy, he’s always on the ready”) seems like an outtake from Billy Joel’s Piano Man , also from ’73.

And you don’t need to be an astrophysicist to guess the inspiration behind The Place We Call Mars . “How did I know where the end might begin,” Tilbrook sang on the Bowiesque number, “when the story was so hard to tell?”

Kacey Musgraves’s Middle of Nowhere tour brings hits and humour to Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena

Conceptual albums were in vogue in the early 1970s, from David Bowie’s The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars to the Who’s Quadrophenia to the Eagles’ Desperado . Artists of that decade had faith that their fans had the interest and attention span to indulge their high-minded musical visions. Now? Not so much.

Some fans of Lily Allen complained because on her current tour the British pop star is performing only the songs of West End Girl , the album inspired by her divorce from actor David Harbour. Allen performs the record in its entirety as a theatrical experience, with no interaction with the crowd at all. Responding to the criticism, she said not breaking the fourth wall was an “artistic choice” to help with the storytelling.

That Allen isn’t playing her previous hits on the West End Girl tour is another artistic choice − one that has affected ticket sales. A Montreal concert was cancelled and other shows were shifted to smaller venues.

I give full credit to artists who stick to their guns. In 2005 at Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena (then under a different corporate name), Elton John told his audience that he didn’t care if they wanted to hear his new album or not, he was going to perform the first eight songs of Peachtree Road anyway. “If we don’t play them,” he explained, “you aren’t going to hear them.”

The sadness of superstar Noah Kahan uplifts his Toronto concert

He meant that radio wasn’t playing tracks off the album. Radio isn’t playing cuts from Trixies either, but that’s not necessarily why Squeeze is performing it in full. They were just in Toronto, at Massey Hall, two years ago. With the full Trixies in the set list, fans are getting a much different show − not another greatest hits tour.

Not that Squeeze ignored those hits. They closed the concert with a string of them, which brought the audience back to their feet. Among them were Black Coffee in Bed , Third Rail , Goodbye Girl and Tempted (“by the fruit of another”).

Still, the music of Trixies was the reason to show up on a drizzly night at the amphitheatre, if only to hear The Jaguars , a snazzy rocker about a band trying very hard to entertain uninterested people.

The song could be autobiographical: “The rock ’n’ roll is sounding way ahead of its time,” Tilbrook sang, “all filled with one regret, you ain’t seen nothin’ yet.”

Squeeze is right on time with newly recorded music from 1974. It’s 2026 and the band is up to its old Trixies in the best way possible.

Squeeze plays Vancouver’s Queen Elizabeth Theatre on Sept. 12.

It’s a concept album released earlier this year based on music he and co-founder Chris Difford wrote as teenagers in 1974. When the songs failed to land them a record contract at the time, they were put away in a drawer as a time capsule of sorts.
“This,” Tilbrook said, “is what it sounds like.”
Squeeze played the album in its entirety, top to bottom. This was the Trixies segment of the band’s current Tried, Tested and Trixies tour. What did it sound like? Like a band reinventing itself.

The crowd, which had been on their feet, sat down en masse , as if instructed to do so. The mood had shifted; the air of nostalgia was gone. This was going to be a rock ’n’ roll recital, not a boomer dance party.
Olivia Rodrigo’s Lilith Fair was sanctuary in turbulent times between Canada and the U.S.

Difford, 71, and Tilbrook, 69, don’t talk much on stage to begin with. But for the Trixies concert centerpiece they clammed up like mussels in a shell. No banter. Musical segues between songs set in a fictional night club added to the dreamy vibe.

The music is moodier, more muscular and mostly without the pop hooks that mark the tuneful rock that made Squeeze legends in dorm rooms on both sides of the Atlantic. It should come to no one’s surprise that the teenaged lyrics of Trixies are not particularly sophisticated. From the album-opener What More Can I Say : “The tables have been cleared, the strangers have been feared, the lipstick has been smeared.”

And to think, Tilbrook and Difford would grow up to write cheeky lines about William Tell and earn comparisons to John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Speaking of which, the Trixies song Don’t Go Out in the Dark is reminiscent of McCartney’s Let Me Roll It from 1973. A line from Hell on Earth (“the bouncer’s name is Eddy, he’s always on the ready”) seems like an outtake from Billy Joel’s Piano Man , also from ’73.

And you don’t need to be an astrophysicist to guess the inspiration behind The Place We Call Mars . “How did I know where the end might begin,” Tilbrook sang on the Bowiesque number, “when the story was so hard to tell?”
Kacey Musgraves’s Middle of Nowhere tour brings hits and humour to Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena

Conceptual albums were in vogue in the early 1970s, from David Bowie’s The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars to the Who’s Quadrophenia to the Eagles’ Desperado . Artists of that decade had faith that their fans had the interest and attention span to indulge their high-minded musical visions. Now? Not so much.

Some fans of Lily Allen complained because on her current tour the British pop star is performing only the songs of West End Girl , the album inspired by her divorce from actor David Harbour. Allen performs the record in its entirety as a theatrical experience, with no interaction with the crowd at all. Responding to the criticism, she said not breaking the fourth wall was an “artistic choice” to help with the storytelling.

That Allen isn’t playing her previous hits on the West End Girl tour is another artistic choice − one that has affected ticket sales. A Montreal concert was cancelled and other shows were shifted to smaller venues.

I give full credit to artists who stick to their guns. In 2005 at Toronto’s Scotiabank Arena (then under a different corporate name), Elton John told his audience that he didn’t care if they wanted to hear his new album or not, he was going to perform the first eight songs of Peachtree Road anyway. “If we don’t play them,” he explained, “you aren’t going to hear them.”
The sadness of superstar Noah Kahan uplifts his Toronto concert

He meant that radio wasn’t playing tracks off the album. Radio isn’t playing cuts from Trixies either, but that’s not necessarily why Squeeze is performing it in full. They were just in Toronto, at Massey Hall, two years ago. With the full Trixies in the set list, fans are getting a much different show − not another greatest hits tour.

Not that Squeeze ignored those hits. They closed the concert with a string of them, which brought the audience back to their feet. Among them were Black Coffee in Bed , Third Rail , Goodbye Girl and Tempted (“by the fruit of another”).

Still, the music of Trixies was the reason to show up on a drizzly night at the amphitheatre, if only to hear The Jaguars , a snazzy rocker about a band trying very hard to entertain uninterested people.
The song could be autobiographical: “The rock ’n’ roll is sounding way ahead of its time,” Tilbrook sang, “all filled with one regret, you ain’t seen nothin’ yet.”
Squeeze is right on time with newly recorded music from 1974. It’s 2026 and the band is up to its old Trixies in the best way possible.
Squeeze plays Vancouver’s Queen Elizabeth Theatre on Sept. 12.

stories.title: 'Apples and oranges': PQ leader not concerned with Carney win in Quebec byelection
stories.summary: The Bloc Québécois May have lost Chicoutimi —Le Fjord to Carney’s Liberals on Monday, but that is not a concern for its provincial cousin.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
St-Pierre Plamondon pushed back against suggestions that Carney’s popularity could hurt the separatist party’s chances

Ottawa — The Bloc Québécois May have lost the federal byelection of Chicoutimi —Le Fjord to Mark Carney’s Liberals on Monday evening, but that is not a concern for the Bloc’s provincial cousin which will be facing the Quebec electorate in just over a month.

Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.

Access articles from across Canada with one account.

Enjoy additional articles per month.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was asked on the campaign trail on Tuesday how he interprets the results in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, which saw Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil celebrate a smashing win at 51.3 per cent while Bloc candidate Caroline Dubé got 32.9 per cent.

“There are no real parallels to be drawn between a riding at the federal level and the fundamental choice a people makes regarding a government for a four-year term at the Quebec level,” St-Pierre Plamondon said. “So, I don’t really have an interpretation.”

Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said the PQ is happy to join forces with the Bloc when it suits them, and vice versa, but now is not one of these moments.

“They must have nice family gatherings,” Milliard said with a smirk.

The PQ is still in first position in Quebec, but the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) has been creeping up in the polls, in part thanks to the trade war with the United States. The situation has also benefitted Carney judging by the byelection results.

St-Pierre Plamondon pushed back against suggestions that Carney’s popularity in Quebec could hurt the separatist party’s chances to form government on October 5.

The PQ leader said it is like comparing “apples and oranges.”

A federal Liberal source, speaking on a not-for-attribution basis to talk more freely, said Gobeil benefitted from the collapse of trade talks with the U.S. but he was also a known figure in the region, having been at the head of the biggest dairy lobby in the province.

The source seemingly agreed with St-Pierre Plamondon that the results in the federal byelection would not necessarily be replicated during the Quebec election.

The Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean region, north of Quebec City, holds a high proportion of “pragmatic separatists” who still intend to vote PQ at the provincial level but are prepared to support Carney at the federal level while Quebec is still a part of Canada.

A Bloc source agreed that the byelection results would have been vastly different if Carney had made concessions to the Trump administration on issues like supply management.

“It would have changed everything,” they said.

The Canada-U.S. relationship could still fluctuate in the next few weeks, and the political predictions in Quebec with it. Canada is expected to impose counter-tariffs on its biggest trading partner in a week, which could lead to further trade retaliation.

For Quebec, that could mean more companies closing doors and more job losses.

If the PQ forms government, St-Pierre Plamondon vowed to build a relationship with Carney based on “respect that we don’t have at the moment.” That means not waiting near the phone for Ottawa to update Quebec on the ongoing trade talks, he said.

St-Pierre Plamondon accused the federal government of not having properly consulted Quebec whilst negotiating with the U.S. on decisions that could have negatively impacted its businesses and workers. “I don’t consider that normal,” he said.

A Quebec source had confirmed to the National Post during the trade negotiations with the U.S. that Ottawa was not sharing specific details with provinces, only offering general information on what was happening at the negotiating table.

Once a deal was almost final, Carney briefed his provincial counterparts and reportedly asked them to consider bringing back U.S. alcohol on their shelves. Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said she asked for further information before taking a final position.

Talks between Canada and the U.S. fell apart on August 21. Carney said the U.S. “asked too much and offered too little,” and asked his negotiators to come back to Ottawa.

The U.S. has since imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of Canadian products.

Carney has vowed to strike back with “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation, something that Fréchette said on Tuesday would be “problematic” for Quebec. She said her government has conveyed to Ottawa they would prefer “targeted” measures.

“We want to protect workers and businesses across Quebec, and we must not let these retaliatory tariffs add to the pressure,” she told reporters on the campaign trail.

Fréchette refused to go more into detail on which retaliatory tariffs she considers would hurt industries her province.

National Post calevesque@postmedia.com

stories.title: Fanshawe College partially evacuated after reports of smoke coming from transformer
stories.summary: Multiple buildings at London’s Fanshawe College were evacuated Tuesday after an electrical transformer reportedly began emitting smoke.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Multiple buildings at London’s Fanshawe College were evacuated Tuesday after an electrical transformer reportedly began emitting smoke.

Spokesperson Elaine Gamble said a precautionary decision was made to evacuate F, G, H, L and K buildings for staff and students.

Signs were posted on multiple doors of connecting and adjacent buildings.

The buildings remain closed. London Hydro crews remain on scene.

stories.title: Cardinal Marc Ouellet speaks out after defamation suit win
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouelette expressed his gratitude today after winning a civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet, right, walks with one of his lawyers during a break at the courthouse in Montreal on Thursday, March 5, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Christinne Muschi

Montreal - Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouelette expressed his gratitude today after winning a civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit.

Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ruled on Monday that Paméla Groleau’s accusations against Ouellet were unfounded and ordered her to pay him $100,000.

Ouelette issued a brief written statement today from his residence in Rome, Italy.

In it, he expresses his gratitude to the civil justice system and thanks his lawyers and the witnesses who testified.

Groleau had accused Ouellet of touching her without consent on three occasions between 2008 and 2010, while she was training or working for the church.

Ouelette reiterated his plan to donate the $100,000 in damages to organizations fighting sexual abuse against Indigenous Peoples in Canada.

“I pledge to continue the fight within the Church and in society against every form of abuse, particularly sexual abuse, and I unreservedly support substantiated victims in their pursuit of restorative justice,” he writes.

Castonguay’s 52-page ruling, handed down Monday at the Montreal courthouse, is harsh on Groleau.

The judge concluded that her testimony “was neither credible nor reliable.” He noted that she changed her account of the facts several times and that the alleged incidents took place during public events attended by other people.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: New Brunswick wants public feedback on data centre plan
stories.summary: A news release says the draft policy will support Canada's efforts to control its own data and develop Canadian artificial intelligence.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The New Brunswick government wants residents to weigh in on its data centre policy as it considers a proposal for a facility in the province’s southwest.

The province created a framework for data centre development it says will prevent spikes in electricity costs for ratepayers and minimize the facilities’ impact on the environment.

A news release says the draft policy will support Canada’s efforts to control its own data and develop Canadian artificial intelligence.

The public can share their thoughts on the plan until Oct. 2 through an online form on the government’s website.

The Liberal government’s request for feedback comes as it reviews plans for a proposed data centre west of Saint John, N.B.

The 390-megawatt Spruce Lake AI Hub, pitched by Beacon Data Centres and VotaGrid, is currently under regulatory review.

stories.title: Champagne says U.S. move to invite Russia to G20 meeting caused ‘a lot of discomfort’
stories.summary: Ottawa — Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says Russia's presence at a G20 meeting hosted by the United States has made many countries uncomfortable.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted September 1, 2026 3:46 pm.

Last Updated September 1, 2026 5:52 pm.

Ottawa — Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says Russia’s presence at a G20 meeting hosted by the United States has made many countries uncomfortable.

The United States invited Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov to attend the Tuesday meeting of G20 finance ministers in Asheville, N.C.

“It created a lot of discomfort around the table, not only from Canada, but I would say from a number of colleagues around the table,” Champagne told reporters in a video conference.

“Canada is steadfast in our resolve to support the Ukrainian people. And we have made sure that our discomfort is being heard by colleagues with respect to who is in attendance at the meeting. “

Moscow remains a G20 member despite its 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The G7 expelled Russia from its ranks after the initial 2014 invasion and seizure of Crimea.

The United States did not allow South Africa to attend Tuesday’s meeting. U.S. President Donald Trump has accused the country of pursuing a genocide against white people — a claim no major human-rights organizations has said is accurate.

Trump said his government invited Russia because “we like getting along with everybody.”

Citing an unidentified source, The Associated Press reported that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Siluanov that the United States will not give Russia economic relief until it ends its war in Ukraine.

Russia’s embassy in Ottawa did not immediately respond when asked for comment on the remarks by Champagne.

“What Ukraine is facing — the escalation and the conflict, the devastation that we’re seeing — requires all of us to show great, great, great unity with the brave people of Ukraine,” he said.

Also on Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed support for Germany after Berlin blamed Russia for an attempted explosive drone attack near a Ukrainian plane at the Leipzig airport last month.

“Attacking a Ukrainian cargo plane on German soil was an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence — and it will fail,” Carney wrote on the platform X after speaking with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

“Our support for Ukraine in the face of Russia’s aggression is unshakable,” Carney wrote.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Check vaccinations before heading back to school: chief public health officer
stories.summary: Toronto — Canada's chief public health officer is urging parents to check that routine childhood vaccinations are up-to-date as kids head back to school.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Nicole Ireland, The Canadian Press

Posted September 1, 2026 3:45 pm.

Last Updated September 1, 2026 5:07 pm.

Toronto — Canada’s chief public health officer is urging parents to check that routine childhood vaccinations are up-to-date as kids head back to school.

In an interview on Tuesday, Dr. Joss Reimer said measles is still spreading, while vaccine misinformation continues to circulate online.

The national measles immunization rate for two-year-olds is about 85 per cent, falling short of the 95 per cent needed for herd immunity, Reimer said.

Although rates of infection in the multi-province measles outbreak that began in 2024 — and cost Canada its measles elimination status late last year — appear to be going down, kids who aren’t vaccinated are always at risk because people bring the virus into the country and it’s “incredibly infectious,” she said.

Most provinces have declared the outbreak over at various times over the last year but recent cases have been reported in Manitoba, according to the Public Health Agency of Canada website.

Children should receive two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine — the first dose at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at 18 months, or around the time they start school, depending on the province.

Reimer said parents should check their child’s vaccine record and reach out to a primary-care provider or their local public health unit if they can’t find it.

“I know there’s a lot to think about when it’s back-to-school. But this is a great time that we want you to just trigger your memory to double-check this before your kids end up in that space where viruses can spread so easily,” she said.

It can be hard for parents to wade through misinformation stoking fear about vaccines online and find science-based health advice, she said.

“Sometimes when people aren’t even looking for it, they’re still being bombarded by misinformation through algorithms,” Reimer said.

“Of course parents have questions. We want parents to have questions when they’re thinking about any intervention with their children, but I just want to make sure that they also have access to reliable answers,” she said.

Parents can find evidence-based information on childhood vaccination through public health and medical association websites and the Canadian Paediatric Society, Reimer said.

But it’s even more important to make sure people have access to fact-based information at the community level through the people they trust, she said.

“Most people will never meet me in person. And so whether or not they trust me in my role … (in) government, I need to make sure that what I’m saying reflects what their family doctor is saying (and) reflects what they’re finding online so that they’re hearing accurate information hopefully as often as they’re seeing that misinformation,” Reimer said.

“People really, at the end of the day, they trust the people in their lives,” she said.

A family doctor or nurse practitioner is an important source of information who patients and parents trust, highlighting the need to make sure every Canadian has a primary-care provider, Reimer said.

Public health workers also need to connect with community leaders and religious leaders to ensure they have accurate information about vaccination they can share, she added.

Reimer said she also thinks the majority of people who are behind on getting their kids immunized are not anti-vaccine.

“ I think most of the time it comes (down) to competing priorities. Life is difficult when it’s hard to pay the bills, when it’s hard to make ends meet. Focusing on preventive care — that can be hard to get that to the top of the to-do list.”

Reimer said she worries about other vaccine-preventable diseases taking hold, such as mumps and rubella, which the MMR shot also protects against.

Australia is currently in the midst of diphtheria outbreaks, she said.

“There’s no reason that this couldn’t happen here as well,” Reimer said, noting that vaccination rates for the serious bacterial infection are below 80 per cent for two-year-olds in Canada.

Children should receive multiple doses of the tetanus, diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough) and polio vaccine, starting at two months of age, according to the Canadian Immunization Guide.

stories.title: Q+A: Canadian band Men Without Hats on longevity and returning to London
stories.summary: The band behind “The Safety Dance” is nearing its 50th anniversary and remains busier than it was in the 1980s.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The band behind “The Safety Dance” is nearing its 50th anniversary and remains busier than it was in the 1980s.

Canadian new wave and synth-pop band Men Without Hats returns to London on Friday for Fairway Fest at East Park. Known primarily for its 1982 hit “The Safety Dance,” the band is approaching its 50th anniversary next year. Ivan Doroschuk, the band’s lead vocalist and only remaining founding member, spoke with Lfp’s Ryan Goodison about why Men Without Hats has lasted so long and what to expect from the upcoming show.

Q: You’ve been making music as Men Without Hats for nearly 50 years. What still excites you about getting into the studio and making new music?

A: It was just that the songs happened. Different people have different ways of working this craft, and I kind of just watershed (ideas). I sort of sit around, and all the songs kind of come to me at once. And that’s what happened this time, too. What keeps me interested is the fans, basically, the crowds that we play for. We’ve been playing live a lot since I put the band back together 15 years ago, and we’re busier now than we were in the ’80s. And just the crowd reaction is great.

Q: Other musicians speak about how songs come to them, and the process is more or less trying to catch them. Would you say that’s similar to your writing process?

A: Yeah, I’ve said that before. I believe the songs exist out there somewhere, and we’re just the channel. The musician is just channeling the message and the music and everything. It’s already out there, you know. We just funnel it down through our fingers or voices or whatever we do and get it out there to the people, passing along the energy.

Q: Take me back to those early days. How did Men Without Hats come together and was music always the goal for you as a young man?

A: I was in film and communications at McGill University in the late ‘70s. I was sort of contemplating a career in the graphic arts, and it was an era where there were a lot of DIY movements. You didn’t have to be a virtuoso at anything. You didn’t have to have a film degree to make a movie. Video cameras were readily available, synthesizers were becoming affordable. People were just grabbing anything and making art with it. So, I met a bunch of guys who wanted to start a band. In the beginning, it was a punk band. There were no keyboards at all, and we were doing cover songs and starting to write our own songs. At one point, I made a conscious decision that I wanted to reach more people. I realized that I wanted to do this as a career, and I wanted to reach more people. Punk music was a lot of fun, but it was a niche market. And since I had the training, the piano background and the classical music training, I had the tools to do it.

Q: Why do you think Men Without Hats has lasted so long?

A: I think people still need to hear the fact that they can dance if they want to. It’s as simple as that. We were fortunate enough to touch on subjects back in the ‘80s that are still relevant today. Even “Pop Goes the World” – when I wrote that, it was the green movement. What I was saying in interviews and stuff was, if we don’t stop mistreating Mother Earth, she’s going to blow up. These are subjects that are still being talked about today. Especially in “The Safety Dance” – you can dance if you want to, you don’t have to follow the crowd. You don’t have to succumb to peer pressure. Especially in today’s sort of atmosphere of social media, where there is a lot of peer pressure. I think people relate to that message.

Q: Speaking of “The Safety Dance,” that’s become so much bigger than just a hit song – it’s something that keeps finding new generations. When you perform it now, do you experience it differently than you did way back when?

A: It’s bigger than the band. It’s almost as if it doesn’t belong to us anymore. You know, it belongs to everybody out there, and I feel sometimes like a musical museum curator going around the world presenting this musical artifact to people that brings them incredible joy. Every time we play, people ask me, “Don’t you get sick of singing that song? You must have sung it like a million times.” But I don’t. That smile it brings to people’s faces – it freaks me out every time. I never sort of envisaged the success that it would have.

Q: There’s definitely a nostalgic element to a Men Without Hats show. But you’re also touring this new album, so how do you balance playing the songs people came to hear while showing off the new stuff?

A: I’ve learned over the years that people are there to hear a certain sort of set list. So we don’t, like some bands, go out there and play completely new material. When I was a young artist, that’s what I would do. We would go out there and play a set that was composed mostly of new material, and I couldn’t understand why people wanted to hear the albums that they knew. But now, over the years, I’ve wised up and learned that this is why we’re still around. These are the songs that are the reason people are still coming to hear us.

Q: What do you remember about playing in Southwestern Ontario and around London? What are the crowds like?

A: They’re great. That’s where we first started out. We had two bases that we would tour extensively. One was Ontario, just because there was the population and the number of clubs there were. We could go there and book a tour, and then as we’d get playing, people would hear about us, and we could actually book shows ahead while we were on the road.

A: It was just that the songs happened. Different people have different ways of working this craft, and I kind of just watershed (ideas). I sort of sit around, and all the songs kind of come to me at once. And that’s what happened this time, too. What keeps me interested is the fans, basically, the crowds that we play for. We’ve been playing live a lot since I put the band back together 15 years ago, and we’re busier now than we were in the ’80s. And just the crowd reaction is great.
Q: Other musicians speak about how songs come to them, and the process is more or less trying to catch them. Would you say that’s similar to your writing process?

A: Yeah, I’ve said that before. I believe the songs exist out there somewhere, and we’re just the channel. The musician is just channeling the message and the music and everything. It’s already out there, you know. We just funnel it down through our fingers or voices or whatever we do and get it out there to the people, passing along the energy.
Q: Take me back to those early days. How did Men Without Hats come together and was music always the goal for you as a young man?

A: I was in film and communications at McGill University in the late ‘70s. I was sort of contemplating a career in the graphic arts, and it was an era where there were a lot of DIY movements. You didn’t have to be a virtuoso at anything. You didn’t have to have a film degree to make a movie. Video cameras were readily available, synthesizers were becoming affordable. People were just grabbing anything and making art with it. So, I met a bunch of guys who wanted to start a band. In the beginning, it was a punk band. There were no keyboards at all, and we were doing cover songs and starting to write our own songs. At one point, I made a conscious decision that I wanted to reach more people. I realized that I wanted to do this as a career, and I wanted to reach more people. Punk music was a lot of fun, but it was a niche market. And since I had the training, the piano background and the classical music training, I had the tools to do it.
Q: Why do you think Men Without Hats has lasted so long?

A: I think people still need to hear the fact that they can dance if they want to. It’s as simple as that. We were fortunate enough to touch on subjects back in the ‘80s that are still relevant today. Even “Pop Goes the World” – when I wrote that, it was the green movement. What I was saying in interviews and stuff was, if we don’t stop mistreating Mother Earth, she’s going to blow up. These are subjects that are still being talked about today. Especially in “The Safety Dance” – you can dance if you want to, you don’t have to follow the crowd. You don’t have to succumb to peer pressure. Especially in today’s sort of atmosphere of social media, where there is a lot of peer pressure. I think people relate to that message.

Q: Speaking of “The Safety Dance,” that’s become so much bigger than just a hit song – it’s something that keeps finding new generations. When you perform it now, do you experience it differently than you did way back when?

A: It’s bigger than the band. It’s almost as if it doesn’t belong to us anymore. You know, it belongs to everybody out there, and I feel sometimes like a musical museum curator going around the world presenting this musical artifact to people that brings them incredible joy. Every time we play, people ask me, “Don’t you get sick of singing that song? You must have sung it like a million times.” But I don’t. That smile it brings to people’s faces – it freaks me out every time. I never sort of envisaged the success that it would have.

Q: There’s definitely a nostalgic element to a Men Without Hats show. But you’re also touring this new album, so how do you balance playing the songs people came to hear while showing off the new stuff?

A: I’ve learned over the years that people are there to hear a certain sort of set list. So we don’t, like some bands, go out there and play completely new material. When I was a young artist, that’s what I would do. We would go out there and play a set that was composed mostly of new material, and I couldn’t understand why people wanted to hear the albums that they knew. But now, over the years, I’ve wised up and learned that this is why we’re still around. These are the songs that are the reason people are still coming to hear us.
Q: What do you remember about playing in Southwestern Ontario and around London? What are the crowds like?

A: They’re great. That’s where we first started out. We had two bases that we would tour extensively. One was Ontario, just because there was the population and the number of clubs there were. We could go there and book a tour, and then as we’d get playing, people would hear about us, and we could actually book shows ahead while we were on the road.

stories.title: 7K walking pads sold at Canadian Tire recalled due to electrical hazard
stories.summary: Health Canada says anyone who purchased the PowerG Walking Pad since January 2025 should 'immediately stop using the recalled product.'
stories.author: Katie Scott
stories.content:
Health Canada has issued a product recall for 7,000 PowerG Walking Pads sold in Canada at Canadian Tire due to an electrical hazard.

In a recall notice issued last week , Health Canada says anyone who purchased the PowerG Walking Pad since January 2025 should “immediately stop using the recalled product and return it to a Canadian Tire store for a refund or in-store credit.”

“The affected product does not meet the requirements of the relevant standard for this product category, which poses an electrical hazard,” the recall notice says.

The recall involves the PowerG Walking Pad, Model Number 499-4052 (UPC 8 46325 03115 8).

Health Canada notes there have been no serious incidents or injuries reported in Canada as of Aug. 10.

Consumers who need more information on the recall can contact Canadian Tire by telephone or visit the company’s website .

stories.title: B.C. MLA Hon Chan pleads not guilty in alleged intimate partner violence case
stories.summary: The BC Prosecution Service says counsel for the Richmond Centre MLA entered the not-guilty plea last Thursday, choosing a jury trial.
stories.author: Globalnews Digital
stories.content:
British Columbia legislator Hon Chan has pleaded not guilty to charges of assault and uttering threats in a case of alleged intimate partner violence.

The BC Prosecution Service says counsel for the Richmond Centre MLA entered the not-guilty plea last Thursday, choosing a jury trial.

The service says Chan has also waived his right to a preliminary inquiry, meaning the matter will move directly to BC Supreme Court.

Chan is next set to appear in court in Vancouver on Sept. 16.

He was elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative banner but was removed from caucus in March by interim leader Trevor Halford after the charges came to light.

Chan has previously said he disagrees with the allegations, which date back to 2024.

stories.title: Canada's living standards 'languishing' behind U.S. as gap in economic performance widens: study
stories.summary: Canada's economic performance has fallen further behind that of the U.S. over the past quarter century, according to a new study.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Up until 2014, Canada largely kept pace with, or in some cases exceeded, the U.S. across multiple economic measures, the Fraser Institute found

Canada’s economic performance has fallen further behind that of the U.S. over the past quarter century, with the gap in GDP per person more than doubling and the Americans pulling ahead on incomes, employment, investment and productivity.

That’s according to a new study published by the Fraser Institute , which found that, in 1999, inflation-adjusted GDP per person in Canada was $48,076, while in the U.S. it was $58,842. By 2024, GDP per person had grown to $83,286 in the U.S. compared to just $59,529 in Canada — meaning the gap had widened from $10,766 to $23,757 over 25 years.

The study compared economic outcomes in the two countries by looking at measures including living standards, incomes, employment, investment, and productivity. In every category, Canada has fallen further behind over the first quarter of the century, it found.

For example, in 2010 (the earliest year of comparable data), inflation-adjusted median employment income was $6,126 higher in the U.S. than in Canada. By 2024, that gap had increased to $8,663.

“When comparing the economic performance of Canada relative to the U.S. since the beginning of the 21st century, it’s abundantly clear that Canadian policymakers have failed to create an environment where we can prosper,” said Jake Fuss, director of fiscal studies at the Fraser Institute, in a news release.

He added that the ability to transform raw materials and other inputs into demanded goods and services increased by more than double the amount (26.7 per cent versus 67.9 per cent) in the U.S. compared to Canada, “which explains much of our languishing living standards.”

The Fraser Institute outlines three factors that explain the widening gap in economic performance between the two countries.

The first is a decline in private sector employment as a share of total employment in Canada. This decreased from 81.2 per cent to 78.5 per cent, meaning the government sector outgrew the private sector. The opposite occurred in the U.S., as private sector employment increased from 85.8 per cent of total employment to 86.5 per cent.

Meanwhile, labour productivity — a key driver of income growth — in the U.S. grew by 67.9 per cent between 1999 and 2025 compared to a 26.7 per cent increase in Canada during the same period.

Finally, business investment in Canada — which equips workers with the tools and technology they need to produce goods and services — dropped from nearly 90 cents per worker for every dollar invested in the U.S. to 54 cents between 2007 and 2024.

That said, the Fraser Institute study suggests that Canada’s trailing economic performance didn’t begin until 2014. Prior to this, Canada largely kept pace with, or in some cases exceeded, the U.S. across multiple measures, it said.

The think tank doesn’t look into the potential reasons for the change in 2014, but Grady Munro, senior policy analyst at the Fraser Institute and one of the study’s authors, offers some insight into the major factors that he says likely played a role.

“One example is that in 2014 we saw a collapse in oil prices in Canada, which resulted in a decline in business investment in the economy,” he said in an interview with National Post. “But that can’t necessarily explain the decade of economic stagnation that followed, and so that’s where, in large part, government policy factors played a role.”

He suggested that increased regulation on sectors like energy resources, combined with tax increases on high- and middle-income earners and increases in federal debt, reduced the attractiveness of Canada for business investment.

In 2015, the Trudeau government introduced a new top tax bracket on income over $200,000, which raised the top federal personal income tax rate from 29 per cent to 33 per cent. And the national debt doubled in less than a decade, increasing from $687 billion in 2014-15 to nearly $1.5 trillion in 2025-26.

“We know that investment is a huge determinant of productivity,” Munro added, “which then impacts the incomes that Canadians earn.”

Canada slightly outperformed the United States on inflation-adjusted GDP per person between 1999 and 2014, with Canada’s growing 19.9 per cent compared to 17.8 per cent in the U.S. However, since then, Canada’s GDP per person as a share of the United States’ has fallen from 83.1 per cent to 71.5 per cent as of 2024.

The Fraser Institute says this reflects the fact that per-person GDP growth in Canada largely stagnated during this time, while growth continued in the United States at a strong pace. From 2014 to 2024, GDP per person in Canada grew just 3.2 per cent compared to 20.1 per cent in the U.S.

When it comes to improving Canada’s economic performance, Munro suggested that a reemphasis on balanced budgets, spending restraint, and beginning to limit debt accumulation are the places to start.

stories.title: Port of Churchill resumes grain shipments for 1st time in 6 years
stories.summary: A ship is being loaded with 30,000 tonnes of wheat durum from Saskatchewan-based AGT Foods this week, destined for Europe.
stories.author: Marney Blunt
stories.content:
For the first time in six years, grain shipments have resumed out of the Port of Churchill this week.

A ship is being loaded with 30,000 tonnes of wheat durum from Saskatchewan-based AGT Foods this week, destined for Europe.

“What we’re witnessing is the return of Churchill as a vital arctic gateway,” federal minister of northern and arctic affairs Rebecca Chartrand said during a ceremony to mark the shipment on Monday.

The ship is the first of three ships slated to leave the port, which is Canada’s only arctic seaport, this season. Another ship will arrive this week to be loaded with zinc concentrate and potash, mined in Manitoba.

“The Port of Churchill is a corridor of opportunity and the benefit that we see in a world that is changing,” Manitoba agriculture minister Ron Kostyshyn said.

Operations are the Port of Churchill grinded to a halt in 2016 due to deteriorating rail line conditions, while the port and railway were owned and operated by U.S.-based company OmniTRAX.

The Manitoba-based Arctic Gateway Group acquired the Port of Churchill in 2018 and resumed operations the following year, before stopping again in 2020 as further work on the port and rail line were needed.

“This was a set of assets that was neglected for decades, ironically by American interests,” Arctic Gateway Group president and CEO Chris Avery said.

“And our ownership group (and partners) had the foresight to put this together, had the foresight to say, as my chairman says, ‘Enough is enough, we’re going to take control of this set of infrastructure. We’re going to take control of it (as) Canadians and as northern Manitobans and as First Nations.'”

“And what great foresight that was, because today, if this was American-owned infrastructure, we wouldn’t be having this same conversation,” Avery added.

The shipment comes as Manitoba eyes the possibility of year-round shipping from the Port of Churchill. Three recent studies found that year-round shipping is possible due to climate change shrinking the sea ice season. The studies also show year-round shipping is possible with current ice class vessels and without the use of icebreakers.

However, one of the studies by FedNav, Canada’s largest ocean bulk-shipping company, paints a less optimistic picture, cautioning the varying sea ice conditions and the shallow and narrow final approach to the port could present challenges.

The port is also being considered as a potential hub for shipping liquified natural gas, something Prime Minister Mark Carney wants to see happening out of the Port of Churchill by 2030.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew recently said expanding the Port of Churchill, which would include further upgrading the rail line and building an offshore LNG terminal, would cost between $70-80 billion. The premier plans on pitching the port to international investors during a summit in Toronto this month.

But in a deep seaport surrounded by beluga whales, polar bears, and the pristine subarctic wilderness of where the arctic tundra, boreal forest, and arctic marine meet, environmental concerns remain.

“As you look towards the vessel today, you see the abundance of beauty, you see the beluga whales and the importance of them. You see the bears, the land, the environment, everything that surrounds us. We have a world-class tourism destination. That is increasingly important to our communities, communities throughout Canada,” Churchill Mayor Michael Spence said.

Mayor Spence says any decisions made will balance economic opportunities with environmental responsibility.

“There’s a lot of opportunity for growth here, there’s opportunity for us to prosper, there’s opportunity for continuous growth within not only northern Manitoba communities but also in Manitoba and Canada as a whole,” he said.

“But the importance of doing it is doing it the right way and doing it responsibly. As northern and Indigenous people, we know the importance of what we’re responsible to do and making sure we do it the right way and leading the way in protecting the environment. We always need to remember that.”

“As you look towards the vessel today, you see the abundance of beauty, you see the beluga whales and the importance of them. You see the bears, the land, the environment, everything that surrounds us. We have a world-class tourism destination. That is increasingly important to our communities, communities throughout Canada,” Churchill Mayor Michael Spence said.
Mayor Spence says any decisions made will balance economic opportunities with environmental responsibility.

“There’s a lot of opportunity for growth here, there’s opportunity for us to prosper, there’s opportunity for continuous growth within not only northern Manitoba communities but also in Manitoba and Canada as a whole,” he said.

“But the importance of doing it is doing it the right way and doing it responsibly. As northern and Indigenous people, we know the importance of what we’re responsible to do and making sure we do it the right way and leading the way in protecting the environment. We always need to remember that.”

content_blocks.text: For the first time in six years, grain shipments have resumed out of the Port of Churchill this week.
A ship is being loaded with 30,000 tonnes of wheat durum from Saskatchewan-based AGT Foods this week, destined for Europe.

stories.title: New Brunswick horse virus scare shows need for public large-animal care, says vet
stories.summary: An equine veterinarian says a recent New Brunswick health advisory about a virus impacting horses underscores the need for publicly funded services for large animals.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
An equine veterinarian says a recent New Brunswick health advisory about a virus impacting horses underscores the need for publicly funded services for large animals.

The province’s chief veterinary officer issued a health advisory Sunday warning of a potential exposure to the Equine Herpesvirus Type 1 at a horse show in Sussex, N.B., last month.

Jordan Koivu, owner of Maritime Equine Veterinary Services, says some horse show operators have cancelled their events, and the virus appears to have been contained.

She says the situation shows horse owners need quick access to veterinary care.

Koivu says the New Brunswick government’s decision to privatize field veterinary services for large animals beginning March 31, 2027, will lead to delayed diagnosis and treatment.

The province’s Liberal government has said public tax dollars shouldn’t be used to subsidize hobby farms, non-commercial livestock and equine facilities.

Koivu, who practices in two Maritime provinces, says some New Brunswick veterinarians have already left for jobs in other jurisdictions, leaving rural horse owners worried about what comes next.

“If the horse is sick and they need to have a veterinarian see it, it might take three or four days to get a veterinarian out to see the horse,” she said by phone Tuesday.

“And, by then, it could have already got eight other horses sick.”
