stories.title: How the cap on international study permits is changing campuses this fall
stories.summary: As post-secondary students get ready to return to campuses for the fall semester, Canada’s international student arrivals are tracking well below the target it has set for this year.
stories.author: Kamil Karamali
stories.content:
Toronto — As post-secondary students get ready to return to campuses for the fall semester, Canada’s international student arrivals are tracking well below the target it has set for this year — resulting in Ontario colleges suspending programs and universities and student groups pushing Ottawa to hand out more study permits.

Ottawa’s target for this year is 155,000 new international student arrivals, but data from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (Ircc) shows just 22,405 arrived during the first six months of 2026, tracking well below the full-year target.

However, international student arrivals are highly seasonal and typically surge ahead of the fall semester.

In January 2024, then-Immigration Minister Marc Miller announced a temporary cap on international study student permits. There were 292,885 new international student arrivals in 2024 — followed by a more than 60-per-cent drop in 2025, to 115,005. That’s much lower than the target that was actually announced for 2025, at 305,900 new arrivals.

The international student population has dropped one-third since 2024, according to an email statement from Ircc, with the goal of reducing pressures on housing, infrastructure, and services.

“We are seeing those positive signs that recent measures are working,” Briannah Dale, spokesperson for Ircc, said in an email to CTV News.

“A recent TD Economics report found that cuts to immigration levels have already eased the pressure on social and economic infrastructure, lowering condo demand for both home ownership and the secondary rental market,” added Dale. “Lower immigration rates have also caused a reduction in asking rents across major cities in Canada.”

Colleges hit harder than universities

Since the temporary cap was issued, Ontario colleges have been hit the hardest, with hundreds of programs suspended and thousands of job losses

Centennial College has had a total of 61 programs suspended between the two years — 54 in 2025 and an additional seven this year.

“Current students who are progressing through affected programs as scheduled can continue their studies toward completion and will have the opportunity to graduate,” said a Centennial College spokesperson to CTV News via email.

Meanwhile, Fanshawe initially announced 40 program suspensions last year, followed by another 10 later that year and nine additional suspensions announced this March.

“Over the last two years Fanshawe has experienced an approximately 40 per cent decline in total student term enrolments due to changes in federal policies related to international students,” a spokesperson from Fanshawe College told CTV News, which highlights it’s welcoming more than 2,000 international students this year.

Algonquin College, meanwhile, approved the suspension or cancellation of another 30 programs effective this fall. Neither college responded to CTV News’ request for comment.

“We’re seeing a decrease in the amount of students on our campuses, meaning there’s a decrease in services as well from that result in terms of students,” Georgina Cabrol, president of the College Student Alliance, said in a Zoom interview with CTV News Sunday.

“From my perspective, we’ve seen a loss in our academic support, such as career services, loss of job employment for students on campus — and it’s just been quite a situation where individuals have been impacted in various ways.”

Ontario initially cushioned universities from much of the impact of the federal cap. The province maintained 2023 application levels at 22 of its 23 universities, compared with just 11 of 24 colleges, saying its allocations would prioritize public programs supporting in-demand jobs.

‘Attracting higher-quality students’

In Ircc’s email to CTV News, Dale says that the current policy is focusing on attracting “higher quality students” and keeping the “world’s best talent” — highlighting that new arrivals of study permit holders at the university level increased by ten percentage points, from 30 per cent in 2024 to 40 per cent in 2025.

“As overall international student admissions decrease, the proportion of university students relative to college students is increasing,” said Dale. “Ircc is expecting this trend to continue with new measures directed at graduate students in 2026 and a continued focus on attracting talent at the master’s and PhD level.”

Data from the University of Toronto shows that although international student intake fell six per cent in the fall of 2024, the institution is now anticipating a nine per cent increase in its international student body this fall.

“When it comes to Trinity, our number (of international students) generally is about 30 per cent,” said Kristen Moore, director of student experience at Trinity College to CTV News Sunday. “That’s been pretty consistent for us over the last few years.”

“It’s fair to say that Toronto fared better than many other universities in the province and in the country, because of here of the international appeal of our programs is very strong,” said Vice-Chancellor of Trinity College at University of Toronto, Nicholas Terpstra, to CTV News Sunday. “We have not had the kind of fall-off, drop-off in international numbers of some other smaller universities have had.”

More stringent requirements

While universities have generally been less affected than colleges, international students who were accepted to Canadian schools say the process of obtaining a study permit has become more difficult.

“I got my (student) visa in under 10 days, so it was very much a miracle for me to get it,” said Aurin Kabir, who is an international student at Toronto Metropolitan University, told CTV News Sunday. “But I know some students who are waiting for almost a year to two years for that visa — and to be honest, a very uncertain thing now.”

The Bangladeshi student studying economics said the process of applying for a student visa from Canada has gotten even more “difficult” since the Canadian government limited the number of study permits it administers.

“When I applied, you had to show proof of almost $25,000 Canadian — but before that it was only $15,000, so it’s almost double now,” she added. “We have to show in our bank that we had that much to cover our first year here in Canada, we have to show proof of assets and other stuff — and we have to show proof that we have intent to go back to Bangladesh after I’m done with my studies. You have to show that intent.”

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada requires a single applicant outside Quebec to demonstrate at least $22,895 for living expenses, in addition to tuition and transportation costs. That requirement rises to $23,448 for applications submitted beginning Sept. 1.

stories.title: Art Gallery of Ontario's CEO Stephan Jost to depart at the end of this year
stories.summary: Toronto - The Art Gallery of Ontario says its top executive is stepping down after a decade in the role.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The Art Gallery of Ontario says its top executive is stepping down after a decade in the role.

In a news release, the AGO says director and CEO Stephan Jost is leaving at the end of this year.

Make us a preferred source on Google

cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com

sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star

bHasMigratedAvatar : false

By Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press

The AGO credits Jost with securing significant art collections during his tenure, including a recent donation of 450 works from the late patrons Carol and Morton Rapp.

It says Jost also led a project to expand the gallery space by 40,000 sq. feet, set to open next year.

The AGO has also weathered controversy in recent months. The Globe and Mail earlier this year reported on the fallout after the gallery backed away from acquiring work by Jewish-American photographer Nan Goldin, who had been critical of Israel’s miliary campaign in Gaza.

The AGO says it will launch a global search for Jost’s replacement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: U.S. Senator to introduce bill to repeal Trump’s latest tariffs on Canada
stories.summary: Legislation is unlikely to pass, but comes as Democrats focus on affordability issues heading into the midterm elections
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is set to introduce legislation to stop U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest tariffs as Democrats ramp up their affordability messaging ahead of midterm elections.

The new bill backed by the Democrat from New York attempts to rein in the latest tariffs on Canadian goods and the separate duties the Trump administration says are linked to forced labour in supply chains.

“While inflation rages, families struggle to pay their bills and small businesses close, Trump – detached from reality – continues his bluster on the global stage, doubling down on a chaotic trade war that has meant only pain for American families, farmers and manufacturers,” Schumer said in a news release Tuesday.

“Republicans won’t stand up to Trump’s nonsense and Americans are crying out for relief.”

The legislation is largely symbolic, since it’s unlikely to pass a Republican-controlled Congress or overcome Trump’s presidential veto.

But it gives Democrats ammunition against Republicans – who are heading into November elections as an unpopular war on Iran drives up inflation and gas prices, and as affordability remains the top issue cited by voters.

Trump last month hit Canada with 50-per-cent tariffs on multiple goods, ranging from hockey sticks and cement to honey, after trade talks between the two nations broke down.

Canada is set to respond with its own set of retaliatory duties next week.

The Trump administration in July also used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to hit Canada and dozens of other countries with double-digit tariffs, after claiming those countries weren’t doing enough to fight forced labour in supply chains.

The Canadian government has told the Trump administration that new legislation combatting forced labour in supply chains should have shielded Canada from those 10 per cent tariffs.

Those duties do not apply to goods compliant under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma.

A coalition of U.S. states is already challenging the use of Section 301 for the forced-labour duties.

Schumer’s new legislation – which would repeal both sets of tariffs and require refunds – comes as polling shows that Trump’s tariffs on Canada and the president’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” are widely unpopular.

A new Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found a majority of Americans oppose both moves.

The nationwide Aug. 28 to Aug. 30 poll of 1,023 registered voters – which was conducted online, so it can’t be assigned a margin of error – found only 20 per cent of respondents support the higher tariffs on Canada and 14 per cent support changing the name of Lake Ontario.

The bilateral tensions could prove to be a boon for Democrats in high-stakes contests in states that do substantial trade with Canada, including Michigan, Maine and Ohio. Some Republicans are already breaking away from Trump’s trade policy and messages disparaging Canada.

Wisconsin Public Radio reported that Tom Tiffany, the Trump-backed Republican candidate for governor in that state, told reporters last week that the Great Lakes should keep their original names. Republican Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont last week called the move disappointing.

Schumer’s bill is co-sponsored by 13 other Senate Democrats, including Ron Wyden of Oregon. They’ve called repeatedly for Congress to take back its power over taxes and tariffs from the executive branch.

“Congress has to stand up to Trump, end his trade war with Canada and repeal the outdated law he’s using to tax nearly everything we need to get by,” Wyden said in the news release.

“Republicans won’t stand up to Trump’s nonsense and Americans are crying out for relief.”
The legislation is largely symbolic, since it’s unlikely to pass a Republican-controlled Congress or overcome Trump’s presidential veto.

But it gives Democrats ammunition against Republicans – who are heading into November elections as an unpopular war on Iran drives up inflation and gas prices, and as affordability remains the top issue cited by voters.
Trump last month hit Canada with 50-per-cent tariffs on multiple goods, ranging from hockey sticks and cement to honey, after trade talks between the two nations broke down.
Canada is set to respond with its own set of retaliatory duties next week.

The Trump administration in July also used Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to hit Canada and dozens of other countries with double-digit tariffs, after claiming those countries weren’t doing enough to fight forced labour in supply chains.
The Canadian government has told the Trump administration that new legislation combatting forced labour in supply chains should have shielded Canada from those 10 per cent tariffs.
Those duties do not apply to goods compliant under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma.
A coalition of U.S. states is already challenging the use of Section 301 for the forced-labour duties.

Schumer’s new legislation – which would repeal both sets of tariffs and require refunds – comes as polling shows that Trump’s tariffs on Canada and the president’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America” are widely unpopular.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll released Tuesday found a majority of Americans oppose both moves.

The nationwide Aug. 28 to Aug. 30 poll of 1,023 registered voters – which was conducted online, so it can’t be assigned a margin of error – found only 20 per cent of respondents support the higher tariffs on Canada and 14 per cent support changing the name of Lake Ontario.

The bilateral tensions could prove to be a boon for Democrats in high-stakes contests in states that do substantial trade with Canada, including Michigan, Maine and Ohio. Some Republicans are already breaking away from Trump’s trade policy and messages disparaging Canada.

Wisconsin Public Radio reported that Tom Tiffany, the Trump-backed Republican candidate for governor in that state, told reporters last week that the Great Lakes should keep their original names. Republican Gov. Phil Scott of Vermont last week called the move disappointing.

Schumer’s bill is co-sponsored by 13 other Senate Democrats, including Ron Wyden of Oregon. They’ve called repeatedly for Congress to take back its power over taxes and tariffs from the executive branch.
“Congress has to stand up to Trump, end his trade war with Canada and repeal the outdated law he’s using to tax nearly everything we need to get by,” Wyden said in the news release.

stories.title: 49 Quebecers become millionaires after $55M Lotto Max win
stories.summary: Forty-nine Quebecers are now millionaires after winning a share of a $55 million Lotto Max jackpot. Some of them only learned the news when Loto-Québec contacted them, with reactions ranging from laughter and disbelief to tears.
stories.author: Marisela Amador
stories.content: Forty-nine Quebecers are now millionaires after winning a share of a $55 million Lotto Max jackpot. Some of them only learned the news when Loto-Québec contacted them, with reactions ranging from laughter and disbelief to tears. Most of the new millionaires didn’t know each other, but they had all purchased at least one share of the winning Formule groupe ticket on the Loto-Québec website. On Tuesday, the winners gathered at Loto-Québec’s head office in Montreal to receive their share of the prize money. The 49 jackpot winners come from 12 different regions across the province, from the Outaouais to the Côte-Nord. Laurentians resident François B. said he purchased his ticket just minutes before the draw and checked the results the following morning. “My heart skipped a beat!” he said. He added that he plans to buy a more luxurious vehicle and spoil his children. ‘It’s hard to believe’ Another winner, Côte-Nord resident Jacques V., said he became emotional upon discovering his win. “I had two sleepless nights. It’s hard to believe, but it feels good.” Loto-Québec said it was the first time in its history that it had handed out so many cheques worth more than $1 million in a single day. “It’s incredible to think that 49 families here in Quebec will enjoy part of this jackpot. Loto-Québec generates significant spinoffs for the community, in addition to the money paid out to lottery winners,” said Isabelle Jean, executive vice-president and COO of Lottery Games at Loto-Québec. “This summer alone, dozens of Quebecers shared jackpots of $25 million, $40 million and $55 million, becoming millionaires in the process. We’re so proud of this contribution.” According to Loto-Québec, the online Formule groupe allows players to purchase one or more shares in a lottery group and pool them with those of other group members.

stories.title: Stephan Jost to depart role as Art Gallery of Ontario CEO
stories.summary: AGO accessioned more than 18,000 works of art since Jost joined in 2016
stories.author: Lana Hall
stories.content:
The Art Gallery of Ontario has announced that director and chief executive Stephan Jost will be stepping down, effective Dec. 31, 2026.

Jost joined the AGO in 2016 after holding roles at the Honolulu Museum of Art in Hawaii, the Shelburne Museum in Vermont and the Mills College Art Museum in California.

Under his leadership, the AGO accessioned more than 18,000 works of art and secured more than $500-million in commitments in gifts of art and funds for the museum. Jost also led a successful campaign to expand the AGO, namely through the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary gallery, which will expand the Ago’s gallery space by 40,000 square feet when it opens in 2027.

The Impressionist Revolution at the AGO revisits the movement’s radical roots

“Over the summer, I reflected on arriving at the AGO 10 years ago and establishing the Strategic Plan we call AGO 2028,” Jost said in a press release. “I realized that we have met our goals ahead of schedule. Now is the time to set the AGO up for the future with new leadership.”

In an interview, Jost said he does not have another role lined up, and plans to take “a bit of a break” for three to nine months before seeking a leadership role elsewhere.

“Let me be blunt. There’s no shortage of opportunities for major museum directors,” he said.

The AGO has said they will appoint someone on an interim basis before commencing a global search for a new director and CEO.

Jost’s tenure has not been without controversy. During his time at the AGO, three curatorial staff members stepped down, including chief curator and deputy director Julian Cox, modern and contemporary curator John Zeppetelli, and inaugural curator of Indigenous art Wanda Nanibush.

Earlier this year, the AGO dissolved a committee that declined to acquire a Nan Goldin artwork after a debate over whether the Jewish-American artist’s views are “antisemitic,” prompting four resignations and a governance review at the gallery.

Understanding the politics of art gallery volunteer committees after the Ago’s failed Nan Goldin acquisition

In an e-mail statement at the time, Jost acknowledged that the committee’s purpose had been undermined by discourse that has spilled into the public. “I can assure you we are focused on our mission and working to take the necessary actions to ensure our processes are about art and respectful dialogue,” he said.

Now, Jost said he’s proud of the programming the AGO has done to attract younger and more diverse audiences over the past decade. Fifty two per cent of the gallery’s visitors, not including school groups, are now under the age of 39, and 60 per cent come from “non-European heritage,” he said.

“That’s a shift that we’ve done very intentionally to reflect Toronto,” he said. “... The last 10 years haven’t been without challenges for any cultural leader. But we had a plan and stuck to it, and I feel good about that.”

In a press release, AGO board of trustees co-president Beth Horowitz praised Jost’s programming shifts and initiation of the gallery’s expansion.

Marsha Lederman: The AGO didn’t just embroil itself in controversy over Nan Goldin’s work – it missed out on a magnificent piece of art

“Stephan has transformed the AGO over the past decade. The collection is broader, deeper and more inclusive,” she said. “His leadership of the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery project – fully funded and on track – is his legacy and will have a lasting impact.”

Reflecting on conversations about art and nationalism that have dominated cultural headlines in the wake of the trade war with the United States, Jost said it’s more important than ever for cultural institutions to frame global conversations through Canadian art.

“If we don’t use Canadian content and artists to tell the world what’s important, other places we will.”

stories.title: Mysterious floating island reappears on B.C. lake
stories.summary: Boaters should resist urge to visit island, which could be based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris, BC Hydro spokesperson says
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
Geologist John Joseph Clague said when he first heard that a floating island, bigger than a football field, had been spotted on a lake in British Columbia’s northern Interior, he dismissed it as an “AI stunt.”

But Clague – a professor of earth sciences at Simon Fraser University and an emeritus scientist of the Geological Survey of Canada – is now convinced that the island is very real, but is mystified by its origins.

Boaters have been being warned to stay off the island that reappeared on Monday on Williston Lake, the reservoir for the W.A.C. Bennett Dam.

BC Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer said it had travelled about 30 kilometres, adding to the mystery surrounding the island that he theorized had been formed when it was lifted free by rising water levels in the reservoir.

Clague, who has previously worked around the Williston Lake area, was not convinced by that explanation. He said he had seen evidence of erosion along the lake, but “nowhere near that in scale.”

“There is erosion occurring, and trees do collapse into the lake, but they don’t kind of form this very large mat of forested material,” said Clague. “This is unusual. I’ve never heard of such a thing before.”

He said it also remained a mystery why the island had not broken apart after travelling so far.

“I think a lot of people view it as something that’s very thick, but it can’t be thick if it’s moving around the lake at speeds,” said Clague, “So, you know, it’s a curiosity.”

BC Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer says he initially thought reports of a floating island covered in trees on Williston Lake in northern British Columbia were a hoax, before satellite images confirmed its existence. It then vanished, but has now reappeared, 30 kilometres from where it was previously seen.

The Canadian Press

Rocky Avery shared images of the island that drew worldwide attention after it was spotted by a friend at the lake north of Avery’s hometown of Mackenzie last month.

He said the water under the island at the time was about 60 metres deep.

“When I saw the video, it was just kind of in awe because you can see from his boat – he was making the ripples, and you could see along the island it was all just going up and down, and it was actually real,” said Avery. “It was crazy.”

Avery notified BC Hydro and members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation of the discovery.

Gammer said he too initially thought the reports of a floating island covered in trees and foliage were a hoax when BC Hydro received them on Aug. 13.

“I checked internally and nobody that I have with contacts in the company had heard of this either. So, at the time, we basically thought it was maybe a hoax, and we didn’t give it much more attention,” said Gammer, manager of northern community relations with BC Hydro.

But a few days later, engineers with the Crown utility spotted it on satellite imagery in Finley Bay, near the centre of the lake.

“This is a rare occurrence, and certainly the first that we’ve heard of for Williston reservoir,” said Gammer.

He said they tried to track the island but it seemed to vanish, before it was spotted again on Monday against the shoreline where the Ospika River flows into the lake.

“It’s moved about 30 kilometres northwest on the reservoir into a more remote location,” said Gammer. “It looks like the island appears to be intact.”

Gammer said he also received a photo from a boater, providing double confirmation of the island’s reappearance. Based on satellite imagery, the island is about 140 metres long and about 70 metres wide, he added.

He said boaters should resist the urge to visit the island, theorizing that it was based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris that May have broken free from the shore when the lake recently filled for the first time since 2012.

Gammer said the island’s origin was not certain but it was normal for trees that fall into the reservoir to clump together in sheltered bays.

“You can imagine, like a tree falling down in the forest, and the trunk is laying flat, and over a long period of time, it starts to break down, and other plants, moss, and even trees start growing on top,” said Gammer.

The rising waters of the reservoir then could have lifted the mass free, calling it the “best theory” of how the island came to be.

Gammer said waves in the reservoir can become violent during a windstorm and he feared they could tear apart the mass of logs and woody debris.

“It’s just naturally unstable, and so it’s unsafe to climb onto the island or land a boat on it. It would be dangerous to do that,” he said.

BC Hydro would continue to monitor the island to see if it started moving again, Gammer said.

“I mean, there will be people who will probably want to study it and get close to it. So, there May be more information to come about the island as the weeks go by,” said Gammer.

Avery cheered news the island hadn’t sunk, after being told by members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation that they too had spotted it again.

“We’re just waiting for the water to calm down so we can take a jet boat and take a better look at it,” said Avery, adding a former chief from the nation would join the trip to inspect the island.

Avery said he had lived in the area for more than 48 years and never heard of anything like the island before.

He said he wanted the island to be named Rocky Island – “even though it’s not that rocky.”

Rocky Avery shared images of the island that drew worldwide attention after it was spotted by a friend at the lake north of Avery’s hometown of Mackenzie last month.
He said the water under the island at the time was about 60 metres deep.

“When I saw the video, it was just kind of in awe because you can see from his boat – he was making the ripples, and you could see along the island it was all just going up and down, and it was actually real,” said Avery. “It was crazy.”
Avery notified BC Hydro and members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation of the discovery.
Gammer said he too initially thought the reports of a floating island covered in trees and foliage were a hoax when BC Hydro received them on Aug. 13.

“I checked internally and nobody that I have with contacts in the company had heard of this either. So, at the time, we basically thought it was maybe a hoax, and we didn’t give it much more attention,” said Gammer, manager of northern community relations with BC Hydro.
But a few days later, engineers with the Crown utility spotted it on satellite imagery in Finley Bay, near the centre of the lake.
“This is a rare occurrence, and certainly the first that we’ve heard of for Williston reservoir,” said Gammer.
He said they tried to track the island but it seemed to vanish, before it was spotted again on Monday against the shoreline where the Ospika River flows into the lake.
“It’s moved about 30 kilometres northwest on the reservoir into a more remote location,” said Gammer. “It looks like the island appears to be intact.”

Gammer said he also received a photo from a boater, providing double confirmation of the island’s reappearance. Based on satellite imagery, the island is about 140 metres long and about 70 metres wide, he added.

He said boaters should resist the urge to visit the island, theorizing that it was based on an unstable mass of logs and decaying debris that May have broken free from the shore when the lake recently filled for the first time since 2012.
Gammer said the island’s origin was not certain but it was normal for trees that fall into the reservoir to clump together in sheltered bays.

“You can imagine, like a tree falling down in the forest, and the trunk is laying flat, and over a long period of time, it starts to break down, and other plants, moss, and even trees start growing on top,” said Gammer.
The rising waters of the reservoir then could have lifted the mass free, calling it the “best theory” of how the island came to be.
Gammer said waves in the reservoir can become violent during a windstorm and he feared they could tear apart the mass of logs and woody debris.
“It’s just naturally unstable, and so it’s unsafe to climb onto the island or land a boat on it. It would be dangerous to do that,” he said.
BC Hydro would continue to monitor the island to see if it started moving again, Gammer said.
“I mean, there will be people who will probably want to study it and get close to it. So, there May be more information to come about the island as the weeks go by,” said Gammer.
Avery cheered news the island hadn’t sunk, after being told by members of the Tsay Keh Dene First Nation that they too had spotted it again.
“We’re just waiting for the water to calm down so we can take a jet boat and take a better look at it,” said Avery, adding a former chief from the nation would join the trip to inspect the island.
Avery said he had lived in the area for more than 48 years and never heard of anything like the island before.
He said he wanted the island to be named Rocky Island – “even though it’s not that rocky.”

stories.title: Carney urges Trump administration to ‘stop doing memes’ and get serious about trade talks
stories.summary: Carney didn't hesitate to defend walking away from the table when it became clear Canada's sovereignty was at stake.
stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
Posted September 1, 2026 1:46 pm.

Prime Minister Mark Carney still believes the United States and Canada can reach a “mutually beneficial” trade deal, but first President Donald Trump and his administration need to show Canadians some respect and get serious about negotiations, he told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday.

Since trade talks fell apart , President Trump has not only unleashed additional tariffs, but his usual barrage of social media tirades directed at Canada — a nation he feels has long taken advantage of the U.S. on the subject of trade.

With a sharpie scrawl, Trump even declared he was renaming Lake Ontario ‘Lake America’ and has claimed Canada has nothing the U.S. wants or needs.

U.S. Department of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth added to the animosity with a distasteful social media post mocking female members of a Cadet Training Centre in Vernon, B.C.

Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss seemed to defend Hegseth’s post, saying it “speaks for itself.”

On Tuesday, Carney said the post was “beneath their office” and indicative of a nation that isn’t taking Canada, or the increasingly precarious trade situation, seriously.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those (trade) discussions, we can have those discussions,” the PM said. “It’s not constructive,” he said of the online trolling, “but that’s their democracy.”

In all fairness, not all Canadian politicians have chosen the high road during the cross-border sparring.

Notably, Ontario Premier Doug Ford has called Trump “a loser” and mocked him for his previous bankruptcies in the private sector, before toning things down and admitting he got a bit carried away.

Carney, meanwhile, refuted speculation that Ford had anything to do with trade talks falling apart.

“The premiers play a very important role in this process, labour plays an important role in this process, all stakeholders play a role in this process,” Carney said. “We consult with the premiers, take into account their views … (but) the decisions on trade are the decisions of the government of Canada, I’m the Prime Minister, ultimately I’m responsible, with the cabinet, for those decisions.”

While Carney is hopeful a deal can be reached, he didn’t hesitate to defend walking away from the table when it became clear Canada’s sovereignty was at stake.

“The attitude of the United States in these discussions, and subsequently, has been one that core Canadian industries would either be subsidiaries effectively of the United States’ industries, or would put in place terms where those industries would be gradually wound down in Canada and wiped out, of course we are not going to accept those terms.”

Canada has since fired back at the United States with counter tariffs , but Carney still remains hopeful that cooler heads May prevail.

“There is a mutually beneficial deal, there were elements of that mutually beneficial deal that we were moving towards … but we never viewed that we had that deal and it diverged towards the end, and at some point maybe it will converge again.”

stories.title: Calgary home with pro-Trump flags becomes vandalism target in cross-border trade war
stories.summary: The homeowner says while his life is in Canada, he's a strong supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Some Calgarians frustrated by the renewed U.S. tariff trade war appear to be taking out their anger on one pro-Trump home by using eggs, dog feces and online suggestions of arson.

The homeowner says while his life is in Canada, he’s a strong supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump. He calls the anger fundamentally offside.

“The position of some would be to say, ‘Hey, this guy, he doesn’t agree with what we agree in, politically (even though) he goes to work, he pays his taxes … (so) let’s run them out of town,’” the homeowner said in an interview.

“That’s not a good look in my opinion, in any democratic society.”

He spoke on the condition of anonymity, noting that the police have become involved, and he and his wife fear for their safety.

Since the recent attention, he said, many people have approached him positively, while others have egged the house and thrown bagged dog excrement onto the property. Some have made comments on social media suggesting torching their home.

A spokesperson for Calgary police confirmed they had received a report of vandalism on Aug. 23, and that the homeowners were concerned about online attacks, but they say there were not sufficient grounds to support criminal charges.

The homeowners say they were born and grew up in the United States, moving to Canada for work reasons more than a decade ago.

Their home near Calgary’s downtown displays two large pro-Trump flags. A massive American flag often hangs from their balcony.

“We’re proud Americans, we support the president, and that was the idea behind the flags,” the homeowner said, stating the intention was originally to showcase their patriotism. He said it has developed into a sign of acceptance of conservatives who, he believes, have had their views suppressed and marginalized.

One of the pro-Trump flags says Trump: Make America Great Again, while the other says Trump 2028: Third Term and Beyond. The homeowner says while he supports the Trump administration’s policies — such as taxes, immigration and spending — the reference to 2028 is a joke given that presidents cannot, under the U.S. Constitution, serve a third term.

It’s not the first time his home has been in the firing line, he said. A retaining wall was defaced with graffiti during the 2024 U.S. presidential election that saw Trump defeat Democrat challenger Kamala Harris.

He said the pro-Trump flags were up long before the tariff war, which began just over a week ago, when the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about $28 billion in Canadian exports. Canada has responded with its own tariffs, which take effect Sept. 8.

The Calgary house is not the only collateral damage. Last week, Trump signed an order changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America to hit back against sharp criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

Asked why they remain in Canada even with their support for the administration, the homeowner said it’s because they have built a life in the country.

Also, he said the trade fight, as with past trade fights, is fleeting. Canada and the U.S. will eventually “kiss and make up,” he said.

“It’s just a matter of when.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Quebec government websites changing ‘Lake America’ back to Lake Ontario on maps
stories.summary: The Quebec government is taking steps to keep the name of Lake Ontario after President Trump signed an order to change lake's name to 'Lake America.'
stories.author: Joe Lofaro
paragraphs: It’s Lake Ontario, as far as the Quebec government is concerned.
For a brief period on Monday, users visiting the provincial transportation ministry’s interactive traffic map saw “Lake America” appear on their screen.
The change on Quebec511.info came after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in the Oval Office last week to change the name of the smallest of the Great Lakes to “Lake America.”

A spokesperson for the Ministère des Transports et de la Mobilité durable said the name of the lake was changed because the map uses data from Google Maps. The online tech giant confirmed that Google Maps also changed the name of the lake because it relies on information from government sources, notably the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (Gnis).

“Depending on the regional settings applied by this provider, certain geographic names May vary, and a recent adjustment made by Google explains the unusual display observed,” wrote Émilie Lord, a transportation ministry spokesperson, in an email.
“The issue has been corrected. The official name, ‘Lake Ontario,’ is now displayed.”
Google has said, however, that users in Canada using Google Maps should still see Lake Ontario, and that only U.S. users would see “Lake America” after the company updated its maps on Saturday.
The Ministry of Transport isn’t the only government website to show the wrong name.

Quebec’s liquor control board, known as the Société des alcools du Québec (SAQ), told CTV News that it has asked its third-party provider “to make the correction on our website first thing this morning to revert the name to Lake Ontario.”
Former U.S. ambassador to Canada Gordon Giffin on the ‘Lake America’ fiasco and why he believes the name change will be reversed.
The maps change also affected the website of the Sqdc, the government-owned corporation that handles the sale of recreational cannabis.

“The naming issue on the maps used by the Sqdc was corrected on Monday morning. It was caused by a supplier, who was able to resolve the issue as soon as it was brought to their attention,” a spokesperson said in an email.
Name changed on other government maps
Several government agencies in Ontario, such as Metrolinx, HydroOne, and the Lcbo , also displayed “Lake America,” blaming third-party mapping services for the change. They later reversed the change.
Meanwhile, MapQuest has said it will refuse to change the name of Lake Ontario on its maps.

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in an interview that Trump contacted Apple directly to force the company to change the name Lake Ontario to “Lake America” and that the change would happen very soon.
With files from CTV News’ Kayla Thompson and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Élections Québec says it will send out voting information in French only to comply with language laws
stories.summary: This year’s documents will include a QR code for voters to access information online in English, spokesperson says
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
However, this year’s documents will include a QR code for voters to access information online in English, she said. Indigenous voters and those eligible to receive English instructions must contact Élections Québec to request English documents.

St-Arnaud-Drolet said the elections authority will multiply its efforts to reach anglophone and allophone voters throughout the campaign period.

“We will run advertisements in English-language media … as well as on several websites and online streaming platforms, such as Spotify,” she said.

The agency said voters should receive information cards by Sept. 18, ahead of the election on Oct. 5.

stories.title: Ontario to remove stretch of Toronto bike lane after recent court win
stories.summary: Work will begin ‘almost immediately’ to remove a stretch of the Bloor Street bike lane east of Islington station, minister Prabmeet Sarkaria says
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
A stretch of bike lane on a major Toronto road is set to be removed, Ontario’s transportation minster said Tuesday as the province pressed ahead with its plan to overhaul the cycling network over the city’s objections after a recent court win.

The province said it had put out a bid request to study and design options to restore vehicle traffic on bike lane sections of Bloor Street, Yonge Street, Avenue Road and around Queen’s Park.

The successful bidder will also be expected to look for ways to retain or reconfigure the bike lanes, “where they make sense and do not make gridlock worse,” the province said in a news release.

In the meantime, work will begin “almost immediately” to remove a stretch of the Bloor Street bike lane east of Islington station, minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said. He did not say how much would be removed and his office did not immediately respond to a request for details.

“Getting these bike lanes out of the way, restoring vehicle lanes, will allow us to get people moving quicker and faster in one of the busiest cities in the world,” he said at a news conference.

Ontario’s top court clears way for Toronto bike lane removal

It comes after Ontario’s top court earlier this month overturned a ruling that blocked Premier Doug Ford’s government effort to remove the bike lanes.

Cyclists who brought the legal challenge argued the government pursued the plan even though its own advisers and experts agreed it would not accomplish its stated goal to reduce congestion, and could possibly make it worse. They pointed to an engineering study commissioned by the province that suggested removing the targeted bike lanes could increase collisions for cyclists, drivers and pedestrians by 54 per cent.

Ford’s government has said it wants bike lanes moved to secondary roads. Critics say that’s untenable for many sections of Toronto’s targeted lanes without creating disconnected stretches more dangerous to cyclists.

Work to restore a vehicle lane while also keeping the bike lane along a stretch of Bloor Street between Kipling and Islington stations was completed last year at an initially estimated cost of $750,000.

Mayor Olivia Chow has called that work a win-win solution and her office has in the past issued statements that avoided direct confrontation with the province on the issue.

Opinion: The question on bike lanes shouldn’t be about constitutional rights but if they save lives

But on Tuesday, she struck a more combative tone. Chow, who is running for re-election, said the provincial government should focus on dealing with U.S. tariffs, “not picking endless political fights with the city of Toronto.”

“I believe strongly in Toronto’s autonomy and right to govern itself,” Chow said in a statement.

The city has pegged the cost to remove the province’s targeted bike lanes at about $48-million. The province has disputed the estimate without providing its own. Asked at Tuesday’s press conference how much the work would cost, Sarkaria said he would wait for the bids.

A spokesperson for Chow said the city had repeatedly put forward designs with both bike lanes and restored vehicle lanes, including options without road construction.

“You will need to ask the Ministry of Transportation why they decided to ignore these solutions that keep all road users safe,” Chow’s press secretary Braman Thillainathan wrote in an e-mail.

The Canadian Press has reached out to the transportation ministry and Sarkaria’s office for comment.

stories.title: Unifor begins contract talks with Stellantis, vows to fight Brampton plant closing
stories.summary: Union pushing to reach agreement with automaker after members ratified deals with Ford and General Motors
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Unifor kicked off contract talks with automaker Stellantis NV on Tuesday, the first negotiations to take place since Canada-U.S. trade talks failed and U.S. President Donald Trump renewed his threats to destroy the Canadian automotive industry with more tariffs.

Lana Payne, Unifor national president, described the negotiations as the toughest to take place with the Detroit Three automakers, maybe ever.

Unifor is pushing to reach an agreement with Stellantis by Sept. 11 after members ratified deals with Ford and General Motors that provide 3-per-cent raises in each of the contracts’ three years.

Unifor turns focus to Stellantis after reaching deals with GM and Ford

Unifor has vowed to fight to match the other agreements and keep the Stellantis Brampton assembly plant from closing for good, while securing production volumes at factories in Windsor and Toronto.

The Stellantis talks have begun after trade negotiations between Canada and the U.S. fell apart on Aug. 21. The U.S. has applied 50-per-cent tariffs on a range of Canadian imports, and said it will impose the same levy on cars, steel and auto parts on Jan. 1. Canada announced retaliatory tariffs, deepening the divisions between the trading partners.

The U.S. last year ignited the trade war with 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars, minus U.S. content, and 50 per cent on steel and aluminum. Canada responded with 25-per-cent tariffs on the U.S. content of U.S.-made cars, with exceptions for automakers that build a certain number of vehicles in Canada.

Ms. Payne said the tariffs have created an “existential crisis for our auto industry,” warning that the levies on auto parts would shut down the North American auto industry within 10 days.

“The most powerful leader in the world has said that he does not want us building cars or trucks or anything,” Ms. Payne said at a press conference on Tuesday.

“There is going to be a time when this will be behind us, and we have to make sure that we’re protecting the auto footprint in Canada for when we get to that moment,” Ms. Payne said.

Stellantis employs more than 9,000 Unifor workers, most of those at the Windsor assembly plants making Chrysler minivans and Dodge Chargers. The carmaker also runs a casting plant in the west end of Toronto.

The Brampton plant closed in 2023 and has 2,200 Unifor workers on layoff. The plant was to be retooled to make the Jeep Compass, but Stellantis moved planned production of the SUV to the U.S. shortly after Mr. Trump announced tariffs on Canadian-made cars last year.

The plant’s future is a priority in the talks, Unifor said.

Without elaborating, Ms. Payne said Stellantis once told the union the plant might return to production by 2028 or 2029 as it introduces 11 new models. But in August, she said, the company told Unifor it planned to begin talks with a third party about a possible sale of the factory.

The federal government in April rejected a proposal by Stellantis’ Chinese partner Leapmotor to assemble kit cars at the plant. Bloomberg on Monday reported Chinese car company BYD has inquired about building buses there.

“Our focus remains on finding a sustainable manufacturing solution for Brampton Assembly,” Stellantis said in a statement on Tuesday, in response to questions about the plant.

Stellantis Canada president Trevor Longley said in a separate statement the company has invested more than $8-billion in Canada since 2022, a reflection of the long-term future of Canadian manufacturing and the company’s confidence in the country and its workforce.

“As the automotive industry continues to navigate significant economic, trade and competitive pressures, our goal is to reach an agreement that recognizes the contributions of our employees while helping ensure our Canadian operations remain competitive,” Mr. Longley said.

James Stewart, a Unifor negotiator and local president of the Windsor plant, said Stellantis workers are “anxious” about the future. The laid-off Brampton workers have been living a “nightmare” for almost three years, he said.

Stellantis weighs selling idled plant in Brampton, Ont., union says

“Our members don’t need to speculate about the damage these tariffs are causing, not to mention the threat of new tariffs,” Mr. Stewart said. “Our members in all our facilities are living it first-hand. They are concerned about what the future holds for their jobs, for their workplaces and for their families.”

On Sunday, Unifor’s GM employees ratified a deal that covers 4,600 workers at Ontario plants in Oshawa, Woodstock, St. Catharines and Ingersoll. Workers at the Ingersoll factory, which ended production last year, will receive extended jobless benefits.

In announcing the agreement, GM said it will spend an additional $144-million at its Oshawa plant to begin production of the GMC Sierra heavy-duty truck, which will be made alongside the plant’s current product, the Chevrolet Silverado HD. GM also announced a $215-million investment at its propulsion plant in St. Catharines that will make the factory the sole source for the new transmissions.

The investments mean GM has recently announced about $1.4-billion in spending on the Ontario plants, “reinforcing the important role Canadian operations will continue to play in GM’s North American manufacturing network,” the automaker said in a statement.

The Ford agreement also included new investments of US$500-million at its Essex engine factory and US$400-million at its Oakville pick-up assembly plant.

Ms. Payne said Ford and GM investments signal the automakers are looking past the current trade turmoil, protecting jobs and their abilities to produce in Canada.

“They both understand that unscrambling the integrated market, the integrated supply chains that we have in the auto industry, is just not possible. They are playing the long game, and we expect Stellantis to play the long game,” she said.

stories.title: Here's what Mark Carney said when asked if he would run in the next federal election
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney was asked if he would lead the Liberals into the next federal election after the party won three by-elections.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The prime minister said more than a hundred words and none of them were 'yes'

Prime Minister Mark Carney was asked if he plans to lead the Liberals into the next federal election during a brief scrum outside the prime minister’s office in Ottawa Tuesday morning.

Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.

Access articles from across Canada with one account.

Enjoy additional articles per month.

Notably, in the more than 100 words of Carney’s response, the word “yes” didn’t appear.

Carney was speaking to reporters after the federal Liberals reclaimed a majority in the House of Commons Monday with three byelection victories , bringing them back to 173 seats.

Here’s how he responded to the question about his future:

“I’ve just led the party into two byelections, and I’m very pleased that we won all three. (Editor’s note: three byelections were held Monday night.)

“I’m pleased to have a remarkable caucus. I view my role as my colleagues do: to do our job. We’re sent to Ottawa for a reason. We’re sent here at a critical time.

“I’m blessed by having three great colleagues who are going to be coming in from very different backgrounds, very different ridings, and we’re going to stand up for Canada.

“We’re going to build this country. We’re going to help unite this country and we’re going to build it for all.

“And I’m going to focus on that and that’s my that’s my concern.”

Dropping the writ and calling a snap election is at Carney’s discretion. The next general federal election in Canada must be held by Oct. 15, 2029 — the third Monday in October of the fourth calendar year since the last polling day, per the Elections Canada Act.

stories.title: B.C. coast, parts of Vancouver Island set to see heavy rains, strong winds
stories.summary: The weather statement also covers the west coast of Vancouver Island stretching from Zeballos in the north to Sooke near the Victoria area.
stories.author: Staff
paragraphs: By Staff The Canadian Press
Posted September 1, 2026 1:04 pm
Updated September 1, 2026 1:05 pm
Environment Canada says the first fall storm of the season is set to bring heavy rain and strong winds to parts of the British Columbia coast.
Environment Canada has issued a special weather statement for B.C.’s north and central coasts, including Prince Rupert, Kitimat and Bella Bella.
The weather statement also covers the west coast of Vancouver Island stretching from Zeballos in the north to Sooke near the Victoria area.

Environment Canada says the storm is expected to bring heavy rainfall Tuesday that could trigger localized flooding and increase the risk for landslides, while winds are expected to peak Tuesday night.
The weather forecast agency says water pooling and flooding May be more prevalent in areas that have seen drought conditions that are widespread across southern B.C.

The BC Wildfire Service says in its update that the province is set for more “fall-like” weather with increased relative humidity and seasonal temperatures, but cautions that drought conditions persist in the southern Interior and southeastern B.C.
While Environment Canada has categorized the weather event as a fall storm, fall officially begins in B.C. on Sept. 22.

stories.title: A sixth straight day of Russian strikes hammers Kyiv, killing at least 12
stories.summary: Russia launched a large aerial assault in and around Ukraine’s capital overnight into Tuesday morning, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than a dozen others, including three children, local authorities said.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Kyiv, Ukraine — Russia bombarded the Ukrainian capital for more than 12 hours overnight and into Tuesday, killing at least a dozen people in another aerial onslaught that authorities said was aimed at menacing civilians.

The strikes marked an unprecedented sixth straight day of heavy Russian attacks on Kyiv since Russia launched the full-scale invasion of its neighbor more than 4.5 years ago. The consecutive aerial assaults are designed to grind down civilians by disrupting daily life, Ukrainian officials have said.

The cruise and ballistic missiles, jet-powered drones, glide bombs and artillery salvos targeted Kyiv as well as eight other regions. The strikes wounded more than a dozen people, including three children, just as millions of Ukrainian schoolchildren returned to classes Tuesday to start their fifth school year since the invasion.

The European Union’s top diplomat said Russia’s army is struggling to make progress on the front line and wants to scare off Ukraine’s Western backers with its air campaign.

“Russia’s war is becoming more ruthless and destructive, but it’s unfortunately not closer to ending,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc’s defence ministers in Ireland. “Russia’s army is bogged down on the ground, and that is why they are killing civilians from the skies.”

Attack hit residential buildings

The latest attack struck civilian infrastructure and residential buildings in several districts of Kyiv, authorities said, with eight people killed in the city itself and four others in the surrounding region.

Six employees of state-owned railway company Ukrzaliznytsia were among those killed in Kyiv when a ballistic missile hit a depot and other property, company Chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said in a social media post.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the dead included an Indian citizen.

Nearly 350 emergency workers were deployed in Kyiv and the surrounding region, Zelenskyy said.

The Russian Defence Ministry said its forces carried out a “massive strike” on Ukraine with “precision-guided weapons” and long-range drones. The assault targeted facilities that manufacture and store weapons as well as military-related infrastructure, it said.

Ukraine’s air force said the attack began at 6 p.m. Monday, using ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, as well as 218 drones and decoys. About a third of the drones were jet-powered, making them much harder to intercept than propeller-driven versions.

The main Russian targets were in the Kyiv and southern Odesa regions, the air force said in a statement.

The attack on the Odesa region on the Black Sea damaged civilian infrastructure and wounded one person, regional head Oleh Kiper said.

Two residential buildings were damaged, while a fire broke out at a textile factory. Russian forces also struck the Orlivka international ferry crossing on the border with Romania, he said.

Russia also shelled the northern Zhytomyr region, starting fires at an industrial facility and a warehouse, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said.

In the capital, first responders worked to clear rubble from damaged apartment buildings and free trapped residents.

Russia says it intercepted more than 500 Ukrainian drones

Meanwhile, the Russian Defence Ministry said Tuesday that its air defenses overnight intercepted 516 Ukrainian drones over 18 Russian regions, as well as the illegally annexed Crimean Peninsula and the Black Sea.

In the Leningrad region, the drone attack sparked a fire in the port of Ust-Luga, Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said, as Ukraine extended its campaign to hurt Russia’s oil sector, which is a mainstay of the economy.

Ust-Luga is one of Russia’s largest oil and gas export terminals, more than 800 kilometres (500 miles) away from Ukraine. It has been repeatedly targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks this year.

Elsewhere, the war in Ukraine was discussed Monday at a summit in Kyrgyzstan involving the leaders of China, Russia and India. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Russian President Vladimir Putin through a translator that India supports efforts to end the fighting.

“We need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities,” Modi said, adding that “this is very important for all of humanity.”

In other developments Tuesday, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives. German leaders announced that they would shut down a Russian consulate, among other measures against Moscow.

The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on Aug. 4, and the device was defused. Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption across Europe with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.

Samya Kullab, The Associated Press

stories.title: U.S. military says it's hitting new targets in Iran as hostilities flare again
stories.summary: The U.S. military says it’s striking new targets in Iran as hostilities flare again after a month without military action.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content: Washington — The U.S. military says it’s striking new targets in Iran as hostilities flare again after a month without military action. U.S. Central Command said Tuesday that the strikes “follow recent attempted attacks by the Irgc against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region.” On Sunday, the U.S. military said it struck rocket launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, which were intercepted, while United Arab Emirates said it stopped an Iranian drone over its waters. President Donald Trump acknowledged Monday that more strikes might be necessary. Ben Finley, The Associated Press

stories.title: Major labour group challenges Quebec's union governance and transparency law
stories.summary: Montreal - A major Quebec labour group has launched a legal challenge of a new provincial law that affects union governance and transparency.
stories.author: Lia Lévesque The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A major Quebec labour group has launched a legal challenge of a new provincial law that affects union governance and transparency.

The Confédération des syndicats nationaux, one of the largest union federations in the province, is challenging the law at the Quebec Superior Court.

The challenge comes after the federation and eight other large labour groups in Quebec filed a complaint about the law to the International Labour Organization in July.

The law introduces a new category of optional union dues on top of the regular union fees that are deducted on employee paycheques.

Unions would need rely on the optional dues to fund activities such as advertising campaigns or legal challenges, under the new law.

The provincial government has said the law would benefit workers and give them a better understanding of how their dues are used.

The new law also forces labour organizations to publish information on their finances and secret ballot procedures.

In the new legal challenge, the labour federation alleged that the law violates the freedom of association and freedom of expression. It is asking the Superior Court to declare the law unconstitutional, invalid, and unenforceable.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: Loblaw increases number of new stores planned for 2026
stories.summary: Loblaw Cos. Ltd. is increasing the number of new stores it plans to open this year
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content: Brampton — Loblaw Cos. Ltd. is increasing the number of new stores it plans to open this year. The company behind Loblaws and Shoppers Drug Mart said Tuesday it now expects to open about 75 new locations this year, up from earlier plans for about 70. Loblaw chief executive Per Bank says Canadians are being thoughtful about every dollar they spend. “We see that in how they shop our stores, the brands they choose, and how they use our loyalty and e-commerce solutions,” Bank said in a statement. “We have a significant investment program underway, and we’re putting that capital behind the parts of our business that meets the needs of Canadians. That includes accelerating our network expansion efforts to reach more customers, faster.” Loblaw has opened 38 new grocery stores and pharmacies in Canada, including 21 grocery stores and 17 Shoppers Drug Mart locations, so far this year. The new stores are part of $2.4 billion in planned capital spending for 2026, the second year of the company’s five-year plan to invest $10 billion in Canada by 2030. Loblaw said it has spent about half of the total for 2026 so far, with plans for the remaining money to include accelerating the opening of new stores, renovating existing locations and continuing to develop new store formats and concepts. Bank said the company has been happy with how its new stores are performing. “As they mature, we’re seeing strong double-digit same-store sales growth. That gives us confidence in our expansion strategy and in continuing to invest behind the formats customers are choosing,” he said. Loblaw’s grocery expansion has been focused on its No Frills and Maxi banners. Grocers have been expanding their discount footprint across Canada since 2023 as shoppers have been grappling with food inflation coming out of the pandemic. Meanwhile, pharmacy and health-care services have been projected to grow significantly, partly led by sales of generic weight-loss drugs. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. bar operator fined $3K after undercover inspector offered ‘bump,’ confronted with knives
stories.summary: A bar operator in Haida Gwaii has been fined $3,000 after an undercover liquor inspector was offered what appeared to be cocaine before being confronted by two men with knives inside the establishment.
stories.author: Becca Clarkson
stories.content: A bar operator in Haida Gwaii, B.C., has been fined $3,000 after an undercover liquor inspector was offered what appeared to be cocaine before being confronted by two men with knives inside the establishment. The inspector was inside the bar at Misty Harbour Inn in Daajing Giids about an hour before closing time on March 1, according to a decision posted by the B.C. Liquor and Cannabis Regulation Branch. What happened inside the bar The adjudicator heard that the inspector had ordered a beer and was standing at the bar when he was approached by a man claiming to be the owner. After some conversation, the man, identified as Patron 1, asked the undercover inspector if he’d like to do a “bump” while producing a bag containing what appeared to be white powder—which the inspector declined. The decision notes a “bump” is slang for inhaling a small dose of a drug such as cocaine. At this point, the adjudicator heard the patron began joking that the inspector was a police officer and repeated the accusation when introducing him to the bar’s third-party operator. Patron 1 later ordered 18 “vodka mixed shots” for customers at the bar. The adjudicator found both he and the third-party operator consumed shots before displaying knives in view of staff and patrons. According to the decision, Patron 1 opened a folding knife with a “4-to-5 inch blade” and pointed it toward the inspector. “The TPO then pulled out a curved, non-foldable knife from the waist area of his trousers and began twirling the knife in a figure-8 motion,” the decision reads. The situation escalated from there, with Patron 1 allegedly raising his fists, asking the inspector if he wanted to fight, taking photographs of him and telling other patrons he was a police officer. The inspector left the bar 45 minutes after arriving “due to personal safety concerns” and contacted RCMP. The consequences The third-party operator was arrested the following day and officers seized multiple knives from him, according to the decision. “Criminal charges arising from the incident were subsequently laid. The charges had not been determined at the time of the hearing,” the decision states. The bar’s liquor licence was suspended from March 6 to March 20. A hearing was later held, resulting in a $3,000 fine after the regulator found the establishment had allowed a person with a knife to remain on the premises. While the regulator had sought a $5,000 penalty, the adjudicator decided to impose a lesser fine, reasoning the establishment had already served a 14-day licence suspension and had no prior history of this contravention. The fine must be paid by Sept. 25.

stories.title: Federal gas tax cut expected to end Labour Day amid calls for an extension
stories.summary: The federal government's excise tax cut on gasoline and diesel is set to expire on Labour Day, amid calls for it to be extended.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
By Patricia D'Cunha

Posted September 1, 2026 12:42 pm.

The federal government’s excise tax cut on gasoline and diesel is set to expire on Labour Day, amid calls for it to be extended beyond that date.

As of Tuesday, the average cost for the price of gas at fuel pumps in Toronto is 182.9 cents a litre and around $2.30 for diesel. Some industry experts say those numbers could go up further over the long weekend.

Back in April, the federal government announced a suspension of the fuel excise tax on gasoline and diesel until Sept. 7 as gas prices soared due to the Iran war. The tax break saves Canadians 10 cents per litre on regular gasoline and four cents on a litre of diesel.

In early August, Ontario Premier Doug Ford called on Prime Minister Mark Carney to extend the suspension until at least Jan. 1, 2027, or even make it permanent.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he wants the excise tax relief extended until at least July 1, 2027, at which time it can be reviewed.

The Canadian Taxpayers Federation is also calling on Ottawa to keep the tax break in place.

“An average family who fills up their minivan about once a week will save about $400 with a gas tax that is not being applied. If you look at someone who fills up their pick-up truck once a week, they save about $470 every single year if there is no federal gas tax,” said Noah Jarvis, the group’s Ontario director, ON Tuesday.

It’s not yet known if the federal government will extend the tax break.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will be making an announcement on Wednesday afternoon “as part of the government’s efforts to help Canadian families and businesses lower everyday costs,” a release states.

With files from The Canadian Press; and Shauna Hunt, CityNews

stories.title: $55M win means new Jeep, paid-off house for some in Quebec lotto group
stories.summary: The Crown corporation in Quebec announced on Monday that 49 people won the $55-million jackpot in the Aug. 21 Lotto Max draw, with each person winning about $1 million.
stories.author: Sean Previl
paragraphs: Not a lot of people can say they’ve won a big lottery jackpot, but after an August Lotto Max draw, 49 people in Quebec can now make that claim — a “landmark first,” Loto-Québec says.
The Crown corporation in Quebec announced on Monday that 49 people won the $55-million jackpot in the Aug. 21 Lotto Max draw.
It’s the first time such a large group has won a million-dollar jackpot in a single lottery win, Loto-Quebéc said. Each individual is receiving $1.1 million.
“First of all, it’s unbelievable, we still today, as a colleague here that won [said], you don’t believe it … we’re on a cloud since a week,” Richard Poirier said.
Poirier was one of three people from the Outaouais who won, alongside 46 others from various regions of Quebec. The group gathered in Montreal at the corporation’s head office on Tuesday.

The 72-year-old won as part of a group of people who did not know each other through Loto-Québec’s online Formule groupe. This allows players to purchase one or more shares in a lottery group and then pool them with those of other group members. Each winner had purchased at least one share of the winning Formule groupe ticket.
Even though it meant playing with multiple other people he didn’t know, Poirier said he didn’t find it a weird prospect.
“I’m so happy and proud that everybody here, 49 winners,” he said.
1:27 Montreal-area family wins $40-million lottery jackpot, vows to avoid impulse spending

Now that he’s won $1.1 million, Poirier said he’s quit the two part-time jobs he worked as a clerk at a store, where he decided to work after retiring in 2014, and plans to golf and will be more regularly attending his gym. He said his wife had already taken her retirement in May.
He also plans to buy a Jeep in cash, a purchase he previously planned to make with credit but can now make outright.
“I’m a simple person, I appreciate life and health and I won’t change at all, not a bit,” he said.
For 43-year-old Naeim Nouzad of Dorval, the $1.1 million is an early birthday gift — he turns 44 on Sept. 18.
“I was really excited and I couldn’t believe it,” he told reporters. “I had an online course and the whole class I was flying, that was a good feeling.”
Retirement is not in his plans, but Nouzad said he hopes to use the money to pay off his house and see how he can help his two sisters. He’s also going to buy a gift for his nephew as his first plan.

He said he normally checks his email when he wakes up Saturdays and sees maybe he won $1 or $2 in the lottery, but saw “too many numbers” without his glasses on. He then went to check the app and saw he won $1.1 million, but when he noticed it was a group that won, he figured he’d get about $22,000.
It was a call to Loto-Québec that confirmed the full $1.1 million was the split amount. He said Tuesday it was a “good feeling” winning alongside so many people.
“When I was entering the building, I was thinking each one has their own dream and you can see on their face that they’re really happy, it was really a good feeling,” he said.

There were 15 winners from Monteregie, 17 from Montreal, two each from the Laurentides and the Capitale-Nationale, five from Lanaudiere, three from the Outaouais, and one each from Abitibi-Temiscamingue, Laval, Cote-Nord, Estrie, Mauricie and Nord-du-Quebec.
“It’s incredible to think that 49 families here in Quebec will enjoy part of this jackpot,” said Isabelle Jean, executive vice-president and COO of Lottery Games at Loto-Québec.
According to Loto-Québec, it’s the first time the corporation has handed out this many cheques worth more than $1 million in a single day.
— with files from Global News’ Dan Spector

“I was really excited and I couldn’t believe it,” he told reporters. “I had an online course and the whole class I was flying, that was a good feeling.”

Retirement is not in his plans, but Nouzad said he hopes to use the money to pay off his house and see how he can help his two sisters. He’s also going to buy a gift for his nephew as his first plan.

He said he normally checks his email when he wakes up Saturdays and sees maybe he won $1 or $2 in the lottery, but saw “too many numbers” without his glasses on. He then went to check the app and saw he won $1.1 million, but when he noticed it was a group that won, he figured he’d get about $22,000.

It was a call to Loto-Québec that confirmed the full $1.1 million was the split amount. He said Tuesday it was a “good feeling” winning alongside so many people.

“When I was entering the building, I was thinking each one has their own dream and you can see on their face that they’re really happy, it was really a good feeling,” he said.

There were 15 winners from Monteregie, 17 from Montreal, two each from the Laurentides and the Capitale-Nationale, five from Lanaudiere, three from the Outaouais, and one each from Abitibi-Temiscamingue, Laval, Cote-Nord, Estrie, Mauricie and Nord-du-Quebec.

“It’s incredible to think that 49 families here in Quebec will enjoy part of this jackpot,” said Isabelle Jean, executive vice-president and COO of Lottery Games at Loto-Québec.

According to Loto-Québec, it’s the first time the corporation has handed out this many cheques worth more than $1 million in a single day.

stories.title: Nepalese community in Nova Scotia rallies as death toll rises after flash flooding
stories.summary: As the death toll rises following last week's flash floods in central Nepal, the Maritimes' Nepalese community is waiting anxiously to hear from friends and family members.
stories.author: Ella Macdonald, Rebecca Lau
paragraphs: As the death toll rises following last week’s flash floods in central Nepal, the Nepalese community in the Maritimes is waiting anxiously to hear from friends and family members.
The combined death toll in Nepal and China surpassed 900, with more than 4,700 people still missing.
The Nepalese Society of Nova Scotia gathered over the weekend in downtown Halifax to light candles and mourn the lives lost in the catastrophic flash floods.
“We do have a number of Nepalese community [members] who have had their immediate family members or their community members still missing,” said Aayush Shrestha, who belongs to the society.
The society’s vice-president, Abilasha Niraula, says the images have been devastating.

“It felt like AI when I first saw [the videos] because there was no possible way the flood could be that big, but it was true. And later on, I found out that the place I used to work on was an affected district and people I know were affected. It made it very personal to me.”
For Sujit Acharya, who owns MomoNepal, there’s concern that the glacial collapse that triggered last Wednesday’s flash flood is a warning sign that more people will soon be at risk.

“I would like to say it is not a natural disaster. It is a human, manmade disaster. And we all are equally responsible for it, every single person living on this planet. Our country, and also India, is sitting just below that huge, huge mountain of ice,” he said.
“And then when it starts melting because of the temperature rise, it’s going to take everything away.”
He and other members of the community are raising money for the government of Nepal Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund.
Acharya has started a GoFundMe campaign for Nova Scotians who want to donate money.
For long-term assistance, however, he says humanity needs to take immediate action on climate issues.
“[We need to] think about the climate crisis whenever we try to do any purchases or involve in certain kind of activities,” he said.
Shrestha echoes that sentiment and encourages Canadians to share their expertise.
“Canada has one of the best flood detection programs; such technical assistance would be super helpful to Nepal.”

stories.title: This Yorkville hotel bar is temporarily serving a $1K cocktail that comes with a ride in a Rolls-Royce
stories.summary: This downtown Toronto hotel is rolling out the red carpet this Toronto International Film Festival in the form of a $1,000 cocktail that comes with a chauffeured ride in a Rolls-Royce.
stories.author: Alex Arsenych
stories.content: This downtown Toronto hotel is rolling out the red carpet this Toronto International Film Festival in the form of a $1,000 cocktail that comes with a chauffeured ride in a Rolls-Royce. Guests going for a pre-show cocktail at d|bar, tucked inside of the Four Seasons Hotel in Yorkville, can opt for a “tableside cocktail experience” by ordering the aptly-named The Final Cut XO Sazerac. The cocktail, crafted by assistant d|bar manager Holly Forgrave, is brimming with high-end spirits. The Final Cut is primarily made of Remy Martin XO Cognac, and 16-year-old Lagavulin Single Malt Scotch Whisky, which retails around $350 and $175 a bottle at the Lcbo, respectively. The cocktail is complete with absinthe, Peychauds bitters, lemon oil and sugar. Oh, and a ride within a two-kilometre radius in the hotel’s new Rolls-Royce house car. The experience is only on the menu once a night, available any time after 4 p.m. starting Sept. 8 throughout the duration of Tiff. It also has to be purchased at the bar, with no advance reservations. The 51st edition of Tiff runs from Sept. 10 to Sept. 20.
