stories.title: Schwartz’s Deli swaps black cherry soda for local alternative as U.S. tariffs bite
stories.summary: On a typical summer day at Schwartz’s Deli, in Montreal, there's a lineup at the door as tourists and locals wait to get their smoked-meat sandwich.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
paragraphs: On a typical summer day at Schwartz’s Deli, in Montreal, there’s a lineup at the door as tourists and locals wait to get their smoked-meat sandwich.
But now, something has changed.
For decades, customers would be able to order a can of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda alongside their sandwich.
While Cott’s used to be a local brand, it was bought out in 2018 by a multinational beverage company, Refresco, which said it has stopped production of the drink in Canada.
The supply change has prompted the iconic smoked-meat deli to to turn to a local made-in-Quebec alternative, Fleischer’s Original Black Cherry Soda.
This comes as a growing cohort of businesses embrace a Buy Canadian mantra in a landscape disrupted by tariffs and the trade war with the United States.
And some customers at the Montreal landmark smoked-meat shop seem to be enthusiastic about the newest item on the menu.
“It’s always good to support locally,” said Liam Keenan, who was visiting from Toronto and getting ready to tackle the classic Schwartz’s trio: smoked-meat sandwich, pickle, and black cherry soda.
Keenan had been to Schwartz’s once before. He said he noticed the canned drink looked different this time, but that it still tasted great.
Originally, Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was made in Montreal. It had been part of Schwartz’s history since its early years, almost a century ago.

“People appreciated (it) being local and different and a little sweet, with the spices from the smoked meat,” Frank Silva, Schwartz’s general manager, said in a recent interview. “People got hooked on it, so people come here for a smoked meat sandwich and a black cherry. That was always the case.”
But Silva said the canned version of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was discontinued by the manufacturer, in part because of American tariffs on aluminum.

“It was very popular here, but I don’t think they sold to too many other places. So when the cost for aluminum went up, they decided to eliminate black cherry in a can,” Silva said, from behind the counter of the crowded deli, between two smoked-meat sandwich orders.
A 2023 change in the provincial recycling system, which implemented a 10-cent deposit for canned drinks, May also have played a role in the end of Cott’s Canadian production, he said.
Soft-drink producer Refresco declined The Canadian Press’s interview request, but confirmed they stopped manufacturing Cott products in Canada.
After the supply ran out in March, Silva said he was happy to make the switch to Fleischer’s.
A can of Fleischer’s black cherry soda costs around twice as much as Cott’s did, but because of its bigger size, many customers share it, said Silva.
“It’s a bigger can, and it’s local, it’s Canadian, so people are really getting into it,” he said.
A few tables over, Ann Thinghuus and her two children were sharing a can of Fleischer’s to go along with their smoked-meat.

“It works really well with the sandwich, it’s super refreshing, and we did notice that there’s a Canadian flag on the can, so we’re pretty happy about that too,” said Thinghuus, who is from Vancouver.
She said supporting a Canadian business was a big plus, “especially with what’s going on” in the past few weeks.
Montreal-born brewer Victor Lukoshius owns a facility that produces beer and the Fleischer’s soda in St-Hyacinthe, east of the city.
Lukoshius set out to create a new version of the cherry-flavoured soft drink two years ago, when he heard Cott’s might be ending its production.

“I grew up just like everybody else, drinking black cherry as we’re eating smoked meat sandwiches,” he said. “We wanted to take on the challenge of producing something for the smoked meat, the delis, the Jewish delis, the hotdog places, to maintain and keep that tradition.”

Lukoshius sources his ingredients locally and the cans are printed in Montreal. He said Fleischer’s isn’t sheltered from tariffs and inflation, but that he is willing to shoulder some extra costs to keep black cherry soda flowing.
“We’re biting the bullet, we are paying more for it. We have smaller production, but I think we’re doing well,” he said.

Saibal Ray, a professor of operations management at McGill University, said tariffs placed on aluminum have affected the beverage industry even though their main goal was to target the aerospace industry, auto manufacturing and appliances.
Cans can represent up to a third of the cost of producing a soda, said Ray, who has expertise in supply chain management.

He explained that since most cans are produced in the United States using Canadian aluminum, they are tariffed at least twice. So Ray said it’s not surprising that niche products like black cherry soda would be swallowed up.
“It’s a very small margin business,” he said. “When the price increases by that much, most of your margin goes away, and then only the very large volume (products) can play a role.”
At Schwartz’s, the numbers show that customers’ thirst for black cherry soda remains strong. Silva said his new supplier is now trying to keep up with their orders of 12-can cases.
“This morning, I ordered 100 cases, and he only had 87,” said Silva. “I just spoke to him, he’s trying to get me some more.”
Whatever happens with trade negotiations and tariffs, Silva doesn’t plan on going back.
Even if the cans of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda return, he said customers would stick with the made-in-Quebec can of Fleischer’s.

stories.title: New foreign investment in Mexico stalls as companies fret over Usmca uncertainty
stories.summary: The uncertainty is deterring new investments and prompting some companies already in Mexico to proactively look elsewhere. More than a dozen business leaders told Reuters that they are reconsidering their investment plans, in some cases drawing up proposals to pull out of Mexico and relocate to Asia.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content: When Randy Carr opened a factory in central Mexico in 2005, he was drawn by the country’s low wages and free-trade agreement with the United States. Over the next 20 years, the plant, which produces embroidered patches and custom emblems, grew into an 800-worker operation. But in 2025, after U.S. President Donald Trump began threatening tariffs on Mexico and Canada, Carr quickly moved to diversify. He set his sights on the Dominican Republic. “It all started with the February decision to hit Mexico and Canada with 25 per cent tariffs,” he said. “The writing was on the wall.” Mexico has so far largely escaped the heaviest of Trump’s sweeping tariffs that have fueled a bitter trade dispute with Canada and other U.S. allies. But Trump has repeatedly attacked the U.S.-Mexico-Canada free trade pact known as Usmca, and in July Washington declined to renew it, instead opting for annual reviews, leaving companies unsure what tariff regime they May face from one year to the next. The uncertainty is deterring new investments and prompting some companies already in Mexico to proactively look elsewhere. More than a dozen business leaders told Reuters that they are reconsidering their investment plans, in some cases drawing up proposals to pull out of Mexico and relocate to Asia. Compounding their concerns is Mexico’s sweeping 2024 judicial reform, which replaced appointed judges with elected ones, unsettling companies worried about the rule of law. NEW Investment Wobbles Executives from three auto parts companies, all based in the central state of Aguascalientes, told Reuters they are considering leaving Mexico and relocating to Vietnam, whose auto parts industry has expanded rapidly over the past decade with the arrival of Japanese, Korean, and European automakers. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal business considerations. Two other executives from multinational companies told Reuters they were reassessing their projects in Mexico and had entered a “wait-and-see” phase while the future of the trade pact became clearer. “If we are going to have a constant renegotiation until July of next year, let’s just turn off the lights, close the doors and go invest somewhere else because that’s just pure uncertainty,” said Pedro Casas, CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico, which represents more than 1,450 companies in the U.S. and Mexico. The Usmca trade pact is essential for Mexico’s economy: some 80 per cent of all Mexican exports go to the U.S. and nearly 89 per cent of that daily $1.5 billion worth of goods fall under the treaty’s umbrella. Overall foreign direct investment in Mexico hit a record high of nearly $35 billion in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary numbers. But almost all of that came from reinvested earnings, with just 7.8 per cent representing new investments. Preliminary data shows new foreign investment fell 13 per cent in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier — a sign that Mexico May be struggling to attract fresh capital. Greenfield investment in Mexico, a measure of foreign spending on new factories and warehouses, fell by nearly half to $24 billion in 2025 from the previous year, according to the latest figures available from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. “If you are already in Mexico and have a plant, investing in machinery and equipment to produce more makes sense,” said Carlos Serrano, chief economist at Bbva Mexico. “But if you are a new firm, and you see all this uncertainty, not only with Usmca but also the judicial system, you will not build a new plant.” Growing Exports Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum has maintained that the country’s economy remains resilient despite the trade tensions with the United States. She has championed what she calls “Plan Mexico,” an ambitious strategy that seeks to revitalize manufacturing in Mexico and boost domestic industries. Mexico’s economy grew 1.4 per cent in the second quarter, its fastest pace since early 2022. Much of that strength has come from exports of computers, servers and other AI-related data-processing equipment to the U.S., highlighting Mexico’s continued dependence on its neighbor to the north and their free trade agreement. While that’s a boon for Mexico’s economy, it has driven the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico to record levels — which could backfire politically, given Trump’s stated mission of reducing trade imbalances with friend and foe alike. Mexico’s central bank, in its August quarterly report, said exports are expected to expand moderately in the near future, noting that the terms of the Usmca are still in effect. But, it noted, “the lack of a definitive resolution regarding its future remains an adverse factor for investment decisions.” Carr’s business, World Emblem, opened its new plant in the Dominican Republic in June and currently employs about 25 people, with plans to hire more. The lower costs and generous tax incentives offset the 10 per cent U.S. tariff on imports from the country, he said. Simultaneously, Carr plans to shrink the company’s 800-employee footprint in Mexico by half through attrition. “It’s a hedge,” he said. “We just have too much at stake right now in Mexico.” (Reporting by Diego Oré and Emily Green, Editing by Rosalba O’Brien)

stories.title: Trio of buyers in showdown over home across from uptown Toronto park
stories.summary: This three-bedroom house in Davisville was listed for nearly $1.5-million and greeted 100 buyers over one weekend alone
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
232 Belsize Dr., Toronto

Asking price: $1,495,000 (July, 2026)

Selling price: $1,742,500 (July, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $841,000 (June, 2010); $611,000 (July, 2005); $450,000 (May, 2001)

Taxes: $9,338 (2026)

Days on the market: Seven

Listing agents: Robert Greenberg and Amir Kiabi, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

This three-bedroom house was undergoing improvements with a new paint job, refinished hardwood flooring and an updated deck, while its owners were watching for a dip in inventory levels in the area, around Mount Pleasant Road and Davisville Avenue. Spying an opening in July, their agent listed the home for nearly $1.5-million and greeted 100 buyers over one weekend alone. On the offer date, three offers were delivered.

“At the time of listing, there was virtually no competition,” agent Amir Kiabi said.

“It paid off; the house was also presented well.”

The buyer took ownership of the home across from Glebe Manor Square with an offer $247,500 over the asking price.

“In Davisville, there’s always more demand for this type of property in a crème de la crème location,” Mr. Kiabi said.

“It’s in front of the parkette, ON a very quiet street and one of the best streets in Davisville.

“It’s also in the Maurice Cody school district, Hodgson Middle School, which is brand-new, and Northern [Secondary School]. These public schools are among the most sought-after in Toronto.”

This two-storey house, built about 100 years ago, has 1,548 square feet of living space, including an office, a living room with a gas fireplace and a family room addition with vaulted ceilings and access to a deck and patio.

The kitchen and two bathrooms were recently remodelled, and recreation areas downstairs were fitted with new windows.

There is one-car parking on a mutual driveway on the 25- by 125-foot lot.

“It had a one-level addition and the basement was renovated,” Mr. Kiabi said.

“But you could do more later, giving the buyer flexibility to do a second-floor addition or extending the basement.”

stories.title: Increased speed limit takes effect between Windsor and Toronto
stories.summary: Highway travelers between Windsor and Toronto are able to move a little faster along Highway 401 as of Monday.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Highway travelers between Windsor and Toronto are able to move a little faster along Highway 401 as of Monday.

The latest in a series of provincial speed limit increases has taken effect, raising the speed limit from 100 to 110 kilometres per hour along the stretch from Tilbury in the southwest to Toronto.

“It’s actually pretty nice. I didn’t realize it until you just said it, but I do remember seeing 110 speed limit,” said driver Ken Moore, who stopped for a break at the ONroute stop on Highway 401 east at Ingersoll, Ont. on Monday.

“The majority of the people on the highway travel at much higher speeds prior to the 110 increase,” said driver John Thomson, who also made a pit stop.

While commercial transport trucks are already regulated with speed limiters set at 105 km/h, truck driver Manav says the new speed limit of 110 km/h gives truck drivers more breathing room.

“Trucks are heavy loaded, you know. On the downhill sometimes you cannot push the brakes too hard. So that is a good change for us,” he said.

Marco Beghetto, media spokesperson for the Ontario Trucking Association, calls for consistent enforcement for all highway users.

“A portion of the truck population is abiding by the speed limiter rule at 105. A portion of the truck population is going to do what the cars are now allowed to do, which is a buck 20 plus. So yes, you’re going to have more vehicles doing a variation of different speeds, which I can see can be problematic,” he told CTV News.

“Any increase in speed is not an invitation to drive even more at an excessive speed,” said Derek Rogers, media relations coordinator for West Region OPP.

Rogers says the higher speed limit will not change their job of keeping roads safe.

“Either driving too fast, or driving too fast for the conditions. So really, from an OPP perspective, it doesn’t change. Our focus is on responsible driving behaviour, and that focus remains in place,” he said.

The final phase of speed limit increases for 2026 will take effect at the end of September. The changes cover 938 kilometers in total, with 89 per cent of the province’s highway network up to 110 km/h.

“The people who are going to exceed by a lot are still going to do it. I don’t see it having changed a lot. Just people are not getting speeding tickets as much now,” said driver Dave Perrotta.

stories.title: Thai resort readies for U.S. carrier’s 5,000 sailors
stories.summary: A U.S. aircraft carrier at the centre of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content: A U.S. aircraft carrier at the centre of a political row over conditions on board was set to arrive in Thailand on Tuesday, the first port call for its 5,000 crew since November. The resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for U.S. troops since the Vietnam War, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln. “About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” provincial Governor Narit Niramaiwong told AFP. The nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago. Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on board -- including attempted suicides -- have made headlines in the United States, provoking criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump’s war against Iran. Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the massive carrier would dock just after midnight (around 1701 GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port. Around 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups until the carrier departs on Sunday. “They come to relax because it’s been almost 280 days since anyone came ashore,” Poramase said in a Facebook post. “Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.” No jet skis or cannabis Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam War in the 1960s, when U.S. soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation (R&R). The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism. Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the U.S. arrivals. In his Facebook post, the mayor said he was hoping the soldiers could bring in up to 100 million Thai baht (US$3 million) during their stay -- a boon to the city during low season. They have been banned from water sports such as jet skis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, he added, encouraging them to take part in the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites. “We’re happy to get business from anybody,” Nicko, the French owner of a go-go bar in Pattaya, told AFP. “We’ll have to be careful because as we know, things can get out of hand with alcohol involved.”

stories.title: Grandma’s recipes inspire London family’s new Egyptian restaurant
stories.summary: The Hyde Park BIA says Teta’s is London’s first dedicated Egyptian restaurant.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
paragraphs: A London Egyptian family that started with a food truck is now recreating the flavours of their Cairo kitchen at a nostalgic restaurant in Hyde Park.
Teta’s Egyptian Kitchen, which translates to “Grandma’s” in Arabic, serves different menus for brunch, lunch and dinner at 1035 Gainsborough Rd.
From the outside, it looks like a house on a busy Hyde Park street. But step through the door and Arabic music plays in the background, transporting diners to Cairo.
“We just want to make an experience even with the music we’re playing,” said manager Mariam Nadeem.

An Egyptian oud sits on the counter by the windows, a pear-shaped, 11-string instrument that predates the modern guitar. On the wall behind it, the restaurant’s mission statement reads in English and Arabic: “From Cairo, with Love.”
The restaurant, located in a former Thai restaurant, is small and fully renovated, with about 20 seats.
Rugs and lamps hang from the ceiling, and the open kitchen is visible from the dining area. Family photos line the walls alongside scenes of the Pyramids and Nile River.
One photo stands out for Nadeem: her grandmother, Teta Madiha, who died in 2018.

“Everything (on the menu) is my grandma’s recipe,” she said. “We’re trying to specialize and keep the recipes very true to home. We really wanted to make sure that she’s highlighted here . . . Even when she’s not here, she’s still able to bring us together.”
When Nadeem’s grandmother visited from Egypt, she cooked for the family and also sold food to the community.

“She also always wanted to start her own restaurant, her own business,” Nadeem said. “And then when my grandma passed away, my mom knew she wanted to actually open a restaurant, but at the time, with COVID, it wasn’t the right time.”
Nadeem and her mother, Rasha Abdelfatah, who owns the restaurant, entered the food business in 2021 with Koshri Express, selling Egyptian street food.
“A food truck is limiting with the snow and weather in Canada, and it’s very labour-intensive,” said Nadeem, 24, who is also a registered nurse.
They opened the restaurant in June with brunch service until 3 p.m. and have since expanded their hours. Brunch has become one of the restaurant’s busiest meals, Nadeem said.
“It’s a very generous portion,” Nadeem said. “That’s the thing with Egyptian food, we make sure there’s a lot.”
They source products such as seasonings, bread and cheese from Egypt. The taameya for the sandwich takes two days to prepare, with the beans soaked overnight before use, Nadeem said.
The Egyptian and Arabic community is “pretty big,” but the restaurant and its menu were also shaped by requests from food truck regulars of different backgrounds.
“There’s a lot of Middle Eastern food in London but not specialized Egyptian,” Nadeem said. “So we’re like, if we don’t do it (open an Egyptian restaurant), someone’s going to beat us to it.”
The Hyde Park BIA said it is excited to welcome the restaurant to the neighbourhood.

“London has a phenomenal food scene, but bringing the city’s very first dedicated Egyptian restaurant right here to our community is incredibly exciting,” said Donna Szpakowski, CEO and general manager of the Hyde Park BIA.
“Teta’s is a true family affair, bringing nostalgia, together with their unique family recipes to create a great local dining experience.”
Teta’s is open Wednesday to Friday from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., Saturday from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6:30 p.m.

stories.title: Ontario EV battery plant to anchor new industrial megasite
stories.summary: Advanced manufacturing facility comes as federal government targets greater EV uptake
stories.author: Zakiya Kassam
stories.content:
St. Thomas, Ont., long-known as the Railway Capital of Canada, will soon be recognized as being home to the country’s largest electric vehicle (EV) battery plant.

The gigafactory – owned by EV battery manufacturer PowerCo , a subsidiary of Volkswagen Group – will include six production blocks across 370 acres, the size of more than 200 soccer fields .

The plant, expected to start production in 2027, is just a part of the vision for St. Thomas’ 1,500-acre Yarmouth Yards industrial park. The mega-site will accommodate other industrial businesses, as well as new and expanded infrastructure, to support the city’s burgeoning industrial scene.

“The selection of St. Thomas by PowerCo is truly a catalyst for what is a generational investment in the infrastructure of the city,” says Sean Dyke, CEO of the St. Thomas Economic Development Corporation . “Without PowerCo, the vision for where we are now and for what the future St. Thomas will look like would never have come to be.”

The project comes as Canada strives to expand domestic EV production and support the adoption of zero-emission vehicles across the country, with the federal government targeting 75 per cent of new vehicle sales to be EVs by 2035 and 90 per cent by 2040.

Attracting the manufacturing capacity required to achieve these goals depends on having the right infrastructure – a growing challenge in the national industrial real estate market.

While the PowerCo facility in St. Thomas will be a private commercial operation, the federal government is investing $16-billion to support production and the tax adjustments required to make the after-tax value of the investment comparable to in the United States.

Evan Robinson, a spokesperson with Ontario’s Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade , says the province is interested in supporting projects such as the PowerCo gigafactory since it “competes with jurisdictions around the world for major advanced manufacturing investments.”

One way the province is supporting the project is through the expansion of Highway 3 in St. Thomas by providing a “critical transportation link” to the PowerCo plant.

The City of St. Thomas is managing the infrastructure within the Yarmouth Yards property, which it acquired between 2022 and 2023. “Having shovel-ready land takes years, and without it, it’s very difficult for investors to see themselves in that location,” says Mr. Dyke. “It’s one of the most important factors in any site selection process.”

The infrastructure advances, combined with PowerCo’s multi-billion-dollar commitment, is already attracting new industrial players to Yarmouth Yards. Norwegian battery materials company Vianode will operate on around 280 acres of the site, according to the city .

“When governments make major investments in transmission, roads, water, waste water and serviced employment land… that infrastructure doesn’t only have value to the original company,” says Brent Rudell, broker of record at Cushman & Wakefield Southwestern Ontario . “You potentially make an entire area more competitive for the next company that comes along.”

Built with tenants such as PowerCo and Vianode in mind, the facilities coming to Yarmouth Yards will be designed for energy-intensive manufacturing.

Access to high-capacity power is becoming a non-negotiable for many industrial real estate players. The Independent Electricity System Operator (Ieso) forecasts that Ontario’s electricity demand will surge by 75 per cent by 2050, with electric vehicle supply chain manufacturing being one of two main drivers.

But outfitting an older facility with greater electrical capacity is not always possible, and when it is, the upgrades May take a considerable amount of time to complete.

Joe Rosati, senior vice-president at Lennard Commercial Realty , expects this will dictate future demand for industrial real estate. He says he thinks energy-intensive processes will be drawn to purpose-built industrial facilities that can be easily adapted.

“St. Thomas is a good example,” Mr. Rosati says.

Advanced manufacturing also creates industrial real estate demand from the broader network of companies that support it.

“It isn’t necessarily the battery manufacturer or auto maker itself. There is a whole ecosystem around these large investments: Parts suppliers, automation companies, engineering companies, logistics, specialized manufacturing and other businesses that want to locate within the same corridor,” says Mr. Rudell. “That creates opportunities for Southwestern Ontario because we already have a very strong manufacturing base.”

Mr. Rosati points out that EV operations aren’t the only industrial users that require substantial power capacity.

“Even for more conventional industrial properties, we’re seeing more occupiers require more and more power and landlords are often having to upgrade the power infrastructure at their facilities,” he says.

PowerCo’s project in St. Thomas will have a potential annual battery production capacity of up to 90 gigawatt-hours, enough to power around one million EVs per year. It will also create up to 3,000 new jobs directly and thousands more indirectly, according to Volkswagen Canada.

But the EV market is currently underpinned by volatility. This spring, Volkswagen announced it is ending production of its electric ID.4 SUV at its Tennessee assembly plant – one of two assembly facilities that PowerCo’s St. Thomas operation would have supplied.

The cancellation coincided with sluggish EV consumer demand in North America. Between the first quarters of 2025 and 2026, EV sales fell 27 per cent in North America, despite declining only three per cent globally, according to industry resource Electrek .

In Canada, zero-emission vehicles accounted for around 11 per cent of new vehicle registrations in this year’s first quarter, according to Statistics Canada . While that figure was up almost 16 per cent annually, it was also the first year-over-year increase since the fourth quarter of 2024.

The slow EV uptake is what makes the broader industrial strategy for Yarmouth Yards so important, says Mr. Dyke.

“Our vision for Yarmouth Yards is twofold. We certainly want to grow and support the EV supply chain as much as possible, but my expectation is that it will naturally fill with a broader advanced manufacturing base as a number of sectors are growing right now, from automotive to defence to food processing.

“We are in the perfect position to support all of these and are surrounded by a region with similar strengths.”

stories.title: Texas’ halt on powering data centres reflects U.S. reckoning over ‘ghost’ demand
stories.summary: Data centres have requested roughly as much electricity across the middle swath of the United States as it takes to power every home in the country, but much of that demand May be an illusion.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content: Data centres have requested roughly as much electricity across the middle swath of the United States as it takes to power every home in the country, but much of that demand May be an illusion. In an attempt to find out what is real, Texas recently became the first major data centre hub to freeze new grid connections for the facilities and investigate their plans. Other U.S. states are taking similar steps to fix the intensifying problem that is vexing regulators and politicians nationwide. A Reuters review of utility and grid data found that electricity requests from very large power users, mostly data centres, exceed 700 gigawatts — or more than 10 times industry estimates of current U.S. data centre power use — across portions of the Midwest, Mid-Atlantic and the South. Consumer advocates and regulators have cautioned that many requests are likely to be duplicative, or made by companies without the funds or expertise to see the projects through, threatening to stymie grid planning that is crucial to keeping the lights on. Some of those warnings are now being validated, with major utilities cutting their data centre demand figures once financial guardrails, like requiring upfront payments, are put in place. The uncertainty is leading data centre hot spots like Texas, Pennsylvania and Ohio to enact rules to filter out projects that could drive up prices and provoke political backlash without ever even getting built. “When you don’t know what is real, you really don’t know how to build the infrastructure for it,” Texas Public Utility Commission Chairman Thomas Gleeson said at an industry conference in March. Ghost demand As Big Tech’s planned AI data centre spending tops US$700 billion this year, companies and landowners with access to power or grid connections have rushed to cash in on the boom by securing electricity supplies needed to run those facilities. Since 2023, requests from data centres and other large energy users to connect to the Texas grid have soared from about 48 gigawatts to more than 474 gigawatts, according to documents from grid operator Ercot and Governor Greg Abbott, making it the fastest-growing region for AI and cloud server warehouses in the world by some measures. Outside of Texas, data centre electricity demand requests in 10 of the biggest U.S. utilities in the Midwest, Mid-Atlantic and U.S. South, including AEP Ohio, Southern Co and PPL, have reached about 270 gigawatts, according to a review of the latest utility quarterly earnings calls with investors. There is no set standard for how utilities report requests for electricity from data centres, with some disclosing only projects that have signed contracts and others tallying up inquiries from projects without firm commitments. When states and utilities have taken a closer look at data centre electricity projects, however, and enacted requirements like large upfront deposits, chunks of that demand can fall away. “The entities that rushed into the space, because there was a sort of pot of gold, are maybe now learning the hard way just how difficult some of this is to actually construct and bring online,” said Daniel Farris, an attorney at Foley & Lardner, who advises data centre developers and hyperscalers. The latter refers to companies such as Amazon, Alphabet’s Google and Microsoft, which operate massive data centre networks. Chicago-based Exelon cut its tally of high-probability data centre demand by about 40 per cent to 11 gigawatts, it said in an investor presentation on July 30, after the company began imposing stricter collateral requirements. In Ohio, electric utility AEP Ohio’s data centre power demand pipeline dropped by more than half following state rules adopted last year that included grid connection study fees for data centres of up to US$100,000. The uncertainty around data centre electricity use, said Tyson Slocum, director of the Energy Program at consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, raises the risk that utilities either under-build and threaten the stability of the grid, or overbuild to serve projects that never materialize, leaving average Americans footing the bill. “I think part of what (Texas) is trying to do is to create some order, and impose some transparency, ON an industry that in much of the country is still like the Wild West,” Slocum said. Electricity requests from proposed data centres have already increased costs in PJM Interconnection, the nation’s largest grid covering 13 states, including Data Centre Alley in Virginia. Growth in existing and forecast data center demand drove a US$29.4 billion increase in capacity costs for homes and businesses in the PJM footprint over roughly the past four auctions that determine those prices, according to grid monitor Monitoring Analytics. Even after utilities dramatically reduce demand forecasts, however, they are still left with enough substantiated data centre requests to overwhelm grids running short on supplies. “The reality is that the load is showing up, and generation is not at the pace we need it to,” said PJM spokesman Jeff Shields. Auditing the unknown In Texas, the cornerstone of Abbott’s order is a comprehensive audit, requiring that proposals to power up data centres reveal who ultimately owns the centres, instead of earlier rules that allowed only an affiliate company to be disclosed. The state Public Utility Commission, chaired by Gleeson, and grid operator Ercot will be in charge of implementing the directive, which also asks for details about whether data centre projects rely on taxpayer-funded incentives, water use and on-site power generation plans. “The Puct and Ercot cannot make decisions to guarantee grid stability and reliability based on substantially incomplete information,” Abbott said in an update on his order. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, whose state’s abundant electricity supplies and natural gas have drawn a flurry of data centre interest, has since made a similar move. Shapiro signed a data centre executive order on Aug. 18 that includes stricter permitting requirements for projects of 25 megawatts or more and greater disclosure of project plans and end users. Of the more than 100 data centres proposed in the state, only 20 have applied for permits needed to move the projects forward, a member of the governor’s office told Reuters. Most of the proposals have not secured power sources or a customer that would be critical to funding the server warehouses, the official said. Reporting by Laila Kearney in New York; Additional reporting by Kavya Balaraman in Bengaluru; Editing by Liz Hampton and Matthew Lewis

stories.title: ‘Immediately stop using’: Thousands of walking pads sold at Canadian Tire recalled
stories.summary: Health Canada has announced a recall for an electric walking pad sold at Canadian Tire due to an 'electrical hazard.'
stories.author: Aarjavee Raaj
paragraphs: Health Canada has announced a recall for an electric walking pad sold at Canadian Tire due to an “electrical hazard.”
The recall involves the PowerG Walking Pad, Model Number 499-4052 (UPC 8 46325 03115 8), the federal agency said in a recall notice posted last week.
“The affected product does not meet the requirements of the relevant standard for this product category, which poses an electrical hazard,” the notice said.

stories.title: ‘Dream job: Retirement’: Canadian little leaguer goes viral after World Series
stories.summary: A 12-year-old from Vancouver is going viral after his appearance at the Little League World Series. And it's not for his playing.
stories.author: Shannon Paterson
paragraphs: “It’s like a dream come true. It’s a baseball paradise, basically. You play on the best fields in the world, and you get interact with other countries,” said Huang, who plays for Vancouver’s Little Mountain Baseball.
The games are televised, and the broadcast crew at Espn wanted to learn a little bit about every player.
“There’s a survey, they ask you about your favourite foods, your favourite actors and stuff like that. One of the questions was, what’s your dream job?” said Huang.
During an at bat against South Korea, his answer appeared on screen. Daniel’s dream job? Retirement.
“I did not know that is what he said on his answer, retirement,” said Daniel’s coach Brad Dorwart. “Someone sent that in our group chat, and I just rolled my eyes. Of course he did.”
“He’s always the guy who makes jokes,” said Daniel’s mom Nicky. “He always comes up with the response that is very not typical. So, I wasn’t super shocked, but I also had a good laugh.”
After Barstool Sports posted about Daniel saying “This Kid Gets It” to its nearly seven million X followers, Huang was internet famous.
“And still today, people are sending me links and news where Daniel’s name is mentioned. It’s actually pretty cool,” said his mom.

“It was pretty sad to have such an amazing season come to an end, but I think it was a really good game. They had pretty good sportsmanship and it showed that they worked hard to get here, so they deserved it,” Daniel said.

“One of your jobs as a coach is to teach them the skills, but also let them understand that it’s OK, the sun will come up tomorrow. It’s a game. We all want to win the game, but it’s a game,” said Dorwart.
For Daniel, it was the end of an era. This was his last season of little league.
“He’s definitely retired from Little League, but not from work,” joked his coach. “You have to start before you retire.”
And Daniel’s not planning on starting work anytime soon.
“It’s just best if I don’t have to work these next couple of years,” he said. “Just enjoy and relax.”

stories.title: The election campaign to replace Macron in France is heating up as the summer vacation season ends
stories.summary: Here’s what to know at these early stages of what promises to be among the most consequential leadership votes anywhere in the world next year, and which comes as France is grappling with multiple challenges, including the disruptions of Donald Trump’s U.S. presidency.
stories.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: Paris — With the end of France’s summer vacation season, the election campaign to replace Emmanuel Macron as president next May is bursting to life.

An unusually large and broad field of candidates is forming to lead the European Union’s largest country, its second-largest economy and only nuclear-armed power, their appetites whetted by the fact that Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive presidential term himself.
Some won’t get the support they will need from sponsors and their political camps to be on the starting line when the first round of voting is held on April 18.

Still, a crowded field could boost far-right candidate Marine Le Pen — just as it did for Jean-Marie Le Pen, her father, in 2002. The record 16 candidates splintered the first-round vote, creating an electoral earthquake when the elder Le Pen qualified for the decisive second round.

Socialist Party leader Olivier Faure became the latest to declare his candidacy this weekend. He joined more than two dozen others who say that they intend to stand or are contemplating a run in 2027.

Here’s what to know at these early stages of what promises to be among the most consequential leadership votes anywhere in the world next year, and which comes as France is grappling with multiple challenges, including the disruptions of Donald Trump’s U.S. presidency.
Polls suggest Le Pen is the candidate to beat

After decades of trying, first by her father and then her, Marine Le Pen’s fourth campaign for the French presidency is already shaping up as the strongest opportunity for her nationalist, anti-immigration National Rally party to take power.

Such an outcome would rock the European Union, putting a politician, who has long been hostile to the bloc of 27 nations and many of their collective rules and policies, in charge of one of the EU’s most important countries.

“It’s clearly a crucial election, just because the far right might win this one and it never was the case before,” said Gilles Ivaldi, a researcher at the Paris-based Sciences Po university who specializes in populism and radical right-wing politics.
“With Le Pen as president, we know that the EU will be weakened. To what extent we don’t know, but we know she’s against the EU,” he said. “This would create a lot of instability.”

Polls have for months suggested that Le Pen is the front-runner and could possibly sail into the winner-takes-all runoff on May 2 as the first-round vote leader, which would be a first for her. She trailed Macron in the 2017 and 2022 first-round voting and then lost decisively to him in round two.

It was a giant upset when her father qualified in 2002 for round two. His associations with people who collaborated with France’s Nazi occupiers in the Second World War and his multiple hate-speech convictions, including Holocaust denial, made him anathema to many voters.

This time, it would a giant upset if his 58-year-old daughter doesn’t advance. Marine Le Pen has worked for years to distance herself from his extremism. She’s already begun reaping the fruits at the ballot box: Since 2024, her National Rally has become the largest party in parliament’s powerful lower house.

She got another boost in July when a Paris appeals court cleared her path for another presidential campaign, by shortening a ban on seeking elected office that a lower court had handed down to Le Pen for embezzlement.
Behind Le Pen, the picture is uncertain
With Le Pen widely expected to secure one of the spots in the decisive second-round duel, the battle for the other is becoming hard fought, its outcome highly uncertain.

For now, Le Pen’s strongest opponents include veteran far-left and anti-capitalist firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who hopes to make his first runoff after placing third in 2022 and fourth in 2017 and 2012, and two former prime ministers under Macron — Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal, both centrists.

Other prominent possibilities include conservative former Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau and multiple figures from the mainstream left, including European Parliament lawmaker Raphaël Glucksmann and Ecologists leader Marine Tondelier, campaigning before the expected birth within weeks of her second child.

Those seven took part in a debate last week at the storied Roland Garros tennis arena in Paris. In what served as an unofficial starting gun for the campaign, they batted around proposals for fixing some of France’s economic problems. Some took shots at Le Pen, which she hit back.

The potential scenario of a Le Pen-Mélenchon second-round duel that polls suggest could end with a Le Pen victory could ultimately prompt some candidates to drop out, to concentrate votes behind mainstream alternatives.
“What we don’t know is who’s going to be against her” in a possible second-round matchup, Ivaldi said. “The more the fragmentation, the more the chances that Mélenchon will be that person.”
Wars, Trump and Macron’s mixed legacy hang over the election
No French presidential election campaign this century has taken place in such choppy waters.

The Iran war has hit France’s stagnating economy with higher energy costs. The war in Ukraine has Paris worrying that Russia might next target one of France’s Nato allies, a potential path to wider conflict.

Trump’s presidency is rattling French faith in the trans-Atlantic alliance. The manufacturing and exporting might of China and the artificial intelligence revolution are heightening concerns of France being left behind economically and technologically.
But France’s mounting and increasingly expensive public debt is narrowing the financial room for maneuver that Macron’s successor will inherit.
Many voters also blame Macron for France’s woes and took their anger to the streets during his two-term presidency.

Ultimately, the election May hinge on whether voters want to upset the established order by propelling Le Pen and Mélenchon into a duel of the right and left extremes, or will back a more mainstream candidate, as a possibly safer option.
“It will be quite interesting to see which of these two forces will win in the end,” Ivaldi said. “These are two different forces, two antagonistic forces that are playing against one another.”
John Leicester, The Associated Press

stories.title: Summer heat lingers across southern Ontario as meteorological fall begins
stories.summary: Summer-like heat and humidity will continue across southern Ontario Tuesday, despite the official start of meteorological fall, according to CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
paragraphs: Summer-like heat and humidity will continue across southern Ontario Tuesday, despite the official start of meteorological fall, according to CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. A muggy start is expected, with temperatures climbing into the upper 20s and low 30s. London is expected to reach 30 C, while parts of the region could hit 33 C. A heat warning is in effect for Essex County. Some cloud cover is expected in the morning, followed by a mix of sun and cloud in the afternoon. There is a 60 per cent chance of scattered showers and thunderstorms Wednesday, with another hot and humid day expected. Thursday will be mainly cloudy, with a high of 27 C. “We have moisture and instability and the risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms over the next couple of days,” said Atchison. The weather should settle heading into the Labour Day long weekend, with a mix of sun and cloud from Friday through Monday and highs of 24 to 26 C. Despite the start of meteorological fall, summer-like conditions are expected to linger across southern Ontario.

stories.summary: Club offered services for cancer patients and their families, including group therapy
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
paragraphs: Three years ago, kindergarten teacher Laura Hughes learned she had breast cancer. Three days after her diagnosis, she contacted Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto, hoping to access support.
The weekly online group that she found through Gilda’s quickly became a lifeline during her medical journey.

She began attending virtual sessions on Friday afternoons, which followed her chemotherapy appointments earlier in the day. Through the group, she connected with other patients grappling with cancer at a time when she felt particularly alone.
“I could just safely connect with my friends in this group, and they knew all the right questions to ask because they had all been there that same week,” she said.
Like the other Gilda’s Club chapters across the United States and Canada, the Greater Toronto club offered services for cancer patients and their families, including group therapy.
It abruptly announced on Aug. 21 that it had ceased operations after nearly 25 years, with no explanation given.
Days later, ON Aug. 24, records show the organization filed for bankruptcy. It is scheduled to meet with creditors on Sept. 10.
Patients who recently received therapy through Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto have been directed to other resources, including the organization’s Simcoe Muskoka chapter.
Last week, the sister club said it would support individuals and families affected by the Toronto closing.
“Our focus is on helping people feel welcomed, supported and connected to the resources that are right for them,” executive director Lana Hann said.
Ms. Hughes was among the patients saddened to learn of the shutdown.
She described how the members of her online group later forged in-person connections and even showed up for each other at the hospital.
“They would sit with me in the waiting room, as I would for them,” she said. “It was pretty amazing.”
Three years after meeting online, they continue to see each other regularly and have a group chat they call “Friday Friends,” a nod to those weekly Zoom sessions that first drew them together.
Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto closed weeks after the group lost its charitable status with the Canada Revenue Agency.
CRA requires charities to comply with the Income Tax Act, including filing annual returns.
The agency’s website shows the organization’s status was revoked on July 11 after it missed a deadline to file a return. The group cited the loss of its charitable status in its bankruptcy filing.
A representative for the organization could not be reached for comment through an e-mail address listed on its website. An automatic reply said the account is no longer monitored.
“We are deeply grateful to everyone who has been part of this community and for the compassion, generosity, and sense of connection fostered over the years,” it said.

Gilda’s Club works to address the emotional and social changes that result from patients’ cancer diagnoses. Cancer specialists say patients and loved ones May experience emotional challenges, such as depression and anxiety, and barriers in interpersonal relationships.

The organization was named after the late actress Gilda Radner, who began her career in Canada in the early 1970s at the comedy theatre Second City Toronto. Ms. Radner died in 1989, three years after her own diagnosis with ovarian cancer.

Garrett Harrison, who works in arts management for the City of Oakville, accessed group therapy online through Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto after his mother was diagnosed with ovarian cancer in August, 2025.

He first learned about the organization’s work through his time at Second City. In January, Mr. Harrison began attending weekly therapy sessions online on Wednesday nights, alongside other caregivers.

Over eight weeks, around eight to 10 people joined the sessions and shared their experiences. The discussion was guided by a psychotherapist. The caregivers found it helpful to access online therapy while meeting loved ones’ medical needs.

Mr. Harrison said he lost his 72-year-old mother, Liz Zavitz , ON Friday, March 6, before the last scheduled Wednesday night group session. Ms. Zavitz, a devoted educator and theatre enthusiast, died just 200 days after her diagnosis.
Her son, an only child, decided he would attend that concluding therapy session, even though he found it very difficult.
“I was very quiet,” he said. ”I just wanted to show my support."
Mr. Harrison also hoped to access grief support services through Gilda’s Club. He said learning about the club’s closing through an e-mail was “very disheartening.”
“I’ve kept in touch with a few people from my group, and we were all very confused and shocked,” he said, adding they too maintain a group chat on WhatsApp.
Other organizations that support cancer patients and their families were also saddened to learn of the club ceasing operations.
On Instagram, Childhood Cancer Canada called Gilda’s a valued partner and a place where families could find “connection and community during some of the most unimaginable moments of their lives.”

Brenda Delodder, chief executive officer of the Wellspring Cancer Support Foundation, also offered support to volunteers and staff. Beyond treatment, she said, individuals need to be able to access understanding, guidance and community.
Mr. Harrison echoed this sentiment and said he hopes the situation with Gilda’s Club Greater Toronto can be resolved.
If not, he added, ”I hope others are able to step up and fill the hole that will be left with all the families.”
With reports from Stephanie Chambers in Toronto
Editor’s note: A photo caption accompanying this article incorrectly named Garrett Harrison’s mother. Her name was Liz Zavitz.

stories.title: For Hamiltonians battling addiction, peer support is a dose of empathy
stories.summary: Pilot program at St. Joseph’s Healthcare gives recovered drug users a chance to help others
stories.author: Molly Hayes, Photography by Laura Proctor
stories.content:
workers with similar experiences offer hope and healing

Perched on a hospital bed on the third floor of St. Joseph’s Healthcare in Hamilton , Madison Tatlock remembers watching her boyfriend nod off in a recliner there, after the birth of their baby 3½ years ago.

He was high, she remembers – and she remembers getting him to sneak in drugs for her, too, before he fell asleep against the freezer in the obstetrics unit’s communal kitchen and got kicked out.

For the most part, Ms. Tatlock acknowledges, her memories of that postpartum period are foggy, and tainted by shame. She and her boyfriend, Matthew Cheeseman, were both well over a decade into active addiction at the time, both heavily using fentanyl and crystal meth.

The then-29-year-old couldn’t be trusted alone with her baby. Mr. Cheeseman, then 37, wasn’t allowed into the hospital, period, after the freezer incident, unless he was escorted by his mother. Ms. Tatlock recalls how family members would visit with baby gifts, and then just sit there, silently.

“Everyone was just really sad,” she says.

But just a few years later, the pair are back roaming the same hospital’s halls – this time with employee badges. They are members of a novel, hospital-wide peer support program that helps patients struggling with substance use, from admission through discharge and beyond.

For two days this summer, The Globe and Mail was granted rare access to the team, shadowing Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman throughout the hospital to get a glimpse of their work firsthand.

The four-year pilot project, which launched in March, 2025, is being funded through a $4.3-million grant from Health Canada’s Substance Use and Addictions Program .

A year and a half in, colleagues say the project has not only filled a critical gap in care for some of the hospital’s most vulnerable patients, but has also empowered those providing the support with a sense of purpose. Since its inception, the peer support team has logged more than 14,000 patient interactions, across virtually every unit of the hospital.

“It’s quite incredible when you see the impact that this small team is having,” says Brooke Cowell, the hospital’s chief nursing executive and executive vice-president of clinical operations.

The patients they see are not necessarily admitted because of substance use, Tim O’Shea, an infectious disease specialist and co-head of the hospital’s addictions medicine program, explains.

“They could be in hospital because they have had a heart attack, a stroke, or need gallbladder surgery,” he says. “But the substance use piece is going to play into the quality of care that they get, because if it’s ignored, obviously that’s going to get in the way of them getting the care that they need.”

Discrimination and stigma are still deeply ingrained within the health care system , and sanctimony from providers has historically left many people – especially those who are homeless or use drugs – reluctant to seek care at all.

As big Canadian cities and small towns alike continue to struggle with converging crises of housing affordability, mental health and addictions, peer workers have become critical in helping to build back support and trust.

“We’re trying to provide good care to people, and this is a way to help provide good care – by making people more comfortable, more trusting,” Dr. O’Shea says.

“It provides better outcomes for the patients.”

At the start of their shift one Monday morning in July, Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman join their team – which also includes social workers, physicians and a part-time nurse – around a boardroom table. It’s time to go over their patient list, which on this day includes roughly 10 people.

There’s a woman who had been admitted the day before, in psychosis. She was too agitated to speak with support workers when she first arrived, but they are hoping she might be up for a visit today.

There’s another patient they’ve been working with for months, since his admission for surgery on both knees, due to septic arthritis. He is just about ready to go home – but needs help getting wheelchair accommodations for his apartment before he can be discharged.

There’s a man who was transported from the local jail, and is in withdrawal in the ICU.

Another man on the list was admitted a few days ago, after an overdose, and is being treated for a serious blood infection. Despite his condition, he is itching to leave; he is worried about losing his bed – and the belongings he left behind – at a local homeless shelter.

Leaving against medical advice is one of the main things the team is trying to prevent, because they know these patients will likely wind up back in the emergency room, usually sicker than when they left.

The peers have conducted hundreds of surveys with patients so far. Virtually all of the nearly 200 patients they spoke with upon intake reported having previous hospitalizations. The average number of hospitalizations in the past year was 4.52 – and the average number of times they left against medical advice was 1.36. The top reasons patients gave for having left early included drug cravings and withdrawal symptoms, but also not feeling welcome or supported within the hospital – which is what the team is hoping to prevent.

During The Globe’s visit, that support takes on different forms. Sometimes a peer worker simply pops by a patient’s room to say hello, and to let them know they’ve been where they are. Other times they take the patient out for a cigarette break, or help co-ordinate a visit from a relative or friend. One former patient they are still working with recalls how touched he was that when he grew bored and restless in the hospital during his months-long stay, they were able to bring him his guitar.

As they build relationships throughout their patients’ stays, Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to connect some people with community resources, assist them with replacing their government IDs, and even help them secure or hang onto housing.

The team follows a harm-reduction model, meaning no one is pressed into addiction treatment. If a patient does want to use drugs, the peers will try to ensure they are doing so safely and offsite. But the majority of patients they’ve worked with – 86 per cent of 187 patients specifically surveyed about their substance use – said they were ready to make a change.

The team works with substance-use physicians such as Dr. O’Shea, who can prescribe medications, such as suboxone, to ease pain or withdrawal symptoms.

In at least a dozen cases she can think of – the ones that make her eyes well up, just thinking about them – Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to get patients into treatment programs. In at least five cases, the programs were the very same ones that she and Mr. Cheeseman credit with saving their own lives.

Back in August, 2022, when Ms. Tatlock saw the two red lines pop up on her pregnancy test, she panicked.

She and Mr. Cheeseman were both homeless at the time, and had not known each other long. They were both deeply unwell and in survival mode.

The couple turned to Dr. O’Shea and peer support worker Marcie McIlveen, whom they’d gotten to know through their outreach work in the community .

With their help, Ms. Tatlock was admitted into St. Joseph’s Inpatient Program for Substance Use in Pregnancy (iPROSPR), where she attempted four different times, unsuccessfully, to titrate off the drugs. They got her a prenatal bed at the Ywca.

Social worker Sarah Simpson, who worked with Ms. Tatlock at the time on the women’s health, newborn and pediatric care unit, remembers her as one of the sickest patients ever admitted to the program. Her addiction was just so severe.

At one point, while Ms. Tatlock was in the hospital during her pregnancy, Mr. Cheeseman was admitted to another floor after suffering from a stroke – his second in only a few years. He’d also previously had open-heart surgery and a pacemaker installed, and had been hospitalized multiple times after overdoses.

“I’ve been all over this hospital,” he remembers today, shaking his head.

It was Mr. Cheeseman who got sober first. When he checked into a detox centre in Sarnia, Ont., in the fall of 2023, Ms. Tatlock – still high and totally paranoid – remembers thinking he was lying and cheating on her.

But then he graduated to a transitional program. And then a sober living house, St. Stephen’s House in London.

As the months passed, and he talked more and more about his hopes for their little family, she realized he was really doing it this time – and began wondering if she could do it, too. By January, 2024, just before her baby’s first birthday, she did.

Though their baby had gone into foster care after leaving the hospital, they kept up visits, and eventually Mr. Cheeseman was even able to take the baby on his own to visit Ms. Tatlock, in treatment. They’d go on stroller walks. Take the baby to the library. Slowly, a new life came into view. By the time the baby was 2, they had regained full custody.

They got an apartment across the street from a big park. Mr. Cheeseman’s mom helped cover their rent while they were on social assistance.

But even with the mountainous task of achieving sobriety behind them, the two new parents had trouble picturing their next steps. Neither had worked in years. They both had criminal records. Who would hire them?

In the fall of 2024, Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman bumped into Ms. McIlveen, who told them about the peer support pilot she was helping to establish at the hospital, and suggested they apply.

They were in disbelief at her faith in them. She’d seen them at their absolute lowest.

But Ms. McIlveen says that’s the whole point.

It’s common now for her team to be stopped by other staff members in the hospital, she says, who want their advice on a patient. The country is in a public-health epidemic, and her team are the experts.

Rebecca Wasser, another social worker on the baby unit, says Ms. Tatlock is a role model for her patients.

“Madison is an inspiration for so many people, to say, like, ‘If she can do it, I can do it,’” Ms. Wasser explains. “You know, it’s hard, and she … has a way of talking with these patients and with moms, to be like, ‘This is hard, but, like, let’s do this.’ She’s really motivating for them.”

The couple’s success is bittersweet for Dr. O’Shea. He says he has worked with so many others who are just like Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman, but who have not been able to find the same opportunities.

“I think that they are exceptional in a lot of ways – not to say that they’re not – but I think that there’s potential for lots and lots of people to be able to recover and to contribute in lots of different meaningful ways, if they have the right supports and the right motivations around them,” he says.

He hopes that when the grant runs out, the program will receive permanent, core funding.

The hospital’s leadership team sees the pilot’s value, says Donna Johnson, who oversees the peer support team as the hospital’s clinical program director of general internal medicine. “Certainly, we will look at what opportunities we have for ongoing funding,” she says.

“I don’t know how we would manage without them,” she adds. “I’m just always in awe of the impact they have.”

Ms. Simpson, the social worker who helped Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman when their baby was born, still gets goosebumps when she sees the pair walking into work in the mornings.

Perched on a hospital bed on the third floor of St. Joseph’s Healthcare in Hamilton , Madison Tatlock remembers watching her boyfriend nod off in a recliner there, after the birth of their baby 3½ years ago.
He was high, she remembers – and she remembers getting him to sneak in drugs for her, too, before he fell asleep against the freezer in the obstetrics unit’s communal kitchen and got kicked out.

For the most part, Ms. Tatlock acknowledges, her memories of that postpartum period are foggy, and tainted by shame. She and her boyfriend, Matthew Cheeseman, were both well over a decade into active addiction at the time, both heavily using fentanyl and crystal meth.

The then-29-year-old couldn’t be trusted alone with her baby. Mr. Cheeseman, then 37, wasn’t allowed into the hospital, period, after the freezer incident, unless he was escorted by his mother. Ms. Tatlock recalls how family members would visit with baby gifts, and then just sit there, silently.
“Everyone was just really sad,” she says.

But just a few years later, the pair are back roaming the same hospital’s halls – this time with employee badges. They are members of a novel, hospital-wide peer support program that helps patients struggling with substance use, from admission through discharge and beyond.
For two days this summer, The Globe and Mail was granted rare access to the team, shadowing Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman throughout the hospital to get a glimpse of their work firsthand.
The four-year pilot project, which launched in March, 2025, is being funded through a $4.3-million grant from Health Canada’s Substance Use and Addictions Program .

A year and a half in, colleagues say the project has not only filled a critical gap in care for some of the hospital’s most vulnerable patients, but has also empowered those providing the support with a sense of purpose. Since its inception, the peer support team has logged more than 14,000 patient interactions, across virtually every unit of the hospital.
“It’s quite incredible when you see the impact that this small team is having,” says Brooke Cowell, the hospital’s chief nursing executive and executive vice-president of clinical operations.
The patients they see are not necessarily admitted because of substance use, Tim O’Shea, an infectious disease specialist and co-head of the hospital’s addictions medicine program, explains.

“They could be in hospital because they have had a heart attack, a stroke, or need gallbladder surgery,” he says. “But the substance use piece is going to play into the quality of care that they get, because if it’s ignored, obviously that’s going to get in the way of them getting the care that they need.”

Discrimination and stigma are still deeply ingrained within the health care system , and sanctimony from providers has historically left many people – especially those who are homeless or use drugs – reluctant to seek care at all.

As big Canadian cities and small towns alike continue to struggle with converging crises of housing affordability, mental health and addictions, peer workers have become critical in helping to build back support and trust.
“We’re trying to provide good care to people, and this is a way to help provide good care – by making people more comfortable, more trusting,” Dr. O’Shea says.
“It provides better outcomes for the patients.”

At the start of their shift one Monday morning in July, Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman join their team – which also includes social workers, physicians and a part-time nurse – around a boardroom table. It’s time to go over their patient list, which on this day includes roughly 10 people.
There’s a woman who had been admitted the day before, in psychosis. She was too agitated to speak with support workers when she first arrived, but they are hoping she might be up for a visit today.

There’s another patient they’ve been working with for months, since his admission for surgery on both knees, due to septic arthritis. He is just about ready to go home – but needs help getting wheelchair accommodations for his apartment before he can be discharged.
There’s a man who was transported from the local jail, and is in withdrawal in the ICU.

Another man on the list was admitted a few days ago, after an overdose, and is being treated for a serious blood infection. Despite his condition, he is itching to leave; he is worried about losing his bed – and the belongings he left behind – at a local homeless shelter.

Leaving against medical advice is one of the main things the team is trying to prevent, because they know these patients will likely wind up back in the emergency room, usually sicker than when they left.

The peers have conducted hundreds of surveys with patients so far. Virtually all of the nearly 200 patients they spoke with upon intake reported having previous hospitalizations. The average number of hospitalizations in the past year was 4.52 – and the average number of times they left against medical advice was 1.36. The top reasons patients gave for having left early included drug cravings and withdrawal symptoms, but also not feeling welcome or supported within the hospital – which is what the team is hoping to prevent.

During The Globe’s visit, that support takes on different forms. Sometimes a peer worker simply pops by a patient’s room to say hello, and to let them know they’ve been where they are. Other times they take the patient out for a cigarette break, or help co-ordinate a visit from a relative or friend. One former patient they are still working with recalls how touched he was that when he grew bored and restless in the hospital during his months-long stay, they were able to bring him his guitar.

As they build relationships throughout their patients’ stays, Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to connect some people with community resources, assist them with replacing their government IDs, and even help them secure or hang onto housing.

The team follows a harm-reduction model, meaning no one is pressed into addiction treatment. If a patient does want to use drugs, the peers will try to ensure they are doing so safely and offsite. But the majority of patients they’ve worked with – 86 per cent of 187 patients specifically surveyed about their substance use – said they were ready to make a change.
The team works with substance-use physicians such as Dr. O’Shea, who can prescribe medications, such as suboxone, to ease pain or withdrawal symptoms.

In at least a dozen cases she can think of – the ones that make her eyes well up, just thinking about them – Ms. Tatlock says they have been able to get patients into treatment programs. In at least five cases, the programs were the very same ones that she and Mr. Cheeseman credit with saving their own lives.
Back in August, 2022, when Ms. Tatlock saw the two red lines pop up on her pregnancy test, she panicked.
She and Mr. Cheeseman were both homeless at the time, and had not known each other long. They were both deeply unwell and in survival mode.
The couple turned to Dr. O’Shea and peer support worker Marcie McIlveen, whom they’d gotten to know through their outreach work in the community .

With their help, Ms. Tatlock was admitted into St. Joseph’s Inpatient Program for Substance Use in Pregnancy (iPROSPR), where she attempted four different times, unsuccessfully, to titrate off the drugs. They got her a prenatal bed at the Ywca.

Social worker Sarah Simpson, who worked with Ms. Tatlock at the time on the women’s health, newborn and pediatric care unit, remembers her as one of the sickest patients ever admitted to the program. Her addiction was just so severe.

At one point, while Ms. Tatlock was in the hospital during her pregnancy, Mr. Cheeseman was admitted to another floor after suffering from a stroke – his second in only a few years. He’d also previously had open-heart surgery and a pacemaker installed, and had been hospitalized multiple times after overdoses.
“I’ve been all over this hospital,” he remembers today, shaking his head.

It was Mr. Cheeseman who got sober first. When he checked into a detox centre in Sarnia, Ont., in the fall of 2023, Ms. Tatlock – still high and totally paranoid – remembers thinking he was lying and cheating on her.
But then he graduated to a transitional program. And then a sober living house, St. Stephen’s House in London.

As the months passed, and he talked more and more about his hopes for their little family, she realized he was really doing it this time – and began wondering if she could do it, too. By January, 2024, just before her baby’s first birthday, she did.

Though their baby had gone into foster care after leaving the hospital, they kept up visits, and eventually Mr. Cheeseman was even able to take the baby on his own to visit Ms. Tatlock, in treatment. They’d go on stroller walks. Take the baby to the library. Slowly, a new life came into view. By the time the baby was 2, they had regained full custody.
They got an apartment across the street from a big park. Mr. Cheeseman’s mom helped cover their rent while they were on social assistance.

But even with the mountainous task of achieving sobriety behind them, the two new parents had trouble picturing their next steps. Neither had worked in years. They both had criminal records. Who would hire them?
In the fall of 2024, Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman bumped into Ms. McIlveen, who told them about the peer support pilot she was helping to establish at the hospital, and suggested they apply.
They were in disbelief at her faith in them. She’d seen them at their absolute lowest.
But Ms. McIlveen says that’s the whole point.

It’s common now for her team to be stopped by other staff members in the hospital, she says, who want their advice on a patient. The country is in a public-health epidemic, and her team are the experts.
Rebecca Wasser, another social worker on the baby unit, says Ms. Tatlock is a role model for her patients.

“Madison is an inspiration for so many people, to say, like, ‘If she can do it, I can do it,’” Ms. Wasser explains. “You know, it’s hard, and she … has a way of talking with these patients and with moms, to be like, ‘This is hard, but, like, let’s do this.’ She’s really motivating for them.”

The couple’s success is bittersweet for Dr. O’Shea. He says he has worked with so many others who are just like Ms. Tatlock and Mr. Cheeseman, but who have not been able to find the same opportunities.

“I think that they are exceptional in a lot of ways – not to say that they’re not – but I think that there’s potential for lots and lots of people to be able to recover and to contribute in lots of different meaningful ways, if they have the right supports and the right motivations around them,” he says.
He hopes that when the grant runs out, the program will receive permanent, core funding.

The hospital’s leadership team sees the pilot’s value, says Donna Johnson, who oversees the peer support team as the hospital’s clinical program director of general internal medicine. “Certainly, we will look at what opportunities we have for ongoing funding,” she says.
“I don’t know how we would manage without them,” she adds. “I’m just always in awe of the impact they have.”

She keeps a daycare class photo they gave her of their now-three-year-old on her office corkboard, the smiling toddler a reminder of what her patients are capable of.

“I tear up, truly, every single time I think about the resilience of that couple and the successes that they’ve had,” she says. “When they were with us at the time, I wasn’t confident that that was ever going to be.”

She jokes about how domesticated they’ve become. They juggle daycare drop-offs and Costco runs. Mr. Cheeseman loves to cut the grass. They recently got a kitten, Sesame (as in the street).
