stories.title: Confusion deepens on Ontario’s new student absence policy after education minister says principals will get final say
stories.summary: The province's principals say they wish they had been consulted beforehand, especially with mid-term marks required a couple of months into the school year.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
The province is targeting students who skip under its new policy that will dock marks for missed classes — but principals get to make the final call whether extended vacations or non-school sports tournaments will count as authorized absences.

These “can still be an excused absence, but the parent has to inform the principal, who can still make the determinant,” Education Minister Paul Calandra said in answering questions about the new rules for Ontario teens while at an unrelated announcement Tuesday in Hamilton.

But with the start of the fall classes already underway in some boards, and starting in most next week, confusion remains about how the policy will work — and be enforced — on the ground, and what will be allowed on a school-by-school basis.

Toronto’s Leaside High School has already sent out a memo to parents, saying allowable absences include “illness or other unavoidable circumstances, such as inclement weather or approved absences such as cultural days and holy days” meaning marks will not be deducted.

However, it adds, “please note that family vacations are not considered excused absences from schools.”

The province’s new rules — which Calandra has said are based on pleas from teachers who saw first-hand the growing numbers of teens missing class on a regular basis — now mandate that attendance and participation comprise 15 per cent of final marks in all classes in Grades 9 and 10, and 10 per cent for those in Grades 11 and 12. Just 40 per cent of high school students meet acceptable standards for attendance, a recent report said.

Calandra insists parents should keep kids in grades 9 through 12 in school. But will it require a culture change?

Excused, or allowable, absences should not impact final grades, but if teens miss 2.5 to 4.5 classes per credit without authorization — or the stamp of approval from a principal — their mark in that area drops to a level 3, or a B, and to a level 2 when they hit five to seven classes.

“Parents still have the ability to excuse their children,” Calandra also said Tuesday. “They’ll have to inform the school, the principal, that it is their intention to excuse their child” for things like outside sports, music, dance or other activities.

“This isn’t targeting those kids who are busy and are doing the right thing,” Calandra added. “What this is about is those kids who don’t have an excused absence from their parents — who sometimes their parents don’t even know that they’re skipping a class ... Ultimately, you have to participate, and you have to be there.”

Concerns around the lack of clear details around the new policy are especially high for students in Grades 11 and 12, given post-secondary schools look at those marks and even a slight drop can make the difference when applying to competitive programs.

The province’s principals are still waiting for more details and say they wish they had been consulted beforehand, especially with mid-term marks required a couple of months into the school year.

These “can still be an excused absence, but the parent has to inform the principal, who can still make the determinant,” Education Minister Paul Calandra said in answering questions about the new rules for Ontario teens while at an unrelated announcement Tuesday in Hamilton.

But with the start of the fall classes already underway in some boards, and starting in most next week, confusion remains about how the policy will work — and be enforced — on the ground, and what will be allowed on a school-by-school basis.

Toronto’s Leaside High School has already sent out a memo to parents, saying allowable absences include “illness or other unavoidable circumstances, such as inclement weather or approved absences such as cultural days and holy days” meaning marks will not be deducted.
However, it adds, “please note that family vacations are not considered excused absences from schools.”

The province’s new rules — which Calandra has said are based on pleas from teachers who saw first-hand the growing numbers of teens missing class on a regular basis — now mandate that attendance and participation comprise 15 per cent of final marks in all classes in Grades 9 and 10, and 10 per cent for those in Grades 11 and 12. stories.title: Say it ain’t snow! Sunshine Village in Banff posts photos of first snow of season
stories.summary: Didn’t they just wrap up a summer snow season at Sunshine Ski Resort?
stories.author: Stephen Hunt
stories.content:
Didn’t they just wrap up a summer snow season at Sunshine Village Ski Resort?

The Banff National Park-based ski resort, which extended ski season for a couple of weeks on June 21, posted photos of its first snow day of the fall on Sunday, a full three weeks before fall officially arrives.

“We’ve got a snow day on our hands,” Sunshine posted. “Hello winter! Who’s ready for ski and snowboard season to begin?”

View this post on Instagram

While it might be presumptuous to answer, ‘absolutely nobody’, the first snow day of 2026 in the Rocky Mountains actually arrived almost a full week later than the first snow day of 2025, which CTV News reported last Aug. 24, 2025.

On that day, four resorts, including Sunshine Village, Nakiska, Lake Louise and Kicking Horse Ski Resort all reported snow.

At Sunshine Village, the snowfall brought on the first snow creature of the season when employee Liv Bergstrom built a snow bear — complete with snowy paws.

Liv Bergstrom made the most of the first snowfall at Banff Sunshine Village over the weekend to build a snow bear.

And on Sunday, Kicking Horse Resort posted some snow day photos of its own on its social media feed.

“First snow has entered the chat,” Kicking Horse posted. “A little snow? No problem. A few more bike laps? Absolutely. Winter mode? Loading...

“One foot in summer, one foot in winter. We’ll take it.”

No word yet on when either resort anticipates opening for winter ski season.

stories.title: Felix Auger-Aliassime advances with opening-round win at U.S. Open
stories.summary: Auger-Aliassime, the third-ranked man at the U.S. Open, won his first-round singles match on Monday night by defeating Australia's Rinky Hijiata 7-5, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5.
stories.author: Meredith Bond
paragraphs: By The Canadian Press
Posted August 31, 2026 11:46 pm.
Felix Auger-Aliassime is well aware that New York claims to be the city that never sleeps.

After starting late and then playing for three hours and 19 minutes — and enduring a 55-minute rain delay between the second and third set — the Montreal tennis star can relate to the lack of rest in The Big Apple.
Auger-Aliassime, the third-ranked man at the U.S. Open, won his first-round singles match on Monday night by defeating Australia’s Rinky Hijiata 7-5, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5.

“We’ve known each other since we were like 10 years old, but this is the first time we’ve played one another. He caused me a lot of problems out there … but most importantly I’m through to the next round,” said Auger-Aliassime after the match.

The Canadian finished with 17 aces, 48 winners and 11 double faults. He had 50 unforced errors. Auger-Aliassime won 18 of 22 service games, and six of 21 return games. He advances to play Russian Karen Khachanov, who beat Roman Burruchaga of Argentina in three straight sets.

Meanwhile, Denis Shapovalov of Richmond Hill, Ont., will play his second-round men’s singles match Wednesday against Luca Van Assche of France. Shapovalov defeated Miomir Kecmanovic of Serbia in four sets on Sunday, while Van Assche beat Britain’s Cameron Norrie, also in four sets.

Leylah Fernandez of Laval, Que., is scheduled to play her second-round women’s singles match Wednesday against Mananchaya Sawangkaew of Thailand. Fernandez bounced Shuai Zhang of China in straight sets on Sunday, while Sawangkaew defeated Panna Udvardy of Hungary in straight sets.

stories.title: Former Calgary teacher and sexual abuse convict Fred Archer back in court
stories.summary: Eighty-two-year-old Fred Archer appeared in a Calgary courtroom Monday to face charges stemming from allegations of sexual incidents going back decades.
stories.author: Tyler Barrow
stories.content:
Eighty-two-year-old Fred Archer appeared in a Calgary courtroom Monday to face charges stemming from allegations of sexual incidents going back decades.

Archer faces charges of sexual assault, sexual interference and sexual exploitation in connection with alleged incidents between June 1994 and September 1995 involving a boy who was then aged 13.

The boy, who cannot be identified due to a publication ban, is referred to as JR in court.

During opening arguments, Crown Prosecutor Gianna Argento told Justice Brandy Shaw that Archer first befriended JR’s father and later developed a “very close relationship” where Archer ended up in a caretaker role over JR.

She told court Archer would look after JR while his father worked out of town for weeks.

Archer is accused of sexually abusing JR during a 15-month period.

JR went to John Ware School, where Archer was a teacher.

Archer’s lawyer, Tim Dunlap, rejected the allegations, telling the court JR’s allegations are “for profit.”

Archer was convicted for abusing boys in the 1990s at Springbank Middle School.

He was also named along with another former teacher in a massive class-action lawsuit against the Calgary Board of Education involving a $15.7-million payment to 55 former students of John Ware School.

The trial is set to last five days.

During opening arguments, Crown Prosecutor Gianna Argento told Justice Brandy Shaw that Archer first befriended JR’s father and later developed a “very close relationship” where Archer ended up in a caretaker role over JR.
She told court Archer would look after JR while his father worked out of town for weeks.
Archer is accused of sexually abusing JR during a 15-month period.
JR went to John Ware School, where Archer was a teacher.
Archer’s lawyer, Tim Dunlap, rejected the allegations, telling the court JR’s allegations are “for profit.”
Archer was convicted for abusing boys in the 1990s at Springbank Middle School.

He was also named along with another former teacher in a massive class-action lawsuit against the Calgary Board of Education involving a $15.7-million payment to 55 former students of John Ware School.
The trial is set to last five days.

stories.title: BC Conservatives lose another MLA, seventh to leave party caucus since mid-August
stories.summary: Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA Á’a:liya Warbus cited a ‘critical breakdown in communications’ in decision to leave party
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The BC Conservative caucus lost another MLA on Monday, the seventh to leave the ranks of the province’s Official Opposition party since mid-August.

The exodus presents a growing challenge to party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay as the former Conservative MP runs in a by-election to win a seat in the provincial legislature.

Monday’s departure of Á’a:liya Warbus, the only Indigenous MLA on the party benches, is the latest domino to fall for the BC Conservatives. A succession of defections, senior staff departures and internal controversies has rocked the party since Ms. Findlay was elected leader in late May, throwing both her leadership and the Conservatives’ future into question.

The upheaval is also a boon to Premier David Eby ’s NDP, which won 47 seats to the Conservatives’ 44 in the 2024 election and could now benefit from a fractured opposition and divided centre-right.

Ms. Warbus, who represented the Chilliwack-Cultus Lake riding and served as the party’s house leader, joins Peter Milobar, Ian Paton, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman. All have left the caucus since Aug. 14 and now sit as independent MLAs.

Mr. Milobar and Mr. Paton last week announced their intention to form a new political party with Mr. Milobar as interim leader. They will be up against former BC Liberal cabinet minister Mike Bernier, who was named leader of the CentreBC party in July, in vying for the votes of those seeking a more centrist political home than Ms. Findlay’s Conservative Party.

The BC Conservatives did not respond to an interview request on Monday.

B.C. premier calls by-election in riding where Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay is set to run

In announcing her decision, Ms. Warbus cited the party’s departure from core issues and a “critical breakdown in communication” under Ms. Findlay’s leadership, both with the public and internally, across MLAs and staff.

“Caucus members have learned of hirings, firings, critic appointments and leadership positions through any and all channels including social media before being informed by leadership,” Ms. Warbus said in a statement.

She also highlighted the inability of the caucus to discuss serious allegations that surfaced last week, which prompted the firing of operations director Apollo Chung after audio recordings circulated purportedly capturing a staffer discussing a fundraiser “so we can steal everything.”

Another recording allegedly captured Ms. Findlay telling caucus members that if an MLA gave up their seat to trigger a by-election, she “could give them a role as a senior adviser in the same portfolio.” Reann Gasper resigned as Abbotsford-Mission MLA on Aug. 22, giving Ms. Findlay a chance to run; she has since become the leader’s deputy chief of staff. It is a violation of the Criminal Code to offer a legislator an inducement to resign from office.

Neither Ms. Findlay nor the party have confirmed the authenticity of the recordings. Ms. Findlay announced Mr. Chung’s firing on Aug. 26 in a one-sentence statement, with no reason given. In a post to social media the following day, she referenced a “surreptitious recording” and called allegations that comments about the party’s future plans May constitute a criminal offence “a political smear job and nothing more.”

A caucus meeting that was planned for Monday was cancelled without explanation on Sunday. Ms. Warbus said it reflected “the lack of value being placed on caucus members and their opinions.”

In an interview, Ms. Warbus said “a number of staff hirings and firings” happened without so much as a courtesy e-mail to MLAs, causing confusion and leaving them not properly informed to speak on behalf of the party and do their jobs effectively. She also underscored the seriousness of the allegations raised by the leaked audio recordings.

“There were some very critical, pivotal points in the past two weeks that deserve time, answers, accountability and transparency,” she said.

Ms. Warbus said unity is needed among like-minded people, and that divisions, personal attacks and culture wars are unhelpful.

“I’m open, and my door’s open, my phone’s open, to anybody that wants to have those conversations,” she said. “I think we have to come together before we can ask British Columbians to govern at all.”

The shocking implosion of B.C.’s Conservative Party

Ms. Warbus is not alone in citing a breakdown of communications as a factor in leaving the party. Randy Hawes resigned as the B.C. Conservatives’ riding association president for Abbotsford-Mission on Aug. 24 after learning through media reports that Ms. Gasper had stepped down.

In an interview, the former BC Liberal MLA and former mayor of Mission said he was shocked by the outcome of May’s leadership contest, when Ms. Findlay was elected on the fourth ballot with 51 per cent of the vote, to Caroline Elliott’s 49 per cent.

“She’s what I would call hardcore right-wing, and I don’t think that’s what the BC Conservative Party was supposed to be,” Mr. Hawes said.

He cited as examples Ms. Findlay’s attack on Mr. Milobar during the leadership contest, suggesting he is in a conflict of interest because his wife is Indigenous, and a July report that Ms. Findlay and her senior staff directed MLAs to no longer use the term “First Nations” in describing people but instead use terms such as “Indian.”

Mr. Hawes also said that Ms. Findlay did not repudiate comments made by her husband, Brent Chapman, the party’s South Surrey MLA, who in old social-media posts described Palestinian children as “inbred walking, talking, breathing time bombs” and suggested mass shootings such as Sandy Hook were fake.

“My conscience will not allow me to sit in a party that has that woman at the head,” Mr. Hawes said.

He, too, is hopeful that Mr. Milobar’s and Mr. Bernier’s groups will work together.

“What’s going on now is insane,” he said. “As far as people who are in the centre, you can’t split that vote. You need a uniting formula.”

stories.title: New $54.3M Regina Mundi school opens, but old building to remain in use amid enrolment growth
stories.summary: Students and staff at Regina Mundi Catholic College are preparing to return to a brand new school this fall, but the school’s former building will remain in use as enrolment continues to outpace capacity.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Students and staff at Regina Mundi Catholic College are preparing to return to a brand new school this fall, but the school’s former building will remain in use as enrolment continues to outpace capacity.

The $54.3-million replacement school, built on the grounds of the existing Regina Mundi campus off Wellington Street South, has capacity for approximately 700 students.

However, the school currently has about 1,100 students enrolled.

As a result, the London District Catholic School Board has decided to keep the former school open for at least another year rather than add up to 24 portable classrooms to accommodate the growing student population.

“We’ve decided to keep the existing school for one year and continually review the plan as we move forward with the students and enrollment that we’re seeing currently today,” said LDCSB’s executive manager of capital projects Daryl Diegel.

The existing building was originally constructed in 1963 as a junior seminary. The new school, which began construction in spring 2024, has been nearly a decade in the making.

While the new facility includes updated technology and classroom spaces designed to connect and work together, elements of the former school have also been incorporated into the design.

Among them is the distinctive arched ceiling in the school’s cafetorium, which was replicated from the original building.

“It’s airy, open and well designed,” said Diegel as he walked down the high ceiling hallways.

The decision to operate both buildings reflects a broader challenge facing the London District Catholic School Board as enrolment continues to grow.

The board says it has grown by more than 30 per cent over the past five years and now serves more than 28,000 students.

It currently has 10 major construction projects underway, including nine new schools and one major addition. The cost of recent and upcoming construction projects is approaching $600 million, before additional land costs.

For now, Regina Mundi students will be split between the new and old buildings.

School officials say that despite operating in two separate spaces, the goal is to maintain the same sense of community.

“Even though we’re working in two buildings, we’re still one school and one family,” said RMC principal, Kevin Barnes.

Students are expected to begin the new school year next week.

stories.title: Nearly 80 rescued from Grand Canyon flooding. 2 others died and 1 is unaccounted for, officials say
stories.summary: Nearly 80 people were rescued during Grand Canyon flooding, while two others died and one is unaccounted for, officials said Monday.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Grand Canyon National Park, Ariz. — -- The bodies of a Texas chiropractor and at least one other person have been found after a major weekend flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon, and forecasters warned more flooding was possible as heavy rain shrouded the canyon walls.

Saturday’s flash flood severely damaged the only water pipeline into the canyon. Officials barred tourists from staying at lodges and hotels inside Grand Canyon National Park and issued emergency water restrictions for year-round residents. Waves of rain hit the Bright Angel Creek area of the tourist destination that hosts 4.4 million visitors a year.

Nearly 80 people were rescued during the flooding. Officials are seeking information on one person who remains unaccounted for.

Incident Cmdr. Dave Black said officials used night vision and other equipment to find people who needed to be evacuated over the weekend.

The flood threatened people who hike far into the Grand Canyon

The flood happened deep in the canyon near where the Colorado River flows, around popular lodges and camping areas where people hiking from one rim of the Grand Canyon to the other stop for the night.

Scores of visitors had to be evacuated from the area by helicopter. They talked of a massive deluge and rangers warning of rockslides, and saw huge pools of logs and debris rolling down the river as they stood nearby awaiting rescue.

Hiker Daniel Evans said it rained several times before the worst 30-minute downpour Saturday afternoon. He had been planning to rest through the hot day and spend the night near the hard-hit Bright Angel campground area.

Earlier, rangers told him it looked to be safe. Then, as the rain poured, they told him it was time to go. He thought of Nepal and the massive floods and landslides that poured down mountain valleys last week.

“The entire time it was raining -- the entire time I’m going through all this and packing -- I’m just keeping my eyes upstream, just praying that a wall of water isn’t coming toward us,” Evans said.

One hiker killed is identified as rescuers search for his friends

The family of John Giusti, 53, said the Texas chiropractor set out Thursday on a trip he dreamed of with two buddies -- Texas martial arts studio owner Brent Rosenkranz, 42, and Wyoming pilot Timothy Smith, 53. They planned to spend two nights at the bottom of the canyon fishing and hiking.

They spoke to their families Thursday and found their campsite Friday. They have not been heard from since, the three families said in a joint statement released Monday.

All three men had ties to Granbury, Texas. Their families said they planned “several days of hiking, camping, fishing and exploring together.”

Park officials said they recovered the body of a 46-year-old man Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River and were trying to recover a second body. Their email provided no other details.

Shannon Cahill said her brother and his daughter are missing somewhere in the Grand Canyon region.

Michael Wilhoit, 53, Mystic Wilhoit, 30, and her boyfriend left Saturday for a three-night camping trip. She hasn’t heard from any of them since. Phone calls go straight to their voicemail, and they have not posted on social media.

“That’s not like Mystic. If she’s doing something, she’s posting. She posts constantly,” Cahill said. Cahill wasn’t sure where they were going to camp.

Late Monday morning, more rain fell as the state Department of Emergency and Military Affairs was coordinating with the park service and county emergency management officials in search and recovery efforts.

It’s `monsoon season’ in the Grand Canyon

Visiting the Grand Canyon can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon, or rainy season. Clear days can quickly give way to thunderstorms and downpours. Forecasters warned more flooding could happen Monday or just about any time storms pop up.

Rain also fell on part of the Dragon Bravo fire scar, a burn area left by a lightning-caused wildfire in July 2025. It burned for days before exploding into a fast-moving conflagration that forced evacuations and consumed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge, some cabins and other structures.

Without vegetation, a barren burn scar allows runoff to flow more quickly.

The steep, rocky nature of the canyon itself funnels water rapidly. What might be a normal summer downpour somewhere else can become a charging wall of water in the canyon.

El Nino has this year’s monsoons in the desert especially intense

This year’s heavy monsoon rains are especially intense because there is a higher amount of water vapour in the atmosphere, mostly because of a strong El Nino, said A. Park Williams, a hydroclimatologist at the University of California, Los Angeles.

The natural warming of parts of the Pacific Ocean can warp weather globally. That extra water vapor in the southwest U.S. gets wrung out in the storm in the form of rainfall, he said.

The link to human-caused climate change and the heavy Arizona rain is pretty strong, said climate scientist Daniel Swain of the California Institute for Water Resources.

A few months ago, Swain and colleagues published a study in the journal Weather and Climate Extremes finding that during the summer, short-term intense downpours in the West -- akin to the one that hit the Grand Canyon -- have become 10 per cent stronger since 2000.

The flood hits water supply in the canyon

The flood was a major blow to an enduring effort to modernize the water pipeline that serves visitors and the roughly 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.

paragraphs: Grand Canyon National Park, Ariz. — -- The bodies of a Texas chiropractor and at least one other person have been found after a major weekend flash flood swept through the Grand Canyon, and forecasters warned more flooding was possible as heavy rain shrouded the canyon walls.

Saturday’s flash flood severely damaged the only water pipeline into the canyon. Officials barred tourists from staying at lodges and hotels inside Grand Canyon National Park and issued emergency water restrictions for year-round residents. Waves of rain hit the Bright Angel Creek area of the tourist destination that hosts 4.4 million visitors a year.
Nearly 80 people were rescued during the flooding. Officials are seeking information on one person who remains unaccounted for.
Incident Cmdr. Dave Black said officials used night vision and other equipment to find people who needed to be evacuated over the weekend.
The flood threatened people who hike far into the Grand Canyon

The flood happened deep in the canyon near where the Colorado River flows, around popular lodges and camping areas where people hiking from one rim of the Grand Canyon to the other stop for the night.

Scores of visitors had to be evacuated from the area by helicopter. They talked of a massive deluge and rangers warning of rockslides, and saw huge pools of logs and debris rolling down the river as they stood nearby awaiting rescue.

Hiker Daniel Evans said it rained several times before the worst 30-minute downpour Saturday afternoon. He had been planning to rest through the hot day and spend the night near the hard-hit Bright Angel campground area.

Earlier, rangers told him it looked to be safe. Then, as the rain poured, they told him it was time to go. He thought of Nepal and the massive floods and landslides that poured down mountain valleys last week.
“The entire time it was raining -- the entire time I’m going through all this and packing -- I’m just keeping my eyes upstream, just praying that a wall of water isn’t coming toward us,” Evans said.
One hiker killed is identified as rescuers search for his friends

The family of John Giusti, 53, said the Texas chiropractor set out Thursday on a trip he dreamed of with two buddies -- Texas martial arts studio owner Brent Rosenkranz, 42, and Wyoming pilot Timothy Smith, 53. They planned to spend two nights at the bottom of the canyon fishing and hiking.
They spoke to their families Thursday and found their campsite Friday. They have not been heard from since, the three families said in a joint statement released Monday.
All three men had ties to Granbury, Texas. Their families said they planned “several days of hiking, camping, fishing and exploring together.”

Park officials said they recovered the body of a 46-year-old man Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River and were trying to recover a second body. Their email provided no other details.
Shannon Cahill said her brother and his daughter are missing somewhere in the Grand Canyon region.

Michael Wilhoit, 53, Mystic Wilhoit, 30, and her boyfriend left Saturday for a three-night camping trip. She hasn’t heard from any of them since. Phone calls go straight to their voicemail, and they have not posted on social media.
“That’s not like Mystic. If she’s doing something, she’s posting. She posts constantly,” Cahill said. Cahill wasn’t sure where they were going to camp.

Late Monday morning, more rain fell as the state Department of Emergency and Military Affairs was coordinating with the park service and county emergency management officials in search and recovery efforts.
It’s `monsoon season’ in the Grand Canyon

Visiting the Grand Canyon can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon, or rainy season. Clear days can quickly give way to thunderstorms and downpours. Forecasters warned more flooding could happen Monday or just about any time storms pop up.

Rain also fell on part of the Dragon Bravo fire scar, a burn area left by a lightning-caused wildfire in July 2025. It burned for days before exploding into a fast-moving conflagration that forced evacuations and consumed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge, some cabins and other structures.
Without vegetation, a barren burn scar allows runoff to flow more quickly.
The steep, rocky nature of the canyon itself funnels water rapidly. What might be a normal summer downpour somewhere else can become a charging wall of water in the canyon.
El Nino has this year’s monsoons in the desert especially intense

This year’s heavy monsoon rains are especially intense because there is a higher amount of water vapour in the atmosphere, mostly because of a strong El Nino, said A. Park Williams, a hydroclimatologist at the University of California, Los Angeles.
The natural warming of parts of the Pacific Ocean can warp weather globally. That extra water vapor in the southwest U.S. gets wrung out in the storm in the form of rainfall, he said.
The link to human-caused climate change and the heavy Arizona rain is pretty strong, said climate scientist Daniel Swain of the California Institute for Water Resources.

A few months ago, Swain and colleagues published a study in the journal Weather and Climate Extremes finding that during the summer, short-term intense downpours in the West -- akin to the one that hit the Grand Canyon -- have become 10 per cent stronger since 2000.

A US$208 million rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year.
While the Grand Canyon has large storage tanks for potable water on the South Rim, they won’t be refilled while the pipeline is out of service.

Jamie Stengle and Ty Oneil, The Associated Press

stories.title: Liberals claim victory in three federal by-elections
stories.summary: The wins in Ontario, Quebec and B.C. bolster the government’s slim majority in the House of Commons
stories.author: Ian Bailey, Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
The federal Liberals won three by-elections on Monday, an outcome that should bolster the party as it deals with a trade war with the United States.

Liberal candidates won one by-election in Ontario, and another in what was expected to be a tight three-way race in Quebec, where the seat was previously held by a Conservative. The final by-election, in the riding of North Vancouver-Capilano, was also an easy win for the Liberals.

The victories in all three ridings bolstered the government’s slim majority in the House of Commons, as additional by-elections loom after the recent departures of several MPs.

Monday’s votes were held amid a tense trade war with the United States, which recently intensified after Prime Minister Mark Carney pulled out of negotiations with the U.S., saying American proposals were unacceptable.

Mr. Carney saluted his party’s winning candidates in Chicoutimi-LeFjord, Beaches-East York and North Vancouver-Capilano in postings on X.

He said Daniel Gobeil, a dairy lobbyist, would be a strong voice for rural Québec and the entire agri-food sector across the country. And he said Tanveer Shahnawaz, the Toronto candidate, knows his community, fights for it and delivers. And of Braeden Caley, the B.C. candidate and the Prime Minister’s former deputy chief of staff, Mr. Carney said he knows “his values, his work ethic, and his character.”

In a longer statement on X, Mr. Carney said: “At this consequential time for Canada, voters have placed their trust in our government’s plan.”

“Despite the headwinds, we are building Canada strong. We are moving fast. And we are just getting started,” he added.

My statement on the by-elections in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, Beaches—East York, and North Vancouver—Capilano. pic.twitter.com/aHkKEaw7C7 — Mark Carney (@MarkJCarney) September 1, 2026

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s X account did not immediately refer to the outcome of the by-elections, but the Conservative Party’s X account thanked the party’s candidates and their teams in all three by-elections not long after polls closed.

Mr. Gobeil decisively claimed the northern Quebec riding of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, a victory that will be seen as a sign of Mr. Carney’s enduring popularity in Quebec amidst the trade conflict.

The Saguenay region where the riding is located is the heart of Quebec’s aluminum industry, hard hit by last year’s U.S. tariffs and new levies imposed after the talks collapsed between Canadian and American negotiators on Aug. 21.

It is the second by-election the Liberals have won in hostile Quebec territory this year, claiming the seat in Chicoutimi that the Conservatives have held since 2018. The Liberals also took the Bloc stronghold of Terrebonne in April.

Monday’s victory came after Mr. Carney nominated the Conservative incumbent Richard Martel to the Senate in July.

A hoarse and smiling Mr. Gobeil called his win a victory for “Canadian unity” and said it would allow him to bring “the people of Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean to the decision-making table.”

“We sent a strong message tonight,” he said.

A former president of les Producteurs de lait du Québec, which represents thousands of dairy farms in the province, Mr. Gobeil is an ardent defender of Canada’s supply management system, which has been a sticking point in trade negotiations with the U.S.

The Conservatives were running Régis Gaudreault, a lawyer and teacher at the Cégep de Chicoutimi. The Bloc candidate was Caroline Dubé, a former director of the office of Bloc MP Mario Simard.

The Liberals also enjoyed comfortable victories in the two other ridings up for grabs: North Vancouver-Capilano and the Toronto riding of Beaches-East York.

Beaches-East York became vacant when Liberal MP Nate Erskine-Smith departed for an unsuccessful attempt to enter provincial politics; he is now running for a seat on Toronto city council.

Mr. Shahnawaz, a onetime assistant to Mr. Erskine-Smith, has now succeeded his former boss as the Liberal MP for Beaches-East York.

Other candidates in the riding included the Conservatives’ Jim Syrbos, the Ndp’s Shannon Devine and the Greens’ Bruce Livesey.

In North Vancouver-Capilano, Mr. Caley claimed victory for the Liberals.

Jonathan Wilkinson had represented the area since 2015, initially as the MP for North Vancouver, and then for the current riding. The former federal cabinet minister was named Canadian ambassador to the European Union earlier this year.

Federal by-elections in 2026 set to cost upwards of $24-million

Given Mr. Caley’s former role in the Carney government, he could potentially be considered as a future cabinet minister.

Other candidates in North Vancouver-Capilano included Conservative Stephen Curran, a lawyer who also contested the riding in 2025; Stephen Tweedale for the NDP; and the Green Party’s Shelley Luce, an environmental scientist.

The three by-elections were held while the House of Commons is on a summer break. MPs return on Sept. 21.

Additional federal by-elections are expected in the coming months. Quebec Liberal MP Steven Guilbeault has resigned his Montreal seat of Laurier–Sainte-Marie, months after he left Mr. Carney’s cabinet over a difference of opinion about the government’s energy and environmental policies. Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall is also expected to officially resign imminently.

Liberal party takes all three by-election races in B.C., Ontario and Quebec.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll stepping down after 18 months on the job: White House
stories.summary: is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Washington — U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader during the Trump administration.

No reason was given for the departure of Driscoll, who is a friend of Vice-President JD Vance, but tensions with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have been widely reported. It marks the latest in a series of shakeups of the military leadership, with the army especially seeing major upheaval.

“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.

“The United States army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

A U.S. army official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said Driscoll spoke with President Donald Trump on the current state of the army and submitted his resignation. The official did not provide additional details. The Pentagon referred questions to the army. Driscoll’s resignation was reported earlier Monday by The Wall Street Journal.

Exit follows other army departures, rollback of drone program

Driscoll’s departure follows the ouster of one of his allies from the army as well as the rollback of a drone program he had championed. Hegseth had suddenly ousted the service’s top uniformed leader, Gen. Randy George, in April, while the army’s commander in Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down in June.

Gen. Christopher LaNeve, who has made a meteoric rise under Hegseth, took George’s place as the army’s acting chief of staff. Under LaNeve, the service is pulling the plug on a drone modernization program. An army unit based in Europe was building its own drones before LaNeve directed it to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion, officials said in August.

stories.title: Family of Indigenous woman killed in hate-fuelled attack angry they weren’t notified of killer’s parole
stories.summary: Brayden Bushby was convicted of manslaughter after throwing a trailer hitch at two women from a passing vehicle in Thunder Bay
stories.author: Willow Fiddler
paragraphs: Family members of an Indigenous woman who died after a hate-fuelled attack say they want the Parole Board of Canada to explain why they weren’t told of a decision to give the man who killed their sister full parole earlier this month.

Indigenous leaders joined Connie and Melissa Kentner on Parliament Hill Monday morning for a news conference calling for a review of the parole board’s decision to release Brayden Bushby, who served five years of an eight-year sentence for manslaughter in the high-profile 2017 death of the two women’s sister, Barbara Kentner, in Thunder Bay.

“When the parole board makes a decision like this, they are not deciding in a vacuum. There is a family on the other side of that decision, which is us. There is a community on the other side of that decision, which is where we live. There are Indigenous women and girls watching. There are families who are asking themselves whether the justice system will protect them and whether their voices will matter if something happens to them,” Connie said.

Mr. Bushby was convicted of manslaughter in 2020 after he pleaded guilty to aggravated assault for throwing a trailer hitch at two of the Kentner sisters from a passing car, hitting Barbara in the stomach and rupturing her small intestine. He was sentenced to eight years in prison in 2021.

On Aug. 13, the parole board granted Mr. Bushby full parole with conditions and notified media of its 13-page decision on the case by e-mail on Aug. 18. At that time, The Globe and Mail contacted Melissa Kentner, who wasn’t aware Mr. Bushby had been released from prison.

She also said no one in her family was contacted by the parole board to inform them of its decision or told that Mr. Bushby was even being considered for full parole, even though family members had registered for such notification.
“They know our e-mails, for some of us, our cellphones haven’t changed since 2017 and still we were not invited to participate in the parole process as victims,” Melissa said in a statement.
The parole board did not respond to a request from The Globe Monday. In its decision, the board said it determined Mr. Bushby would not pose undue risk to the public.
Melissa said she no longer feels safe knowing Mr. Bushby is free, and neither do her children.

Six months after Barbara, a 34-year old Anishinaabe mother, was struck with the trailer hitch hurled at her and Melissa as they walked down a Thunder Bay street, she died from injuries to her abdomen.

Evidence from the preliminary hearing and trial heard that on the night of the assault, Mr. Bushby, a Thunder Bay resident, was intoxicated after a day of ice fishing and drinking. He and three friends went driving around the city, and Mr. Bushby told his friends he wanted to “yell at hookers.”

That night, Melissa said, she saw a vehicle approach them with someone hanging out the window. Then she heard someone yell, “I got one!” as it drove off. Barbara was behind her on the ground and had been hit in the stomach with a trailer hitch she found nearby.
The blunt force trauma ruptured Barbara’s small intestine, requiring emergency surgery.

The forensic pathologist who performed her autopsy said Barbara died of bronchopneumonia and acute chronic peritonitis. She determined that both were consequences of a “traumatic rupture of the small intestine” caused by the blunt force injury.

Barbara also had end-stage liver disease, and while it was a significant contributing factor, it was not a direct cause of her death, the forensic pathologist who conducted the autopsy testified in 2020.
Superior Court Justice Helen Pierce said in her sentencing that Mr. Bushby’s fatal attack was motivated by a hatred of women and disregard for their lives.

Justice Pierce said while there was no evidence Mr. Bushby knew the Kentner sisters were Indigenous on the night of Jan. 29, 2017, it was proven beyond a reasonable doubt that he was motivated by hate toward women.
“Your actions have signalled to Indigenous people across Canada that they cannot expect to be safe, and that their lives are not valued,” she said.
Indigenous leaders from Northern Ontario said greater consideration has to be given in parole board risk assessments that involve Indigenous victims.
“There has to be a review on this particular case,” Deputy Grand Chief Anna Betty Achneepineskum of Nishnawbe Aski Nation said Monday.

In its August decision, the board said it determined “a release on full parole now will not pose undue risk and the release will contribute to the protection of society by facilitating [Mr. Bushby’s] reintegration back into society as a law-abiding citizen.”
Mr. Bushby was previously granted day parole in 2023, allowing him to live at his mother’s home in Thunder Bay, but the parole board revoked his release the following year.
At the time, the board said it found Mr. Bushby had violated several terms of his day parole, including a prohibition on consuming alcohol.

Mr. Bushby had failed a breathalyzer test during a traffic stop, the board said. He had also failed to remain at the scene after he reversed a car into another vehicle, and was a suspect in a car theft investigation, the parole board said in the decision.
He also got a new tattoo of a Confederate flag, which the board said was widely linked to “racist ideologies.”
Mr. Bushby, however, said he fell asleep and didn’t know what the tattoo artist was doing until the piece was done and questioned whether it was relevant to his case.
He also cut a swastika into a correctional facility’s lawn in August, 2025, according to the parole board’s decision.

That night, Melissa said, she saw a vehicle approach them with someone hanging out the window. Then she heard someone yell, “I got one!” as it drove off. Barbara was behind her on the ground and had been hit in the stomach with a trailer hitch she found nearby.

The blunt force trauma ruptured Barbara’s small intestine, requiring emergency surgery.

The forensic pathologist who performed her autopsy said Barbara died of bronchopneumonia and acute chronic peritonitis. She determined that both were consequences of a “traumatic rupture of the small intestine” caused by the blunt force injury.

Barbara also had end-stage liver disease, and while it was a significant contributing factor, it was not a direct cause of her death, the forensic pathologist who conducted the autopsy testified in 2020.

Superior Court Justice Helen Pierce said in her sentencing that Mr. Bushby’s fatal attack was motivated by a hatred of women and disregard for their lives.

Justice Pierce said while there was no evidence Mr. Bushby knew the Kentner sisters were Indigenous on the night of Jan. 29, 2017, it was proven beyond a reasonable doubt that he was motivated by hate toward women.

“Your actions have signalled to Indigenous people across Canada that they cannot expect to be safe, and that their lives are not valued,” she said.

Indigenous leaders from Northern Ontario said greater consideration has to be given in parole board risk assessments that involve Indigenous victims.

“There has to be a review on this particular case,” Deputy Grand Chief Anna Betty Achneepineskum of Nishnawbe Aski Nation said Monday.

In its August decision, the board said it determined “a release on full parole now will not pose undue risk and the release will contribute to the protection of society by facilitating [Mr. Bushby’s] reintegration back into society as a law-abiding citizen.”

Mr. Bushby was previously granted day parole in 2023, allowing him to live at his mother’s home in Thunder Bay, but the parole board revoked his release the following year.

At the time, the board said it found Mr. Bushby had violated several terms of his day parole, including a prohibition on consuming alcohol.

Mr. Bushby had failed a breathalyzer test during a traffic stop, the board said. He had also failed to remain at the scene after he reversed a car into another vehicle, and was a suspect in a car theft investigation, the parole board said in the decision.

He also got a new tattoo of a Confederate flag, which the board said was widely linked to “racist ideologies.”

Mr. Bushby, however, said he fell asleep and didn’t know what the tattoo artist was doing until the piece was done and questioned whether it was relevant to his case.

He also cut a swastika into a correctional facility’s lawn in August, 2025, according to the parole board’s decision.

stories.title: Young people are drinking less. So why are some embracing ‘tanmaxxing’ and smoking?
stories.summary: Health experts are raising concerns as trends like “tanmaxxing” and cigarette smoking gain traction among some young people, despite growing awareness of their links to cancer.
stories.author: Becca Clarkson
stories.content: Health experts are raising concerns as trends like “tanmaxxing” and cigarette smoking gain traction among some young people, despite growing awareness of their links to cancer. At the same time, a recent report from B.C.’s provincial health officer suggests alcohol consumption among young people is at an all time low, prompting questions about why some youth are rejecting one well-known health risk while embracing others. Experts say social media May be helping glamorize behaviours that come with well-established long-term health risks by repackaging them as markers of beauty, rebellion or status. The dangers of ‘tanmaxxing’ One trend drawing particular concern from dermatologists is “tanmaxxing,” in which influencers encourage people to maximize their UV and sun exposure in pursuit of a darker tan. “As far as our level of concern goes, it’s a 10 out of 10,” Dr. Sunil Kalia, chair of the Canadian Dermatology Association Sun Awareness Working Group, said in an interview with CTV’s Your Morning Vancouver. He says youth and adolescence are particularly important periods for skin cancer prevention because much of a person’s lifetime UV damage occurs during those years. “The amount of UV exposure people gets in their youth years is what develops the risk of getting skin cancer later on,” Kalia said, noting that the disease affects one in every five to seven people. While the trend is largely driven by aesthetics, Kalia says excessive tanning can accelerate skin aging and contribute to skin damage and blemishes. He is also concerned by the correlation between tanmaxxing and sunburns. “Even just one sunburn doubles the risk of melanoma, the most deadly type of skin cancer,” Kalia explained. He’s encouraging people to avoid prolonged sun exposure, especially during peak UV hours between 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. Wearing sunscreen, protective clothing and wide-brimmed hats will also help reduce the risk of skin cancer. “We’re also seeing a rise in the use of tanning beds, which are considered as hazardous as other exposures to cancer such as smoking,” said Kalia. Warning signs of a cigarette comeback Cancer experts are also paying attention to a resurgence of cigarette smoking in pop culture and its potential impact on youth behaviour. “Young people May copy celebrities and social media influencers that glamourize smoking,” BC Cancer warned in a statement earlier this year. The latest data suggests B.C. has the lowest adult smoking rate in Canada, at 9.5 per cent compared with a national average of 12.5 per cent. Fifteen per cent of youth aged 12 to 19 reported having smoked tobacco. Despite long-term declines in smoking, recent national data suggests smoking rates May be edging upward. According to the 2025 Canadian Substance Use Survey, 14 per cent of respondents reported smoking a cigarette in the previous 30 days, up from 13 per cent in 2023. Among youth and young adults, the number rose from 14 per cent to 15 per cent over the same period. Researchers writing in the medical journal Tobacco Control have warned that a growing volume of smoking-related content on social media May be helping normalize cigarette use among young people. The journal points to the rise of so-called “cigfluencers”—celebrities and influencers who share photos of themselves smoking online—as well as dedicated accounts such as Instagram’s @cigfluencers. The account’s biography describes itself as “hot people keeping the art of smoking & being cool alive.” According to the article, the account “selectively compiles and amplifies both contemporary and archival imagery” that portrays smoking as “rebellious, glamorous and culturally nostalgic.” Celebrities like Hailey Bieber, Charlie XCX and Heated Rivalry stars Connor Storie and Hudson Williams have been featured on the account.

stories.title: Days after Trump announces Venezuela oil deal, White House fills in some of the details
stories.summary: The White House on Monday said it’s partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners as part of U.S. President Donald Trump’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry, setting up a deal that will give the Pentagon a stake over roughly a fifth of the country’s vast oil reserves.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Washington — The White House on Monday said it’s partnering with North American Blue Energy Partners as part of U.S. President Donald Trump’s push to tap into Venezuela’s oil industry, setting up a deal that will give the Pentagon a stake over roughly a fifth of the country’s vast oil reserves.

The Trump administration released more details about the agreement on Monday night, days after Trump announced what he described as the biggest oil deal in history. The sweeping deal has been met with skepticism from analysts who say it will take years to revive Venezuela’s production, but Trump and his aides are pitching it as a chance to develop a new oil giant in the Western Hemisphere.

As part of the deal, the U.S. is creating a private company as part of a joint venture with Nabep — a detail the White House withheld for days. Nabep, owned by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, is already the second largest operator in Venezuela behind Chevron.

Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez is giving the company 100-year rights over 17 oil fields with proven reserves of 65 billion barrels. Many of those fields were previously owned by Russian or Chinese firms, the White House said.

The deal will give the Pentagon a 35 per cent ownership stake in the company, and the State Department will get a guarantee to purchase 20 per cent of the output at cost, the White House disclosed Monday. Betancourt’s company has agreed to put up US$100 billion in new oil infrastructure.

Trump has been pushing to boost oil production in Venezuela since the January military mission that captured then-president Nicolás Maduro on federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.

The White House claimed the deal would be “at zero cost” to the U.S., and said the government would have veto power on board members — the majority of whom would be U.S. citizens.

“Nabep will have reputable U.S. auditors, lawyers, and advisers and the U.S. government’s agreement with Nabep is governed by U.S. law and is subject to the jurisdiction of U.S. courts,” the White House said in a fact sheet about the deal.

Former U.S. government energy advisers have cautioned that the deal comes with political risk, since future administrations in Venezuela or the United States could challenge the deal.

Collin Binkley, The Associated Press

stories.title: In Rochester, N.Y., businesses and officials defy Trump’s Lake Ontario renaming ‘stunt’
stories.summary: Residents oppose the removal of a name that is interwoven with businesses and landmarks throughout the region
stories.author: Matthew Frank
paragraphs: Don’t talk about politics in the boat.
Since Leandro DaSilva launched Ontario Boat Charters in Rochester, N.Y., six years ago, that has been the rule aboard his vessels.

The 49-year-old has been boating on the lake since he was 13. The water became a place where he could leave the stress of life on the shoreline. He named his boat company after the lake to share his love of it with others.

But after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order last week to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” Mr. DaSilva said he’s worried that the once-peaceful water his business relies on is now tied to political controversy.
“Any time you bring politics into anything, it’s going to divide people, and this new name will divide people more,” he said.

Canadians have swiftly condemned Mr. Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, which straddles the border between Canada and the United States, as an attack on Indigenous culture and an imposition of American nationalism on a lake whose name hasn’t changed in nearly 400 years.
Across the water in Rochester, located 150 kilometres southeast of Toronto, Americans are also opposing the removal of a name that is interwoven with businesses and landmarks throughout the region.

The city council of Rochester issued a proclamation on Friday to maintain Lake Ontario’s name and defy the President’s executive order. The proclamation called the “stunt” a distraction from other issues Americans face, including housing and the economy.
“To ‘change’ the identity of this lake, after centuries of being known by a single name, is as childish as it is futile,” the proclamation stated.
Asked to comment on Rochester’s proclamation, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said the lake’s new name reflects its heritage and place in the U.S.
“As the president said, the majority of the great lake’s volume sits in United States territory,” she said in an e-mail.
Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?
Rochester city council president Miguel A. Meléndez Jr., who brought the proclamation forward, said the name “Lake America” disrespects the people who know Lake Ontario and its Indigenous history.

The lake’s name originated from an Iroquois word meaning “beautiful lake” or “sparkling water.” French explorers initially used other names such as Lac Frontenac, but Lake Ontario became most commonly used on maps.
Mr. Meléndez said the city council needed to take a stand against Mr. Trump because the water is critical to peoples’ livelihoods and Canada is Rochester’s best neighbour.
“It’s something we shouldn’t be picking fights over at this point, and it was important for us to stand up and say something,” he said in a Monday interview.
While the relationship between Canada and the U.S. will need repair, Mr. Meléndez said, he hopes the bond across the water will stay strong and outlast one president’s decisions.
On its website, the city refers to Lake Ontario as the “sweetwater sea.”

Rochester and Toronto once shared a direct connection through a ferry that travelled across Lake Ontario. A planned route between the two cities was first floated in 1979, according to The Globe and Mail’s archives.

In May, 2004, the ferry route was launched after Rochester bought a US$32-million boat. A month after operations began, two Globe reporters raced from Toronto to Rochester to see whether travel by water or land was faster. (The reporter travelling by car handily beat the one taking the ferry.)
But the ferry lost US$10-million in its first 10 months of operating and was ultimately shut down in 2006.

William Keeler, a librarian and archivist for the Rochester Historical Society, said the ferry helped bring the two cities closer together and was an example of cross-border co-operation during its brief existence.

But he also said losing the ferry illustrated Rochester’s shift away from relying on Lake Ontario for trade and instead using the nearly 200-year-old Erie Canal, which flows across upstate New York from Lake Erie to Albany.
Mr. Keeler said that Mr. Trump’s renaming of the lake is an insult to both Americans and Canadians.
“Trump is trying to add one more thing to his legacy,” he said. “The guy is an egomaniac.”

The name “Ontario” extended beyond the lake and has become a signifier for the region, he said. The town of Ontario, N.Y., is roughly 30 kilometres east of Rochester. Multiple beaches, hiking trails and businesses near the lake also incorporate the name.

When Matt Saxon, owner of Rochester-based screen-printing company Lake Ontario Press, saw Mr. Trump’s Friday executive order, he initially joked with customers that he would have to change his company’s name.
As the day went by, he got a flood of messages from customers asking for Lake Ontario-branded clothing to protest “Lake America” and preserve the original name.

On Saturday, he held a pop-up event inviting customers to have their own clothing screen-printed with Lake Ontario designs, and people lined up an hour before opening. Mr. Saxon said he printed at least 300 shirts – one of the best days his business has ever had.
“So many people wanted it,” he said. “There was no way I couldn’t do it. I was going to do something, but I didn’t think I’d be doing it that quickly.”
Mr. Saxon is already planning another event as demand for the designs continues, prompted in part by the lake’s name change starting to appear online.
Google updated its map on Saturday to show U.S. users the name “Lake America.” Canadian users still see Lake Ontario, while people in other countries are shown both names.
The web giant said in a brief statement Saturday that such updates “follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”
On Monday, Mr. Trump also asked Apple to change the name on its maps app.

Regardless of what any map says, Mr. DaSilva said he will always refer to it as Lake Ontario. But he’s concerned that keeping “Ontario” in his company’s name will complicate his boating business with both names in use.
“This is something I have to think about, and I don’t want to spend my energy to change things,” Mr. DaSilva said. “Now, it’s really just a waste of time.”
With reports from the Associated Press

stories.content:
Don’t talk about politics in the boat.

Since Leandro DaSilva launched Ontario Boat Charters in Rochester, N.Y., six years ago, that has been the rule aboard his vessels.

The 49-year-old has been boating on the lake since he was 13. The water became a place where he could leave the stress of life on the shoreline. He named his boat company after the lake to share his love of it with others.

But after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order last week to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America,” Mr. DaSilva said he’s worried that the once-peaceful water his business relies on is now tied to political controversy.

“Any time you bring politics into anything, it’s going to divide people, and this new name will divide people more,” he said.

Canadians have swiftly condemned Mr. Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario, which straddles the border between Canada and the United States, as an attack on Indigenous culture and an imposition of American nationalism on a lake whose name hasn’t changed in nearly 400 years.

Across the water in Rochester, located 150 kilometres southeast of Toronto, Americans are also opposing the removal of a name that is interwoven with businesses and landmarks throughout the region.

The city council of Rochester issued a proclamation on Friday to maintain Lake Ontario’s name and defy the President’s executive order. The proclamation called the “stunt” a distraction from other issues Americans face, including housing and the economy.

“To ‘change’ the identity of this lake, after centuries of being known by a single name, is as childish as it is futile,” the proclamation stated.

Asked to comment on Rochester’s proclamation, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said the lake’s new name reflects its heritage and place in the U.S.

“As the president said, the majority of the great lake’s volume sits in United States territory,” she said in an e-mail.

Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

Rochester city council president Miguel A. Meléndez Jr., who brought the proclamation forward, said the name “Lake America” disrespects the people who know Lake Ontario and its Indigenous history.

The lake’s name originated from an Iroquois word meaning “beautiful lake” or “sparkling water.” French explorers initially used other names such as Lac Frontenac, but Lake Ontario became most commonly used on maps.

Mr. Meléndez said the city council needed to take a stand against Mr. Trump because the water is critical to peoples’ livelihoods and Canada is Rochester’s best neighbour.

“It’s something we shouldn’t be picking fights over at this point, and it was important for us to stand up and say something,” he said in a Monday interview.

While the relationship between Canada and the U.S. will need repair, Mr. Meléndez said, he hopes the bond across the water will stay strong and outlast one president’s decisions.

On its website, the city refers to Lake Ontario as the “sweetwater sea.”

Rochester and Toronto once shared a direct connection through a ferry that travelled across Lake Ontario. A planned route between the two cities was first floated in 1979, according to The Globe and Mail’s archives.

In May, 2004, the ferry route was launched after Rochester bought a US$32-million boat. A month after operations began, two Globe reporters raced from Toronto to Rochester to see whether travel by water or land was faster. (The reporter travelling by car handily beat the one taking the ferry.)

But the ferry lost US$10-million in its first 10 months of operating and was ultimately shut down in 2006.

William Keeler, a librarian and archivist for the Rochester Historical Society, said the ferry helped bring the two cities closer together and was an example of cross-border co-operation during its brief existence.

But he also said losing the ferry illustrated Rochester’s shift away from relying on Lake Ontario for trade and instead using the nearly 200-year-old Erie Canal, which flows across upstate New York from Lake Erie to Albany.

Mr. Keeler said that Mr. Trump’s renaming of the lake is an insult to both Americans and Canadians.

“Trump is trying to add one more thing to his legacy,” he said. “The guy is an egomaniac.”

The name “Ontario” extended beyond the lake and has become a signifier for the region, he said. The town of Ontario, N.Y., is roughly 30 kilometres east of Rochester. Multiple beaches, hiking trails and businesses near the lake also incorporate the name.

When Matt Saxon, owner of Rochester-based screen-printing company Lake Ontario Press, saw Mr. Trump’s Friday executive order, he initially joked with customers that he would have to change his company’s name.

As the day went by, he got a flood of messages from customers asking for Lake Ontario-branded clothing to protest “Lake America” and preserve the original name.

On Saturday, he held a pop-up event inviting customers to have their own clothing screen-printed with Lake Ontario designs, and people lined up an hour before opening. Mr. Saxon said he printed at least 300 shirts – one of the best days his business has ever had.

“So many people wanted it,” he said. “There was no way I couldn’t do it. I was going to do something, but I didn’t think I’d be doing it that quickly.”

Mr. Saxon is already planning another event as demand for the designs continues, prompted in part by the lake’s name change starting to appear online.

Google updated its map on Saturday to show U.S. users the name “Lake America.” Canadian users still see Lake Ontario, while people in other countries are shown both names.

The web giant said in a brief statement Saturday that such updates “follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

On Monday, Mr. Trump also asked Apple to change the name on its maps app.

Regardless of what any map says, Mr. DaSilva said he will always refer to it as Lake Ontario. But he’s concerned that keeping “Ontario” in his company’s name will complicate his boating business with both names in use.

“This is something I have to think about, and I don’t want to spend my energy to change things,” Mr. DaSilva said. “Now, it’s really just a waste of time.”

With reports from the Associated Press

stories.title: Steven Guilbeault formally resigns his seat in Laurier-Sainte-Marie
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to schedule another six byelections for the coming months.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to schedule another six byelections for the coming months.
Liberal MP Steven Guilbeault officially resigned his Montreal seat on Friday, according to the House of Commons website.

The MP for Laurier—Sainte-Marie has said he’s leaving government on a matter of principle because the party’s direction on energy and the environment changed under Carney’s leadership. Ottawa dropped the consumer carbon tax and endorsed building new pipelines out of Alberta.
Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall was also expected to officially resign this week after announcing her plans in June.

Wagantall, a Saskatchewan MP since 2015, announced her resignation this summer after originally saying she planned to stick around until the next election. Nelson Pohl will run under the Conservative banner in her Yorkton-Melville riding in the next election.
Guilbeault and Wagantall are just the latest MPs to exit the Commons in recent months.
Two MPs stepped down this summer to run in Quebec’s provincial election.

Bloc Québécois MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay resigned on June 19 to run for the Parti Québécois, while Alexandre Boulerice resigned his Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie seat on Aug. 25 to run for Québec solidaire.
Ontario Conservative MP Larry Brock has announced plans to step down on Sept. 18 to return to the Crown prosecutor’s office in Brantford, Ont.
Ontario Liberal Shaun Chen resigned as a member of Parliament on Aug. 15, attributing his exit to injuries he sustained in a car accident last fall that led to significant health issues.
The prime minister must call a byelection after a seat becomes vacant, but he has a window of 11 to 180 days in which to do so. The election period must last from 36 to 50 days.
The Liberals also swept three April byelections earlier this year — two in the GTA and one in Quebec.
The Toronto-area races were called to replace former cabinet ministers Chrystia Freeland and Bill Blair.

The April byelection in Quebec’s Terrebonne riding was called after the Supreme Court of Canada nullified the riding’s result from the general election over a clerical error on the return address for some mail-in ballots.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Alvinston Arena Floor Fund almost halfway to goal after help from London Knights exhibition game
stories.summary: The new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena is starting to freeze. The facility, built in 1977, is reaching its end of life with critical repairs needed to the rink floor and refrigeration room.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena is starting to freeze. The facility, built in 1977, is reaching its end of life with critical repairs needed to the rink floor and refrigeration room.

With pinholes in the pipes, the municipality needed to be proactive when it came to the only ice surface in the community.

“It would be shut down for a couple of weeks if you have a major catastrophe,” said Dave Ferguson, mayor of Brooke-Alvinston.

“If that’s the middle of February or hitting a playoff time, it’s going to just wreck everything. So, when you can plan ahead and the ice came in, the cement came in and the boards on budget and on time. That is phenomenal for the small community,” said Ferguson.

Work began on the arena floor project back in May and continues to progress.

“The quotes came back at $1.1 million,” said Ferguson. “The grant from Ontario (Ontario community Sport and Recreation Infrastructure Fund) is half of 2 million, so we could get up to $1 million of grant money matched dollar for dollar. This was cost effective when the tenders came in and when you’re able to include the boards in it, the total project would be about $1.5 million. Half from the government, half from the township.”

With roads and bridges to pay for, the Municipality did not want to include the repair costs on the tax bill of the 2,350 residents.

They started the Alvinston Arena Floor Fund (Aaff) immediately and with sponsors, and private donors included, they are making a significant dent in the goal.

“We’re at about $450,000 so far,” said Jill Joris, fundraising manager for Brooke-Alvinston. “Our goal is $1 million. We have some deals in the works as well, so hopefully those will pan out.”

A major boost came this weekend when the London Knights approached the Municipality about hosting an exhibition game to help raise money for the Aaff.

With the arena under construction, the neighbouring community of Watford allowed them to host the game free of charge.

The 650 tickets were snapped up quickly with the game being played in the hometown of Knights forward, Evan Van Gorp.

“Everywhere I went I just knew pretty much everybody because of the small town,” said Mike Van Gorp, Evan’s father.

“Everybody was coming up and talking to me and Melissa and the atmosphere was just great.”

One reason the game was so exciting was to see that calibre of play in a small venue.

“Everyone is so close to the ice and it is a very small ice surface,” said Mike.

“A lot of the comments were, ‘I can’t believe how fast it is’ and how ‘great the players are and how skilled they are to make decisions in such a small rink like that’. It was pretty cool.”

With help from Sarnia-Lambton Tourism, additional fan-friendly activities were held around the arena hours prior to puck drop.

“There were tons of fans in the stands,” said Joris.

“We had a few at the watch party as well. There were a silent auction and raffle and the donations for that were incredible. My heart grew three sizes that day.”

Small-town arenas are not just skating and hockey. They host the fall fair, baseball and even the rodeo. The hope is that the donations from the Aaff will prolong the life of the building for generations.

“We replaced the cement and we’re going to do the boards next spring,” said Ferguson.

“The ice pad and the boards will be all freshly redone by this time in 2027.”

“A lot of the comments were, ‘I can’t believe how fast it is’ and how ‘great the players are and how skilled they are to make decisions in such a small rink like that’. It was pretty cool.”

content_blocks.alt: Brooke-Alvinston Arena
content_blocks.caption: Ice is starting to form on the new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: With help from Sarnia-Lambton Tourism, additional fan-friendly activities were held around the arena hours prior to puck drop.
“There were tons of fans in the stands,” said Joris.
“We had a few at the watch party as well. There were a silent auction and raffle and the donations for that were incredible. My heart grew three sizes that day.”

Small-town arenas are not just skating and hockey. They host the fall fair, baseball and even the rodeo. The hope is that the donations from the Aaff will prolong the life of the building for generations.
“We replaced the cement and we’re going to do the boards next spring,” said Ferguson.
“The ice pad and the boards will be all freshly redone by this time in 2027.”

stories.title: ATV users open new trail in southern Bruce County
stories.summary: Terry Lamont has been discovering Bruce County’s fields and forests with his ATV since 2006.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Terry Lamont has been discovering Bruce County’s fields and forests with his ATV since 2006.

“I put roughly 8000 km on a year on my ATV, and I volunteer with the club and help do trail maintenance. It’s good for your mind,” said Lamont.

“Let’s you get outside, enjoy the outdoors, away from all the other stuff that goes on in the world, and you can just get out and relax and have a good time.”

Lamont is one of the first ATV enthusiasts to use a new 8-kilometre trail, constructed by the Huron Shores ATV club, spanning four concessions in Southern Bruce County.

“This trail, for a lot of years has been used unofficially by people. And it was getting fairly rundown. Not a lot of management and oversight on the trail,” said Tyler Jonston, president of the Huron Shores ATV Club.

“So, we were prepared to take that on, in partnership with our other trail users and groups. So, we’ll be monitoring the trail, and making sure that everybody’s safe and compliant, so they’ll be able to explore utilizing the trails.”

Unofficial use of hiking trails by ATV users has, for years, caught the ire of local conservation authorities, and hiking groups, by causing ruts and damage. More “sanctioned” places to ride, like the Sideroad 30 trail, should help reduce outcomes like that, caused by a small handful of ATV drivers.

“We’ve cultivated some great relationships with the Municipality of Huron-Kinloss and with Bruce County, proving to them that the ATV club is a great trail partner in trail management and maintenance, as well as oversight for the trails to ensure that we have a safe place to ride,” said Johnston.

“It’s a sanctioned place to ride, so that all of our recreational users have a place that they can enjoy.”

The new trail adds to more than 100 kilometres of trails stretching from Wingham to Port Elgin, maintained by the Huron Shores ATV club. This new section, an important link, joining forest loops in Southern Bruce County together.

“It’s a great thing to have it open. It helps connect all of our other group of trails down in this area, and keeps us off the main paved roads,” said Lamont.

“It allows our ATV users to connect to all our county forest trails down here in the region and gives us an opportunity to be able to do some more exploring down in Southern Bruce,” said Johnston.

stories.title: Homicide charge upgraded in fatal south London home invasion; accused remanded in custody
stories.summary: Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, appeared briefly by video from Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre in London court Monday morning.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A new charge of second-degree murder has officially been laid against a man accused in a south London home invasion after the victim died from her injuries.

Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, appeared briefly by video from Elgin-Middlesex Detention Centre in London court Monday morning. During the approximately three-minute appearance, the second-degree murder charge was read into the record.

Cornejo was remanded into custody and is scheduled to return to court Sept. 10.

The new charge follows the death of a 73-year-old woman who was seriously injured during an alleged break-in at her home near Wellington Road and Base Line Road East on Aug. 22.

London police previously said the woman was sleeping when she was awakened by a loud noise at about 6:10 a.m. Investigators allege an unknown man entered the residence, assaulted and stabbed her before she was able to call 911.

The woman was taken to hospital with serious injuries that were initially believed to be non-life threatening. Police confirmed on Aug. 28 that she died in hospital, and the case is now being investigated as a homicide.

Cornejo was originally charged with aggravated assault, break and enter, assaulting a peace officer and obstructing a peace officer. He now also faces a charge of second-degree murder.

The allegations against Cornejo have not been proven in court.

With files from CTV News London’s Nick Paparella
