Ottawa — U.S President Donald Trump’s Republican Party has revoked the CBC/Radio-Canada’s press access to its upcoming midterm convention, citing the public broadcaster’s now-reversed policy not to refer to 9/11 as “terrorism” without direct attribution, National Post has learned.

A CBC spokesperson confirmed Monday that the Republican National Convention (RNC) had revoked access for both CBC and Radio-Canada to its major party gathering on Sept. 9 and 10, ahead of key mid-term elections.

The unusual press credential revocation came following a week of controversy about an internal memo from the broadcaster reminding reporters and editors of a “longstanding language guidance” not to refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as “terrorism” without attribution.

In an email to National Post, Chuck Thompson, the CBC’s head of public affairs, said the public broadcaster is reviewing the Rnc’s decision. “It is a disappointing development; we hope it will be reconsidered,” he wrote.

The Rnc’s move also appears to be the latest attempt by Trump’s administration and party to fire salvos at Canada since free trade talks between Ottawa and Washington fell apart late last week.

It could suggest Trump’s Republican party is also looking beyond tariffs for ways to pressure Canada during the ongoing trade war.

The RNC did not respond to emailed queries by deadline Monday.

Late Friday afternoon, following media reports about the broadcaster’s memo on the Sept. 11 attacks and ensuing criticism from both sides of the border, the CBC wrote in an editor’s blog that it had reversed the policy.

A few hours later, the RNC sent a heated letter to CBC/Radio-Canada revoking all the public broadcaster’s previous-approved press credentials to the upcoming major political gathering in Dallas, TX. The gathering is an important press event as it will unite Republican heavyweights on the eve of key U.S. mid-term elections.

In the missive, the RNC reprised much of the fiery criticism from Trump administration officials last week regarding the CBC’s former policy on the use of the unattributed use of the word terrorism around 9/11. (Radio-Canada did not have such an editorial policy.)

The letter cited social media posts stating CBC had instructed employees “do not refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks.” It also claimed that the public broadcaster had refused to apologize for the policy.

The letter also said that allowing CBC/Radio-Canada to attend the convention would be an “insult” to victims of the worst terrorist attack in U.S. history.

In the Friday afternoon blog post Basem Boshra, CBC’s senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, wrote that a leaked memo about the policy “has caused significant concern, anger and hurt for many people who believe CBC News seeks to minimize or obscure the horror of that day and who was behind it.”

“That is the last thing we want to do,” said Boshra, who is the senior director of journalistic standards and public trust of CBC News.

Asked if the public broadcaster’s reversal of its longtime policy was at all linked to the Rnc’s decision to revoke its access to the convention, Thompson pointed to Boshra’s blog. Thompson later pointed out the Rnc’s letter arrived hours after the blog post announcing the reversal

Shawn McCarthy, past president of World Press Freedom Canada, said this latest incident is part of the Trump Administration’s “hostile” approach to the news media.

“It’s in keeping with the Trump Administration’s efforts to control the press,” McCarthy said. “They have a horrible record when it comes to press freedoms.”

After Canada said it would respond to Trump’s earlier tariffs with a “dollar-for-dollar” tariff response on American goods, Trump took the unprecedented move of invoking the 1930 Tariff Act to launch another round of tariffs against Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded by calling for a united response from Canada’s provinces, including threats to cut or tariff electricity and critical minerals.

Trump responded by insulting Ford and later signed an order directing the U.S. government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The revocation also raises concerns as to how the White House and Republican Party May try to exert further control on foreign Canadian journalists reporting in the United States.

For example, last month the U.S. government announced it was drastically cutting down visa duration times for foreign journalists from five years to 240 days. That means foreign reporters, including Canadians reporting from the U.S., will have to renew their work visas every eight months and risk having to leave the country if it is not renewed.

The Rnc’s move against CBC-Radio Canada is also the Trump administration’s latest attempt to punish reporters or their employers by denying credentials.

Reports over the weekend said journalists from at least three large American news outlets – The New York Times, Bloomberg News and The Wall Street Journal – were denied credentials to cover the Group of 20 finance meeting next week in North Carolina.

The event is intended to gather finance ministers and central bankers from the world’s leading economies at a critical time, with the global economy under threat from Trump tariffs, wars in Iran and Ukraine

stories.title: Oil prices rise and stocks fall after U.S. hits Iranian sites in the Strait of Hormuz
stories.summary: Wall Street closed out August on a downbeat note as stocks fell and the price of oil rose after the U.S. launched a military action against Iran.
stories.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: NEW York — Wall Street closed out August on a downbeat note Monday as stocks fell and the price of oil rose after the U.S. launched its first military action in a month against Iran.
The S&P 500 index fell 0.3 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.7 per cent and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.1 per cent.

August had no shortage of turbulence for the market, but the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each posted a gain for the month after losing ground in July and June. The Dow, meanwhile, managed its fifth-straight monthly gain.

Monday’s losses were broad, with nearly every sector within the benchmark S&P 500 finishing in the red. Energy stocks, though, notched gains. Exxon Mobil rose 2.7 per cent and Chevron rose 2.1 per cent.
S&P 500 market updates here

On the losing side, Edison International slumped 23.1 per cent and PG&E fell 20.1 per cent for the two steepest declines. That followed reports about potential California wildfire legislation that would allow insurers to sue utilities over related claims.

Amazon fell 2.5 per cent after The Wall Street Journal reported that the Federal Trade Commission and more than 20 states are preparing to sue the online retail giant over claims the company manipulated prices on its platform.

The U.S. war with Iran remained a key focus for Wall Street. U.S. forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates said it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters on Monday.
The aggressive actions follow a lull in activity in the U.S. war with Iran, which has lasted more than six months.

The war has curtailed traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil shipments. Oil prices remain high after an initial surge earlier in the war and that has made everything from gasoline to shipped goods more expensive.

The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 2.7 per cent to settle at Usus$90.49 per barrel on Monday. Brent fell below Usus$80 earlier in August but has since moved higher with no sign of an imminent end to the war.
Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

The national average for gasoline in August has been above Usus$4 per gallon every day of the month for the first time ever, according to the AAA. It has been the most expensive August at the pump on record, outpacing even the enormous supply chain crunch during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022.

Higher energy prices have fueled already stubbornly high inflation. That has been weighing on household spending and consumer confidence. It has also given the Federal Reserve a more complicated path ahead for its interest rate policy.

The rate of inflation remains well above 3 per cent, which is far beyond the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates at least once before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation. On Friday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that inflation is still too high and suggested a rate hike might be necessary in the coming months.

The Fed gets its next inflation update on Sept. 11, just days ahead of its next meeting to determine interest rate policy. Wall Street is forecasting a 66 per cent chance that the Fed will raise its benchmark rate at that meeting, according to CME FedWatch.

“While a September hike is not a foregone conclusion, we expect the Fed to have limited tolerance for meaningful upside inflation surprises,” wrote Brock Weimer, investment strategy analyst at Edward Jones, in a research note.

The yield on the two-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations about Fed moves, held steady at 4.34 per cent, where it was late Friday. That’s up significantly from about 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.75 per cent from 4.73 per cent late Friday. That’s back up around the level seen two weeks ago when the Trump administration took the unusual step of announcing it would intervene in the bond market.
Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA

Any increase to interest rates that could cool inflation also risks hurting the jobs market. Later this week, the U.S. reports August jobs data. In July, the U.S. job market stalled unexpectedly as employers cut 23,000 jobs. Labor Department revisions slashed another 103,000 jobs from May and June payrolls.

Company updates helped move several stocks Monday. GameStop rose 2.9 per cent after the video game retailer provided a preliminary second-quarter earnings outlook above its year-ago results. Shares of Aon slid 9.5 per cent as the company announced that it was buying insurance broker USI Insurance Services from private equity firm KKR in a deal valued at Usus$17 billion, including debt.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 25.62 points to 7,686.14. It rose 2.6 per cent in August and is up 12.3 per cent so far this year.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 374.09 points to 53,185.90. The Nasdaq fell 31.53 points to 26,370.89. The index, which is heavily weighted with big tech stocks, posted a 3.9 per cent gain for the month and is up 13.5 per cent this year.
Markets were mixed in Europe and Asia.
Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press
AP Business Writers Elaine Kurtenbach and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

The war has curtailed traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, which accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil shipments. Oil prices remain high after an initial surge earlier in the war and that has made everything from gasoline to shipped goods more expensive.

The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 2.7 per cent to settle at Usus$90.49 per barrel on Monday. Brent fell below Usus$80 earlier in August but has since moved higher with no sign of an imminent end to the war.

Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

The national average for gasoline in August has been above Usus$4 per gallon every day of the month for the first time ever, according to the AAA. It has been the most expensive August at the pump on record, outpacing even the enormous supply chain crunch during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2022.

Higher energy prices have fueled already stubbornly high inflation. That has been weighing on household spending and consumer confidence. It has also given the Federal Reserve a more complicated path ahead for its interest rate policy.

The rate of inflation remains well above 3 per cent, which is far beyond the Fed’s 2 per cent target. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise interest rates at least once before the year ends in an effort to cool inflation. On Friday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that inflation is still too high and suggested a rate hike might be necessary in the coming months.

The Fed gets its next inflation update on Sept. 11, just days ahead of its next meeting to determine interest rate policy. Wall Street is forecasting a 66 per cent chance that the Fed will raise its benchmark rate at that meeting, according to CME FedWatch.

“While a September hike is not a foregone conclusion, we expect the Fed to have limited tolerance for meaningful upside inflation surprises,” wrote Brock Weimer, investment strategy analyst at Edward Jones, in a research note.

The yield on the two-year Treasury, which closely tracks expectations about Fed moves, held steady at 4.34 per cent, where it was late Friday. That’s up significantly from about 3.50 per cent at the beginning of 2026.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.75 per cent from 4.73 per cent late Friday. That’s back up around the level seen two weeks ago when the Trump administration took the unusual step of announcing it would intervene in the bond market.

Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA

Any increase to interest rates that could cool inflation also risks hurting the jobs market. Later this week, the U.S. reports August jobs data. In July, the U.S. job market stalled unexpectedly as employers cut 23,000 jobs. Labor Department revisions slashed another 103,000 jobs from May and June payrolls.

Company updates helped move several stocks Monday. GameStop rose 2.9 per cent after the video game retailer provided a preliminary second-quarter earnings outlook above its year-ago results. Shares of Aon slid 9.5 per cent as the company announced that it was buying insurance broker USI Insurance Services from private equity firm KKR in a deal valued at Usus$17 billion, including debt.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 25.62 points to 7,686.14. It rose 2.6 per cent in August and is up 12.3 per cent so far this year.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 374.09 points to 53,185.90. The Nasdaq fell 31.53 points to 26,370.89. The index, which is heavily weighted with big tech stocks, posted a 3.9 per cent gain for the month and is up 13.5 per cent this year.

Markets were mixed in Europe and Asia.

Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press

stories.title: Looking for Canadian alternatives to U.S. tech? It’s not easy, experts say
stories.summary: As the world reacted over recent days to Google Maps changing the name of Lake Ontario, MapQuest made a social media post that quickly drew praise and has seen downloads surge.
stories.author: Uday Rana
paragraphs: As leaders on both sides of the border reacted over recent days to Google Maps changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” aligning with U.S. President Donald Trump ’s push, MapQuest made a social media post that quickly drew praise and has seen the app’s downloads surge.
“We’re not changing it,” the company said over a screenshot of the lake on their map platform on Thursday.
MapQuest, which is also an American company, took the marketing campaign further on Sunday, saying, “We are aware that Lake Ontario is being correctly labeled on our map.”
We’re not changing it. pic.twitter.com/NdeE9v2BNO — MapQuest (@MapQuest) August 27, 2026

The app, which many users likely haven’t thought of in years, quickly became the number three most downloaded app among all free apps on Monday, right behind ChatGPT and Meta AI, and saw its Google Trends search traffic up 5,000 per cent compared to the same period last year, with searches up 500 per cent compared to last week in Canada.
Worldwide, searches for the app are up 50 per cent compared to last week and 40 per cent compared to the same period last year.

While the U.S. is the biggest market for MapQuest, Canadians also make up “a very big chunk” of their customer base and the decision to stand by the name has resonated with them, MapQuest CEO Doug Berger said.
“Hundreds of thousands of people have picked up the app and downloaded it. Obviously, people agree with us and we struck a chord,” Berger said.

But while switching from Google Maps to MapQuest takes only a few clicks on your smartphone, switching other digital technology services can be trickier — and often, there aren’t many alternatives to the U.S. tech giants, let alone Canadian options amid the growing Buy Canadian push, experts say.

“There’s a lot of areas, because of how dependent we are on American firms, where they can throttle our access to essential services,” said Emily Osborne, policy researcher at the Canadian Shield Institute, a think tank launched last year and focusing on digital sovereignty and national security.
The institute includes former Blackberry co-CEO Jim Balsillie on its board of directors.

“Cloud infrastructure stands out as an example of this, and you see people concerned about the potential of a kill switch for cloud infrastructure or other essential infrastructure services,” she added.
Making the switch from American tech is easier said than done for most Canadians, Rotman School of Management marketing professor David Soberman said.
“Almost all the dominant companies are American or American owned,” he said.

It can be easier to make the change in some cases compared to others, Soberman said. For example, some Canadians May choose to order from Canadian platforms like SkipTheDishes instead of UberEats, or buy retail goods on Canadian Tire instead of Amazon or Walmart.
“Canadian Tire is pretty competitive, and, in some cases, they might even be less expensive,” Soberman said.
Some Canadian companies, like Toronto-based Hovr and Beck Taxi, are also looking to compete with Uber and Lyft in some of Canada’s biggest cities.
But most U.S. tech has become enmeshed in our lives, Osborne said, meaning it can be harder to change up services like website domains, email hosting, social media and other digital technology.
While some Canadian social media alternatives like Gander and NorthSocial do exist, they cannot match the “scope and scale” of American social media giants, she said.
“It’s difficult to switch away from Meta’s platforms because all of our friends are going to continue using it. It’s hard to convince them all to switch,” she said.
You might be able to find alternatives for individual apps, like Canadian browser Shift in place of Google Chrome or Safari and cDox in place of Microsoft Word and Google Docs.
For those looking for an alternative for Microsoft Teams or Slack, Canadian conference calling software Callbridge might offer an alternative.
However, Osborne said it might end up being less cost effective with big U.S. firms offering bundles, packages and suites of software like Microsoft Office or Google Suite.
“We have some Canadian alternatives to Google Docs or Google Sheets, but there’s no across the board whole alternative to those products,” she said.
In some areas, Canadians have more choice between Canadian and non-U.S. tech offerings.

“We do have a Canadian alternative to Gmail called Typewire, and when there aren’t Canadian alternatives or we’re interested in different alternatives, there’s plenty of EU-based options that we can switch. There’s EU-based email providers like ProtonMail that are a bit bigger that we can also consider switching to,” Osborne said.
And there are areas where there are no alternatives to U.S. tech, like in payment platforms.
While Interac provides some domestic payment infrastructure in Canada, two American companies – Visa and Mastercard – dominate the global credit card network.
Last month, Canadian commercial solutions and payment processing platform Moneris got a new owner in an American private equity firm.

Moneris, one of Canada’s largest commerce solutions providers, was jointly owned by the Bank of Montreal and the Royal Bank of Canada. American private equity firm Francisco Partners, which specializes in dealing with technology companies, bought the platform for $2 billion.
Canadian tech firms being sold off to American private equity has become common.
“We used to have a Canadian alternative to Google Maps called Avenza and we sold it to a Boston private equity firm,” Osborne said.
While the list of Canadian tech firms offering alternatives to American giants May be small, the entrenchment of the “Buy Canadian” movement offers an opportunity for growth, Soberman said.

“If there is a pronounced shift to buying Canadian, that in itself will create an opportunity. After all, we do have Shopify which is a huge Canadian company and others will arise if Canadians start showing those preferences,” he added.
Ottawa could take a page out of the European Union’s book by creating more tools themselves, Osborne said.
“The French government has alternatives to Zoom and to Teams and to a bunch of other American office software products that they’re building in-house for their public servants to use.”

The renewed Buy Canadian surge also provides a marketing opportunity, not just to Canadian firms but also to American firms looking to build bridges with Canadian consumers as MapQuest’s social media campaign shows, Soberman said.
“Something like the changing of Lake Ontario provides an opportunity even for American firms to be deferential to Canadian wishes,” he said.
But being able to sustain any changes is important for keeping any new habit or effort going, experts noted.
“People should always remember in this case is to look for the easiest ways to put your preferences into action and not to punish yourself,” says Soberman.
–With files from Global’s Mackenzie Gray

stories.title: Mark Carney's Liberals sweep three federal byelections amid trade war
stories.summary: The collapse of the trade talks with the United States ultimately led the Liberals picking up a seat in Quebec.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
paragraphs: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney secured his government’s majority by winning all three byelections in British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec on Monday night, upping his seat count to 173 in the House of Commons.

The Liberals were expecting to easily win the two byelections in Toronto and Vancouver, but the race in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord — a riding two hours north of Quebec City — was expected to be a fierce battle between the Liberals and the Bloc Québécois. The collapse of the trade talks with the United States, combined with Carney’s commitment to protect supply management, ultimately led the Liberals picking up the seat in Quebec.

Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil, former head of the Milk Producers of Quebec and a dairy farmer himself, won a resounding victory in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord with 51.3 per cent of the vote while Bloc’s Caroline Dubé, a former political staffer, finished second with 32.9 per cent according to preliminary results. Conservative candidate Régis Gaudreault, a lawyer by profession, finished in third place at 12.5 per cent.
In his victory speech, Gobeil said he was happy the people of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord would have a seat at the table in government and he vowed to become a strong voice for supply management.

A Liberal source told the National Post ahead of the vote that the mood amongst voters had significantly shifted in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord after the trade talks collapsed with the U.S. The source, speaking on a not-for-attribution basis to talk more freely, said people at the doors seemed to rally around Carney’s decision to not concede to the Trump administration’s demands.

The Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean region has been disproportionately affected by the trade war with the U.S. Many workers in the area work in the aluminum and lumber sectors, and there is a large dairy farming industry under supply management. Despite that, voters were ready to support Carney in his decision to walk away from the negotiating table.
“I have to say: the people of Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean are very proud and they don’t let people step on their toes,” the source said.
The seat of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord was left vacant after Conservative MP Richard Martel, a former junior hockey coach, was appointed to the Senate by Carney earlier this summer.

Martel’s move to the Senate, while not a floor-crossing per se, might have left a sour taste in the mouths of some of his voters. But Chicoutimi—Le Fjord was not a Conservative stronghold. In fact, voters in the riding have voted Bloc, Liberal and NDP in the past before they first voted for Martel, whom was well-known in the community, in 2018.

Despite a strong personal brand, Martel barely held onto his seat in 2025. Only three points separated first place from third place in the riding, and Martel won his fourth mandate with a razor-thin majority.

Late Monday evening, Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet conceded the victory to the Liberals and congratulated his candidate for a hard-fought campaign. He also proclaimed that this byelection has demonstrated that there are two main political parties competing on the federal scene: the Liberals and the Bloc Québécois.

Blanchet spent nearly two weeks campaigning with his candidate in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, to the point where his opponents have suggested they’re campaigning against him and not Dubé. Bloc MPs and Parti Québécois candidates also swarmed in the riding in recent weeks to help Dubé, but to no avail.
In comparison, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Carney each visited the riding once ahead of the byelection.
The Bloc had criticized Carney for holding a federal byelection while the Quebec election campaign is underway.

In fact, provincial party signs have popped up along the streets of Chicoutimi in recent days, adding to the federal signs already in place. The confusion was such that Elections Canada had to remind voters that Monday’s federal byelection is separate from the provincial election set to happen on Oct. 5.
The trade war May have helped the Liberals snatch a riding from the Conservatives, but they easily held onto two of their safe seats on Monday.

Tanveer Shahnawaz, a longtime political staffer to former Liberal minister Nathaniel Erskine-Smith, secured 55.7 per cent of the vote in the Toronto riding of Beaches—East York. Shahnawaz said in a speech it will be “an honour of a lifetime” to serve as MP, while his former boss praised his kindness and his hard work in the riding.
The Ndp’s Shannon Devine finished second in the riding with 25.8 per cent of the vote, which NDP Leader Avi Lewis praised as a strong result given the circumstances.
“In Beaches–East York, our party has returned to fighting form. We’ve proved that the sting of last election was a one-time injury,” Lewis said in a statement.

The race in the B.C. riding of North Vancouver—Capilano sought to replace Jonathan Wilkinson, another former minister who is now Canada’s ambassador to the European Union. Carney’s former deputy chief of staff, Braeden Caley, won the seat for the Liberals with 58.6 per cent of the votes, while the Conservatives’ Stephen Curran ended second with 29.2 per cent of the vote.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday morning, Carney congratulated his three candidates for their respective wins and said it is clear from the high scores in these byelections that Canadians support the direction of his government.

“What’s a clear message from last night in three very different ridings across this great diverse country is that Canadians are behind the plan of the government which is first and foremost about building strong at home, diversifying (trade) with reliable partners, building Canada strong for all,” he said.
At least five more byelections are expected to be called in the coming months, including three in Quebec, one in Ontario and one in Saskatchewan.
National Post calevesque@postmedia.com

stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney secured his government’s majority by winning all three byelections in British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec on Monday night, upping his seat count to 173 in the House of Commons.

The Liberals were expecting to easily win the two byelections in Toronto and Vancouver, but the race in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord — a riding two hours north of Quebec City — was expected to be a fierce battle between the Liberals and the Bloc Québécois. The collapse of the trade talks with the United States, combined with Carney’s commitment to protect supply management, ultimately led the Liberals picking up the seat in Quebec.

Liberal candidate Daniel Gobeil, former head of the Milk Producers of Quebec and a dairy farmer himself, won a resounding victory in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord with 51.3 per cent of the vote while Bloc’s Caroline Dubé, a former political staffer, finished second with 32.9 per cent according to preliminary results. Conservative candidate Régis Gaudreault, a lawyer by profession, finished in third place at 12.5 per cent.

In his victory speech, Gobeil said he was happy the people of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord would have a seat at the table in government and he vowed to become a strong voice for supply management.

A Liberal source told the National Post ahead of the vote that the mood amongst voters had significantly shifted in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord after the trade talks collapsed with the U.S. The source, speaking on a not-for-attribution basis to talk more freely, said people at the doors seemed to rally around Carney’s decision to not concede to the Trump administration’s demands.

The Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean region has been disproportionately affected by the trade war with the U.S. Many workers in the area work in the aluminum and lumber sectors, and there is a large dairy farming industry under supply management. Despite that, voters were ready to support Carney in his decision to walk away from the negotiating table.

“I have to say: the people of Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean are very proud and they don’t let people step on their toes,” the source said.

The seat of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord was left vacant after Conservative MP Richard Martel, a former junior hockey coach, was appointed to the Senate by Carney earlier this summer.

Martel’s move to the Senate, while not a floor-crossing per se, might have left a sour taste in the mouths of some of his voters. But Chicoutimi—Le Fjord was not a Conservative stronghold. In fact, voters in the riding have voted Bloc, Liberal and NDP in the past before they first voted for Martel, whom was well-known in the community, in 2018.

Despite a strong personal brand, Martel barely held onto his seat in 2025. Only three points separated first place from third place in the riding, and Martel won his fourth mandate with a razor-thin majority.

Late Monday evening, Bloc Leader Yves-François Blanchet conceded the victory to the Liberals and congratulated his candidate for a hard-fought campaign. He also proclaimed that this byelection has demonstrated that there are two main political parties competing on the federal scene: the Liberals and the Bloc Québécois.

Blanchet spent nearly two weeks campaigning with his candidate in Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, to the point where his opponents have suggested they’re campaigning against him and not Dubé. Bloc MPs and Parti Québécois candidates also swarmed in the riding in recent weeks to help Dubé, but to no avail.

In comparison, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Carney each visited the riding once ahead of the byelection.

The Bloc had criticized Carney for holding a federal byelection while the Quebec election campaign is underway.

In fact, provincial party signs have popped up along the streets of Chicoutimi in recent days, adding to the federal signs already in place. The confusion was such that Elections Canada had to remind voters that Monday’s federal byelection is separate from the provincial election set to happen on Oct. 5.

The trade war May have helped the Liberals snatch a riding from the Conservatives, but they easily held onto two of their safe seats on Monday.

Tanveer Shahnawaz, a longtime political staffer to former Liberal minister Nathaniel Erskine-Smith, secured 55.7 per cent of the vote in the Toronto riding of Beaches—East York. Shahnawaz said in a speech it will be “an honour of a lifetime” to serve as MP, while his former boss praised his kindness and his hard work in the riding.

The Ndp’s Shannon Devine finished second in the riding with 25.8 per cent of the vote, which NDP Leader Avi Lewis praised as a strong result given the circumstances.

“In Beaches–East York, our party has returned to fighting form. We’ve proved that the sting of last election was a one-time injury,” Lewis said in a statement.

The race in the B.C. riding of North Vancouver—Capilano sought to replace Jonathan Wilkinson, another former minister who is now Canada’s ambassador to the European Union. Carney’s former deputy chief of staff, Braeden Caley, won the seat for the Liberals with 58.6 per cent of the votes, while the Conservatives’ Stephen Curran ended second with 29.2 per cent of the vote.

Speaking to reporters on Tuesday morning, Carney congratulated his three candidates for their respective wins and said it is clear from the high scores in these byelections that Canadians support the direction of his government.

“What’s a clear message from last night in three very different ridings across this great diverse country is that Canadians are behind the plan of the government which is first and foremost about building strong at home, diversifying (trade) with reliable partners, building Canada strong for all,” he said.

At least five more byelections are expected to be called in the coming months, including three in Quebec, one in Ontario and one in Saskatchewan.

stories.title: Canada hosts U.S., Chinese military leaders at Indo-Pacific defence forum
stories.summary: Annual gathering of Indo-Pacific military leaders comes at a tense time in Canada-U.S. political relations, and while Ottawa seeks to improve relationship with Beijing.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
paragraphs: Canada is playing host this week to military leaders from both the United States and China amid cross-border tensions with the Trump administration and Ottawa’s attempts to improve relations with Beijing.
Canada’s chief of defence staff, Gen. Jennie Carignan , is co-hosting an annual meeting of military leaders from Indo-Pacific countries this week in Victoria, B.C.
The conference, now in its 28 th year, is co-chaired by the commander of the U.S. Pacific Command, Adm. Samuel Paparo.

Canada’s turn at hosting the 32-nation conference comes amid worsening tension between Ottawa and Washington after negotiations toward a new trade deal between the two countries collapsed earlier this month.

Stephen Saideman, an international affairs professor at Carleton University, said in an interview Monday that he expects many Indo-Pacific military leaders’ conversations will focus on the unpredictable and undependable nature of the U.S. president and his secretary of war, Pete Hegseth.
“It absolutely puts (Canada) in a difficult spot, because all our planning is premised on this relationship with the United States,” said Saideman.
“What Hegseth and Trump are doing is absolutely making it harder for the militaries of the world to cooperate with the Americans. And we’re not an exception in any of this.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that Canada would impose retaliatory tariffs on American products after talks with the Trump administration on a new trade deal collapsed on Aug. 21 – a response to the 50 per cent tariffs Trump has leveled on billions in Canadian products.

Since those talks failed, Trump’s cabinet has blamed Canada for walking away from what they suggest was a good deal. Canadians, however, overwhelmingly support Carney’s decision to walk away, with 63 per cent of Canadians voicing that view in Ipsos polling exclusively for Global News.
An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by Trump.
On Monday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dismissed the idea that Canada could “retaliate,” including taking a shot at the country’s military.

“We’re not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada? What, are they going to take their two submarines from the (West) Edmonton Mall and sic them on us,” Bessent said during an interview with Cnbc.

Throughout Trump’s various threats against Canada, officials have suggested that despite political bluster, the working relationship between American and Canadian military and intelligence agencies remain strong.

That sentiment was shared by Paparo in 2023 when he visited the Hmcs Ottawa to speak about the “strength and solidarity of Canada and the U.S. and the importance of cooperation for an enduring, free and open Indo-Pacific.”
What he will say this year as tensions escalate remains to be seen.

The theme of this year’s Indo-Pacific Chiefs of Defence conference focuses on strengthening collective security in what they call a “dynamic” landscape in the region. In addition to senior military leaders, the conference will hear from undisclosed non-military experts.
Most of the conversation will be behind closed doors, but a joint press availability with Carignan and Paparo is expected on Wednesday at the conference’s close.

stories.title: Stolen Vehicle Found in Oxford County
stories.summary: The Middlesex County OPP arrested and charged a suspect after an investigation spanning two counties.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
paragraphs: Monday, 31 August 2026 16:23
By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM
The Middlesex County OPP arrested and charged a suspect after an investigation spanning two counties.
Middlesex/Oxford - A stolen vehicle investigation spreads over two counties.

Middlesex County OPP were called on Saturday morning to an address on Melvin Drive in Dorchester for a report of a vehicle entry. An unknown person entered a vehicle, but fled once confronted by the homeowner. A short time later, a homeowner at an address on 21st Line in Zorra saw the same suspect inside a vehicle in their laneway.

A U-Haul truck was observed in the ditch near the residence on 21st Line. The vehicle was confirmed to be stolen out of London. After a lengthy search, a 32-year-old St. Thomas man was arrested and taken to the Middlesex OPP detachment. He is facing three charges, which include Possession of Property Obtained by Crime Over $5,000, Theft of Motor Vehicle, and Mischief Under $5,000.
He was held in custody for bail.

stories.title: U.S. judge authorizes involuntary feeding of jailed suspect in deadly National Guard shooting
stories.summary: A man refusing to eat food while jailed on charges he shot two National Guard troops near the White House, killing one of them, can be fed against his will under a U.S. judge’s emergency order.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Washington — A man refusing to eat food while jailed on charges he shot two National Guard troops near the White House, killing one of them, can be fed against his will under a U.S. judge’s emergency order.

U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta agreed Saturday to order “nonconsensual” nutrition and medical treatment for Rahmanullah Lakanwal, who was rushed to a hospital in July after he stopped eating. Mehta said federal Bureau of Prisons medical staff can feed Lakanwal intravenously or through a medical tube to save his life.

Redacted court filings haven’t specified a reason for Lakanwal’s refusal to eat, but prosecutors noted that courts have held that prison officials can involuntary feed “hunger-striking prisoners.”

U.S. Justice Department attorneys asked Mehta to order the emergency lifesaving measures for Lakanwal.

stories.title: London Majors’ first-place hopes hinge on suspended game
stories.summary: The Majors trail Welland 9-2 in the fifth inning and need a comeback to keep their shot at the No. 1 playoff seed alive.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
paragraphs: The Majors trail Welland 9-2 in the fifth inning and need a comeback to keep their shot at the No. 1 playoff seed alive.
The London Majors have less than half a game to avoid a stunning collapse from first place .

The Canadian Baseball League club’s last chance at the pennant will require a massive comeback against Welland Tuesday night (7:05 p.m.) at Labatt Park. The Majors trail the Jackfish 9-2 in the fifth inning of a game suspended Aug. 23 because of inclement weather and already pushed back twice more by rain.
The two rivals were originally scheduled to complete the meaningful contest this past Sunday, but rain forced another delay then and again Monday.

London (31-16) had been in the driver’s seat to secure the No. 1 playoff seed but has suffered through a rare slump at the worst possible time. If the Majors fail to rally and beat Welland (30-17), it will mark a fourth consecutive loss.

Hamilton (31-17), meanwhile, surged to the finish line with six straight wins and is just a half-game back of London. The Cardinals won the season series against both the Majors and Jackfish, so they hold any first-place tiebreakers.

London won the season series against Welland, so barring a miracle turnaround Tuesday, the Majors would earn home-field advantage in a best-of-seven playoff semifinal against the Jackfish, which is poised to start Friday at Labatt Park.
Also Tuesday, the fourth-place Guelph Royals (29-19) will face the fifth-place Barrie Baycats (27-21) in a one-game wild-card battle to determine who faces the first-place finisher.
There is some good news for Majors fans. The team is offering $2 hot dogs for the five-inning game courtesy of TriCar, and tickets for the shortened contest are $5 at the gate.
rpyette@postmedia.com

stories.title: Steven Guilbeault officially resigns Montreal seat of Laurier-Sainte-Marie
stories.summary: Guilbeault says he’s leaving on principal due to party’s direction on energy and environment under Carney
stories.author: Canadian Press Staff
paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to schedule another six by-elections for the coming months.
Liberal MP Steven Guilbeault officially resigned his Montreal seat on Friday, according to the House of Commons website.

The MP for Laurier–Sainte-Marie has said he’s leaving government on a matter of principle because the party’s direction on energy and the environment changed under Mr. Carney’s leadership. Ottawa dropped the consumer carbon tax and endorsed building new pipelines out of Alberta.
Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall was also expected to officially resign this week after announcing her plans in June.

Ms. Wagantall, a Saskatchewan MP since 2015, announced her resignation this summer after originally saying she planned to stick around until the next election. Nelson Pohl will run under the Conservative banner in her Yorkton-Melville riding in the next election.
Mr. Guilbeault and Ms. Wagantall are just the latest MPs to exit the Commons in recent months.
Two MPs stepped down this summer to run in Quebec’s provincial election.

Bloc Québécois MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay resigned on June 19 to run for the Parti Québécois, while Alexandre Boulerice resigned his Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie seat on Aug. 25 to run for Québec solidaire.
Ontario Conservative MP Larry Brock has announced plans to step down on Sept. 18 to return to the Crown prosecutor’s office in Brantford, Ont.
Ontario Liberal Shaun Chen resigned as a member of Parliament on Aug. 15, attributing his exit to injuries he sustained in a car accident last fall that led to significant health issues.
The prime minister must call a by-election after a seat becomes vacant, but he has a window of 11 to 180 days in which to do so. The election period must last from 36 to 50 days.
The Liberals also swept three April by-elections earlier this year – two in the GTA and one in Quebec.
The Toronto-area races were called to replace former cabinet ministers Chrystia Freeland and Bill Blair.

The April by-election in Quebec’s Terrebonne riding was called after the Supreme Court of Canada nullified the riding’s result from the general election over a clerical error on the return address for some mail-in ballots.

stories.title: Committee releases final report into 2020 Nova Scotia mass shooting
stories.summary: The independent committee released its third and final annual report Monday, monitoring the progress towards 130 recommendations released in a 2023 public inquiry.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
paragraphs: The chair of the committee monitoring the implementation of recommendations from the inquiry into the 2020 Nova Scotia mass shooting says more work needs to be done, but she is “optimistic” about the future.

The independent committee released its third and final annual report Monday, monitoring the progress towards 130 recommendations released as a result of the 2023 public inquiry known as the Mass Casualty Commission.
The public inquiry was conducted after a gunman shot and killed 22 people during a 13-hour rampage in the province on April 18 and 19, 2020.

Myra Freeman, chair of the Progress Monitoring Committee (PMC), said there are still approximately 40 recommendations that need to be addressed, but responsibility will now be handed over to the governments of Nova Scotia and Canada, along with the RCMP.

“I’m confident that they will figure out a way,” Freeman said. “We are strongly encouraged by the fact that they have committed this much action, this much progress to date, and they know the importance and the public will remind them.”
The 72-page report emphasizes that progress is being made on some fronts, including regulatory oversight, policing reforms and gender-based violence prevention.

This is the first year the committee delved into the aspects of gender-based violence, which is an area that Freeman said will require much more work from governments, police, community organizations and the public in years to come.

“It requires a societal change, and societal changes don’t happen overnight,” she said. “So what we need is a concerted effort to continue the action to keep people safe, and all of us have a responsibility to do it.”
She said more work also needs to be done on the mental health front .
Freeman said some committee members asked for its mandate to be extended, but she said that was never something she brought forth to the government.
“We recognized this was a finite time,” she said.
But she added that even though the mandate has ended, the work does not stop here.

“We always knew that this work and addressing the recommendations would extend far beyond our three-year mandate,” she said. “We also knew that it was never an endpoint. That it was meant to be a first step and a foundation to a longer commitment for accountability, for transparency and for building stronger, safer communities.”
Nova Scotia is safer now than it was in 2020, Freeman said.
While he said the province is moving forward, Scott McLeod, whose brother Sean was killed in the attacks, said he is taking a “wait and see” approach.
“Some of the stuff that needs to be done isn’t just something that can be scratched down on paper or taught,” he said. “It has to continue to evolve and progress with society the way it is.”

With the bulk of the work now being transferred to governments and the RCMP, McLeod said he hopes institutions commit to sharing their progress towards the inquiry’s recommendations and making their work transparent.

Kristina Fifield, a trauma specialist who worked with the PMC, said that while the government is taking over, the public still has a responsibility to keep pushing for the recommendations to be implemented.
“This is going to require a lot of collective and community advocacy to continue moving this forward,” she said.
In the wake of increases in community-based violence, gender-based violence and intimate partner violence, Fifield said more needs to be done to hold perpetrators accountable and stop the cycle.
“We have a long, dark history of violence and violence being normalized and people protecting people that are using violence,” she said.
In a statement, Premier Tim Houston said the government is prepared to accept responsibility for the work moving forward.
“We will not settle for mere progress,” he said. “We want to make real, meaningful change.”
But the NDP Opposition said it is concerned with how the government is funding some associated services.
“We need to ensure the right resources are in place to build on the work that’s underway and support families and strengthen communities,” a statement from the NDP caucus said.

The government of Canada has taken “significant action” to support the work of the PMC over the past three years, said a joint statement from Gary Anandasangaree, minister of public safety, and Sean Fraser, minister of justice and attorney general of Canada.

That it was meant to be a first step and a foundation to a longer commitment for accountability, for transparency and for building stronger, safer communities.”

Nova Scotia is safer now than it was in 2020, Freeman said.

While he said the province is moving forward, Scott McLeod, whose brother Sean was killed in the attacks, said he is taking a “wait and see” approach.

“Some of the stuff that needs to be done isn’t just something that can be scratched down on paper or taught,” he said. “It has to continue to evolve and progress with society the way it is.”

With the bulk of the work now being transferred to governments and the RCMP, McLeod said he hopes institutions commit to sharing their progress towards the inquiry’s recommendations and making their work transparent.

Kristina Fifield, a trauma specialist who worked with the PMC, said that while the government is taking over, the public still has a responsibility to keep pushing for the recommendations to be implemented.

“This is going to require a lot of collective and community advocacy to continue moving this forward,” she said.

In the wake of increases in community-based violence, gender-based violence and intimate partner violence, Fifield said more needs to be done to hold perpetrators accountable and stop the cycle.

“We have a long, dark history of violence and violence being normalized and people protecting people that are using violence,” she said.

In a statement, Premier Tim Houston said the government is prepared to accept responsibility for the work moving forward.

“We will not settle for mere progress,” he said. “We want to make real, meaningful change.”

But the NDP Opposition said it is concerned with how the government is funding some associated services.

“We need to ensure the right resources are in place to build on the work that’s underway and support families and strengthen communities,” a statement from the NDP caucus said.

The government of Canada has taken “significant action” to support the work of the PMC over the past three years, said a joint statement from Gary Anandasangaree, minister of public safety, and Sean Fraser, minister of justice and attorney general of Canada.

stories.title: Deceased man identified by Winnipeg police, family notified
stories.summary: Police have identified the man who died after being found unresponsive in Winnipeg last month, the service said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
paragraphs: Winnipeg police have identified a man who died after he was found unresponsive last month.

The man, whose identity was not provided by police, was located by officers at the corner of Main Street and James Avenue on July 28. He died in hospital a day later, the Winnipeg Police Service (WPS) said in a news release.
Police issued a composite sketch of the man in hopes of identifying him. Those efforts were successful, the release said, adding that his family has been notified.
Police said further details about the man’s identity will not be shared out of respect for his family.

stories.title: Congo authorities report more than 6,000 confirmed Ebola cases and nearly 3,000 deaths
stories.summary: Congo’s authorities said Monday that the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history has topped 6,000 cases with 2,911 deaths.
stories.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: Bunia, Congo — Congo’s authorities said Monday that the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history has topped 6,000 cases with 2,911 deaths.
More than 1,360 people have recovered from the virus, in what authorities said was an “encouraging” development.

The outbreak in eastern Congo is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers’ strike and intense population movements. The situation is particularly concerning at displacement sites, where residents already live in extremely precarious conditions.
Last week, the virus spilled into two new health zones in the region.

The World Health Organization has said that it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Bodies of those who died of Ebola can be highly contagious and lead to further spread when people prepare them for burial and gather for funerals.

In response to the outbreak, Congolese authorities have mandated that the dangerous work of burying suspected victims be managed wherever possible by authorities, which can be met by protests from families and friends.
The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare type of Ebola that has no approved vaccine or treatment.
Last week, Congo began vaccinating health and other front-line workers with the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type called Zaire.
Clinical trials are underway to find a licenced vaccine for the Bundibugyo virus.

Although the current outbreak was declared in mid-May, officials believe it had been spreading since February. It has spread from three health zones to nearly 60, with most cases and deaths occurring outside the network of monitored contacts and within communities.

Efforts to bring the outbreak under control -- from limited public gatherings to social distancing and airport closures -- have disrupted life in the six provinces, particularly Ituri, which also has been ravaged by rebel violence.
The government has introduced some measures, including installing health and sanitary equipment at some locations, but advocacy groups say more needs to be done to build trust with the community.
While neighbouring Uganda declared itself free of Ebola last month, the risk of further cross-border spread remains, WHO said last week.

stories.title: ‘Lake Ontario’ lyric now anti-Trump rallying cry, says Blue Rodeo’s Greg Keelor
stories.summary: Keelor says Trump’s name change is ‘insulting’ and emblematic of a broader pattern of behaviour
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu
paragraphs: Greg Keelor had been mulling what to say about Donald Trump all night.

Blue Rodeo was about to play Hasn’t Hit Me Yet during their Saturday show at Toronto’s RBC Amphitheatre, and the Canadian band’s frontman knew their 1993 hit contained a newly loaded lyric: “Out in the middle of Lake Ontario.”
Keelor considered using the moment to tear into the U.S. president, who last week signed an executive order to rename the body of water “Lake America.”
“A part of me just wanted to go off on Trump and just call him a lot of bad names,” the singer-songwriter says in an interview Monday.
But he opted for a different approach.
Blue Rodeo's Greg Keelor talks about the viral moment at the band's Toronto show Saturday, when thousands of fans shouted 'Lake Ontario' in unison during their 1993 hit 'Hasn't Hit Me Yet.'
The Canadian Press
“I knew that the song would do the work” he says. “I didn’t have to say much. Just getting to that line was going to blow the roof off the place.”
Turns out he was right.

When Blue Rodeo reached the song, Keelor asked the roughly 16,000 people in attendance to sing Lake Ontario with “full authority and ownership,” with the lake itself stretching out behind the waterfront venue.
They roared the line out.
A map of Lake Ontario appeared on the screens behind the band, a visual Keelor had specifically requested before the show.
The moment has since gone viral, drawing international attention as Trump pushes to put his own stamp on the Great Lake shared by Canada and the U.S.
For Keelor, the response was far more charged than he expected.
“We were all just a little shocked at the wave of emotion that came from the audience when they got to that line,” he says. “It has a different meaning now. I’m very happy for that.”

Keelor says Trump’s name change, which comes amid an escalating trade war between Canada and the U.S., is “insulting” and emblematic of what he sees as a broader pattern of behaviour from the president.
“He’s an ignorant man,” Keelor says. “He’s just a man-baby throwing his food off his tray when he doesn’t like it, pounding his fists on his feeding tray.”
He adds that Trump’s name change on one of the Great Lakes is “just another aspect of his idiocy” and “so un-Canadian.”
But he also sees something unifying in the controversy.
“We’re not pushovers. We dig in,” he says.
To Keelor, Lake Ontario has always meant something more than a name on a map.
He says he wrote the song after walking around Port Hope, Ont., where he felt a deep connection to the water and the surrounding landscape.
“It’s sort of a mystical experience of sharing the oneness of all things, in a way,” he says.
The lake, he notes, predates the countries and borders that now surround it by thousands of years.

“That’s a very powerful body of water,” Keelor says. “Most Canadians, it wasn’t really something in your brain, it was just Lake Ontario. But now it’s taken on a significance and it’s a bit of a line in the sand.”
Trump’s executive order has only added to that symbolism.
“The Indigenous people had a relationship with this lake thousands of years before any of us showed up,” Keelor says.
“It’s unbelievable that the American people would have put him in power. It’s a very depressing thing.”
Keelor says Blue Rodeo has largely stopped touring the U.S.
“Nobody has any appetite to go down there and play,” he says.
Google Maps now displays “Lake America” for users in the U.S., while Canadians continue to see Lake Ontario. International users see both names.
“That corporate complicity is a scary thing,” says Keelor.
“Maps are something we take for granted most of the time, but they’re important. Arbitrary lines that are cut across countries, they mean a lot.”
Blue Rodeo doesn’t hit the road again until October, but Keelor says the current political climate could create an opportunity for the band to do something smaller and more spontaneous.
“Maybe some smaller guerrilla sort of stuff,” he says.
For now, the veteran country rockers are getting used to their unexpected role helping Canadians rage against the American machine.
“We’re very happy to have that line in that song at this particular moment because it is a little bit of a rallying call,” he says.
“If the song galvanizes a mood or an energy in the country, that is amazing.”

“It’s unbelievable that the American people would have put him in power. It’s a very depressing thing.”

Keelor says Blue Rodeo has largely stopped touring the U.S.

“Nobody has any appetite to go down there and play,” he says.

Google Maps now displays “Lake America” for users in the U.S., while Canadians continue to see Lake Ontario. International users see both names.

“That corporate complicity is a scary thing,” says Keelor.

“Maps are something we take for granted most of the time, but they’re important. Arbitrary lines that are cut across countries, they mean a lot.”

Blue Rodeo doesn’t hit the road again until October, but Keelor says the current political climate could create an opportunity for the band to do something smaller and more spontaneous.

“Maybe some smaller guerrilla sort of stuff,” he says.

For now, the veteran country rockers are getting used to their unexpected role helping Canadians rage against the American machine.

“We’re very happy to have that line in that song at this particular moment because it is a little bit of a rallying call,” he says.

“If the song galvanizes a mood or an energy in the country, that is amazing.”

stories.title: Three Londoners among seven charged in $913K drug seizure
stories.summary: Police seized more than 6.5 kilograms of illicit drugs, firearms and over $100,000 in stolen property.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
paragraphs: Police seized more than 6.5 kilograms of illicit drugs, firearms and over $100,000 in stolen property.

Seven people, including three from London, are facing 64 charges following the seizure of more than $913,000 worth of suspected fentanyl, cocaine and methamphetamine, along with more than $100,000 in stolen property, during searches across Southwestern Ontario.
Ontario Provincial Police said Monday the charges stem from a multijurisdictional drug-trafficking investigation that also led to the seizure of more than 6.5 kilograms of illicit drugs and firearms.

The OPP-led Provincial Guns and Gangs Enforcement Team launched an intelligence-led investigation in January into suspected drug trafficking across Southwestern Ontario. Investigators identified two separate criminal networks operating independently: one primarily in Brantford and Brant County, and another in London and on the Oneida Nation of the Thames.
On July 7, officers executed search warrants at four locations in Brantford and Paris with assistance from Oxford County OPP and Brantford police.
On Aug. 12, police executed search warrants at a London residence and on the Oneida Nation of the Thames in collaboration with Oneida police and London police.
As a result of the investigation, officers seized:
6.5 kilograms of suspected fentanyl
420 grams of suspected cocaine
250 grams of suspected methamphetamine
More than $73,500 in Canadian currency
A handgun with an auto-switch
A rifle
Three prohibited magazines, including an over-capacity drum magazine
Ammunition
Brass knuckles
Drug trafficking paraphernalia
Two stolen camper trailers
A stolen 2019 Honda Civic
Police estimate the street value of the drugs at more than $913,000 and the stolen property at more than $100,000.

Five people were arrested and warrants were issued for two others: a 29-year-old Brantford man facing three charges and a 21-year-old London man facing 17 charges. Neither was named in the OPP release.

A 21-year-old London resident is charged with 10 offences and was released from custody pending a Nov. 13 court appearance in London. A 35-year-old London resident is charged with seven offences and was released pending a Sept. 25 court appearance in London.
OPP said the fentanyl seized represents approximately 65,000 potentially lethal street-level doses.
Anyone with information about illegal firearms or the possession, manufacturing or trafficking of illicit drugs is asked to contact OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (Tips).

stories.title: Trump has asked Apple to change Lake Ontario name to 'Lake America' on its maps, interior chief says
stories.summary: Chicago (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump has asked Apple to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” on its maps app, his administration's interior chief said Monday, days after signing an executive order over the body of water now in the spotlight amid his escalating trade war with Canada.
stories.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: Chicago (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump has asked Apple to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” on its maps app, his administration’s interior chief said Monday, days after signing an executive order over the body of water now in the spotlight amid his escalating trade war with Canada.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox’s “Mornings with Maria” program that Trump “reached out to Apple directly.” He said he was confident the “Lake America” name could be seen on its platform soon.

stories.title: London Transit eyes on-demand service for unserved areas, seeks $2M boost
stories.summary: The pilot would test demand in Fox Hollow, south Byron and north Lambeth before committing to conventional bus routes.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
paragraphs: The pilot would test demand in Fox Hollow, south Byron and north Lambeth before committing to conventional bus routes.

London Transit commuters in the city’s northwest and southwest could soon have a connection to the system as the transit authority looks to implement an on-demand service to test ridership in areas not served by conventional transit.

Greenlit by the politician-led commission Monday, London Transit will apply to the city for $3.5 million in assessment-growth funding for 2027 – the net-new property tax revenue generated each year – to introduce new service.

London Transit wants funding for a fixed-route expansion from the Hyde Park Power Centre to Western University , as well as on-demand service in the Fox Hollow neighbourhood and pockets of south Byron and north Lambeth.

“There’s areas of the city that have grown significantly, but we don’t know what the ridership is like. So to commit to a full conventional bus service where you’re running multiple large buses through the neighbourhood, but only having a couple people hop on – that might not be the best use of our funds,” said Skylar Franke, chair of the commission.

“This model . . . it’ll let us understand if there is a growing market in those neighbourhoods, and I think then we can, once we see the ridership levels increase, allocate the appropriate conventional service to it.”
Each year, the city runs an application process for its pot of assessment growth dollars, generated by property taxes from new development that year. The amount can vary from year to year.

Agencies such as police and paramedics, along with city services including garbage collection and road maintenance, can apply for the funding to cover the cost of expanding service to accommodate growth. That funding then continues in subsequent years.

London Transit had its first assessment-growth request approved by the city this year, with $2.1 million going toward new service to Cedar Hollow in the northeast, Innovation Park, Summerside and Sheffield, West Byron, and the Kains Road and Upperpoint Boulevard area.
London Transit eyes new city hall tax cash to fund route expansion

Because of manufacturing and ordering timelines for new buses, those routes won’t begin until 2028, according to a transit staff report. In the meantime, the funding will go toward buying the buses needed.

The same delay would apply to the proposed Route 40 between Hyde Park Power Centre and Western University . The route would cost just over $2 million annually and is expected to see annual ridership of 205,500.

The on-demand service would cost $1.4 million and has forecast annual ridership of 22,700. Kelly Paleczny, general manager of London Transit, told politicians fares would be the same as for standard transit service, but details such as what vehicles would be used will be subject to a final report and proposal from a consultant in October.

“We’ve seen this approach in numerous other jurisdictions be quite successful,” Paleczny said following Monday’s meeting. “It really is an opportunity to get in sooner, and learn that critical information, and then hopefully when we do have the resources to put that route in, it’s going to be more successful.”

The commission also approved submitting the transit agency’s 2027 budget request, which includes an increase of approximately $2.6 million because of rising diesel costs and added service hours previously covered through its reserves.

While London Transit will still dip into its reserves to cover a portion, the budget report asks “administration to submit a budget amendment case increasing the City of London investment by $2,037,800 for 2027 to support the permanent addition of 2,400 service growth hours and the increased cost of diesel fuel.”

London Transit budgeted for diesel at roughly $1.22 per litre, but the recent average price is $1.65 per litre. Franke said London Transit has “already dipped heavily” into its fuel reserve fund and pointed to last year’s budget update, when the agency returned $700,000 to the city after the federal carbon tax was eliminated.

“I’m hopeful that council will recognize we have been very prudent, and at this point, if we want to continue delivering a reliable service and improve on our service targets, we do need that increase,” Franke said.
The commission also amended its budget request to seek advocacy from the provincial and federal governments for relief from diesel and tariff-related cost increases.
“It’s not a local decision, although it has a local impact, so we need to be discussing that with our provincial and federal counterparts,” Franke said.
Both the city’s 2027 budget update and assessment-growth allocations are set to be determined early next year.
jmoulton@postmedia.com

stories.title: Ontario agencies restore Lake Ontario to their websites after Google Maps updated it to Lake America in the U.S.
stories.summary: Four Ontario government websites displayed Lake America over the weekend. The fix was a single Google Maps setting, or no map at all.
stories.author: Mason Kossak
stories.content:
Four Ontario government websites spent at a portion of the weekend showing U.S. President Donald Trump's new name for the shared body of water. No two of them fixed it the same way

Ontario government agencies have restored Lake Ontario to their websites after a Google Maps update replaced it with Lake America over the weekend.

Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.

Access articles from across Canada with one account.

Enjoy additional articles per month.

Metrolinx, the provincial agency that runs GO Transit, disabled the map on its GO stations page where the label appeared, it told Global News . The agency said in an email to National Post that “the issue has since been resolved, and our maps once again show Lake Ontario.”

Maps on sites run by Hydro One, Metrolinx, Infrastructure Ontario and the Lcbo all displayed the American name, Global News reported. Global confirmed the labels itself and found the same on the Loblaws store locator, which CTV News reported was still showing Lake America on Monday morning.

A website that embeds a Google map loads the code from Google’s servers, and unless a developer specifies a region, the map draws American place names. Specifying Canada changes them.

Google’s developer guide says ensuring the correct regional setting for the country where an application is hosted is the developer’s responsibility.

We can help. — MapQuest (@MapQuest) August 30, 2026

Hydro One said in an email to National Post that its outage map showed an incorrect label for Lake Ontario for “a brief period” Sunday because of an issue with a third-party mapping service. The problem was identified and corrected Sunday evening, the utility wrote. It apologized for the error in an earlier statement to Global News.

TD was displaying Lake America but as of Monday afternoon, that problem had been resolved, the bank told National Post.

Loblaw said in an email to National Post that the map on its store locator was showing an incorrect label for Lake Ontario, that the information comes from a third-party mapping service and that it was working to correct it.

The Lcbo did not respond to a request for comment. Google did not provide a statement. Housing, Infrastructure and Communities Canada acknowledged the request and said it would respond. It had not by deadline.

Stephen Crawford, Ontario’s minister of public and business service delivery and procurement, wrote on X that some agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps and that the province is reviewing them.

Some Ontario government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps. Following recent changes by Google, we're actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario As Ontarians, we will always stand up for… — Stephen Crawford (@stcrawford2) August 30, 2026

Google said Saturday that Maps users in the United States would see Lake America, users in Canada would see Lake Ontario and users elsewhere would see both names.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 , “Honoring the American History of the Great Lakes and Renaming Lake Ontario as Lake America,” on Aug. 27. A secretary’s order directed the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to change its database the same day. The record lists Lake Ontario as a variant name alongside the Mohawk Kaniatarí:io, translated as nice lake.

The order says the United States lays claim to most of the lake’s “volume” and is mostly responsible for its security, economic activity and environmental stewardship.

The renaming followed the collapse of trade talks between the two countries this month. Canada and the United States have since announced matching tariffs of up to 50 per cent on some goods.

stories.title: Carney government asks court to quash lawsuit over projected missed emission targets
stories.summary: The federal government is asking a Federal Court judge to toss out a lawsuit accusing Ottawa of having no intention of meeting its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions target.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Ottawa — The federal government is asking a Federal Court judge to toss out a lawsuit accusing Ottawa of having no intention of meeting its 2030 greenhouse gas emissions target.
In recent court filings, government lawyers argued the Federal Court doesn’t have the power to order the government to take steps to meet its emissions targets.
The government also argued it wasn’t up to the court to “opine on the political and policy issues” at the heart of the lawsuit.
“Climate change is a real and important issue. Accountability, however, with respect to concerns expressed by the Applicants, lies with Parliament, not with the Court,” the government wrote.

“There is no basis on which a court could order any of the relief sought in the Application. The Act creates no duties which could be owed to the Applicants and instead establishes a framework that includes a series of targets, plans, assessments, and reporting to track progress on emission reductions over time.”

A group of climate advocates filed a lawsuit against the federal government in June arguing recent policy changes have knocked Ottawa off its track to meet Canada’s legislated greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets.
Environmental Defence, the Canadian Association of Physicians for the Environment and climate activists Marie Maltais, Sophia Mathur and Shirley Barnea brought the lawsuit forward.

They asked the Federal Court to order the government to bring its 2030 emissions reductions plan into compliance with the Net-Zero Accountability Act — or to declare Ottawa’s emission reductions plan unlawful under the act.

The Net-Zero Accountability Act, which passed in 2021, legally commits Canada to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 and requires the government to set national emission reduction targets along the way — though there are no consequences for missing them.
A progress report published in December shows the government is nowhere near on track to meet its current target of cutting emissions to 40 to 45 per cent below 2005 levels.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has been accused of backsliding on climate policy for the better part of the last year.

He eliminated the consumer carbon price in March 2025 — on his first day in office. While he promised a strengthened industrial carbon pricing system, he was accused of weakening that system through an agreement with Alberta in May that has ramifications for every other province and territory.

His government is also moving to repeal the electric vehicle sales mandate — Ottawa has promised stronger tailpipe standards but those are still years away — and to cancel the oil and gas emissions cap. Carney’s government also has delayed methane regulations in Alberta.
In a video released two weeks after the suit was filed, Carney said federal climate policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau was too expensive and divisive.

“I want to be clear on this point. The changes we have made will mean that our emissions will be higher in the next few years than they were projected to be under the previous government’s plan,” Carney said in the video.
“But in my judgment, that plan was not sustainable over the long term.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.
Nick Murray, The Canadian Press
