stories.title: A look at two of Manitoba’s oldest family farms, still in the same hands after 150 years
stories.summary: A drive through rural Manitoba passes farm after farm—grain bins catching the light, cattle scattered across pasture, and the occasional yard with old machinery rusting away. Most have changed hands at some point—sold, bought out by a neighbour, or left behind when nobody in the family wanted to take it over.
stories.author: Milan Lukes
stories.content:
A drive through rural Manitoba passes farm after farm — grain bins catching the light, cattle scattered across pasture, and the occasional yard with old machinery rusting away. Most have changed hands at some point — sold, bought out by a neighbour, or left behind when nobody in the family wanted to take it over.

However, a handful of Manitoba families have held on. Eight Manitoba farms have been recognized by the province for staying in the same family for 150 consecutive years or more, according to a provincial spokesperson.

CTV News spoke with two of those families about their farms’ history and looked at why keeping land in the family May be getting harder to do.

Matheson Family Farm

One of them is the Matheson family farm, south of Stonewall, which has remained in the same family since it was established in 1873.

“(It) is quite amazing, really,” said Tricia Harris, who owns and lives on the farm with her husband Rod. “That it has managed to stay in the family that long, because, as you can tell from the data, it doesn’t happen a lot.”

Tricia, 73, is the fourth generation to hold the land since her great-grandfather, Alexander Matheson, broke ground on it three years after Manitoba became a province — not long after surveyors first mapped out what is now the Rural Municipality of Rockwood.

To understand how the farm came to be, Tricia said you have to go back decades, to the era of the Selkirk Settlement. Also known as the Red River Colony, it was the first European agricultural settlement in Western Canada, with its first group of settlers arriving in 1812.

The colony spanned a vast tract of land, roughly 300,000 square kilometres — granted to Lord Selkirk, a Scottish nobleman, by the Hudson’s Bay Company — centred along the Red and Assiniboine rivers near present-day Winnipeg.

Among those who followed in 1814-15 was Alexander’s father, John “Bushy” Matheson, who arrived as a six-month-old baby with his parents.

“They came and settled along the Red River and farmed there for a number of years,” Tricia said.

She said John “Bushy” grew up in the Red River Settlement and learned multiple languages, including Indigenous languages, Gaelic and French. That multilingualism helped him become a constable there, breaking up disputes and serving warrants.

Tricia said travelling for his job eventually led him to learn of the “good land” in the present-day Stonewall region. In 1873, he moved there with one of his sons, Alexander — then a single man in his 20s — and the two took up adjoining quarter-sections.

Family legend has it that John “Bushy” stumbled onto more than just good land.

“The story is that his dad, John “Bushy,” was just kind of touring around the area on his horse and came across another family that had moved in… and he noticed they had some daughters, so he came home and told [Alexander], ‘I think I met your wife today,’” she said.

“And so, he told his son he better go over there and help them build their house. And he married one of the daughters,” Tricia said. Though how accurate that family tale is, she doesn’t entirely know.

That first year, only 10 acres of Alexander’s section were cleared, and a 1.5-storey log cabin went up. In 1875, Alexander married Catharine — a marriage that would last 65 years and result in five children.

From there, Tricia said the farm passed to Alexander’s youngest son, Willis, in 1917. Electricity reached the property in 1948, and in 1954 the farm passed again, this time to Willis’ niece, Linda, and her husband, Gordon Furness. This was the same year the first tractor arrived. Running water followed later that decade.

Tricia, the daughter of Linda and Gordon, took over ownership with her husband in 1983. She has lived on the farm since she was nine months old, aside from a few years away. Over the generations, the family has raised cattle and grain crops, along with chickens and pigs at various points.

None of the farm’s original buildings remain, Tricia said. However, a stone house built in 1904 by a Scottish stonemason with help from Alexander and his three sons still stands, and it’s where the couple lives today.

“It was built from the stone, the granite stone on the fields as they cleared land and pulled up these great big boulders. They stockpiled them until they had enough to build a two-storey stone house,” she said. “The house was a major accomplishment.”

But the farm’s history hasn’t been without hardship. In 1875, Tricia said detailed farm records kept by Alexander over his 44 years of farming show grasshoppers “completely destroyed” the crop.

She also said the adjoining quarter-section was lost after Willis Matheson couldn’t cover the land’s taxes while paying for his wife’s cancer treatment during the Great Depression.

“So, the farm was reduced in half,” she said.

And in 1965, Tricia said the stone house was “completely gutted” by fire, prompting her parents to rebuild the interior.

Despite the setbacks, the farm has endured, and in 2023, Tricia said about 70 relatives gathered there to celebrate 150 years of it being worked by one family. Among those in attendance was her mother Linda, then 104, who was able to make it to the special occasion.

“It was a great cousins’ reunion at that time,” Tricia said.

The couple, who also worked full time off the farm as teachers, completely retired from farming last year when they sold the last of their cattle.

As for how the farm has stayed in the family so long, Tricia said no one before her ever insisted that the next generation take it over and it’s not a pressure she and Rod are putting on their own four children, all of whom live in Winnipeg.

Still, the land continues to be farmed by a Matheson descendant — one of Tricia’s cousin’s sons, 41, who is the fifth generation to work it. The couple also looks after his cattle on the farm during the summer months.

“He lives just down the road on his own farm,” Tricia said, “which happens to be another Matheson homestead as well.”

Another farm the province recognizes as having stayed in the same family for over 150 years is the Munro family farm, which was established even earlier in 1872. The quarter-section is located just west of Portage la Prairie.

Clarke Munro, 71, and his sister Carol Kruck, 68, are the great-great-grandchildren of Rupert and Allison Munro, the couple who homesteaded the land. Both Clarke and Carol grew up on that farm.

According to Carol, Rupert and Allison were born in Scotland before immigrating and marrying in Clinton, Ont., about 175 kilometres west of Toronto. The couple went on to raise nine children and came to Manitoba in 1870.

Between the family, Clarke said they homesteaded over 1,100 acres at the time in the area. He said he never heard exactly why the family chose to head west.

“I’m just guessing maybe it was the allure of new land,” Clarke said.

The family’s history carries its share of loss, too. Carol recalled that her grandfather was one of three children and the only member of his immediate family to survive tuberculosis, after his parents and siblings all died of the disease.

Clarke said his father, Allan, bought the quarter-section in 1944 from the widow of his great-uncle — one of Rupert and Allison’s sons — shortly after his great-uncle’s death. Allan then moved there from the neighbouring quarter-section, where he’d been living with his own parents, Rupert Allan and Catherine.

The land is now registered in Clarke’s name, alongside his wife Noreen, though he says he moved off the property in his early 20s when he got married. He said his 45-year-old son moved onto the farm over two decades ago, where he farms and lives with his wife and two kids.

“If my grandsons farm, I guess they’ll be the seventh generation,” Clarke said.

“I really think they will be the seventh generation,” added Carol, who lives on an adjacent quarter-section which has also long been in the family.

Clarke said none of the original structures from the 1870s remain on the property, though the farm’s log house, which he was told was original, was still standing when he was a child. He said it was removed several decades ago.

Livestock has been part of the farm’s operation for most of its history. Clarke said the farm has generally kept horses and cattle, aside from a 20 to 30-year stretch without them, and that his grandsons — active in 4-H — even have a few cows and calves of their own. The farm has also raised chickens and ducks over the years.

The family was planning a 150th anniversary celebration in 2022, but Clarke said a shed fire shortly before derailed those plans. The family is now aiming for the next milestone instead.

“We’re going to try to do something for the 155th. That’s the plan right now,” Clarke said.

As for why the farm has stayed in the family for so long, Carol credited their father Allan with handling the succession.

“My dad was a very, very fair person, and Clarke farmed with him as a teenager, and I was a non-farming sibling, but he was gracious,” said Carol, a retired accountant. “I feel he was very ahead of his time. Farm succession is a very problematic thing today, but dad made it so easy. He was very fair. It’s not even, but it’s fair, because Clarke is the farmer in the family.”

The siblings also emphasized that they have no intention to pressure the next generation to keep working the quarter section or carry on the farming tradition.

“I think it would be great, but I’m not putting pressure on them. It’s whatever they want to do,” Clarke said.

“I don’t think they need any pressure,” Carol said. “They want it.”

When asked what it feels like to know their family runs one of the province’s oldest family farms, both siblings landed on the same word: proud.

“I’m so proud of my brother and his children, and my dad, and everyone that has done this. It’s great,” Carol said.

CTV News also reached out to several other family farms recognized by the province that were established in the early 1870s for their story but did not hear back by the deadline.

The Manitoba Family Farm Recognition Program, run by the province’s agricultural department, recognizes family farms that have remained in continuous ownership by direct descendants of the original owner for 100, 125 or 150 consecutive years.

As of mid-July, a provincial spokesperson said 1,923 farms have received recognition under the program’s centennial milestone, and 165 have been recognized for reaching 125 years. Those are all-time figures, the spokesperson added, meaning some of the farms could have since been sold out of the family.

The changing economics of keeping a farm in the family

While families like the Mathesons and Munros have kept their land for generations, one industry advocate says the path to passing down a farm today looks different than it once did.

Colin Hornby, general manager of Keystone Agricultural Producers, said it’s difficult to say definitively whether multi-generational farms are becoming rarer in Manitoba, but he’s noticed a shift towards consolidation.

“What we’re seeing is perhaps what used to be a few family farms within the same family have now become one larger operation,” Hornby said. He added that consolidation lets families split costs and take advantage of economies of scale, such as sharing equipment or buying inputs in bulk for better prices.

Hornby said the total number of farms in Manitoba has substantially diminished over the years, even as the average farm size has grown.

However, a handful of Manitoba families have held on. Eight Manitoba farms have been recognized by the province for staying in the same family for 150 consecutive years or more, according to a provincial spokesperson.
CTV News spoke with two of those families about their farms’ history and looked at why keeping land in the family May be getting harder to do.
Matheson Family Farm
One of them is the Matheson family farm, south of Stonewall, which has remained in the same family since it was established in 1873.

“(It) is quite amazing, really,” said Tricia Harris, who owns and lives on the farm with her husband Rod. “That it has managed to stay in the family that long, because, as you can tell from the data, it doesn’t happen a lot.”

Tricia, 73, is the fourth generation to hold the land since her great-grandfather, Alexander Matheson, broke ground on it three years after Manitoba became a province — not long after surveyors first mapped out what is now the Rural Municipality of Rockwood.

To understand how the farm came to be, Tricia said you have to go back decades, to the era of the Selkirk Settlement. Also known as the Red River Colony, it was the first European agricultural settlement in Western Canada, with its first group of settlers arriving in 1812.

The colony spanned a vast tract of land, roughly 300,000 square kilometres — granted to Lord Selkirk, a Scottish nobleman, by the Hudson’s Bay Company — centred along the Red and Assiniboine rivers near present-day Winnipeg.
Among those who followed in 1814-15 was Alexander’s father, John “Bushy” Matheson, who arrived as a six-month-old baby with his parents.
“They came and settled along the Red River and farmed there for a number of years,” Tricia said.

She said John “Bushy” grew up in the Red River Settlement and learned multiple languages, including Indigenous languages, Gaelic and French. That multilingualism helped him become a constable there, breaking up disputes and serving warrants.

Tricia said travelling for his job eventually led him to learn of the “good land” in the present-day Stonewall region. In 1873, he moved there with one of his sons, Alexander — then a single man in his 20s — and the two took up adjoining quarter-sections.
Family legend has it that John “Bushy” stumbled onto more than just good land.

“The story is that his dad, John “Bushy,” was just kind of touring around the area on his horse and came across another family that had moved in… and he noticed they had some daughters, so he came home and told [Alexander], ‘I think I met your wife today,’” she said.

“And so, he told his son he better go over there and help them build their house. And he married one of the daughters,” Tricia said. Though how accurate that family tale is, she doesn’t entirely know.

That first year, only 10 acres of Alexander’s section were cleared, and a 1.5-storey log cabin went up. In 1875, Alexander married Catharine — a marriage that would last 65 years and result in five children.

From there, Tricia said the farm passed to Alexander’s youngest son, Willis, in 1917. Electricity reached the property in 1948, and in 1954 the farm passed again, this time to Willis’ niece, Linda, and her husband, Gordon Furness. This was the same year the first tractor arrived. Running water followed later that decade.

Tricia, the daughter of Linda and Gordon, took over ownership with her husband in 1983. She has lived on the farm since she was nine months old, aside from a few years away. Over the generations, the family has raised cattle and grain crops, along with chickens and pigs at various points.

None of the farm’s original buildings remain, Tricia said. However, a stone house built in 1904 by a Scottish stonemason with help from Alexander and his three sons still stands, and it’s where the couple lives today.

“It was built from the stone, the granite stone on the fields as they cleared land and pulled up these great big boulders. They stockpiled them until they had enough to build a two-storey stone house,” she said. “The house was a major accomplishment.”
But the farm’s history hasn’t been without hardship. In 1875, Tricia said detailed farm records kept by Alexander over his 44 years of farming show grasshoppers “completely destroyed” the crop.
She also said the adjoining quarter-section was lost after Willis Matheson couldn’t cover the land’s taxes while paying for his wife’s cancer treatment during the Great Depression.
“So, the farm was reduced in half,” she said.
And in 1965, Tricia said the stone house was “completely gutted” by fire, prompting her parents to rebuild the interior.

Despite the setbacks, the farm has endured, and in 2023, Tricia said about 70 relatives gathered there to celebrate 150 years of it being worked by one family. Among those in attendance was her mother Linda, then 104, who was able to make it to the special occasion.
“It was a great cousins’ reunion at that time,” Tricia said.
The couple, who also worked full time off the farm as teachers, completely retired from farming last year when they sold the last of their cattle.

As for how the farm has stayed in the family so long, Tricia said no one before her ever insisted that the next generation take it over and it’s not a pressure she and Rod are putting on their own four children, all of whom live in Winnipeg.

Still, the land continues to be farmed by a Matheson descendant — one of Tricia’s cousin’s sons, 41, who is the fifth generation to work it. The couple also looks after his cattle on the farm during the summer months.
“He lives just down the road on his own farm,” Tricia said, “which happens to be another Matheson homestead as well.”

Another farm the province recognizes as having stayed in the same family for over 150 years is the Munro family farm, which was established even earlier in 1872. The quarter-section is located just west of Portage la Prairie.
Clarke Munro, 71, and his sister Carol Kruck, 68, are the great-great-grandchildren of Rupert and Allison Munro, the couple who homesteaded the land. Both Clarke and Carol grew up on that farm.

According to Carol, Rupert and Allison were born in Scotland before immigrating and marrying in Clinton, Ont., about 175 kilometres west of Toronto. The couple went on to raise nine children and came to Manitoba in 1870.
Between the family, Clarke said they homesteaded over 1,100 acres at the time in the area. He said he never heard exactly why the family chose to head west.
“I’m just guessing maybe it was the allure of new land,” Clarke said.

The family’s history carries its share of loss, too. Carol recalled that her grandfather was one of three children and the only member of his immediate family to survive tuberculosis, after his parents and siblings all died of the disease.

Clarke said his father, Allan, bought the quarter-section in 1944 from the widow of his great-uncle — one of Rupert and Allison’s sons — shortly after his great-uncle’s death. Allan then moved there from the neighbouring quarter-section, where he’d been living with his own parents, Rupert Allan and Catherine.

The land is now registered in Clarke’s name, alongside his wife Noreen, though he says he moved off the property in his early 20s when he got married. He said his 45-year-old son moved onto the farm over two decades ago, where he farms and lives with his wife and two kids.
“If my grandsons farm, I guess they’ll be the seventh generation,” Clarke said.
“I really think they will be the seventh generation,” added Carol, who lives on an adjacent quarter-section which has also long been in the family.

Clarke said none of the original structures from the 1870s remain on the property, though the farm’s log house, which he was told was original, was still standing when he was a child. He said it was removed several decades ago.

Livestock has been part of the farm’s operation for most of its history. Clarke said the farm has generally kept horses and cattle, aside from a 20 to 30-year stretch without them, and that his grandsons — active in 4-H — even have a few cows and calves of their own. The farm has also raised chickens and ducks over the years.
The family was planning a 150th anniversary celebration in 2022, but Clarke said a shed fire shortly before derailed those plans. The family is now aiming for the next milestone instead.
“We’re going to try to do something for the 155th. That’s the plan right now,” Clarke said.
As for why the farm has stayed in the family for so long, Carol credited their father Allan with handling the succession.

“My dad was a very, very fair person, and Clarke farmed with him as a teenager, and I was a non-farming sibling, but he was gracious,” said Carol, a retired accountant. “I feel he was very ahead of his time. Farm succession is a very problematic thing today, but dad made it so easy. He was very fair. It’s not even, but it’s fair, because Clarke is the farmer in the family.”
The siblings also emphasized that they have no intention to pressure the next generation to keep working the quarter section or carry on the farming tradition.
“I think it would be great, but I’m not putting pressure on them. It’s whatever they want to do,” Clarke said.
“I don’t think they need any pressure,” Carol said. “They want it.”
When asked what it feels like to know their family runs one of the province’s oldest family farms, both siblings landed on the same word: proud.
“I’m so proud of my brother and his children, and my dad, and everyone that has done this. It’s great,” Carol said.

According to the province, the oldest family farm on record under the Manitoba Family Farm Recognition Program was established in 1870 — the only recognized farm dating back to that year. It last requested recognition under the program in 2024.

Families can apply for recognition at any time after reaching the 100, 125, or 150-year milestone, a spokesperson said, provided the farm meets the eligibility requirements and has supporting documents to prove ownership.

Where that farm is located, and the family’s story behind it, is hard to say. The family chose not to give permission to share their information on the application form, the provincial spokesperson said. That’s also the case for the farm established in 1871, the second-oldest on record.
As for whether an even older family farm is still out there, being worked by the same family, it’s possible. The spokesperson notes that participation in the recognition program is voluntary.

stories.title: Father-son duo highlight of roadside beef jerky scene for more than 20 years
stories.summary: On Saturday, just east of Sherwood Park, the Alberta Beef Jerky Boy is setting up shop outside the Country Mercantile.
stories.author: Hannah Kavanagh
paragraphs: On Saturday, just east of Sherwood Park, the Alberta Beef Jerky Boy is setting up shop outside the Country Mercantile.

Danny Koenig has been running his side hustle for roughly 20 years. He made it a father-son duo when he brought along 35-year-old Justin, who has cerebral palsy, as a way to bond. Justin says he loves the opportunity to meet new people every Saturday.

“People like our products,” he told CTV News Edmonton. The products, coolers upon coolers of Alberta beef jerky, steaks, cheese, baking and other goods sell out quickly as customers flock during their weekend errands.
The longevity of the roadside stand is a testament to its popularity, some say. Regular customer Al Jacobs says it’s an easy way to support “fresh, convenient” local products.
“It’s like visiting with friends. We end up spending usually a half hour just hanging out and visiting,” he said.
Danny says it’s the community that’s made the work a “legacy.”

“I think people know that you’re giving a good deal. I try to keep my prices down because I don’t have an overhead. I’m honest to people about what I carry … I usually carry the best of the best of the beef,” he said.
“The crowd is overwhelming. They’re beautiful people … I like to talk it through with them, and sometimes we have great moments here.”
He says he’s spoken to people at their lowest, people from out of town, locals who are out running errands and those who just want some good Alberta beef.
Danny works a full-time job but still manages to maintain the bins of beef all 12 months of the year.
“In the fall the beard gets big, and some of the old ladies come up to me and say, ‘Where’s the other guy?’ and I go, ‘I am that other guy,’” he joked.
And he’ll retire, someday – if they let him.
“I believe that people out here want me to be here … I’ve come close a couple times to retirement already, and people say no, so that kind of drives me to do it. It’s a beautiful thing.
“The community out here has been so good to us.”
With files from CTV News Edmonton’s Curtis Goodrum

stories.title: Former Surrey RCMP officer sentenced to 18 months in jail for breach of trust
stories.summary: A former Surrey RCMP officer who pleaded guilty to breach of trust earlier this year has been sentenced, six years after the undercover operation that led to 13 charges against him.
stories.author: Ian Holliday
stories.content:
A former Surrey RCMP officer who pleaded guilty to breach of trust earlier this year has been sentenced, six years after the undercover operation that led to 13 charges against him .

Dawwd Alaaeldine Soukary was sentenced Thursday to 18 months in jail. B.C. Supreme Court Justice Murray B. Blok accepted a joint submission from Crown and defence lawyers recommending that sentence.

The charge Soukary pleaded guilty to in April alleged that he had committed breach of trust by “accessing confidential police databases and files for a purpose inconsistent with his duties as a police officer” between Nov. 30, 2020 and his arrest on Jan. 27, 2021.

Blok’s decision sheds additional light on the context of those breaches.

59 undercover scenarios

According to the decision, the RCMP received a report “supported by Cctv footage” that Soukary was involved in purchasing a significant volume of drugs on behalf of two suspected criminals, referred to in the decision as MN and AH.

The tip was received in August 2020, but investigators “did not gather any further evidence supporting this drug trafficking allegation, and no charges resulted,” Blok’s decision notes.

At the time, Soukary was a probationary officer with the Surrey RCMP. The person who provided the tip said Soukary had indicated that once he was allowed to work without supervision, he planned to use police databases to obtain information for his criminal associates.

“The RCMP formulated and then implemented a plan to recruit Mr. Soukary as an undercover operator for a fictitious undercover operation targeting a fictitious drug trafficker,” the decision reads.

“He was paired with another undercover operator who pretended to be corrupt and associate with drug traffickers. The goal of this fictitious operation was to arrange a purchase of a kilogram of cocaine from a particular big-time (but also fictional) trafficker, but the real target of the operation was Mr. Soukary.”

Beginning in October 2020 and continuing up until his arrest in January 2021, investigators staged “43 undercover scenarios consisting of interactions between Mr. Soukary and his fictitiously corrupt partner, and 16 additional scenarios involving the sham undercover drug investigation,” according to the decision.

The sting culminated with a scenario in which Soukary was given $72,000 to purchase a one-kilogram cocaine brick from the fictional trafficker.

The court decision indicates Soukary told his fake partner that the market value of such a brick was $55,000 to $60,000, and that he intended to negotiate a lower price with the trafficker and then pocket the proceeds.

The fake partner encouraged this behaviour, and when Soukary paid just $63,000 for the drugs, he gave the fake partner $1,000 and kept the remaining $8,000 for himself, according to the decision.

“Mr. Soukary was arrested shortly afterward, at which time $8,000 was found on his person,” the decision reads. “The $63,000 in purchase money was obviously recovered, as it never left RCMP hands, the $1,000 paid to the other undercover operator was also accounted for, and the cocaine (which was real) also never left RCMP control.”

Investigators seized, searched and analyzed Soukary’s phone, finding that he had “repeatedly texted” photos of confidential information he obtained while working solo during the fake undercover investigation to MN and AH.

“There is no evidence that the confidential information Mr. Soukary shared compromised any active RCMP investigations and no evidence that the shared information led to any other criminal conduct,” the decision reads, citing an agreed statement of facts in the case.

‘Substantial triable issues’

Blok’s decision describes Soukary as a 31-year-old son of Egyptian immigrants who was born and raised in Ottawa and grew up in “underprivileged circumstances.”

After his arrest, he resigned from the RCMP and returned to Ottawa, working as a Realtor before “shifting to work at a soccer and athletic performance gym,” according to the decision.

While it’s not mentioned in the court document, Soukary voluntarily terminated his registration with the Real Estate Council of Ontario after the regulator accused him with failing to notify it of criminal charges laid against him.

Soukary entered an undertaking not to reapply for registration with the Reco before July 1 of this year.

Blok’s decision summarizes arguments from both the Crown and defence in support of their joint submission.

Prosecutors noted the seriousness of the offence and the repeated nature of Soukary’s decision to access and share confidential information.

They also highlighted his guilty plea as a “significant sign of remorse,” his lack of a prior criminal record, and his relative youth: He was 25 years old at the time of the offence.

Soukary’s defence lawyers highlighted the RCMP’s tactics in investigating him, noting that the undercover operation “aimed to create a climate that normalized police corruption and tempted him with opportunities to commit offences.”

“The defence notes the significant benefits of Mr. Soukary’s guilty plea and joint submission on sentence,” the decision reads.

“There were substantial triable issues and, in particular, a genuine issue as to the extent to which the police created the circumstances that led to the offences. The evidence would have required the court to carefully consider whether the police conduct crossed the line into entrapment.”

Blok ultimately accepted the joint submission, finding that it was reasonable in the circumstances and would not bring the administration of justice into disrepute or be contrary to the public interest.

The judge sentenced Soukary to 18 months in jail, ordered him to provide a DNA sample, and required him to pay a $200 victim surcharge.

The other 12 charges against Soukary have been stayed by the Crown.

stories.title: Last evacuation order lifted for Ainslie Creek wildfire in B.C.
stories.summary: Regional district says an order has been downgraded to an evacuation alert for 58 addressed properties
paragraphs: The Thompson-Nicola Regional District in southern British Columbia has lifted the last of its evacuation orders related to the out-of-control Ainslie Creek wildfire.
The regional district says an order has been downgraded to an evacuation alert for 58 addressed properties in the Coldwater and Patchett Road areas.
Another 94 properties that had been under evacuation alert were declared all clear.
B.C. ends provincial state of emergency as wildfires continue to burn
An evacuation order issued by the Spuzzum First Nation remained in place as of Saturday afternoon related to the fire that was last measured at 677 square kilometres.
The regional district says in a statement that approximately 248 properties it covers remain on evacuation alert as of Saturday afternoon.
It says property owners are free to return but should use caution and be aware of any hazards in the area.

stories.title: GM plans Ontario pickup production in deal that would pump $1.1-billion into Canada’s auto sector
stories.summary: Tentative agreement with Unifor comes as Canadian automakers grapple with U.S. tariffs and uncertainty over future trade negotiations
stories.author: Allison Lampert
paragraphs: General Motors GM-N plans to assemble a heavy-duty pickup at an Ontario plant as part of a tentative deal with a key union that would pump $1.1-billion into Canada’s auto sector as it reels from U.S. tariffs, a union bargaining report said on Saturday.

The investment comes as Canada’s auto sector grapples with 25 per cent U.S. tariffs on vehicles, with U.S. President Donald Trump pledging to double them to 50 per cent on Jan. 1, 2027. The fate of Canadian auto plants has emerged as a central issue in stalled U.S.-Canada trade negotiations.

GM plans to spend $144-million to add the next-generation heavy-duty GMC Sierra truck to a plant in Oshawa, and pledged not to immediately sell or close a second assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ontario, according to the bargaining report from the union Unifor.
Escalation tactics in trade negotiations with the U.S. prove to be a minefield
The deal is contingent on approval from workers who are voting on Saturday and Sunday. Both Unifor and GM’s Canadian division declined to comment during the vote.
The $1.1-billion investment includes a $691-million commitment to support production of new V8 engines in Ontario that was previously announced in April, the report said.
The tentative agreement was reached last Saturday between GM and Unifor on behalf of 4,600 union members in Canada’s most populous province, Ontario.

U.S. President Donald Trump, who has clashed with Ontario Premier Doug Ford in recent days, has also said he will increase tariffs on all Canadian cars and trucks, automotive parts and steel to 50 per cent starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Autos are a key part of talks between the United States and its northern neighbour to reduce U.S. tariffs on Canadian-produced vehicles. Negotiations ended last week over unresolved issues, such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories.
Canada has said it cannot accept a trade deal with the U.S. unless the agreement ensures the survival of a robust Canadian auto assembly and parts industry.
Opinion: As insults fly between Ford and Trump, consequences loom

United States Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has said Canadian negotiators only raised demands to include medium-and heavy-duty trucks on Friday at 4 p.m. just ahead of a deadline for securing a deal .
The tentative deal with Unifor would invest $215-million to assemble a new generation transmission at a separate factory in St. Catharines, Ontario, starting in late 2029.

GM also committed to not close or sell its Cami assembly plant, formally known as Canadian Automotive Manufacturing Inc., in Ingersoll while it studies alternative production for the factory. The plant would have priority to do defence work for the Canadian Armed Forces, in the event the auto maker secures a contract for such output, the bargaining report said.
Editor’s note: This article has been updated to correct the spelling of St. Catharines, Ontario.

stories.title: Transit, home care and immigration dominate Day 3 of Quebec election
stories.summary: The debate over immigration came on the third day of the provincial election campaign, as Quebec’s party leaders fanned out across the province.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s plan to more than halve temporary immigration in Quebec drew criticism from his rivals Saturday, who accused him of making immigrants bear the blame for problems in public schools and of risking worsening the province’s labour shortage.

St-Pierre Plamondon said a PQ government would reduce the number of temporary immigrants in Quebec from more than 500,000 to between 200,000 and 250,000, arguing current levels have exceeded the province’s capacity to provide housing and public services.

The debate over immigration came on the third day of the provincial election campaign, as Quebec’s party leaders fanned out across the province with promises on public transit, home care, gasoline prices and the economy.

“We’re facing a total loss of control of our immigration system,” he said outside a Quebec City high school where modular classrooms are being used to accommodate students.

St-Pierre Plamondon blamed the governing Coalition Avenir Québec for the sharp rise in temporary immigration, targeting CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette over her previous tenure as immigration minister.

As it reduced temporary immigration, the sovereigntist PQ would protect sectors that rely heavily on temporary workers, including agriculture, manufacturing and health care, while taking regional needs into account, he said.

The party also reiterated its pledge to reduce permanent immigration to 35,000 people a year, down from the government’s current target of 45,000. Until its temporary immigration target is reached, it would select economic immigrants seeking permanent residence from among temporary immigrants already in Quebec rather than from abroad.

St-Pierre Plamondon rejected suggestions that he was blaming immigrants themselves for strains on public services.

“Never will the Parti Québécois blame people who become Quebecers,” he said. “We blame the CAQ and the federal government.”

Also campaigning in Quebec City, Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal criticized St-Pierre Plamondon’s decision to make the announcement outside a school, accusing him of making immigrant children bear the blame for overcrowding and deteriorating school infrastructure.

“I find it appalling that Mr. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon continues to talk about immigration in such a negative way,” Ghazal said. “I was that immigrant child myself, a child of Bill 101.”

Bill 101, Quebec’s landmark French-language law, generally requires children of immigrants to attend French-language schools.

Ghazal blamed successive governments for years of underinvestment in public schools, adding: “We can’t make immigrant children bear the blame for that.”

In Shawinigan, Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard also criticized the PQ proposal, arguing it would worsen Quebec’s labour shortage as businesses grapple with the U.S. trade war.

“It’s the worst time to tell the business community and entrepreneurs that we’re going to have even less labour,” Milliard said.

Earlier Saturday in Drummondville, CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette appealed to sovereigntist voters who are reluctant to hold a referendum in the coming years to back her party rather than the PQ.

“Many people who would be tempted to vote Yes (…) are aware that this is the worst time in the last 50 years to hold a referendum,” she said, pointing to the trade war with the United States.

Fréchette also promised an additional $1 billion over four years for homecare services.

Elsewhere, Ghazal pledged $23 billion over 10 years to repair and expand public transit infrastructure.

Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime promised to pull Quebec out of its cap-and-trade carbon market and suspend the province’s 19.2-cent-per-litre fuel tax for five months, measures he said would lower gasoline prices by about 33 cents a litre.

Milliard also promised to reduce red tape for small and medium-sized businesses.

stories.title: One Canadian found safe after catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods, Anand says
stories.summary: At least 31 other Canadians remain unaccounted for as rescuers search flood-ravaged areas along the Nepal-Tibet border
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
paragraphs: The brother of a Canadian man among those missing after flash floods swept through an area along the Nepal-Tibet border says their family is on edge waiting for information.

Dhaval Shah and his wife Megha Shah, from Port Moody, B.C., were on a spiritual journey in Nepal when the floods hit. Dhaval’s brother Kheval Shah, reached at his home in Mumbai, India, said his family is desperate to know if they’ve been rescued or found.
“Everybody is on edge to get some news, if they’re rescued or found or something. Something which will make the family understand what happened to them,” Kheval Shah said in an interview Saturday.
“We’re hoping that they find them and some miracles happen and we see them again,” he added.

After Nepali authorities updated their figures Saturday, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 676 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities have reported seven deaths and more than 550 missing, while Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 669 with 2,426 people missing.
Families comb through lists of missing people in Nepal as steep mountains hamper rescue efforts
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing in the disaster had been found safely.
“This brings the total number of Canadians whose whereabouts haven’t been confirmed to 31. This number May still fluctuate as new information comes in,” Anand said in a statement.
No Canadians are among the 121 foreign nationals the Nepal Tourism Board said Friday had been rescued.
Nepalese community organizations across the country cancelled annual cultural festivals this weekend following the devastating floods.

This weekend would normally be the annual Teej festival, a Hindu practice celebrating womanhood, but organizers in cities including Toronto, Brampton and Calgary cancelled celebrations in light of the disaster.

Punam Dhungel, president of the Nepali Canadian Women’s Society of B.C., saID her organization canceled their event for the first time, but decided to redirect $15,000 in ticket sales to humanitarian relief efforts.
Rescuers have pulled survivors caked in dark mud and helicopters lifted stranded people to safety after catastrophic floods on the Nepal-China border.
The Associated Press

Many of the missing were believed to have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others. Hundreds of others have been displaced across the Himalayan region.
Religious pilgrims from Canada at building swept away in Tibet-Nepal border floods

Shah said he last heard from his brother on Monday, and a cousin of theirs heard from the couple on Tuesday. He believes his brother and sister-in-law were waiting for immigration offices to open in order to leave Nepal at the Tibet border when the flash floods hit.
He said the Canadian government should press Nepal for answers and more information about missing Canadians.
“I know they’re doing something, but I feel that they must really push... to find where they are and to get some information,” Shah said.
Canada has said it will send $5-million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal as of Saturday.
With reports from the Associated Press and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Doug Ford erects sign to remind Donald Trump 'it's Lake Ontario now and forever'
stories.summary: "Let's be serious. Long before Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after Trump is gone it will still be called Lake Ontario."
stories.author: Anisha Dhiman
paragraphs: 'Let's be serious. Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after President Trump is gone it will still be called Lake Ontario,' Ford said on X
Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a new sign in Winona, Ont. to remind Donald Trump “it’s Lake Ontario , now and forever.”
Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.
Access articles from across Canada with one account.
Enjoy additional articles per month.

Ford’s message comes less than a week after he told the U.S. president to “ kiss my ass ” in response to Trump threatening to impose 50 per cent tariff against Canadian automobiles and auto parts. Trump, in retaliation, called Ford a “flunky.”

In a 39-second video posted on X on Saturday, the Ontario premier said, “You May have heard that President Trump is trying to rename this lake all because he doesn’t like Ontario and Canada standing up for ourselves. But let’s be serious. Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario.”

Ford continued: “And long after President Trump is gone it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”
It’s Lake Ontario, now and always. pic.twitter.com/KNahtPAMeJ — Doug Ford (@fordnation) August 29, 2026

On Thursday, the U.S. president signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, bordered by New York State and Ontario, to “Lake America.” The change, Trump said, will come into effect “immediately.”

After the trade deal fell apart between the two countries on Aug. 21, tensions between Canada and the U.S. have been high. When asked on Thursday if he was trying to send Canada a message with the executive order, Trump said, “Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly,” and that “we defend Canada for nothing; they don’t pay us.”
Trump’s order has drawn flak not just from Canadian politicians but also politicians down south.

“An acronym for the Great Lakes used to be Homes. Thanks to Donald Trump, it’s now Shame,” New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s office said in a post on X. The executive order was branded “ sad and pathetic ” by U.S. Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer. And U.S. Rep. Joe Morelle said on X that “pretending to rename a lake is an attempted distraction from the President’s disastrous trade talks with Canada.”
We’re not changing it. pic.twitter.com/NdeE9v2BNO — MapQuest (@MapQuest) August 27, 2026

Meanwhile, American mapping company MapQuest in a social media post announced “we’re not changing it,” and shared an image of Lake Ontario and surrounding communities. The company jokingly invited social media users to “name it whatever you want at your leisure,” in a follow-up post with some suggestions that include “ Lake Double-Double, Lake Eh and Lake Oh Canada .”

stories.title: Buck Martinez honoured as Blue Jays unveil Hall of Excellence at Rogers Centre
stories.summary: The Toronto Blue Jays opened their new Hall of Excellence on Saturday ahead of an afternoon ceremony for 2026 inductee Buck Martinez at Rogers Centre.
stories.author: John Marchesan
paragraphs: By Tim Wharnsby, The Canadian Press
Posted August 29, 2026 4:07 pm.
Last Updated August 29, 2026 6:22 pm.
John Albert (Buck) Martinez, a cancer survivor, catcher, manager and broadcaster for parts of five decades with the Toronto Blue Jays, was inducted into the club’s new Hall of Excellence on Saturday.

As part of their 50th season celebrations, the Blue Jays unveiled the section to honour the franchise’s greatest contributors. The 11 honourees from the former Level of Excellence were enshrined in the hall, located on the concourse behind right field at Rogers Centre.

The 77-year-old Martinez was honoured before the Blue Jays’ matinee against the Seattle Mariners. His popularity across Canada exploded during his lengthy stint as a team broadcaster, a position he retired from last winter.
“Today blew me away,” Martinez said. “I didn’t have any grasp of the magnitude of today.”
Martinez added he was also blown away when newcomer Brett Bateman stopped him underneath the stands to congratulate him, saying he knew what Martinez meant to the Blue Jays and their fan base.
He also told a story of visiting England in July. Martinez was having a beer with a friend when a group of ladies walked by. They circled back to say hello because they recognized his voice.
He made a point of saying how much Canadians meant to him.

“First thing they tell you is where they’re from,” Martinez said. “They say I’m from New Brunswick. I’m from Calgary. I came in from Winnipeg. They’re so proud that they came this far to watch the Blue Jays, and that’s the impact the Blue Jays have had on this entire country.”
Martinez joins José Bautista, Paul Beeston, George Bell, Joe Carter, Tom Cheek, Carlos Delgado, Tony Fernandez, Cito Gaston, Pat Gillick, Roy Halladay and Dave Stieb in the hall.

The Level of Excellence will remain on the fascia within the ballpark bowl through the remainder of the season. It will be relocated next year within the stadium’s bowl, where the names will remain visible to fans.

The Californian, who now lives in Florida, flew north to Toronto on a plane with Gaston and Bautista. Delgado, Bell, Carter, Stieb, Beeston and Gillick helped open the new hall and take in Martinez’s ceremony.

“He was an awesome teammate,” Stieb said at a morning media availability. “He was especially special for me because, as you know, I was quite a battler out there. I would lose my emotions at times, and Buck just had a knack for calming me down and keeping me focused on the task at hand.”

Building on the legacy of the Level of Excellence, the hall will provide a space to honour players, coaches, managers, builders and broadcasters – past, present and future – to bring generations of fans closer to the people who shaped the Blue Jays, the team said.

Martinez was a Blue Jays catcher (1981-1986) and manager (2001-2002) who enjoyed two stints as a team broadcaster (1987-2000, 2010-2025). The fan favourite was diagnosed with head and neck cancer in April 2022 and lung cancer in May 2025.
He went 100-115 before being let go as Toronto’s manager in May 2002. As a catcher, he was constantly asked about a play in game at Seattle on July 9, 1985.

In the bottom of the third inning, Martinez tagged out Phil Bradley on a throw from right-fielder Jesse Barfield. But Martinez broke his leg and dislocated his ankle in the violent collision at the plate.

Still, a seated Martinez tried to throw out advancing runner Gorman Thomas at third. But his toss sailed into left field, where George Bell threw a strike back to the injured catcher for a memorable 9-2-7-2 double play.
“I picked up the end of the stretcher to help carry him off the field,” Bell said. “He was yelling at me in pain. It turns out his [broken] leg and ankle were rubbing against me.”

“It was an incredible play,” Stieb added. “To have your leg broken and still have the wherewithal to try to throw somebody out was unbelievable.” Martinez retired as a player in 1986 after a 17-year Major League Baseball career with the Blue Jays, Kansas City Royals and Milwaukee Brewers.
His broadcasting career began in 1982 while still an active player for the Blue Jays. Martinez started by covering playoff games and the all-star game for the Telemedia Radio Network.
He began his television broadcasting career in 1987 as a colour analyst and went on to call over 4,000 Blue Jays games over his career.

His final appearance in the broadcast booth came last fall when he called the World Series with longtime broadcast partner Dan Shulman on Sportsnet. The Los Angeles Dodgers defeated the Blue Jays in the deciding seventh game.
Martinez has also provided commentary for Espn, XM Radio, TBS, The Baseball Network, TSN, and MLB International over his career.
In 2023, he was awarded the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame’s Jack Graney Award for his significant contributions to baseball in Canada.

stories.title: Byelection called as B.C. Conservative leader faces questions over leaked audio
stories.summary: B.C. Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay currently does not hold a seat in the legislature. The byelection is set for Sept. 26.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A byelection has been called in British Columbia after a B.C. Conservative MLA resigned last week, giving leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay a chance to sit in the legislature.

But in many ways, the timing could not be worse for Findlay, whose caucus has lost six MLAs in recent weeks.

An audio recording appeared on social media Thursday of a person who sounds like Findlay saying she thought if someone stepped aside as a legislator, “I could give them a role as senior adviser in their same portfolio.”

The MLA who resigned, Reann Gasper, has since become Findlay’s deputy chief of staff.

Findlay has addressed the recording and said suggestions it shows her illegally offering jobs to legislators in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a byelection are “preposterous.”

The B.C. Conservative leader currently does not hold a seat in the legislature. The byelection is set for Sept. 26.

Trevor Bolin, the party’s former leader, said the timing of the audio’s release “couldn’t be worse” because of various issues facing the Conservatives.

“I think, you know, Kerri-Lynne needs to get a handle on not only her leadership with the caucus, but as well as the MLAs and the members in British Columbia,” Bolin told Global News.

Findlay said on social media Thursday that it appeared the “unverified” audio recording was made at a July caucus meeting, calling it a “political smear job.”

It is illegal under the Criminal Code to negotiate a reward or benefit related to resignation from political office, but Findlay said the comments in the recording, published by an anonymous account known as “The Findlay Files,” were “normal political discussions” that did not constitute a criminal offence.

In addition to the Criminal Code bribery prohibition, which is subject to up to five years’ prison, BC legislature standing orders ban the offer of money or other advantages to members for promoting any matter “depending or to be transacted” in the house.

The B.C. RCMP said it was aware of the social media post.

“However, generally speaking, the RCMP does not confirm or deny any investigation, or the identity of any person who May be subject to an investigation, until such time as charges have been laid,” a spokesperson said in an email Friday.

It’s not only the audio hanging over Findlay going into a byelection. Six MLAs have left the party in the past month, four of them in the past week.

The exodus began Aug. 14, when longtime MLA Peter Milobar announced he would leave the party to sit as an independent.

About 10 days later, Ian Paton left the BC Conservatives and signalled he and Milobar planned to form a new party before the fall legislative session.

Since Aug. 24, four others have left: Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman.

Bolin also said he’s hearing six to eight more Conservative MLAs could leave before the fall sitting.

“There’s obviously an issue in the party, there’s an issue in caucus, there’s an issue with the executive,” he said. “Don’t hide from it, don’t deny it, take it head on and fix this issue because the last thing we need is more centre-to-right parties popping up just to split that vote.”

He added he believes the party can recover ahead of a potential general election, which has to be held no later than October 2028, but encouraged Findlay to change the closed-door meetings policy, improve transparency and work with communities and her MLAs.

“Parties last forever, leaders come and go, MLAs come and go, politicians have expiry dates, but at the end of the day, the platforms and the policies that the members put in place are what lasts a lifetime,” he said.

If Findlay chooses to run in the riding, she would face former NDP MLA and agriculture and food minister Pam Alexis. Alexis was elected in the 2020 election before losing to Gasper in 2024 by about 2,600 votes.

OneBC Leader Dallas Brodie said in a post on X on Saturday that her party does not intend to run a candidate despite support she said they have in the Fraser Valley.

“I do not believe it would be ethical to run in a race to try and block a major party leader from getting into the legislature to lead her caucus,” she wrote.

Brodie called on CentreBC and the likely party led by Milobar and Paton to not run candidates, either under their banners or as independents.

Findlay thanked Brodie for her stance and said it would send a message to the B.C. NDP. She did not confirm in the post if she will be running.

Milobar, along with fellow defector Ian Paton, have said they plan to start a new party after leaving Findlay’s caucus. In an interview Saturday, Milobar said they are still working with Elections BC on the process to become official.

He said both he and Paton want their party to be credible and that people “will want to see more meat on the bone of the party that we’re setting up.”

“If it was three months down the road, I’m fully confident we’d be well equipped to put a good effort in and have a credible candidate and be a force, but we’re not in that situation,” he said.

“We’re five days post announcement (of plans for the new party) and the byelection has been called.”

— with files from Global News’ Amy Judd and The Canadian Press

stories.title: This 98-year-old ‘Doll House’ in Regina is getting a makeover
stories.summary: There is a one-of-a-kind residence in the Lakeview neighbourhood of Regina that has stood since 1928. Nicknamed “The Doll House,” 2812 McCallum Ave. is one of Regina’s municipal heritage properties, earning the title in 1983.
stories.author: Ardenn Lloyd
paragraphs: There is a one-of-a-kind residence in the Lakeview neighbourhood of Regina that has stood since 1928.
Nicknamed “The Doll House,” 2812 McCallum Ave. is one of Regina’s municipal heritage properties, earning the title in 1983.

Built as a wedding gift by architect W.G. Van Egmond for his daughter Isabelle, the home features Swiss-chalet design with a steep gable roof, heavy cedar shingles and triangular architecture modeling in every nook and cranny of the home.
But after 98 years of withstanding the prairie weather, the house needed someone to step in to maintain and renovate it.

Daniel Hunt moved in May 1, 2025, after purchasing the house a few months prior. Since then, it has been restoration central. The original wiring, including the electrical fireplace from the late 1920s, was still installed posing a large fire hazard. Hunt also soon discovered the house had never been insulated.

Even the siding of the house itself needed some patchwork done to it. Not as hard of a task as finding the heavy cedar shingles themselves to replace the ones that had broke. The thick cut planks aren’t exactly as common to use today as opposed to a century ago.
Between bringing the house up to modern code and re-painting the exterior, there is nobody else Heritage Regina President Jackie Schmidt would rather have up to the task.

“We were over the moon when we found out who bought this house. [Hunt] has a track record of maintaining heritage properties, he understands what he has to do. he understands that he is just the steward of this property, his job is to take care of it and pass it on to the next person.” she said.
With the help of Hunt, the one-of-a-kind home will hopefully stand for another 100 years, bringing joy to all those who pass by. A heritage mission Hunt himself wants to embody.

“If we don’t live in these homes and value them and put our time and money and effort into them, they go by the way. My philosophy of heritage is if we want to preserve it, it has to be living, we have to live in it,” he said.

Hunt’s job is not finished yet, but the doll house is breathing new life and colour into the Lakeview community. Those interested in the colourful property can see it for themselves with the Heritage Regina Walking Tours.

stories.title: Ford unveils Lake Ontario sign days after Trump’s Lake America order
stories.summary: The two traded personal insults in interviews and social media posts over the past week amid a Canada-U.S. trade war
stories.author: David Shribman
stories.content:
Premier Doug Ford unveiled a Lake Ontario sign at a park on the shores of the Great Lake on Saturday, two days after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to change its name to Lake America.

Clad in a red Canada Soccer jersey, Ford pulled a tarp off the large blue sign, revealing the words “Now and Always” below the lake’s name.

Standing in front of the sign at Fifty Point Conservation Area in Hamilton, Ont., Ford said he wanted to send a message to Trump that Canadians are resilient and strong and “we will never, ever back down from a bully.”

It’s Lake Ontario, now and always. pic.twitter.com/KNahtPAMeJ — Doug Ford (@fordnation) August 29, 2026

The lake will always be known as Lake Ontario in Canada and the rest of the world, no matter what Trump calls it, he added.

Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ford earlier this week sparked by the breakdown of Canada-U.S. trade talks .

The two exchanged insults, with Ford saying the president could “kiss my ass,” among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a “less charismatic, intelligent” version of his late brother, Rob.

Opinion: As insults fly between Ford and Trump, consequences loom

Ford’s latest move failed to impress some who witnessed the sign’s unveiling.

Ankur Patel, who was at the lakefront during the event, said Ford and Trump’s shots at each other and the controversy around the lake’s name change are little more than political theatre.

“It’s just unnecessary, it’s getting more attention than it needs to. I think the focus should be trade negotiation,” he said.

“It doesn’t help or do anything, it just distracts,” Patel said of the sign.

Canada, being the smaller economy, has more to lose in a trade war with the U.S., Patel said, and he would like to see politicians’ energies going toward hashing out a deal.

Explainer: Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

Trump’s executive order renaming the lake only holds water in the U.S. and Prime Minister Mark Carney has shrugged off the change.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America,” Carney wrote on social media Thursday, affirming the Lake Ontario name persists “then, now and always.”

The Lake Ontario sign is just the latest development in the Canada-U.S. trade war, which has seen the U.S. impose 50 per cent tariffs on about $28-billion of Canadian goods.

The federal government has responded with 15 to 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of U.S. products to take effect on Sept. 8.

stories.title: B.C. premier calls by-election in riding where Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay is set to run
stories.summary: Findlay has had a rocky tenure, with six MLAs leaving her caucus to sit as independents this month
stories.author: Gary Mason
paragraphs: B.C. Premier David Eby has called a by-election for next month in the riding of Abbotsford-Mission, where embattled Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay is set to run.

Eby’s New Democrats said Saturday that former agriculture minister Pam Alexis, who lost the seat in the 2024 provincial election by fewer than 3,000 votes, will be back on the ballot in the Sept. 26 vote.

But Peter Milobar, part of the exodus of Conservative MLAs who have left Findlay’s caucus this month , said it’s “highly unlikely” there will be enough time for the new party he is hoping to create to have a candidate in the race.

The seat became vacant when Conservative MLA Reann Gasper resigned earlier this month to give Findlay a chance to get a seat in the legislature. She has since taken a paid position as Findlay’s deputy chief of staff.
B.C. Conservatives to gather for crisis meeting on Monday after departure of five MLAs
Findlay was elected party leader in May but her tenure has been far from smooth, with six MLAs leaving her caucus to sit as independents this month, including five in the span of a week.
The defectors have questioned her leadership and the direction in which she is taking the party, with one suggesting she was “unelectable.”

Milobar, along with fellow defector Ian Paton, have said they plan to start a new party after leaving Findlay’s caucus. In an interview Saturday, Milobar said they are still working with Elections BC on the process to become official.
He said both he and Paton want their party to be credible and that people “will want to see more meat on the bone of the party that we’re setting up.”
“If it was three months down the road, I’m fully confident we’d be well equipped to put a good effort in and have a credible candidate and be a force, but we’re not in that situation,” he said.
“We’re five days post announcement (of plans for the new party) and the byelection has been called.”
Opinion: The shocking implosion of B.C.’s Conservative Party
Findlay posted on social media on Saturday, calling for “unity now.”
“Let’s send the NDP a message that our support is positive, inclusive and determined to build on the foundation that (Gasper) has built in Abbotsford-Mission,” she said.
A statement from Elections BC said candidate nominations close at 1 p.m. on Sept. 5. Advance voting will run from Sept.18 to 23.
Alexis was elected as MLA for Abbotsford-Mission in 2020 and previously has been the mayor of Mission.

In a statement released by the party on Saturday, she said the NDP is working on issues like health care and housing while the provincial Conservatives are “focusing on culture wars over the things that matter most.”
Along with losing multiple MLAs, the Conservative Party has seen multiple high profile departures of staff, including the president and executive director.
Findlay is set to host a press conference in Richmond on Monday with the B.C. Conservative caucus.

“Let’s send the NDP a message that our support is positive, inclusive and determined to build on the foundation that (Gasper) has built in Abbotsford-Mission,” she said.

A statement from Elections BC said candidate nominations close at 1 p.m. on Sept. 5. Advance voting will run from Sept.18 to 23.

Alexis was elected as MLA for Abbotsford-Mission in 2020 and previously has been the mayor of Mission.

In a statement released by the party on Saturday, she said the NDP is working on issues like health care and housing while the provincial Conservatives are “focusing on culture wars over the things that matter most.”

Along with losing multiple MLAs, the Conservative Party has seen multiple high profile departures of staff, including the president and executive director.

Findlay is set to host a press conference in Richmond on Monday with the B.C. Conservative caucus.

stories.title: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to meet with U.S. officials amid trade war
stories.summary: was originally heading to the U.S. on a pre-planned trip, but her office says she's now going to meet with officials amid the trade war.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
plans to meet with U.S. officials next week during a trip south of the border.

According to Sam Blackett, press secretary for Smith, the meetings have been added to a trip planned and booked months ago.

“As the Premier said earlier this week, Canadian legislators should be doubling down on diplomacy with members of the U.S. Congress and lawmakers in both parties to ensure they understand how destructive these tariffs are for the American people, and how we will be there to help as soon as the tariffs are reversed,” Blackett said in an emailed statement.

Smith is expected to meet with Mark Ezell, the commissioner of the Tennessee Department of Tourist Development, Stephanie Coleman, the head of the Nashville Chamber of Commerce and the CEO of the Nashville Convention and Visitors Corp., Deana Ivey.

The premier will be joined by Alberta’s senior U.S. representative Nathan Cooper.

Earlier this week, Smith said the U.S. had “no excuse for their behaviour” after trade talks fell apart, but did not believe Canada could win through “brute force.”

She also rejected calls by the Opposition NDP, along with others such as former premier Jason Kenney, to use Alberta’s energy exports as a high-stakes bargaining chip.

The U.S. has the power to cripple Canada energy-wise, she cautioned.

Smith predicted if Canada were to enact a 50 per cent tariff on the four million barrels of oil exported south each day, the U.S. would retaliate with tariffs of 50 to 100 per cent on refined oil and gas products exported to Canada, such as aviation fuel.

Blackett said Alberta’s diplomatic efforts include participation in organizations like the Council of State Governments (CSG) Midwest, where MLA for Lacombe-Ponoka Jennifer Johnson serves as representative for the province.

Johnson, a backbencher in Smith’s United Conservative caucus, is expected to be joined next week at the U.S. organization’s annual Midwestern Legislative Conference by six members of Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe’s caucus.

Saskatchewan is a full member of the Council of State Governments Midwest, while Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario are affiliate members.

During a news conference this past week, Smith also called for an accelerated approval timeline for the West Coast pipeline her government is pitching, and that she’s formed two committees in response to the breakdown in trade talks.

Smith said one committee, made up of her cabinet members, is set to meet Thursday to discuss following Saskatchewan’s lead by imposing a 50 per cent tax on U.S. alcohol brought into that province.

She said she prefers Moe’s approach to an outright ban on American alcohol in Alberta, noting Canadian products aren’t blocked from going south of the border.

— with files from Global News’ Karen Bartko and The Canadian Press

stories.title: London Transit considering shuttle system linking two unserved areas to bus routes
stories.summary: London Transit is working with a consultant to design a new type of public transit service in London that would link passengers to the existing bus network.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
paragraphs: London Transit is working with a consultant to design a new type of public transit service in London that would link passengers to the existing bus network. An Alternate Service Delivery (ASD) system has been used by other cities in neighbourhoods that May not initially warrant a full conventional route based on estimated ridership demands. A report to the London Transit Commission (LTC) reads, “This type of service has been utilized in many jurisdictions as a way to offer access to public transit to areas in an effort to grow ridership, which ultimately results in the addition of a conventional route when ridership meets the required thresholds.” The ASD service would require passengers in two proposed service zones to schedule a trip on a shuttle using an app. Utilizing a “Stop to Hub” design, the service would include shuttle stops in the ASD zones where passengers would be picked-up and taken to a nearby transit hub where they can join the existing bus system. “It’s an opportunity to get transit into an area where it May not be viable to go in with a conventional route, but we can start to build that ridership,” explained London Transit General Manager Kelly Paleczny. Preliminarily, two ASD zones are being considered: Zone 1– Fox Hollow area bounded by Hyde Park, Wonderland, Fanshawe Park Road and Sunningdale. Stops would be located within the area with main destinations of the Hyde Park Power Centre at Fanshawe and Hyde Park and Masonville Mall. Zone 2– three, non-adjacent areas within north Lambeth and south Byron which fall outside of the 400-meter travel distance to a fixed route service, Stops would be located within each of the zones and connect to major destinations such as Hyde Park and Oxford and Westmount Mall allowing for connections to the fixed route network. Its estimated that the two zones could serve 22,700 riders each year and bring public transit within walking distance (400 metres) of 6,632 homes. Ankit Nagpal lives in Zone 1 and says transit riders face long walks to bus stops on Fanshawe Park Road, “It takes them almost 18 minutes or 20 minutes to get to the nearest transit station.” He explains the neighbourhood has many bus riders who live in basement apartments or ARUs (additional residential units), “I think that would be a great move especially for a neighborhood like this, where we have a lot of students from Western University.” Paleczny emphasizes that the analysis is still underway, “This was identified in our five-year service plan, (as) one of the options moving forward, so we’re working right now with a consulting firm to come up with the actual implementation plan.” The consultant’s report is expected in October. In the meantime, staff are recommending the transit commission include $1.5 million for the ASD initiative in a business case for assessment growth funding from city hall in March, 2027. The LTC will consider a next steps on Aug. 31.

stories.title: Family of Canadians missing in Nepal floods on edge as they wait for information
stories.summary: The brother of a Canadian man among those missing after flash floods swept through an area along the Nepal-Tibet border says their family is on edge as they wait for information.
stories.author: News Staff
paragraphs: By The Canadian Press
Posted August 29, 2026 11:34 am.
Last Updated August 29, 2026 3:58 pm.
The brother of a Canadian man among those missing after flash floods swept through an area along the Nepal-Tibet border says their family is on edge waiting for information.

Dhaval Shah and his wife Megha Shah, from Port Moody, B.C., were on a spiritual journey in Nepal when the floods hit. Dhaval’s brother Kheval Shah, reached at his home in Mumbai, India, said his family is desperate to know if they’ve been rescued or found.
“Everybody is on edge to get some news, if they’re rescued or found or something. Something which will make the family understand what happened to them,” Kheval Shah said in an interview Saturday.
“We’re hoping that they find them and some miracles happen and we see them again,” he added.

After Nepali authorities updated their figures Saturday, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 676 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities have reported seven deaths and more than 550 missing, while Nepal’s disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 669 with 2,426 people missing.
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Saturday that one of the 32 Canadians and permanent residents missing in the region has been located safely.

“Telecommunications in the affected areas of Nepal are being restored and Chinese authorities are now characterizing the risk of secondary flooding as “controllable,” she said in a statement. “Canadians in the region should continue to exercise caution, follow the guidelines of local authorities and Global Affairs Canada travel advisories as the situation evolves.”
The Nepal Tourism Board said Friday that 121 foreign nationals had been rescued.

Many of the missing were believed to have been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others. Hundreds of others have been displaced across the Himalayan region.

Shah said he last heard from his brother on Monday, and a cousin of theirs heard from the couple on Tuesday. He believes his brother and sister-in-law were waiting for immigration offices to open in order to leave Nepal at the Tibet border when the flash floods hit.
He said the Canadian government should press Nepal for answers and more information about missing Canadians.
“I know they’re doing something, but I feel that they must really push… to find where they are and to get some information,” Shah said.
Canada has said it will send $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal, with the money earmarked for organizations like the Red Cross to deliver assistance to people on the ground.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal as of Saturday.

stories.title: Alberta separatists rally ahead of province’s birthday celebrations
stories.summary: Organizers said Alberta would be better off without Canada, called on attendees to stand up to Ottawa
stories.author: Fakiha Baig
stories.content:
Alberta separatists converged outside the legislature in Edmonton on Saturday afternoon ahead of the province’s birthday, with many praying, listening to sermons and saying Alberta would be better off without Canada after having joined Confederation 121 years ago.

“It’s the corruption, the lies from out east. I’m just tired of it,” said Skip Macaulay, a rally attendee who lives in the central Alberta city of Lacombe. “I’m tired of being told how to live my life. I’m a gun enthusiast ... I want change.”

“They don’t listen to what Alberta wants and needs,” said Jill Didow, an Edmonton resident who was also at the rally. “I believe in Alberta independence.”

Alberta officially became a province on Sept. 1, 1905, and various festivities are planned this weekend to mark the anniversary on Tuesday.

The head of the Alberta Prosperity Project, the separatist group that organized the rally, called on attendees to stand up to Ottawa.

“Ottawa is putting its elbows up to protect themselves from us,” Mitch Sylvestre claimed in front of a large crowd of people holding Alberta flags at the start of the rally. “We think that’s backwards.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney first pledged to go “elbows up” for Canada during his election campaign last year in response to threats from U.S. President Donald Trump .

Nenshi urges Smith to cancel referendum on separation vote amid Canada-U.S. trade war

After Sylvestre’s brief speech, two pastors spent a large portion of the rally praying for the independence movement and delivering sermons.

“Provide for us the wisdom and leadership needed as we seek your justice in this province,” said one pastor during a prayer, as some separatists took off their hats and lowered their heads.

Seven weeks away from the province’s separation referendum, the Alberta Prosperity Project said before the rally that all Albertans were welcome at its “gathering for a province in peril.”

The group filed a petition earlier this year pushing for a referendum question asking if Alberta should cease to be a part of Canada and become an independent state.

It was quashed in court in May, although the ruling is being appealed by those behind the petition campaign as well as by Premier Danielle Smith ’s government.

Smith has since scheduled an Oct. 19 referendum , but her ballot will instead ask Albertans whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

The reasons for why the premier called the vote are in dispute.

Smith has said she supports staying in Canada but hundreds of thousands have signed petitions regarding separation and that it’s time to put the issue to rest once and for all.

She has said those wanting to separate are frustrated with Ottawa and “are not fringe voices.”

Smith says Alberta could have a binding referendum on secession in early 2027

Critics, pointing to long-standing opinion polls indicating massive support for Alberta staying in Canada, accuse Smith of self-serving politics by calling the vote merely to placate restive separatist hardliners in her United Conservative Party.

Earlier this week, Thomas Lukaszuk, organizer of the pro-federalist Forever Canadian petition to keep Alberta in Canada, called for Smith to defer the vote in light of the trade war that Trump has launched.
