“Albertans have every right to be angry with a premier who basically thinks that if she’s really nice to Trump, he will be really nice to us,” Nenshi said.

“Let’s not forget, she flew to Mar-a-Lago right after (Trump’s) election to congratulate him. She went to his inauguration and none of it has worked,” he said.

“It’s a great day to celebrate all that we’ve accomplished,” he said. “It’s great day celebrate who we are as Albertans and remember that the core part of being Albertan is being a proud Canadian.”

Smith is set to speak at an Alberta Day event in Calgary on Sunday.

Music, barbecues and beer gardens are also planned for Sunday across Alberta, including at the legislature.

stories.title: Feds pledge support for London manufacturers
stories.summary: Federal government officials held an event in London, promoting their efforts to support local industries.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
paragraphs: Federal government officials held an event in London, promoting their efforts to support local industries.
“The prime minister made a decision – Canada will not accept a bad deal,” said John Zerucelli, secretary of state for labour.
Zerucelli visited Attica Manufacturing in southeast London Friday afternoon.
Attica is a CNC machine shop, which serves a number of industries including the energy, medical, and automotive sectors.
Joined by local area MPs, Zerucelli focused on the impacts of U.S. tariffs on London and how the government’s response will focus on local challenges created by those tariffs.
“We’re going to stand up and stand with Londoners and with all Canadians. The finance minister has been very clear. We have the fiscal firepower,” said Zerucelli.

stories.title: B.C.’s historic Little Red House destroyed by fire
stories.summary: The Langley Heritage Society said in an online post Friday that it was "sad and unfortunate" the home, also known as the McIver House, was never preserved.
stories.author: Nono Shen
stories.content:
A historic home popularly known as the Little Red House has been destroyed by fire after standing in the Township of Langley for almost 140 years.

The township’s archives say the home properly known as Mclver House burned down early on Thursday.

It says the home was built by Murdoch and Annie McIver between 1887 and 1890.

While the Langley Heritage Society says in a social media post that the house in the Glen Valley area had fallen into disrepair, its location in the middle of a turf farm helped make it “one of the most photographed and painted” homes in the area.

It says the Gothic-style farmhouse, which also served as a backdrop for photo shoots and videos, “evoked memories of simpler times.”

Rob Rindt, a Township of Langley councillor, shared videos of the house being engulfed in flames, saying its destruction was “incredibly sad.”

“So many people photographed, painted and stopped to admire this house over the years, and now these images capture its final moments,” he said.

A description of the house in the Township of Langley’s archives, held by its heritage facility known as salishan Place by the River, says the house was built by the McIvers to replace an earlier log cabin, “which was most likely too small to accommodate the McIvers’ growing clan of nine children.”

It says the house was still occupied until the early 1990s “but by 2010 it had been surrounded by a turf farm and was uninhabited and falling into disrepair.”

The heritage society said in an online post Friday that it was “sad and unfortunate” the home was never preserved.

paragraphs: Trump belittled the Democratic governor, claiming that Canada has been taking economic advantage of Hochul as well as New York state
Author of the article:
President Donald Trump hit back at New York Governor Kathy Hochul after she said her state wouldn’t use “Lake America,” the administration’s new name for Lake Ontario.

Trump belittled the Democratic governor in a social media post Friday, claiming that Canada has been taking economic advantage of Hochul as well as New York state. He repeated his charge that the US’s northern neighbor “has been ripping us off for decades on Trade and Tariffs.”
Hochul “allows other Countries and States to take advantage of New York, which gets treated like “garbage,’” he said. Trump urged voters to back Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman.

stories.title: Jason Kenney on Conservative leadership aspirations as MPs doubt Pierre Poilievre’s future
stories.summary: Former federal Conservative cabinet minister and Alberta premier Jason Kenney is throwing cold water on the possibility of a party leadership run, as Conservative MPs privately question Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s future at the helm.
stories.author: Spencer Van Dyk
stories.content:
Former federal Conservative cabinet minister and Alberta premier Jason Kenney is throwing cold water on the possibility of a party leadership run, as Conservative MPs privately question Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s future at the helm.

Asked in an interview on The Graham Richardson Show on Friday whether he would run to replace Poilievre if the opportunity arose, Kenney said: “No.”

“Twenty-five years in elected office, a great privilege, I’m really enjoying having some more normal life in the private sector,” Kenney told Richardson. “Look, I’m 58, never say never, in the future who knows what might happen? But it’s not an aspiration of mine, certainly not in the foreseeable future.”

The question comes as several Conservative MPs privately express deep concerns about Poilievre’s leadership, with some telling CTV News earlier this month they do not believe he will still be leading the party when the next federal election is called.

Specifically, MPs were asked about a recent Nanos Research poll commissioned by CTV News, which concluded that Prime Minister Mark Carney has “no obvious challenger” when presented with a list of Conservative politicians.

Notably, only five per cent of respondents in that poll said Kenney — if he were Conservative leader —would be able to beat Carney in a general election.

Tory MPs should blame Trump for trade war: Kenney

Kenney also discussed the protracted trade war with the United States, saying while he believes Poilievre’s approach to the issue has been “responsible,” he also thinks some Conservative MPs need to more explicitly lay blame for the conflict on U.S. President Donald Trump.

“He made an excellent statement last Saturday in the wake of the U.S. negotiations falling apart,” Kenney said of Poilievre. “He called for once again dollar-for-dollar reciprocal tariffs, which is what he campaigned on.”

But, Kenney added of some Conservatives MPs: “I don’t think that I have seen in their public commentary ascribe responsibility for this trade war to the protagonist, to the person who launched it and sustains it, with belittling attacks on our country’s dignity, threats to our sovereignty and actual practical attacks against our economy, that’s Donald J. Trump.”

The longtime federal cabinet minister chalked the position of some Conservative MPs, who he did not name, up to the amount of time they’ve been on Opposition benches.

“That’s the old saying like ‘to a hammer everything looks like a nail,’” Kenney said. “Well, to a very partisan opposition MP, everything looks like an opportunity to criticize the incumbent government.”

Kenney said the Conservatives need to balance holding the Liberals accountable, especially on domestic policy issues, with blaming the right person for the trade war.

“If you ever want to form government, you’ve got to demonstrate on something like this that patriotism comes before partisanship,” he said. “Which does not mean giving Prime Minister Carney and his Liberal government a blank cheque, it means holding them to account.”

With files from CTV News’ Stephanie Ha, Vassy Kapelos, and Graham Richardson

But, Kenney added of some Conservatives MPs: “I don’t think that I have seen in their public commentary ascribe responsibility for this trade war to the protagonist, to the person who launched it and sustains it, with belittling attacks on our country’s dignity, threats to our sovereignty and actual practical attacks against our economy, that’s Donald J. Trump.”
The longtime federal cabinet minister chalked the position of some Conservative MPs, who he did not name, up to the amount of time they’ve been on Opposition benches.

“That’s the old saying like ‘to a hammer everything looks like a nail,’” Kenney said. “Well, to a very partisan opposition MP, everything looks like an opportunity to criticize the incumbent government.”
Kenney said the Conservatives need to balance holding the Liberals accountable, especially on domestic policy issues, with blaming the right person for the trade war.

“If you ever want to form government, you’ve got to demonstrate on something like this that patriotism comes before partisanship,” he said. “Which does not mean giving Prime Minister Carney and his Liberal government a blank cheque, it means holding them to account.”

stories.title: A Toronto sommelier adds Master of Wine to his credentials
stories.summary: Jake Skakun is one of the seven new Masters of Wine after successfully completing all three stages of the rigorous exam
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Toronto sommelier and restaurateur Jake Skakun is one of the seven new Masters of Wine after successfully completing all three stages of the rigorous exam. A native of British Columbia, Skakun got his start in wine 20 years ago while working in Vancouver as a sommelier and writer. Shortly after moving to Toronto in 2012, he was recruited by trailblazing Black Hoof owner Jen Agg to work at her seafood restaurant, Hoof Raw Bar.

Today, he’s sommelier, general manager and partner in Agg’s network of local restaurants, Le Swan, Grey Gardens, Bar Vendetta and General Public. That schedule and a young family at home wouldn’t allow for much time for studying, Skakun says, but the pandemic provided a window in September 2020 to apply to the Master of Wine program while restaurants were closed. “I’m not someone who does too well with a lot of free time,” Skakun explains.

Skakun, who was introduced Aug. 20 as one of 427 active MWs across 31 countries, including nine based in Canada, told The Globe how fortuitous timing and his experience working as a sommelier in Toronto helped him master the necessary academic theory and practical knowledge of wine to pass the extensive examination process.

What inspired you to pursue the Master of Wine qualification?

The first or second wine class I took was with Barb Philip in Vancouver, who received her Master of Wine in 2007. Since then, I have had a lot of admiration and respect for her and the Institute of Masters of Wine. While I always enjoyed taking wine education classes, I never thought I would ever go the distance to the MW until during the early stage of the pandemic, when I realized I had the time and thought to see how far I could go.

The Master of Wine exam is notoriously difficult. Passing the various stages requires a significant investment of time and resources. What made you think you would succeed?

Early on, I felt confident that it was something I could do, especially the tasting aspect. I taste a lot of wines working in the restaurants, I’m often meeting with wine representatives. Something about the timing worked out perfectly. I passed theory on my first attempt and shortly after, my daughter was born. The following year, I passed the practical tasting exam. Had the sequence been reversed, I would not have had enough time each day to thoroughly study the theory with a little one in at home. Everything just fell into place.

Your research paper was a case study of Ontario wine served on tap in Toronto restaurants, which is a format that you’ve been using at Grey Gardens and elsewhere for the past seven years.

I joked with my wife that I am the world’s foremost expert on the topic of wine in kegs. My interest in wine on tap came from a restaurant perspective, especially one in a big city that’s an hour away from a wine-producing region. There’s a wasteful element using bottled wine for wines served by the glass. There are cost reductions and service efficiencies that appealed to me. I was curious why more restaurants weren’t embracing the format.

Editor’s note: This article has been updated to correct the surname of Barb Philip.

stories.title: Federal Court staff working weekends, vacations to keep up with cases: chief justice
stories.summary: The Federal Court has jurisdiction over a number of immigration matters, such as visa applications, refugee claims, admissibility cases and removals.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
A massive increase in immigration cases in the last six years has created unmanageable workloads at the Federal Court , says Chief Justice Alan Diner.

The Federal Court has jurisdiction over a number of immigration matters, such as visa applications, refugee claims, admissibility cases and removals.

Diner, who was sworn in as the top judge for the Federal Court on July 6, said when he joined the court in 2014, it typically saw between 5,000 and 6,000 immigration cases a year.

In 2021, immigration filings quickly began to climb, with 9,700 cases brought before the court that year. Now Diner said the Federal Court is on track to see upwards of 33,000 immigration filings this year alone.

“The judges have the pedal to the metal and are trying to do their utmost,” Diner said.

“They’re working around the clock, working weekends, working vacations, court staff, the same thing, available evenings, available weekends to try and deal with this volume.”

The rapid increase in immigration-related cases coincides with an increase in the number of permanent and temporary immigrants, in addition to asylum seekers, in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

More than 14,000 immigration cases were filed between Jan. 1 and June 30, with 28,000 pending. Almost 1,000 cases have been granted hearings for a judicial review.

“It would be a lie for me to say this is without challenges. Judges are being pressured, court staff are being pressured, and I’m very proud of the way they’re handling this unprecedented increase, but we’re doing what we can,” Diner said.

The passage of Canada’s border security bill, C-12, in March is also creating additional pressures on Federal Court resources.

That bill says the Immigration and Refugee Board will only hear cases from people who make a refugee claim within their first year in Canada. The law is retroactive to arrivals in Canada after June 24, 2020 and applies to all claims made on or after June 3, 2025.

If someone makes a refugee claim more than a year after the first time they arrived in Canada, they are only eligible for a pre-removal risk assessment. The only avenue to appeal a negative assessment is through the Federal Court.

Diner said since C-12 became law the Federal Court has received more than 2,000 applications challenging the constitutionality of the law.

These challenges are going through case management, where judges will make a ruling on the core constitutional question based on a smaller number of cases.

Diner said the Federal Court is also seeing a “huge increase” in requests for a stay of deportation since C-12 was passed. He said the court usually saw 300 to 400 applications a year, but is now looking at more than 1,100 cases.

There are 44 Federal Court judges, including Diner. He said they have seen a roughly 600 per cent increase in the number of immigration cases since 2020 with no change in the number of judges.

He said the Federal Court needs more judges to keep up with the workload and the government has been made aware of the request.

“So, difficult for the same number of judges to do six times the amount of work,” Diner said.

“But obviously it’s incumbent on us to improve to the extent that we can, and be innovative and modernize and use technology to try and somehow stem this flow.”

A spokesperson for Justice Minister Sean Fraser said he is “mindful” of the significant caseload increase facing the Federal Court, and is committed to supporting fair, timely access to justice.

The spokesperson said both the department and minister assess requests for additional resources, and “evidence of growing caseloads and backlogs are important factors in those assessments.”

Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner said the increased caseload isn’t surprising, given the increase in immigration over the last decade that includes the period when Fraser was minister.

She said the government was also warned about “instant challenges” to C-12 when it was being studied at committee.

“I think that the government needs to take a bit of a pause and look at why there is such a volume of caseload and then try to address some of the determinants of those causes,” Rempel Garner said.

“Their poor management of the file, putting it mildly over the last decade, has had an impact on the court system. Of course it has.”

The Federal Court registry issued a notice last month noting document processing times have increased due to a “significant surge” in filings. The notice says the goal is to process documents within 48 hours, but delays could be up to eight weeks — especially for immigration-related matters.

Diner said the court is doing what it can to increase efficiency. He said this is one of his main priorities as chief justice.

This includes expanding on digitization work that really started to advance during the COVID-19 pandemic and looking at automation and artificial intelligence tools that could assist in managing high caseloads.

The use of AI in the court could one day go beyond just administration.

“That’s obviously something we’re going to have to consider. Not to make decisions, but to see where we can assist in the process, given this unprecedented surge,” Diner said. “We do know that AI is increasingly being used and obviously we also have to consider if the judiciary can use AI to help cope with this unprecedented volume.”

Immigration related filings made up about 86 per cent of the matters brought to the Federal Court in the first six months on the year, and are consistently the majority of files brought to the court in a given year.

While the court continues to manage the major increase in immigration cases, Diner said the demand is increasing in other areas of their jurisdiction, including national security matters, class actions and judicial reviews.

“Working weekends, working holidays, working through your vacations is not really an acceptable answer to how we’re going to have long term well-being,” he said.

“When you’re under the kinds of pressure that I’ve talked about, you can imagine that people end up feeling sensitive, burned out, and so forth … The judges are always going to work hard, the employees are always going to work hard. But we have to ensure the well-being of our complement.”

stories.title: ‘Unprecedented’ increase in immigration cases creates unmanageable workloads for Federal Court, says chief justice
stories.summary: When Alan Diner became top judge in 2014, there were between 5,000 and 6,000 immigration cases a year. Now, the Federal Court is on track to see upwards of 33,000 filings this year alone
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
A massive increase in immigration cases in the last six years has created unmanageable workloads at the Federal Court, says Chief Justice Alan Diner.

The Federal Court has jurisdiction over a number of immigration matters, such as visa applications, refugee claims, admissibility cases and removals.

Diner, who was sworn in as the top judge for the Federal Court on July 6, said when he joined the court in 2014, it typically saw between 5,000 and 6,000 immigration cases a year.

In 2021, immigration filings quickly began to climb, with 9,700 cases brought before the court that year. Now Diner said the Federal Court is on track to see upwards of 33,000 immigration filings this year alone.

“The judges have the pedal to the metal and are trying to do their utmost,” Diner said.

“They’re working around the clock, working weekends, working vacations, court staff, the same thing, available evenings, available weekends to try and deal with this volume.”

The rapid increase in immigration-related cases coincides with an increase in the number of permanent and temporary immigrants, in addition to asylum seekers, in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

More than 14,000 immigration cases were filed between Jan. 1 and June 30, with 28,000 pending. Almost 1,000 cases have been granted hearings for a judicial review.

Immigration Department faces almost 300 court challenges over denial of asylum hearings

“It would be a lie for me to say this is without challenges. Judges are being pressured, court staff are being pressured, and I’m very proud of the way they’re handling this unprecedented increase, but we’re doing what we can,” Diner said.

The passage of Canada’s border security bill, C-12, in March is also creating additional pressures on Federal Court resources.

That bill says the Immigration and Refugee Board will only hear cases from people who make a refugee claim within their first year in Canada. The law is retroactive to arrivals in Canada after June 24, 2020 and applies to all claims made on or after June 3, 2025.

If someone makes a refugee claim more than a year after the first time they arrived in Canada, they are only eligible for a pre-removal risk assessment. The only avenue to appeal a negative assessment is through the Federal Court.

Diner said since C-12 became law the Federal Court has received more than 2,000 applications challenging the constitutionality of the law.

These challenges are going through case management, where judges will make a ruling on the core constitutional question based on a smaller number of cases.

Diner said the Federal Court is also seeing a “huge increase” in requests for a stay of deportation since C-12 was passed. He said the court usually saw 300 to 400 applications a year, but is now looking at more than 1,100 cases.

Bill C-12 curbing asylum, immigration rights becomes law amid warnings of court challenges

There are 44 Federal Court judges, including Diner. He said they have seen a roughly 600 per cent increase in the number of immigration cases since 2020 with no change in the number of judges.

He said the Federal Court needs more judges to keep up with the workload and the government has been made aware of the request.

“So, difficult for the same number of judges to do six times the amount of work,” Diner said.

“But obviously it’s incumbent on us to improve to the extent that we can, and be innovative and modernize and use technology to try and somehow stem this flow.”

A spokesperson for Justice Minister Sean Fraser said he is “mindful” of the significant caseload increase facing the Federal Court, and is committed to supporting fair, timely access to justice.

The spokesperson said both the department and minister assess requests for additional resources, and “evidence of growing caseloads and backlogs are important factors in those assessments.”

Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner said the increased caseload isn’t surprising, given the increase in immigration over the last decade that includes the period when Fraser was minister.

She said the government was also warned about “instant challenges” to C-12 when it was being studied at committee.

“I think that the government needs to take a bit of a pause and look at why there is such a volume of caseload and then try to address some of the determinants of those causes,” Rempel Garner said.

“Their poor management of the file, putting it mildly over the last decade, has had an impact on the court system. Of course it has.”

The Federal Court registry issued a notice last month noting document processing times have increased due to a “significant surge” in filings. The notice says the goal is to process documents within 48 hours, but delays could be up to eight weeks — especially for immigration-related matters.

Diner said the court is doing what it can to increase efficiency. He said this is one of his main priorities as chief justice.

This includes expanding on digitization work that really started to advance during the COVID-19 pandemic and looking at automation and artificial intelligence tools that could assist in managing high caseloads.

The use of AI in the court could one day go beyond just administration.

Immigration Department experimenting with AI to advise newcomers on where to settle

“That’s obviously something we’re going to have to consider. Not to make decisions, but to see where we can assist in the process, given this unprecedented surge,” Diner said. “We do know that AI is increasingly being used and obviously we also have to consider if the judiciary can use AI to help cope with this unprecedented volume.”

Immigration related filings made up about 86 per cent of the matters brought to the Federal Court in the first six months on the year, and are consistently the majority of files brought to the court in a given year.

While the court continues to manage the major increase in immigration cases, Diner said the demand is increasing in other areas of their jurisdiction, including national security matters, class actions and judicial reviews.

“Working weekends, working holidays, working through your vacations is not really an acceptable answer to how we’re going to have long term well-being,” he said.

“When you’re under the kinds of pressure that I’ve talked about, you can imagine that people end up feeling sensitive, burned out, and so forth … The judges are always going to work hard, the employees are always going to work hard. But we have to ensure the well-being of our complement.”

stories.title: ‘We cannot absorb 25%’: Southwestern Ontario farm sector braces for tariff hit
stories.summary: The 25 per cent counter-tariffs will hit some U.S.-made farm equipment parts, adding pressure to already thin margins.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
The 25 per cent counter-tariffs will hit some U.S.-made farm equipment parts, adding pressure to already thin margins.

Farm machinery manufacturers and sellers in Southwestern Ontario are bracing for higher costs and weaker sales as the Canada-U.S. trade war reaches the agricultural sector.

Canada’s counter-tariffs on some U.S.-made farm equipment and parts could reach 25 per cent, while recent U.S. tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Canadian-made goods are expected to raise costs for farmers and manufacturers on both sides of the border.

Industry observers say the already thin margins for farmers, equipment manufacturers and retailers could be squeezed even tighter.

“We cannot absorb 25 per cent, that is our own government taxing us, that is what is happening,” said Terry Caldwell, owner of Hyde Brothers, a business that sells farm equipment in Hensall.

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. recently broke down, prompting U.S. President Donald Trump to impose $28 billion in tariffs on a range of Canadian goods entering the U.S.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with $27.6 billion in counter-tariffs on some U.S. goods entering Canada.

The good news for farmers is that large pieces of farm equipment entering Canada will be spared the counter-tariffs, according to several agriculture-focused publications.

The 25 per cent tariff set to take effect Sept. 8 instead applies to smaller parts and components used in larger machines, including combine parts, baler parts, some mowing equipment, livestock trailers and parts, grain trailers and parts, truck parts, some engine components and conveyors, according to agricultural news site RealAgriculture.

“Tractors, combines, and most other major farm implements are not on the list,” the report stated.

But the cost of parts that Caldwell and other farm equipment businesses sell to farmers will still rise, adding another expense in an already difficult market.

“It is terrible, it is getting tough to make a fair living,” he said. “I look at my fuel bills and they have already doubled from a year ago.”

Those higher costs will ultimately be passed on to farmers, whose margins are already thin.

“I am also a farmer and we cannot raise the price on a bushel of corn, or no one will buy it,” he said. “People need to keep things going. Things break and you need a part, but 25 per cent more is not good.”

Caldwell plans to meet with sales staff in September to determine how the business will respond. One option is to carry less equipment on site and order it only when needed as a way to control costs.

“Market forces are bearing down on us. We May have to find something else to do, we May have to stop this. That number is not going to work.”

Caldwell sells Canadian-made Versatile farm equipment from Manitoba, along with American- and Japanese-made machinery. But even Canadian equipment can contain parts from the U.S., meaning it May not escape the impact of tariffs, he said.

Southwestern Ontario is home to many small agricultural machinery manufacturers that sell parts and equipment in both Canada and the U.S., said Trevor Newman, operating officer with Penta Equipment in Glencoe, which exports farm equipment it manufactures to the U.S.

“We are getting fatigued around the whole tariff conversation. It has made it difficult to get a business model that is predictable, there is uncertainty,” Newman said.

To reduce the tariff impact, Newman said the company is looking to buy more parts from Europe or manufacture more components itself.

“We are living in a very uncertain environment. As a group of manufacturers we learned to be resilient. We will figure this out.”

stories.title: LTC seeks additional $2M for 2027 budget
stories.summary: London Transit is asking for an additional $2 million in the city’s 2027 budget to cover rising diesel costs and maintain recent service improvements.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
paragraphs: London Transit is asking for an additional $2 million in the city’s 2027 budget to cover rising diesel costs and maintain recent service improvements.
A staff report going before the commission next week recommends asking city hall for the additional funding to address higher diesel costs and make recent transit service improvements permanent.
London Transit Commission general manager Kelly Paleczny says most of the increase is related to the rising cost of diesel fuel.

“A majority of this is the diesel fuel prices,” Paleczny said. “The other piece is there was some additional service hours that were added as part of the 2026 service plan by the commission. They were funded in 2026 through reserves, but now we’re looking for that permanent source of funding.”
Staff also noted the commission has come in $2.1 million under budget over the past two years.
The commission is expected to consider the funding request at its meeting next week.

stories.summary: Alberta independence boosters are planning to rally outside the legislature today ahead of festivities marking the province's 121st birthday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

Posted August 29, 2026 8:00 am.

Last Updated August 30, 2026 1:58 pm.

Edmonton — Alberta separatists converged outside the legislature in Edmonton on Saturday afternoon ahead of the province’s birthday, with many praying, listening to sermons and saying Alberta would be better off without Canada after having joined Confederation 121 years ago.

“It’s the corruption, the lies from out east. I’m just tired of it,” said Skip Macaulay, a rally attendee who lives in the central Alberta city of Lacombe. “I’m tired of being told how to live my life. I’m a gun enthusiast … I want change.”

“They don’t listen to what Alberta wants and needs,” said Jill Didow, an Edmonton resident who was also at the rally. “I believe in Alberta independence.”

Alberta officially became a province on Sept. 1, 1905, and various festivities are planned this weekend to mark the anniversary on Tuesday.

The head of the Alberta Prosperity Project, the separatist group that organized the rally, called on attendees to stand up to Ottawa.

“Ottawa is putting its elbows up to protect themselves from us,” Mitch Sylvestre claimed in front of a large crowd of people holding Alberta flags at the start of the rally. “We think that’s backwards.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney first pledged to go “elbows up” for Canada during his election campaign last year in response to threats from U.S. President Donald Trump.

After Sylvestre’s brief speech, two pastors spent a large portion of the rally praying for the independence movement and delivering sermons.

“Provide for us the wisdom and leadership needed as we seek your justice in this province,” said one pastor during a prayer, as some separatists took off their hats and lowered their heads.

Seven weeks away from the province’s separation referendum, the Alberta Prosperity Project said before the rally that all Albertans were welcome at its “gathering for a province in peril.”

The group filed a petition earlier this year pushing for a referendum question asking if Alberta should cease to be a part of Canada and become an independent state.

It was quashed in court in May, although the ruling is being appealed by those behind the petition campaign as well as by Premier Danielle Smith’s government.

Smith has since scheduled an Oct. 19 referendum, but her ballot will instead ask Albertans whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

The reasons for why the premier called the vote are in dispute.

Smith has said she supports staying in Canada but hundreds of thousands have signed petitions regarding separation and that it’s time to put the issue to rest once and for all.

She has said those wanting to separate are frustrated with Ottawa and “are not fringe voices.”

Critics, pointing to long-standing opinion polls indicating massive support for Alberta staying in Canada, accuse Smith of self-serving politics by calling the vote merely to placate restive separatist hardliners in her United Conservative Party.

Earlier this week, Thomas Lukaszuk, organizer of the pro-federalist Forever Canadian petition to keep Alberta in Canada, called for Smith to defer the vote in light of the trade war that Trump has launched.

Lukaszuk said he was writing on behalf of the more than 400,000 Albertans who signed his petition.

“We submit that this is not the time for unnecessary domestic conflict; this is the time for Albertans to stand together with our fellow Canadians and collectively rally against this unprecedented economic threat,” Lukaszuk wrote.

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi, who held a “Vote for Canada” rally in Calgary on Saturday, has also called for the fall referendum to be put off or kiboshed.

During his rally, he called the vote “crazy,” especially in light of the trade war.

He also criticized Smith’s meeting with U.S. officials next week. Smith said Wednesday after Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart that the United States had “no excuse for their behaviour” but that she didn’t think Canada could win through “brute force.”

Nenshi said that Smith’s meetings with U.S. officials are pointless.

“Albertans have every right to be angry with a premier who basically thinks that if she’s really nice to Trump, he will be really nice to us,” Nenshi said.

“Let’s not forget, she flew to Mar-a-Lago right after (Trump’s) election to congratulate him. She went to his inauguration and none of it has worked,” he said.

Nenshi also marked Alberta’s birthday during his rally.

“It’s a great day to celebrate all that we’ve accomplished,” he said. “It’s great day celebrate who we are as Albertans and remember that the core part of being Albertan is being a proud Canadian.”

Smith is set to speak at an Alberta Day event in Calgary on Sunday.

Music, barbecues and beer gardens are also planned for Sunday across Alberta, including at the legislature.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 29, 2026.

Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Voters head to the polls in three by-elections across Canada
stories.summary: Federal by-elections are taking place Monday in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord in Quebec, Beaches-East York in Toronto and North Vancouver-Capilano
stories.author: Ian Bailey
paragraphs: Amid escalating trade tensions with the United States, voters are going to the polls Monday in three federal by-elections that could indicate how Canadians are feeling about the conflict.

The by-elections are being held in the Quebec riding of Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, Beaches-East York in Toronto and North Vancouver-Capilano. All three ridings opened up as MPs − two Liberals and a Conservative – stepped down for other opportunities in politics and the public service.
Pollster Nik Nanos says the collapse of trade talks May end up being especially germane to the vote in Quebec.

“The trade war May have an impact on the Quebec by-election because the Liberal candidate is a dairy farmer,” said the chief data scientist at Nanos Research, referring to Daniel Gobeil, the former president of the Dairy Farmers of Quebec.
In a statement, Mr. Nanos said that because the riding has been competitive it will be interesting to see if the trade war puts Mr. Gobeil over the top.
Meanwhile, Liberal Braeden Caley, a former senior aide to Prime Minister Mark Carney, is among the candidates in North Vancouver-Capilano.
Federal by-elections in 2026 set to cost upwards of $24-million
Ahead of Monday’s by-elections, the Liberals have a slim majority in the House of Commons.
Elections Canada has reported that 39,500 people had voted in advance polls in the by-elections – 11,800 in Beaches-East York, 11,000 in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord and 16,700 in North Vancouver-Capilano.
Here’s the situation in each riding:

Chicoutimi-Le Fjord: Conservative MP Richard Martel first won this largely francophone Quebec riding that includes some of the city of Saguenay in a 2018 by-election. This year, he was appointed to the Senate, precipitating his exit from the House and the resulting by-election.

The former head coach in the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League won re-election in the 2025 general election with 34 per cent of the vote compared with 31.19 per cent for the Bloc candidate, and 31.12 per cent for the Liberals.

In the by-election, the Conservatives are running Régis Gaudreault, a lawyer and teacher at the Cégep de Chicoutimi. The Bloc candidate is Caroline Dubé, a former director of the office of Bloc MP Mario Simard. The Liberal candidate is Mr. Gobeil.

Daniel Béland, James McGill Professor and director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada, says the enduring popularity of Mr. Carney in Quebec, related to his role in the continuing trade war with the United States, seems to be boosting support for Mr. Gobeil.

Mr. Béland said this by-election stands out among the three. “It is the one in which a partisan shift is most likely as the Conservatives seem poised to lose a seat at the expense of the Liberals, or, perhaps the Bloc,” he said in a statement.

Beaches-East York: Voters are going to the polls in this Toronto riding because Nathaniel Erskine-Smith, the Liberal MP since 2015, resigned in July after his bid to seek the leadership of the Ontario provincial Liberals went awry.
Mr. Erskine-Smith, briefly a housing minister under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, has since announced that he will seek to become a Toronto city councillor.

In the by-election, Tanveer Shahnawaz, Mr. Erskine-Smith’s former constituency assistant, constituency office manager and special ministerial assistant, is running to succeed his former boss. The former MP won the riding with 67.75 per cent of the vote in 2025.
During that election, the Conservatives ran second with 23.5 per cent of the vote, and the NDP candidate was third with 6.85 per cent.
In the by-election, the Conservative candidate is restaurant operator Jim Syrbos and the NDP is running Shannon Devine, an executive director for the Toronto and York Region Labour Council.
North Vancouver-Capilano: By the time the riding of North Vancouver was renamed North Vancouver-Capilano in 2022, Jonathan Wilkinson had been the Liberal MP for seven years.

Before Mr. Wilkinson went to Ottawa as part of the Trudeau team that took power in 2015, the riding had been represented by members from the Progressive Conservatives, the Reform Party, the Canadian Alliance and the Conservatives.
More recently, Mr. Wilkinson was appointed ambassador to the European Union, and his departure prompted the by-election in the riding.

In 2025, the former environment and energy minister won the riding with 59.8 per cent of the vote. Conservative Stephen Curran, a lawyer running again this year, had 33.6 per cent and the NDP candidate had four per cent.

This time, the Liberal candidate is Mr. Caley, a former deputy chief of staff to Mr. Carney. He was also a director of policy and communications for Gregor Robertson, now the federal Housing Minister, when Mr. Robertson was mayor of Vancouver between 2008 and 2018.
Other candidates include Stephen Tweedale for the NDP and the Green Party’s Shelley Luce, an environmental scientist.

stories.title: Economists have some ideas about how to Trump-proof the economy
stories.summary: The government's initial response was to offer support payments for companies and workers hit by this latest round of American tariffs.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
paragraphs: The most powerful policy play, they say, would be an overhaul of Canada's tax system
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is under attack, bombarded by U.S. tariffs and a trade partner that moves goalposts on a whim.
Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.
Access articles from across Canada with one account.
Enjoy additional articles per month.
The federal government’s initial response was to offer short-term support payments for companies and workers hit by this latest round of American tariffs.
But economists say it’s the long-term policy moves that will do much more to inoculate the Canadian economy against the Trump tariffs, not to mention fuel a higher national standard of living.

The most powerful policy play, they say, would be an overhaul of Canada’s tax system because that could improve national competitiveness, something that was sorely needed even without the Trump tariff threat. They argue that tax changes, specifically cuts to personal and corporate income, would encourage increased investment and exports, which would then fuel increased economic growth.
“Canada really needs to do something large on tax reform,” said Jack Mintz, the p resident’s fellow at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy. “I think it’s even more crucial today.”

While Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has yet to signal the government’s broad goals for its upcoming budget this fall , the stars May have aligned for big change. The trade rupture has given Ottawa and the provinces rare political cover to make moves that might have been unpopular during normal times. The Liberals are also led by an economist, have a majority and are likely at least a couple of years from the next election.

The Liberal government might be leaning that way. Even before the trade war with the U.S., the party had vowed to hold a review of the corporate tax system during last year’s federal election campaign, although that promise that has not yet been kept.
The question is whether the Carney government will seize this moment to boost the economy or defy Winston Churchill’s quip to “never let a good crisis go to waste.”

It’s not just economists feeling the tides of change. The leaders of two of Canada’s largest banks, Scott Thomson of the Bank of Nova Scotia and Darryl White of the Bank of Montreal, said Tuesday that the tariff fight should trigger the federal government to act.

“There is an opportunity for the Canadian federal and provincial governments to recognize the moment for what it is and use it to drive transformational policy change,” White told equity analysts, “and not let this moment go to waste.”
A handful of economists surveyed by National Post were largely consistent in what they’d like to see the government do to spur and Trump-proof the economy.
Each said that their recipes for growth include, and usually begin with, income tax cuts: both corporate and personal.

Tim Sargent, director of economic growth and prosperity at University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy, said these two taxes touch and influence virtually every inch of the economy, which means that reducing them would also mean widespread improvements to competitiveness.

Despite some tepid cuts to personal income taxes in recent decades, economists say Canadians still pay way too much and the problem has been getting worse. Canada now relies more on personal income taxes for its revenue than any other G7 country.

While governments’ slice from Canadians’ pay cheques has been climbing for decades, Mintz pointed out that personal income taxes accounted for 11 per cent of GDP in 2010, but grew to 13 per cent by 2023. Personal income taxes are now responsible for easily the biggest chunk of government revenue, and almost twice the amount of any other form of federal or provincial tax.

While governments need money to pay for health care, education, defence and other big spending items, economists say it’s critical that legislators take the minimum and in a way that is as harmless as possible.

Don Drummond, a former high-ranking official at the Department of Finance and chief economist at TD Bank, said the four big tax baskets in order, from most to least harmful, are: corporate income, personal income, employment insurance and other payroll, then consumption taxes such as the GST.
Lower personal income taxes spur growth, economists say, because when people have fatter wallets, they tend to spend it, invest it, or use it to reduce debt which are all good things for the economy.

That’s particularly the case when governments cut “marginal” income taxes — the percentage that is taken off the next dollar that someone earns, not the entire amount. That is seen as an important distinction because that marginal rate influences whether people are motivated to work or invest more and high marginal Canadian rates kick in at relatively low levels, economists say, compared to other G7 countries.
Lower personal income taxes also help stave off the migration of highly skilled and entrepreneurial people to other countries.
And if you think cutting personal income taxes has political enemies, try selling corporate income tax cuts.

But economists argue that lower corporate income taxes are good for the economy, perhaps the greatest bang for the public buck, because they encourage and lower the long-term costs of investments in buildings, factories, and research.
And anything that leads to lower business costs should also lead to more productive employees and lower costs, at least where markets are competitive.

More profitable companies are also more valuable, giving them more equity heft to acquire competitors instead of the other way around. They can also pay employees more, which leads to more personal spending and investing, more government tax revenue, and reduces one of the key foreign lures that leads to “brain drain.”

To make those changes even more appealing, economists say, the government revenue lost by corporate income tax cuts is mitigated by a number of factors, such as the increased tax revenue derived from new investments spurred by the changes. Tax cuts also lead to behavioural changes, they say, such as multi-nationals moving profits to jurisdictions with lower rates.
In short, corporate income tax cuts don’t cost as much as they might appear.

In 2000-01, the federal corporate income tax rate stood at 28 per cent, and took in $28.3-billion. Flush at that time with growing revenue, Ottawa started cutting that tax and others. By 2012, it had been cut almost in half to today’s rate of 15 per cent. Ottawa took in $36.1 billion that year. In the last fiscal year, companies paid $97.1 billion in income tax, despite the lower rate
How is that possible? Economists say there are a few factors at play, including economic growth, multi-nationals accounting tools and higher corporate profits.

Sargent said Canada needs a national edge over the U.S., its biggest competitor for investment and production, and having a more efficient tax system that spurred and attracted investment would qualify.

While Canada used to have an edge in this regard, it’s been lost in recent years. In 2018, the U.S. cut its federal corporate income tax rate in 2018, which left its combined average federal-state rates at 25.7 per cent, compared to 26.1 per cent for Canada’s combined federal-provincial rate.

In a study released earlier this year, Mintz and two colleagues called for a “big bang” to Canada’s tax policy because they argued that the country’s tax system is contributing to weak economic performance. Despite the Canadian economy posting strong second quarter growth on Friday, the bigger picture remains less rosy. Over the last decade, Mintz said, the country has posted the slowest per-capita income growth in the G7 over the last three decades.

The “big bang” paper calls for the federal government to rely less on those taxes – namely corporate and personal income taxes — that hurt the economy the most, while shifting the burden to sales taxes and perhaps a new employer-paid payroll tax to help pay for health costs. They also call for cuts to government spending.
Part of the prescription in that paper is for a sharp cut in corporate income taxes to 10 per cent from today’s 15.

Doug Porter, chief economist at BMO Financial Group, suggested a more cautious approach, but with similar themes: slight trim to corporate income taxes and an across-the-board cut to marginal personal income taxes. Porter also said governments should broaden the base of taxpayers by reducing some exemptions and write-offs.
Either way, it’s not like a concerted effort at improved competitiveness hasn’t been tried before.
The most famous recent example of the benefits of lower corporate income taxes is Ireland.

In 1997, Ireland accelerated a plan to boost its economy, kicking off a series of corporate income tax cuts that dropped the rate to 12.5 per cent from 32 per cent over six years. Ireland already had low taxes for those companies exporting manufactured goods and some services and was enjoying a period of strong growth. But the big tax cut – accompanied by new investments in education and other policy changes – was the centrepiece of the plan, leading to a “Celtic tiger” that produced one of the world’s fastest-growing economies.
But it’s not just corporate and personal income tax cuts that economists point to for change.

There’s near unanimity among economists and just about everybody else that inter-provincial trade barriers are an economic menace that has been hurting Canadians’ pocketbooks since before Confederation.
Drummond said creating a legitimate Canadian economic union should be an important early step to economic growth.

Solving that dilemma was a s ignature piece of Carney’s economic plan. Ottawa has for the most part done what it can on this front as the federal barriers — which were never really the big problem — have largely been removed. But the broader goal of free trade within Canada, despite today’s trade challenges and a Constitution that says products from one province shall “be admitted free into each of the other provinces,” governments continue to reject the benefits of economic union.
There is some debate among economists about how much of an economic boost would be triggered by the elimination of provincial trade barriers,

Most studies have concluded that interprovincial trade barriers cost the Canadian economy between $50 billion and $130 billion a year in economic activity, or about 1.9 to 4.9 per cent of the gross domestic product. The International Monetary Fund recently estimated that Canada could boost its economy by seven per cent if it removed internal trade barriers. A recent analysis by Deloitte Canada estimated that a full elimination of the barriers could increase the Canadian economy by $881 billion over time.

Benjamin Tal , the deputy chief economist of Cibc World Markets, said the Canadian economy would also get an important boost if it were “opened up” to greater levels of fo reign investment. The keys to that goal, Tal said, are loosening ownership caps on foreign investment, streamlining regulations and speeding up project approvals.

The Carney government has made that third objective a priority by, among other things, opening up a new major projects office. That’s part of Ottawa’s effort to diversify trade, with the goal set last year of doubling non-U.S. exports over the next decade.

stories.title: As she launches her campaign, Quebec's Fréchette hopes the Carney formula will work twice
stories.summary: 'I think people can figure out which side Mark Carney's on,' said Jonathan Kalles, a former Quebec advisor to Justin Trudeau.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
paragraphs: Ottawa — Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette launched her province’s election campaign by talking about the importance for Quebec to transform its economy in the face of the trade war with the U.S. because their old relationship is over.
If that message sounds oddly familiar, it’s because it is.
That is exactly the message that Prime Minister Mark Carney has been repeating since the 2025 election that saw the Liberal Party of Canada get elected for a fourth mandate against all odds.
On Thursday, a reporter asked Fréchette if she was trying to emulate Carney.
“My name is Christine Fréchette — and it’ll stay that way,” she said with a laugh.

Fréchette took the reins of the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) in April, succeeding its founder and longtime leader François Legault. The CAQ was expected to be wiped off the electoral map with the separatist Parti Québécois (PQ) poised to form a majority government.

But Fréchette took the bull by the horns, multiplying announcements in the province and adopting a new collaborative tone with Ottawa that led to the conclusion of pending deals with Quebec worth billions for infrastructure and major contracts.

Provincial and federal sources consulted for this story said that Fréchette and Carney have a “transactional” relationship which has benefitted both sides — showcasing Fréchette as a dealmaker and Carney as practicing “cooperative federalism.”
But they argue that Ottawa would be wise to take a step back now that the campaign is underway and let the different parties battle it out for the election on October 5.

“They shouldn’t do anything that smells of interfering. Quebec voters will look very unfavourably on the federal government doing anything that hints of picking a winner,” said Jonathan Kalles, a former Quebec advisor to former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

“I think people can figure out which side Mark Carney’s on. At least in terms of who he doesn’t want to win, I don’t think he needs to say that. And I think if he does, it would look bad, and it wouldn’t help whichever other party he, in essence, wants to win.”

Once Fréchette became premier, she travelled to Ottawa to meet with the prime minister — instead of him coming to Montreal or Quebec City — and Carney pointed out there were many years-long pending deals between both levels of government.
“He couldn’t wrap his mind around why we could not agree on good news,” said one senior government source.
Kalles, now senior vice president at Vantage, said the personalities and backgrounds of Trudeau and Legault were so different that their talks weren’t “always constructive.”
“Fréchette comes in and she’s looking to demonstrate that she can get concrete things done. And I think Mark Carney understood that, so he was in a deal mode,” Kalles said.

The first major announcement came in June when Quebec and Ottawa signed five infrastructure agreements worth nearly $10 billion which would pave the way for major investments in public transit, health care, housing and education over the next decade.

Earlier in August, the federal government also helped Quebec broker a new energy framework with Newfoundland and Labrador that the PQ promised it would review once in power and ask for compensation for Quebec’s loss of Labrador nearly a century ago.

And only three days before the start of the campaign, Carney was by Fréchette’s side in Lévis, Quebec, to announce that the federal government will invest $11 billion for Davie Shipyard to build six new icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard.

The multiple announcements between both leaders so close to the election did not go unnoticed by reporters, who asked Fréchette if Carney is becoming her “best friend” for the upcoming campaign and Carney if he would like Fréchette to win the election.
Carney took the podium first to say it is his job to work with premiers, unions, business leaders and all Canadians in a spirit of collaboration.

“That’s my choice,” he said in French. “It’s the only choice and I am happy that Madame Fréchette has the same attitude in terms of working in collaboration to create good jobs and bright futures for people.”
“When Madame Fréchette became premier, she said, ‘Let’s get to work.’ These are good words for me,” he added.
In a similar fashion, Fréchette said it is her job to work with anyone who wants to advance Quebec’s interests.
After the announcement, Carney crossed the St. Lawrence River to meet with the leader of the Quebec Liberal Party (QLP) Charles Milliard, for a brief lunch.

It was the first meeting between the two men and sources said they spoke about their vision of how to respond to the trade war. After lunch, Carney took the initiative to go around the patio, with Milliard, to shake hands with customers.

A provincial source said the Liberal Party of Canada has more natural links with the QLP than the CAQ. For instance, two of Carney’s top advisors — chief of staff Marc-André Blanchard and deputy chief of staff Andrée-Lynne Hallé — were involved with the provincial Liberals years back.
Kalles said he didn’t see Carney’s meeting with Milliard as an endorsement.

“I don’t think we know who’s going to win this election, so I think it’s trying to build a relationship — especially in the current circumstances of an economic crisis and the tariff crisis — and at least break the ice with any of the potential winners.”
No such meetings were in the works for PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon or other provincial leaders before the start of the campaign, Carney’s office said.
And Carney will not be making partisan announcements with any of the contenders during the Quebec election either.
If the PQ were to form government in October, a senior government source said the prime minister would treat it no differently than other provinces.
For now, Fréchette is the one who seems to be benefitting from the current trade war with the U.S. while St-Pierre Plamondon and Milliard are losing ground.

A Synopsis-La Presse poll released Friday showed that the CAQ has soared to 27 per cent of voting intentions in Quebec among decided voters, a statistical tie with the PQ which now stands at 28 per cent. The QLP is in third place at 20 per cent.
In this scenario, the PQ would still form a minority government, but any movement upwards for the CAQ could compromise this scenario for the separatist party.

Jonathan Valois, a former CAQ chief of staff and PQ member of the National Assembly, said the polling shows that Quebecers are striving for more stability amid the trade war, and that as a result, all provincial parties will be forced to readjust their messaging.
“The campaign is going to be a long one, but it certainly sends very clear signals to political parties regarding the mood of the electorate concerning this American threat,” he said.

Valois said that while Fréchette has benefitted from her close proximity to Carney — who remains widely popular in Quebec — she also struck the right tone in demanding more information on the tentative Canada-U.S. deal before talks collapsed last week.

Earlier this week, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Carney walking away from a trade agreement and blaming it in part on the lack of protections for the French language because he was trying to prevent the PQ from winning in Quebec.
Valois said that while details around this issue are still fuzzy, Carney defending the protection of the French language from the U.S. is a “gift from heaven” for the CAQ.
“This makes things a bit easier for Christine Fréchette, who wanted to show that she is aligned with Mark Carney but also a staunch defender of Quebec’s distinct character.”
“Right now, the stars are aligned for her.”

Ottawa — Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette launched her province’s election campaign by talking about the importance for Quebec to transform its economy in the face of the trade war with the U.S. because their old relationship is over.

If that message sounds oddly familiar, it’s because it is.

That is exactly the message that Prime Minister Mark Carney has been repeating since the 2025 election that saw the Liberal Party of Canada get elected for a fourth mandate against all odds.

On Thursday, a reporter asked Fréchette if she was trying to emulate Carney.

“My name is Christine Fréchette — and it’ll stay that way,” she said with a laugh.

Fréchette took the reins of the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) in April, succeeding its founder and longtime leader François Legault. The CAQ was expected to be wiped off the electoral map with the separatist Parti Québécois (PQ) poised to form a majority government.

But Fréchette took the bull by the horns, multiplying announcements in the province and adopting a new collaborative tone with Ottawa that led to the conclusion of pending deals with Quebec worth billions for infrastructure and major contracts.

Provincial and federal sources consulted for this story said that Fréchette and Carney have a “transactional” relationship which has benefitted both sides — showcasing Fréchette as a dealmaker and Carney as practicing “cooperative federalism.”

But they argue that Ottawa would be wise to take a step back now that the campaign is underway and let the different parties battle it out for the election on October 5.

“They shouldn’t do anything that smells of interfering. Quebec voters will look very unfavourably on the federal government doing anything that hints of picking a winner,” said Jonathan Kalles, a former Quebec advisor to former prime minister Justin Trudeau.

“I think people can figure out which side Mark Carney’s on. At least in terms of who he doesn’t want to win, I don’t think he needs to say that. And I think if he does, it would look bad, and it wouldn’t help whichever other party he, in essence, wants to win.”

Once Fréchette became premier, she travelled to Ottawa to meet with the prime minister — instead of him coming to Montreal or Quebec City — and Carney pointed out there were many years-long pending deals between both levels of government.

“He couldn’t wrap his mind around why we could not agree on good news,” said one senior government source.

Kalles, now senior vice president at Vantage, said the personalities and backgrounds of Trudeau and Legault were so different that their talks weren’t “always constructive.”

“Fréchette comes in and she’s looking to demonstrate that she can get concrete things done. And I think Mark Carney understood that, so he was in a deal mode,” Kalles said.

The first major announcement came in June when Quebec and Ottawa signed five infrastructure agreements worth nearly $10 billion which would pave the way for major investments in public transit, health care, housing and education over the next decade.

And only three days before the start of the campaign, Carney was by Fréchette’s side in Lévis, Quebec, to announce that the federal government will invest $11 billion for Davie Shipyard to build six new icebreakers for the Canadian Coast Guard.

The multiple announcements between both leaders so close to the election did not go unnoticed by reporters, who asked Fréchette if Carney is becoming her “best friend” for the upcoming campaign and Carney if he would like Fréchette to win the election.

Carney took the podium first to say it is his job to work with premiers, unions, business leaders and all Canadians in a spirit of collaboration.

“That’s my choice,” he said in French. “It’s the only choice and I am happy that Madame Fréchette has the same attitude in terms of working in collaboration to create good jobs and bright futures for people.”

“When Madame Fréchette became premier, she said, ‘Let’s get to work.’ These are good words for me,” he added.

In a similar fashion, Fréchette said it is her job to work with anyone who wants to advance Quebec’s interests.

After the announcement, Carney crossed the St. Lawrence River to meet with the leader of the Quebec Liberal Party (QLP) Charles Milliard, for a brief lunch.

It was the first meeting between the two men and sources said they spoke about their vision of how to respond to the trade war. After lunch, Carney took the initiative to go around the patio, with Milliard, to shake hands with customers.

stories.title: Surge in student violence brings Canadian teachers to a breaking point
stories.summary: Educators press ministries and school boards to act as resources fall short for increasingly complex classrooms
stories.author: Dave McGinn
stories.content:
Teachers face more violence as resources fall short for complex classrooms and kids who need support

Bridget Healy was attacked on the eighth day of the school year. The first week had been full of violence.

Ms. Healy was teaching a Grade 4 class at a school in Innisfil, Ont., in the fall of 2023. A safety plan had been put in place for one of the 23 students – a blueprint for how to respond if the student’s behaviour put others at risk.

The student was known to act out, but was not deemed violent enough by administrators to require full-time support. Instead, one educational assistant split her time between Ms. Healy’s classroom and the one next door. “The classroom next door also had a violent student, but he was six foot tall and 200 pounds, and so that’s where the EA spent most of her time,” Ms. Healy said.

She had a walkie-talkie to communicate with her colleague if she ever needed help. She had used it every morning: “Every single day since the start of school he would come right up to my face, scratch me, hit me and I would walkie for help and they would come.”

On the eighth day, the student, who was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, began hitting Ms. Healy. She called for help and followed the safety plan: Walk away without acknowledging the student. “But he ran faster than the EA could catch him, and he clocked me in the back of the head three times. And the EA had to pull him off me,” Ms. Healy said.

She knew she had suffered a concussion, having experienced similar symptoms after a car accident and after a work injury as a teenager. A doctor soon confirmed her suspicions. It took months before she could return to school.

Ms. Healy’s story is an extreme example of a phenomenon that has become a regular occurrence in classrooms across Canada.

Data from across the country gathered by The Globe and Mail show that acts of violence against elementary and high-school teachers are on the rise. The causes are complicated: overcrowded and increasingly complex classrooms, a lack of funding for support staff such as EAs and social workers, and inadequate screening for behavioural concerns.

Students involved in such incidents are often struggling with mental-health issues or have developmental disabilities such as autism. There are often inadequate resources to support them.

Many teachers are at breaking point. They are urging education ministries and school boards to solve the problem – but not everyone can agree on how.

Statistics from several school boards and governments across the country suggest a troubling rise in violence against teachers.

Incidents range from verbal threats and spitting to kicking, punching, hair-pulling, stabbing with pencils and throwing desks and chairs. Since the return to classrooms after COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, these acts have become more frequent.

The Toronto District School Board, the largest in the country, recorded 5,138 violent incidents by a student against a staff member in the 2024-25 school year, up from 4,077 incidents in the 2018-19 school year, an increase of 26 per cent.

The total student population at the board dropped slightly over that period as violence increased.

A spokesperson for the board said these numbers need to be taken with a grain of salt. “We take all reports of violence in the workplace very seriously,” Ryan Bird said in a statement.

“These numbers represent incidents that have been reported by staff, but not yet investigated, and cover a wide range of situations which May or May not have resulted in an injury. It’s important to note that some of these incidents include multiple employees reporting the same incident.”

But similar increases have been reported elsewhere. The Peel District School Board, the second largest in Ontario, recorded 7,039 such incidents in compliance with the Ontario Health and Safety Act in 2024-25, up from 3,102 in 2018-19 – a 127-per-cent increase.

Multiple staff members May submit reports relating to the same incident, and so the number of reports May be higher than the number of incidents.

In the last school year, Edmonton Public Schools, the largest public-school division in the Alberta capital, recorded 25,783 incidents of violence against staff members, a 161-per-cent increase over the 9,883 incidents reported in the 2018-19 year.

A spokesperson for the board said several factors help to explain the size of the increase. The total counts the number of times a student engaged in violent behaviour, rather than individual events. (For example, if a student spat at a teacher three times in a row, that would count as three incidents.) The spokesperson said there has also been a greater focus on encouraging staff to report incidents. The total student population has also increased by more than 20 per cent over the same time period.

Not all boards track these data. Other jurisdictions report violent incidents in the aggregate, which can also include altercations between students.

In Nova Scotia, for example, there were 27,117 incidents of violence at schools throughout the province in the 2024-25 school year. That’s 82 per cent more than the 14,864 incidents reported in 2018-19, Department of Education figures show. The data do not break down how many of the incidents consisted of student-on-teacher violence.

There are other data points that suggest the problem is getting worse. Some provinces report a rise in the number of teachers and teacher assistants on short-term and long-term disability leave as a result of violence.

Last year in British Columbia, there were 575 successful short-term and long-term disability claims arising from “an act of violence or force” filed by secondary, elementary and kindergarten teachers and teacher assistants, according to data from WorkSafeBC, the provincial Workers’ Compensation Board. That is an increase of more than 100 per cent since 2018, when there were 285 such claims.

Alberta has witnessed a similar trend. In 2025, there were 230 accepted workers’ compensation claims by elementary and secondary school teacher assistants that were the result of violence, according to data from the Workers’ Compensation Board of Alberta. “If you did that in any school, elementary or high school, the number on that board would be zero,” he said.

She had a walkie-talkie to communicate with her colleague if she ever needed help. She had used it every morning: “Every single day since the start of school he would come right up to my face, scratch me, hit me and I would walkie for help and they would come.”

On the eighth day, the student, who was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, began hitting Ms. Healy. She called for help and followed the safety plan: Walk away without acknowledging the student. “But he ran faster than the EA could catch him, and he clocked me in the back of the head three times. And the EA had to pull him off me,” Ms. Healy said.

As she slowly recovered from the concussion she suffered at the hands of a student, Ms. Healy could not work for several months, relying on a Workplace Safety and Insurance Board claim to pay her bills.
She returned to the classroom in January, 2024, working two days a week at a smaller school near her home. “I couldn’t drive, and I couldn’t be in a classroom by myself,” she said.
When she was finally able to work full-time, she transferred to another school to teach kindergarten. But even with younger students, Ms. Healy still experienced violence on a regular basis.
Her class of 26 students included 13 who she said were likely neurodivergent and needed extra support.

The school board had denied a request for a dedicated EA to help one of the students, Ms. Healy said. One day in June of 2025, she said, that student destroyed the classroom, throwing its small chairs and desks and using everything they could grab as a projectile.
Violence has been a consistent theme throughout her career so far, Ms. Healy said. She believes smaller class sizes are the first step to solving the problem.
“If there weren’t so many students in my classrooms, then so many of these problems could be avoided,” she said.
The punching incident still haunts her, although she said it never made her question whether or not she wants to continue to be a teacher.
“But it certainly made me question how long I’m going to be able to survive in this system.”
