stories.title: Strong support for Canada axing U.S. trade talks, retaliatory tariffs: poll
stories.summary: The Ipsos poll for Global News suggests the Liberal government still enjoys broad backing from Canadians, but that support dips among younger voters.
stories.author: Sean Boynton
stories.content:
Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs , a new poll suggests, which is translating to persistent support for Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals.

However, the Ipsos polling conducted exclusively for Global News and released Saturday also shows that support varies by age, with fewer Generation Z and Millennial adults backing the Liberals and their approach to the growing U.S. trade war.

“These people are living in what we like to call ‘the endurance economy’: they’re just getting by from day to day, and they’re enduring economic life right now,” said Darrell Bricker, chairman of Ipsos Canada.

“I think one of the takeaways here is that while Canadians are generally supportive of the idea of pushing back hard on the United States … if any of those things could bring a personal risk, if you’re somebody who’s living in that endurance economy, you’re less likely to support it.”

The poll found 63 per cent of Canadians surveyed feel Canada was right to stand firm in the trade negotiations, “even if it meant higher costs and job losses,” while just 18 per cent said Canada should have made additional sacrifices to get a deal.

An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week after trade talks collapsed.

But those numbers fall to 48 per cent of Gen Z adults and 57 per cent of Millennials who support Canada standing firm, and 59 per cent of Millennials who were happy to see Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. By comparison, about 80 per cent of elderly boomers supported both of those positions.

Bricker said the disparity points to economic realities for those different age groups.

“The people who were the ‘elbows up’ crowd in the last election campaign, who voted for the Liberals and continue to vote for the Liberals, they’re older, they’re more economically established, they tend to have higher degrees of education, they tend be more affluent,” Bricker said.

“So as a result of that, there’s less risk for them. So they can be all ‘elbows up,’ but it doesn’t cost them as much as it’s going to cost the other people they’re asking to have their elbows up.”

The age gap also extends to who Canadians said they would vote for if an election were to be held tomorrow.

While the Liberals maintain a healthy lead of 44 per cent support overall among those surveyed, compared to 33 per cent for the Conservatives, 40 per cent of Millennials chose the Conservatives over the Liberals, who see just 30 per cent support in that age group.

The Liberals’ support is down by just one point since April, while the Conservatives saw no change. The NDP at 10 per cent and the Bloc Quebecois at eight per cent nationally are each up one point since April.

“I have not in my consciousness recalled as tumultuous a week, or couple of weeks, or couple of months, in Canadian politics since probably 1995, when we went through the sovereignty referendum,” Bricker said.

“You would expect that you would see a lot of change in terms of political support, and we’re seeing virtually none (since the federal election). … I would say a lot of what’s going on right now is basically baked in, in terms of how it relates to federal politics.

Bricker added Canadians are likely not anticipating another election anytime soon, meaning they’re not thinking hard about their vote intentions right now.

Asked if they felt Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and his party would have done a better job handling the trade issues with the U.S. than Carney, 37 per cent overall said yes, with 67 per cent of Conservative voters agreeing.

A sizeable 62 per cent of respondents said they would like to see Parliament recalled before it’s due to reconvene in late September in order to debate and vote on Canada’s response to the U.S., which Bricker said could pose a vulnerability to an otherwise politically strong Carney.

“Canadians know their institutions actually matter to them,” he said. “Not recalling Parliament and not having a conversation through our political institutions is something that does represent a little bit of a vulnerability … (but) I would say, at this stage of the day, a mere crack.”

The poll also found strong support for a slew of other retaliatory measures that Canada could take against U.S. trade actions, from imposing tariffs on critical minerals and energy (both 73 per cent) to limiting those exports south of the border (71 per cent for critical minerals and 69 per cent for crude oil, natural gas and electricity).

Two-thirds said they would like to see an “aggressive” tax on U.S. tech giants operating in Canada, while 64 per cent were supportive of logistically slowing down U.S. imports by tightening border inspections on incoming goods.

The least popular option presented — letting the Canadian dollar weaken naturally to make Canadian exports more globally competitive — saw 45 per cent support.

On “Buy Canadian,” 80 per cent said they supported government purchasing and infrastructure projected prioritizing Canadian materials and contracts, with 60 per cent saying they will make an effort to prioritize Canadian products, services and companies themselves.

Between two-thirds and 80 per cent of respondents were supportive of other possible government support measures in the trade war, such as helping businesses expand to markets outside the U.S., providing job training and retraining programs for affected workers, and offering loans, emergency aid, extended Employment Insurance, or financial incentives to businesses.

Sixty-seven per cent of Canadians said they would like to see a major COVID-era subsidy program put in place to support Canadian workers affected by tariffs by both countries in the trade war, up eight points since last July.

And while 52 per cent overall said they are personally willing to undergo some “significant” economic pain to help Canada weather the storm, that number once again was lower among Generation Z (41 per cent) and higher among boomers (67 per cent).

“I thought the numbers would be stronger,” Bricker said.

“As you start going down the list and people start considering things that might be a little bit more onerous, or things that they’re really not that certain what it means, you start to see things get a little bit more wobbly. On the side of support right now, but definitely not as baked in and strong.”

These are some of the findings of an Ipsos poll conducted between August 26 and 27, 2026, ON behalf of Global News. For this survey, a sample of 1,001 Canadians aged 18+ was interviewed online. Quotas and weighting were employed to ensure that the sample’s composition reflects that of the Canadian population according to census parameters. The precision of Ipsos online polls is measured using a credibility interval. In this case, the poll is accurate to within ± 3.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, had all Canadians aged 18+ been polled. paragraphs: Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs , a new poll suggests, which is translating to persistent support for Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals.

However, the Ipsos polling conducted exclusively for Global News and released Saturday also shows that support varies by age, with fewer Generation Z and Millennial adults backing the Liberals and their approach to the growing U.S. trade war.

“These people are living in what we like to call ‘the endurance economy’: they’re just getting by from day to day, and they’re enduring economic life right now,” said Darrell Bricker, chairman of Ipsos Canada.

“I think one of the takeaways here is that while Canadians are generally supportive of the idea of pushing back hard on the United States … if any of those things could bring a personal risk, if you’re somebody who’s living in that endurance economy, you’re less likely to support it.”

The poll found 63 per cent of Canadians surveyed feel Canada was right to stand firm in the trade negotiations, “even if it meant higher costs and job losses,” while just 18 per cent said Canada should have made additional sacrifices to get a deal.

An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week after trade talks collapsed.

But those numbers fall to 48 per cent of Gen Z adults and 57 per cent of Millennials who support Canada standing firm, and 59 per cent of Millennials who were happy to see Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. By comparison, about 80 per cent of elderly boomers supported both of those positions.
Bricker said the disparity points to economic realities for those different age groups.

“The people who were the ‘elbows up’ crowd in the last election campaign, who voted for the Liberals and continue to vote for the Liberals, they’re older, they’re more economically established, they tend to have higher degrees of education, they tend be more affluent,” Bricker said.
“So as a result of that, there’s less risk for them. So they can be all ‘elbows up,’ but it doesn’t cost them as much as it’s going to cost the other people they’re asking to have their elbows up.”
The age gap also extends to who Canadians said they would vote for if an election were to be held tomorrow.

While the Liberals maintain a healthy lead of 44 per cent support overall among those surveyed, compared to 33 per cent for the Conservatives, 40 per cent of Millennials chose the Conservatives over the Liberals, who see just 30 per cent support in that age group.

The Liberals’ support is down by just one point since April, while the Conservatives saw no change. The NDP at 10 per cent and the Bloc Quebecois at eight per cent nationally are each up one point since April.

“I have not in my consciousness recalled as tumultuous a week, or couple of weeks, or couple of months, in Canadian politics since probably 1995, when we went through the sovereignty referendum,” Bricker said.

“You would expect that you would see a lot of change in terms of political support, and we’re seeing virtually none (since the federal election). … I would say a lot of what’s going on right now is basically baked in, in terms of how it relates to federal politics.
Bricker added Canadians are likely not anticipating another election anytime soon, meaning they’re not thinking hard about their vote intentions right now.

Asked if they felt Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and his party would have done a better job handling the trade issues with the U.S. than Carney, 37 per cent overall said yes, with 67 per cent of Conservative voters agreeing.

A sizeable 62 per cent of respondents said they would like to see Parliament recalled before it’s due to reconvene in late September in order to debate and vote on Canada’s response to the U.S., which Bricker said could pose a vulnerability to an otherwise politically strong Carney.

“Canadians know their institutions actually matter to them,” he said. “Not recalling Parliament and not having a conversation through our political institutions is something that does represent a little bit of a vulnerability … (but) I would say, at this stage of the day, a mere crack.”

The poll also found strong support for a slew of other retaliatory measures that Canada could take against U.S. trade actions, from imposing tariffs on critical minerals and energy (both 73 per cent) to limiting those exports south of the border (71 per cent for critical minerals and 69 per cent for crude oil, natural gas and electricity).

Two-thirds said they would like to see an “aggressive” tax on U.S. tech giants operating in Canada, while 64 per cent were supportive of logistically slowing down U.S. imports by tightening border inspections on incoming goods.
The least popular option presented — letting the Canadian dollar weaken naturally to make Canadian exports more globally competitive — saw 45 per cent support.

On “Buy Canadian,” 80 per cent said they supported government purchasing and infrastructure projected prioritizing Canadian materials and contracts, with 60 per cent saying they will make an effort to prioritize Canadian products, services and companies themselves.

Between two-thirds and 80 per cent of respondents were supportive of other possible government support measures in the trade war, such as helping businesses expand to markets outside the U.S., providing job training and retraining programs for affected workers, and offering loans, emergency aid, extended Employment Insurance, or financial incentives to businesses.

Sixty-seven per cent of Canadians said they would like to see a major COVID-era subsidy program put in place to support Canadian workers affected by tariffs by both countries in the trade war, up eight points since last July.

And while 52 per cent overall said they are personally willing to undergo some “significant” economic pain to help Canada weather the storm, that number once again was lower among Generation Z (41 per cent) and higher among boomers (67 per cent).
“I thought the numbers would be stronger,” Bricker said.

“As you start going down the list and people start considering things that might be a little bit more onerous, or things that they’re really not that certain what it means, you start to see things get a little bit more wobbly. On the side of support right now, but definitely not as baked in and strong.”

These are some of the findings of an Ipsos poll conducted between August 26 and 27, 2026, ON behalf of Global News. For this survey, a sample of 1,001 Canadians aged 18+ was interviewed online. Quotas and weighting were employed to ensure that the sample’s composition reflects that of the Canadian population according to census parameters. The precision of Ipsos online polls is measured using a credibility interval. In this case, the poll is accurate to within ± 3.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, had all Canadians aged 18+ been polled. The credibility interval will be wider among subsets of the population. All sample surveys and polls May be subject to other sources of error, including, but not limited to coverage error, and measurement error.

stories.title: Fire wrecks B.C.'s historic Little Red House, beloved by painters and photographers
stories.summary: A historic home popularly known as the Little Red House has been destroyed by fire after standing in the Township of Langley for almost 140 years.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A heritage house, shown in this Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026 handout photo, that stood for more than 130 years in Township of Langley, B.C., has burned down. THE Canadian Press/Handout — Ken Baber (Mandatory Credit)

A historic home popularly known as the Little Red House has been destroyed by fire after standing in the Township of Langley for almost 140 years.

The township’s archives say the home properly known as Mclver House burned down early on Thursday.

It says the home was built by Murdoch and Annie McIver between 1887 and 1890.

While the Langley Heritage Society says in a social media post that the house in the Glen Valley area had fallen into disrepair, its location in the middle of a turf farm helped make it “one of the most photographed and painted” homes in the area.

It says the Gothic-style farmhouse, which also served as a backdrop for photo shoots and videos, “evoked memories of simpler times.”

Rob Rindt, a Township of Langley councillor, shared videos of the house being engulfed in flames, saying its destruction was “incredibly sad.”

“So many people photographed, painted and stopped to admire this house over the years, and now these images capture its final moments,” he said.

A description of the house in the Township of Langley’s archives, held by its heritage facility known as salishan Place by the River, says the house was built by the McIvers to replace an earlier log cabin, “which was most likely too small to accommodate the McIvers’ growing clan of nine children.”

It says the house was still occupied until the early 1990s “but by 2010 it had been surrounded by a turf farm and was uninhabited and falling into disrepair.”

The heritage society said in an online post Friday that it was “sad and unfortunate” the home was never preserved.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Brews News: Railway City brings back updated honey elixir
stories.summary: St. Thomas brewery also renamed its Crew lager Canada Southern after a rail firm that used to operate in the railway city
stories.author: Wayne Newton, Special to Postmedia News
stories.content:
Honey, we missed you.

Back on the board this month is Woodworth and Edwards Original Honey Elixir, the very local brown ale from the once-again very local Railway City Brewing in St. Thomas.

The marketing evokes a travelling medicine show — a nod to the health benefits of honey – and creates a fictional business partnership of Woodworth and Edwards. Woodworth Avenue in St. Thomas runs near the spot where Jumbo the Elephant was hit and killed by a train in 1885. Edward Street is home to the brewery.

The liquid honey added to the boil to create Honey Elixir comes from an apiary 20 kilometres away, more famous for entertaining children with a bee-themed adventure park. Yes, Clovermead also produces honey in addition to smiles.

Honey Elixir was one of Railway City’s early brews. An undated clipping from a newspaper featuring then-brewmaster Barb Ziola and Christy Hiemstra, of Clovermead, is part of the honey-history display at the entrance to the popular Aylmer theme park.

While the gist of Ziola’s Honey Elixir recipe has come and gone as a seasonal during the years, another of her brews originally intended as a one-off continues to be Railway City’s top seller: Dead Elephant. That beer got a boost early when it won the IPA category at the Ontario Brewing Awards and was the speaker’s choice winner when St. Thomas’s Steve Peters was Speaker of the Ontario Legislature.

At the ice cream headquarters of Ben and Jerry’s in Vermont, there’s a literal graveyard of flavours that lived and died. If Railway City were to create something similar, it would include beers such as Colonel Talbot’s Coffee Stout and Fire Roasted Mocha Porter.

With the brewery back in the hands of a local ownership group that includes day-oner Paul Corriveau, are there other beers returning, even if for a short while? Witty Traveller, a Belgian wheat beer, is a contender.

But not everything can be backward-looking.

During Railway City’s day-long re-launch Aug. 22, current head brewer Amanda Fehr introduced an excellent golden ale, Back on Track. It’s not intended to be available long-term, but that’s what they said about Dead Elephant.

There’s also a renaming of the flagship lager. What was Crew is now the more locally-focused Canada Southern, named in honour of one of the railways that once ran through St. Thomas.

What say you, craft beer fans? Is Railway City on track?

As Crew became Canada Southern Lager at Railway City, it looks to me like Cowbell’s Standard Light Lager is a rebranding of 2025’s Elbows Up. Both are/were 4 per cent alcohol light, crisp lagers with Canadian ingredients.

There’s another railway-themed craft brewery in southern Ontario: Broken Rail in St. Marys. It has a fresh hazy pale ale, named Rule 43. Train people know what that means. It’s the protocol to reduce speed during track repairs. Broken Rail Rule 43 is brewed inside a restored Grand Trunk station.

Change is not unique to Railway City Brewing this year. On the shore of Lake Ontario in Mississauga’s Port Credit neighbourhood, Stonehooker will close if a buyer can’t be found. It opened in 2019. No brewery events are planned after Labour Day. Stonehooker will continue selling beer until the cans and cases are gone.

Ready for cooler days ahead: Patina Irish Red is back at Storm Stayed on Wharncliffe Road, London.

Local craft beer, local great food, and now local wine from Crew: Colchester Ridge Estate Winery, of Harrow, is waiting at Cured Craft Brewing Co. in Leamington. On the beer side for first timers, SOS (Southern Ontario Stout) or Honey Badger, a wheat beer, are highly recommended. They are best paired with a free-admission day at Point Pelee.

Wayne Newton is a freelance journalist based in London.

BrewsNewsTravels@gmail.com

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: August 29, 2026
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney asked premiers to remove the U.S. booze ban.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney asked premiers to remove the U.S. booze ban.

I was a Jack Daniels whiskey fan, enjoying a sip now and again. Then, U.S. alcohol was removed from the Lcbo shelves. I found Barnburner, a distilled whiskey made in Ontario. It’s better value and I think it tastes better.

So, go ahead and reverse the booze ban. I still will not buy U.S. alcohol.

Steve Dibert, London

If the Lcbo starts selling American liquor again, it should reduce the shelf space and raise the price by 50 per cent.

If someone has to have an American product, they can pay more for it and we’ll make more money selling it. If the Americans complain, tell them the high price of diesel fuel has increased freight costs.

How can city hall allow e-scooters and e-bikes to run out of control on our streets? We have disasters waiting to happen. City council must address this situation immediately.

Ron Reesor, London

Regarding the Ask Rebecca advice column My friends’ warnings are making me question my retirement plans (Aug. 19).

The idea that you’ll be bored in retirement is a tired old myth. I, and everyone I know, found in retirement the time for other pursuits like hobbies, interests, projects, and travel. When retired, you aren’t limited by paltry vacation allowances. Retirement really is freedom. If you’re not yet ready for full retirement, see if your employer could keep you on part time or get a part-time job.

Doug Payne, London

When the Bank of Canada keeps the interest rate lower than the U.S., the Canadian dollar looses value. Everything we buy from outside Canada costs us more because of the exchange rate. The lower interest rate pushes the price of housing higher, because people can borrow more money.

You’d think our independent central bank would have learned when they put the interest rate near zero and housing prices skyrocketed. Then, they put the interest to eight per cent to slow inflation instead of putting the interest rate to something reasonable like four per cent. The exchange rate is self-inflicted pain.

Al Hutchison, St Thomas

In his column Climate change reality not spurring action (Aug. 22) Gwynne Dyer writes of the need to get serious about climate change.

He cherry-picks the latest extreme weather events to make his case, the first hurricane in Hawaii in 34 years and the summer heat dome over Europe.

His solution is to rid the world of fossil fuels and to move to net-zero as soon as possible. Increasingly, however, modern thought emphasizes people focus on adaptation rather than the radical and extreme net-zero approach. That approach, embraced by Europe, has resulted in a 300 to 400 per cent spike in energy prices compared to North America.

Air conditioning is almost non-existent in Europe due to high energy costs and net-zero thinking. The lack of air conditioning has contributed to the high number of deaths from the heat wave.

The human race has been around for thousands of years and has survived all kinds of challenges by learning to adapt to our environment. Climate change reality should spur us to action, but not in the direction Dyer suggests.

Daniel Mailer, London

Gwynne Dyer notes climate change denial is now becoming resignation toward the coming disaster so we don’t have to do anything that would require higher taxes and severely curtailing familiar lifestyles in the way every major country did during the Second World War.

I remember my parents, living in New York State during the Second World War, saving their gas ration cards all year so they could drive to visit grandparents in Iowa in the summer. In addition, having lived through the Depression, they grew their own food where possible, mended their clothes, played cards for entertainment, and used every teabag four times.

I worry that, as a group of First World humans, we have lost our capacity for frugality and perspective.

Carol Lewis, London

stories.title: These Ontario doctors know how dangerous e-scooters can be. But keeping them from kids isn't easy
stories.summary: With e-scooter hospitalizations up nearly 40% across Canada, they say parents need to rethink how they view the devices.
stories.author: Amarachi Amadike
stories.content:
Over the past year, Diana Craiovan has spent much of her time analyzing data that paints a grim image of e-scooter use among children. A mother of two kids, age five and nine, she worries about the impact of these devices on Ontario’s youth as an increasing number of children end up in hospital.

“My kids have the regular scooters and (they) even find those fast,” she said. “I can’t imagine allowing them on a device that goes that fast.”

Craiovan, the program lead for hospital data management at the Canadian Institute for Health Information (Cihi), said her older child has not yet asked for an upgrade to a motorized scooter. Even if her children were older, however, she said she would not allow one in her home.

“Some of these e-scooters can go up to 25 kilometres an hour,” she said, roughly twice the speed of a typical kick scooter.

She was alarmed to discover that e-scooter-related injuries increased by 40 per cent nationally over the past year, with 837 hospitalizations recorded between April 2025 and March 2026.

Our city is one of the few in North America where riding one is against the law. Shauna Brail says yea and Erica Lam nay in our bridging the

Children under 15 account for much of that increase, she said in an interview, with injuries among that age group up 180 per cent over the same period. Data from the Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program also revealed that 10 kids died from e-scooter accidents in 2025. Six were in Ontario.

The staggering numbers have parents grappling with whether motorized scooters should be treated as toys or as vehicles subject to licensing and age restrictions — a question that takes on particular weight for parents who work as emergency physicians and see the results of accidents in the ER.

But as e-scooters become increasingly popular among children and teens, parents are finding themselves caught between wanting their kids to fit in and worrying about what can happen when things go wrong.

E-scooters’ greatest danger

Dr. Fraser Mackay, an ER physician and member of the Canadian Association of Emergency Physicians, said his response to his children asking to buy e-scooters would be “tough s—-,” even though they have “lots of friends with e-scooters, going down to seven and eight years old.”

“The main issue is the head injuries,” he said, adding that while they are not the most common injuries, they are the most devastating.

According to unpublished SickKids data from 2021 to 2025, many of the injuries involve head trauma, with 62 per cent of all accidents occurring without a helmet.

“You’re safer on a bicycle than you are on an e-scooter for a whole series of reasons,” Mackay said. “It is a motorized vehicle that’s supposed to be on the road and not on the sidewalk.”

Toronto is looking at a licensing e-bikes, which could close a gap in protections for delivery

Mackay said telling a 12-year-old to ride a motorized vehicle on the road is “ludicrous,” highlighting what he called the “bizarre” nature of municipal and provincial approaches to e-scooter regulations across the country.

“Right now, it’s a total Wild West, and we’re seeing the results of that.”

In Ontario, e-scooters can be used on private property, but municipalities must opt into the province’s pilot program if they want to permit e-scooters on public roads. Toronto has not opted in, so e-scooters cannot legally be ridden on the city’s public roads, bike lanes, sidewalks, trails, paths or in parks. In other words, owning an e-scooter, or riding one on private property, such as a driveway, is not prohibited, but taking it onto Toronto’s public streets is.

Why do parents buy e-scooters?

Dr. Josh Ramjist, a father of two children age four and seven, said the easy access creates a “developmental mismatch,” as young children are not skeletally or socially mature enough to operate the devices.

“They can’t handle the speed, their reflexes aren’t fast enough, and they’re in a crowded environment,” he explained.

Common and less common activities without protection can pose a high risk of injury, physicians say.

At The Hospital for Sick Children, where Ramjist practices, past emergency patients often return for follow-up appointments. Most parents get rid of their child’s e-scooter after an accident, he said.

“Almost all of them have given away (their devices), or just thrown the e-scooters in the trash,” he said. “It’s regret. I don’t think any well-meaning parent buys something for their kid with the intent that they’re going to get hurt by it.”

Ramjist noted that there is a misconception among parents that e-scooters are toys.

“The reality is that these are proper motorized vehicles,” he warned. “And the injury patterns resemble that.”

Experts say that, unlike conventional scooters, e-scooter accidents can result in injuries that resemble those seen in “standard motor vehicle accidents.”

“These kids are ending up with devastating injuries, sometimes debilitating injuries,” Ramjist said.

Potholes add another layer of risk. Pothole-related insurance claims from drivers increased almost 50 per cent from last year, and physicians say they are seeing the impact on e-scooter riders in emergency departments.

Dr. Caroline Rutten, a pediatric radiologist at The Hospital for Sick Children, said the hospital is seeing many young children come in after falls involving potholes, a statement corroborated by the hospital’s unpublished data, which reveals 69 per cent of accidents are due to falls without a collision.

“That has nothing to do with the child behaving safely and respecting speed limitations,” she said. “It’s just … the environment is very risky, and these devices are not very safe or stable. So accidents just happen very quickly.”

Rutten told the Star she has spent much of her time convincing family members not to allow her nieces and nephews on e-scooters, even though their friends May ride them.

“The average documented speed is around 25 kilometres an hour. That is motor-vehicle-level speed,” she warned them. “Would you let a 13-year-old child on a motorbike?”

Toronto has not opted in, so e-scooters cannot legally be ridden on the city’s public roads, bike lanes, sidewalks, trails, paths or in parks. In other words, owning an e-scooter, or riding one on private property, such as a driveway, is not prohibited, but taking it onto Toronto’s public streets is.

Dr. Josh Ramjist, a father of two children age four and seven, said the easy access creates a “developmental mismatch,” as young children are not skeletally or socially mature enough to operate the devices.
“They can’t handle the speed, their reflexes aren’t fast enough, and they’re in a crowded environment,” he explained.

At The Hospital for Sick Children, where Ramjist practices, past emergency patients often return for follow-up appointments. Most parents get rid of their child’s e-scooter after an accident, he said.

“Almost all of them have given away (their devices), or just thrown the e-scooters in the trash,” he said. “It’s regret. I don’t think any well-meaning parent buys something for their kid with the intent that they’re going to get hurt by it.”

content_blocks.text: Ramjist noted that there is a misconception among parents that e-scooters are toys.
“The reality is that these are proper motorized vehicles,” he warned. “And the injury patterns resemble that.”
Experts say that, unlike conventional scooters, e-scooter accidents can result in injuries that resemble those seen in “standard motor vehicle accidents.”

content_blocks.text: “These kids are ending up with devastating injuries, sometimes debilitating injuries,” Ramjist said.

Potholes add another layer of risk. Pothole-related insurance claims from drivers increased almost 50 per cent from last year, and physicians say they are seeing the impact on e-scooter riders in emergency departments.

Dr. Caroline Rutten, a pediatric radiologist at The Hospital for Sick Children, said the hospital is seeing many young children come in after falls involving potholes, a statement corroborated by the hospital’s unpublished data, which reveals 69 per cent of accidents are due to falls without a collision.

“That has nothing to do with the child behaving safely and respecting speed limitations,” she said. “It’s just … the environment is very risky, and these devices are not very safe or stable. So accidents just happen very quickly.”
Rutten told the Star she has spent much of her time convincing family members not to allow her nieces and nephews on e-scooters, even though their friends May ride them.

stories.title: Donald Trump claims Lake Ontario is now ‘Lake America.’ Here’s what you need to know about the cross-border battle
stories.summary: Trump’s executive order May change the name in the U.S., but Canada isn’t required to follow suit. Here’s who gets to decide and where the centuries-old name came from.
stories.author: Anastasia Blosser
paragraphs: A lake can be many things: a border, a body of water, a source of drinking water and, apparently, a battleground in a trade war .

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, following a bitter public spat with Ontario Premier Doug Ford and the collapse of trade talks between Canada and the United States.
Trump announced the change Thursday after Canada launched a new round of counter-tariffs on American products.
President Donald Trump says he's renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States as he escalates his trade war with Canada. (Aug. 28, 2026)

“They can continue to make their cars for Canada, but … we don’t want them to make cars for the United States of America,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “So the lake change, the Lake of America, was something I’ve been thinking about for a long time.”

Trump’s threat to rename the Great Lake came after he traded insults with Ford, who called the president a bully and told him to “kiss my ass.” Trump responded by comparing the premier to his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford, saying Doug Ford was a less charismatic version of him.
Trump also repeatedly accused Canada of “ripping off” the United States and said his administration did not expect to continue doing business with Ontario “much longer.”
Ford has since softened his language, calling for the two sides to reach a deal. But he said he did not regret his earlier comments, which he said resonated around the world.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has dismissed Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario, saying Canada will not recognize the change.
Other politicians on both sides of the border have also said they will continue using the lake’s familiar name.

“Lake Ontario is and will always be Lake Ontario, and no executive order will change that,” Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a statement on X. “It doesn’t belong to President Donald Trump to rename on a whim.”
Trump said it was “effective immediately” days after he said on social media that he was “giving
Ford likewise posted: “It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever.”
The renaming has particular significance for the Wendat Nation, whose language is believed to be the source of the name Ontario.
“Outraged, appalled, shocked: there are no other words to describe how I feel,” Grand Chief Pierre Picard of the Wendat Nation said in a statement.
“President Trump is attempting to eradicate our history,” Picard said.
In Canada, geographical names are overseen by the Geographical Names Board of Canada, which was established in 1897 and has approved more than 350,000 names over its history.

Individuals and organizations can propose names or name changes for Canadian geographical features. Those requests require information such as the reason for the proposed change, the origin and meaning of the name and evidence from local residents about how the area is commonly referred to.

Canada is not required to recognize geographical name changes made by another country. That means even if Trump’s administration uses “Lake America” for the portion of the lake on the U.S. side, he cannot dictate what other countries call the lake.

Lake Ontario is not the first border-straddling body of water that Trump has attempted to rename. One of his first moves after returning to office in January 2025 was signing an executive order directing the U.S. government to use “Gulf of America” instead of the Gulf of Mexico.
The Gulf of Mexico has carried its name for more than 400 years, and Trump’s order only holds water in the United States.

Trump also ordered the restoration of the name “Mount McKinley” for North America’s highest peak. Former president Barack Obama had changed the official U.S. name to Denali in 2015, reflecting the name preferred by local residents and Indigenous Peoples.
In February 2025, Republican congressman Buddy Carter introduced a House bill that would authorize Trump to acquire Greenland and rename it “Red, White and Blueland,”
U.S. map company MapQuest has already said it will not adjust its site to reflect Trump’s executive order.
“We’re not changing it,” Mapquest said in a post on social media, displaying a map of the lake bearing the familiar “Lake Ontario” moniker.
In a followup post, MapQuest joked that anyone determined to give the lake a new name could use an online generator, offering “Lake Are We Doing This Again?” as one possibility.
The Star has reached out to Apple to ask whether their maps will adopt “Lake America,” but had not received a response.
U.S. President Donald Trump asked Apple on Monday to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” on its map service.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox’s daytime program that Trump “reached out to Apple directly.” He said he was confident the “Lake America” name could be seen on its platform soon.

Google said in a statement published Saturday that it had changed the name of the lake on its U.S. service to Lake America, while in Canada it would remain Lake Ontario. Users outside the two countries would see both names on Google Maps. Google said the change reflects its “long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”
Google said this name change was due to the Geographic Names Information System (Gnis) formally changing the name from Lake Ontario to Lake America in the United States.
Other Canadian services that use Google Maps like Ontario 511 which provides images from over 900 cameras on roads across the province May have changed the name to Lake America.

Google Maps now uses “Gulf of America” for users in the United States, while users elsewhere see both names, with “Gulf of America” appearing in brackets. Apple Maps has also adopted the new name for the gulf.
The Associated Press, meanwhile, has declined to change its style guide, which is widely used by American news organizations.
The name Lake Ontario predates both Canada and the United States.

Historians believe Ontario has Iroquoian roots, with interpretations including “beautiful lake,” “great lake” or “sparkling water,” according to the Canadian Encyclopedia. Europeans were using the name Ontario for the lake by 1641, and it appeared on maps by 1656.
The name eventually became attached to the province itself during confederation, meaning Ontario is named after the lake and not the other way around.

Carney pointed to the Wendat origins of the name in a social media post, writing that Ontari’io means, roughly, “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” The beginning of the word, “Ontar,” means lake or body of water.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” Carney posted on social media.

Historians believe Ontario has Iroquoian roots, with interpretations including “beautiful lake,” “great lake” or “sparkling water,” according to the Canadian Encyclopedia. Europeans were using the name Ontario for the lake by 1641, and it appeared on maps by 1656.

The name eventually became attached to the province itself during confederation, meaning Ontario is named after the lake and not the other way around.

Wendat Nation Grand Chief Pierre Picard said the U.S. president “is attempting to eradicate our

Carney pointed to the Wendat origins of the name in a social media post, writing that Ontari’io means, roughly, “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.” The beginning of the word, “Ontar,” means lake or body of water.

“The name is more than 400 years old, predating both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States of America. We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always,” Carney posted on social media.

With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Medical tattoos mark next step in Peloza’s health journey after chemotherapy
stories.summary: Councillor Elizabeth Peloza is providing a health update in her ongoing series about her cancer journey called Healing in the Public Eye.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Councillor Elizabeth Peloza is providing a health update in her ongoing series about her cancer journey called Healing in the Public Eye.

Tonight, she shares her milestone completing chemotherapy, and the start of radiation treatments.

“It was a great day, I was never so excited to be having toxic chemicals put in me,” London City Coun. Elizabeth Peloza recalls about her final chemotherapy treatment.

Peloza has been sharing her breast cancer journey with CTV News in a special series called Healing in the Public Eye.

Recently, Peloza sat down to share her thoughts about reaching the milestone in her treatment.

“I got to ring the bell that signals the end of chemo,” she said about the tradition of ringing a brass bell inside the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at the London Health Sciences Centre.

“When anyone in that space rings the bell, the auditorium echoes with people clapping,” Peloza explains. “Everyone is celebrating with you because they are in that same place themselves or with a loved one.”

She’s was also excited for the removal of a peripherally inserted central catheter, known as a Picc line, that delivered the chemotherapy drugs close to her heart.

Running a finger over the small scar on the inside of her arm she explains, “I can now sleep comfortably, not worry about putting clothes on and catching it, and I can shower without having to bag it up.”

However, ringing the bell and removing the Picc line isn’t the end of Peloza’s cancer treatments.

“Everyone’s journey can include different things and can be in a different order,” she explains. “For me, it was the surgery first, then chemo, and now I’m going into radiation. For me, it’ll be 19 rounds of radiation.”

Early in her radiation treatments, she’s mentally preparing for side effects.

“I’ve been told it could feel like a sunburn, and then you keep going tanning every day,” Peloza said.

She’s aware that patients can experience fatigue at various times during the treatments.

However, each radiation treatment is much quicker than chemotherapy.

“Radiation is super fast,” she explains. “The bed is already precisely set-up to your exact measurements (regarding) where they need to place you for treatment. You hop on the bed, it takes a couple minutes, and then off you go with your day.”

Previously, chemotherapy treatments would require up to six hours at the cancer centre.

“They put three really small dots on my body, which are a permanent tattoo that they use to align the machine when I go in for radiation treatment,” she explains.

Asked if those were her first tattoos, she laughs.

“I was never cool enough to have a tattoo, so now I’ve got my first, second, and third tattoo all at the same time,” Peloza said.

She’s unsure whether to keep the tiny tattoos after her breast cancer journey is over.

“They’ll be a reminder. But the (surgery) scars are another reminder whenever I look down.”

stories.title: Head of federal agency helping to organize Carney’s investment summit resigns
stories.summary: Laurel Broten to depart Invest Canada two weeks before high-profile event is set to take place, source says
stories.author: Jameson Berkow
stories.content:
The head of the federal agency tasked with helping to organize Prime Minister Mark Carney’s high-stakes Canada Investment Summit is resigning.

Laurel Broten, chief executive officer of Invest in Canada, informed her staff last week that she will be leaving her position as of Sept. 1, according to a source familiar with the matter. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source, who was not authorized to disclose that information.

Ms. Broten is a former Ontario cabinet minister and Bay Street litigator. She has led the agency responsible for attracting foreign direct investment in Canada since 2022. Messages left on Ms. Broten’s voicemail and an email sent to her personal account were not immediately returned.

Invest in Canada is helping coordinate the Prime Minister’s inaugural gathering of top global business leaders in Toronto on Sept. 14 and 15 alongside two of the country’s largest institutional investors who are serving as co-hosts: The Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

The summit, which is expected to bring together the largest group of financial decision-makers ever to assemble in Canada, has garnered even more attention in the wake of a rapidly evolving trade war with the United States. As many as 250 executives from 28 countries that collectively manage nearly $120-trillion are expected to attend the event. Mr. Carney is under pressure to deliver on a promise to attract $500-billion in new private-sector investment over the next five years.

Ms. Broten has been playing a key role in planning the summit’s logistical details, the source said, including booking venues and selecting plenary session topics. Another source disputed that characterization, saying her main contribution has been the provision of a small number of Invest in Canada staff to support the primary organizers.

The date of her resignation means she is leaving two weeks before the most high-profile event in her agency’s history is due to take place.

Updated: This story was updated on Saturday to clarify Ms. Broten’s role and her effective departure date.

Editor’s note: This article was updated to clarify that the Invest in Canada agency helped to organize the summit.

stories.title: ‘It’s scary’: Neighbours concerned after fatal home break-in
stories.summary: An elderly woman who was stabbed and assaulted in a break and enter at her London home early Saturday morning has died, according to the London Police Service.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
An elderly woman who was stabbed and assaulted in a break and enter at her London home early Saturday morning has died, according to the London Police Service.

The case has now been turned over to the LPS Major Crimes Section to investigate as a homicide in collaboration with the Chief Coroner’s Office.

“There was a few squad cars there, and I didn’t know what happened until I saw forensics there,” said James Horner, who lives across the street from where the incident occurred. He learned of his neighbour’s death while speaking to CTV News Friday morning.

“That’s hard to take in. It shouldn’t happen to somebody like that. It sucks. The only thing I can think of, it sucks. It’s sad. And it’s not the outcome I would have wanted to hear,” he said.

On Saturday morning just after 6 a.m., police responded to a break and enter at 10 Raywood Avenue. An elderly woman had been awoken by a loud noise and found a man in her home. She was assaulted and stabbed, and taken to hospital with injuries described at the time as serious but non life-threatening.

On Friday, police announced that she died in hospital of her injuries.

The London city tax registry identifies the owner of the home as 73-year-old Lillian Anne Leonard.

Neighbour Steve Walker says he didn’t know her, personally. But he’s rattled by the incident, nonetheless.

“It’s scary. Yeah, it’s scary. I mean I think she was an older woman living here by herself and, yeah. It’s horrible,” he remarked.

Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London has been charged with second degree murder, along several other offences in connection with the Saturday morning incident.

The charges are as follows:

Second Degree Murder

Aggravated Assault

Break and enter with intent

Assault a peace officer with a weapon

Obstruct peace officer

LPS says as officers attended the residence the accused began throwing broken glass at police. One officer sustained minor injuries.

On Friday, shards of broken glass remained on the front and back porches, and front lawn of the home. A front window and back door had been boarded up.

The incident appears to be random.

“We do believe this was an isolated incident,” said LPS Inspector Jerry Rozic. “They were not known to each other. And I also want to reassure the public that the accused is in custody at this time. He was arrested at the scene,” he said.

The Raywood Avenue home where the incident occurred is currently the closest house to the corner at Wellington, with a vacant lot in between. A number of houses have been taken down to make way for the new transit line. Some neighbours believe that has left the neighbourhood, and Raywood Avenue in particular, more exposed.

“All these big trees have been cut down, which is another sad thing. But all the construction that has been going on here, the neighbourhood has been compromised somewhat with maybe crime. It’s sad,” said neighbour Mark Todd.

LPS is asking the public to contact them with any information relating to the case or the suspect’s whereabouts leading up to the incident.

In the meantime, Nelson Enrique Cornejo is scheduled to appear in court on Monday, Aug. 31.

“There was a few squad cars there, and I didn’t know what happened until I saw forensics there,” said James Horner, who lives across the street from where the incident occurred. He learned of his neighbour’s death while speaking to CTV News Friday morning.
“That’s hard to take in. It shouldn’t happen to somebody like that. It sucks. The only thing I can think of, it sucks. It’s sad. And it’s not the outcome I would have wanted to hear,” he said.

content_blocks.alt: James Horner
content_blocks.caption: James Horner, neighbour, reacts to the break-and-enter at 10 Raywood Avenue. (Bryan Bicknell/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: On Saturday morning just after 6 a.m., police responded to a break and enter at 10 Raywood Avenue. An elderly woman had been awoken by a loud noise and found a man in her home. She was assaulted and stabbed, and taken to hospital with injuries described at the time as serious but non life-threatening.
On Friday, police announced that she died in hospital of her injuries.
The London city tax registry identifies the owner of the home as 73-year-old Lillian Anne Leonard.
Neighbour Steve Walker says he didn’t know her, personally. But he’s rattled by the incident, nonetheless.
“It’s scary. Yeah, it’s scary. I mean I think she was an older woman living here by herself and, yeah. It’s horrible,” he remarked.

content_blocks.alt: 10 Raywood Avenue
content_blocks.caption: Back door at 10 Raywood Avenue on Aug. 28, 2026. (Bryan Bicknell/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London has been charged with second degree murder, along several other offences in connection with the Saturday morning incident.
The charges are as follows:
Second Degree Murder
Aggravated Assault
Break and enter with intent
Assault a peace officer with a weapon
Obstruct peace officer
LPS says as officers attended the residence the accused began throwing broken glass at police. One officer sustained minor injuries.
On Friday, shards of broken glass remained on the front and back porches, and front lawn of the home. A front window and back door had been boarded up.

content_blocks.alt: 10 Raywood Avenue
content_blocks.caption: Front window ledge at 10 Raywood Avenue on Aug. 28, 2026. (Bryan Bicknell/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: The incident appears to be random.

“We do believe this was an isolated incident,” said LPS Inspector Jerry Rozic. “They were not known to each other. And I also want to reassure the public that the accused is in custody at this time. He was arrested at the scene,” he said.

The Raywood Avenue home where the incident occurred is currently the closest house to the corner at Wellington, with a vacant lot in between. A number of houses have been taken down to make way for the new transit line. Some neighbours believe that has left the neighbourhood, and Raywood Avenue in particular, more exposed.

“All these big trees have been cut down, which is another sad thing. But all the construction that has been going on here, the neighbourhood has been compromised somewhat with maybe crime. It’s sad,” said neighbour Mark Todd.
LPS is asking the public to contact them with any information relating to the case or the suspect’s whereabouts leading up to the incident.
In the meantime, Nelson Enrique Cornejo is scheduled to appear in court on Monday, Aug. 31.

stories.title: ‘Very scary’: E-scooter injuries among London children more than double, LHSC data shows
stories.summary: The number of children treated for e-scooter-related injuries at London’s Children’s Hospital more than doubled this spring compared with the same period last year, according to new data from London Health Sciences Centre.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
paragraphs: The number of children treated for e-scooter-related injuries at London’s Children’s Hospital more than doubled this spring compared with the same period last year, according to new data from London Health Sciences Centre.
The hospital treated 22 children for e-scooter-related injuries between April and June 2025. That number rose to 58 during the same three-month period this year — an increase of about 164 per cent.
The figures come as e-scooter use continues to be permitted on London streets under a provincial pilot program.

Londoner Lindsey Greeno uses her e-scooter as her main mode of transportation. “I use it both to get to work. And like right now, I’m using it to get to the gym. So it’s. I rely on it very heavily,” said Greeno.
She said she wears a helmet and follows the city’s rules.
But the rise in injuries has prompted concerns about the safety of the devices, particularly among younger riders.
Data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows hospitalizations involving children and adults riding e-scooters rose by almost 40 per cent in the past year.
The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program also reported that 10 children died in 2025 while using e-scooters or e-bikes.
Dr. Sheena Belisle, a paediatric emergency physician at LHSC, said children arriving at the emergency department are presenting with a wide range of injuries.

“We see the full spectrum of injuries present to the pediatric emergency department,” Belisle said. “Everything from very mild injuries which might include bruises, cuts, scrapes to more serious injuries like broken bones and concussions to very significant injuries, which might include intra abdominal injuries and brain bleeds. So it can be very scary.”
The increase in injuries comes after London city council extended its e-scooter pilot program in May.
The decision included measures aimed at improving safety and enforcement, including an education campaign, proactive enforcement, and a new $100 fine for parents of riders under 16.
Under London’s rules, e-scooter riders must be at least 16 years old. Riders under 18 are required to wear a helmet.
Ward 10 Coun. Paul Van Meerbergen said he remains concerned about children riding e-scooters illegally.

“Frankly, it’s illegal. We passed a by-law that anyone under 16 is forbidden from riding these bikes, these e-scooters on London’s streets, but yet you look around and there they are,” said Van Meerbegen.
Ward 1 Coun. Hadleigh McAlister supported extending London’s pilot program but said the province should ultimately be responsible for regulating e-scooters.

“Ultimately the province needs to be the one regulating them,” said McAlister. “We heard from staff about difficulties regarding enforcement. Even with an outright ban, it would be tough to stop them.”
For now, e-scooters remain permitted on London roads with speed limits below 50 kilometres per hour, as well as in bike lanes and on multi-use pathways.
The province’s e-scooter pilot program is scheduled to end Nov. 27, 2029.

paragraphs: Search efforts are underway for a missing swimmer in the Ausable River in the Township of Bosanquet.
OPP received a report just before 3:00 p.m. Friday of a missing 66-year-old London resident.
The individual was last seen at the dock attached to an address on Canal Street in Grand Bend.
Police say updates will be provided when available.

stories.title: ‘We’ve been so worried’: Another B.C. couple missing after Nepal flash flooding
stories.summary: Their daughter says they were on a guided pilgrimage in the region of Nepal and haven't been heard from since the morning of Aug. 26.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Travis Prasad
stories.content:
The number of Canadian citizens and permanent residents unaccounted for since the Nepal flash flooding has risen to 32, including Coquitlam couple Sumit and Shubakshi Rawla.

Their daughter says they were on a guided pilgrimage in the region and haven’t been heard from since the morning of Aug. 26.

“We’ve been so worried,” Kenisha Rawla told Global News.

“Me and my sister personally have made over 200 phone calls to our parents just hoping that even for a moment if they get a second of signal they can contact us.”

The foreign affairs minister is urging caution as the search continues.

“Those 32 Canadians are unaccounted for but no Canadian deaths have been confirmed,” Anita Anand said on Friday.

The Rawlas were travelling with Port Moody residents Dhaval and Megha Shah , who also remain unaccounted for.

“They were somewhere in that location and the company lost contact with anybody at around 8:30 that morning,” Nikita Shah, relative of Megha and Dhaval Shah said on Thursday.

“So we don’t know where they have been since then.”

Thousands are still missing after the tragedy and at least 579 people are confirmed dead.

The scale of the destruction is visible at one Nepal’s main border crossings into China, where the area is buried in mud and debris.

“Further north, some of the communities are completely cut out,” Tamara Demuria, Corus International Chief Humanitarian Officer, said.

“We cant even get there to assess what’s left. The damage is way more severe.”

Ottawa is providing $5 million in humanitarian aid and sending five consular officials to Nepal.

But some want Canada to go further.

“We really want to really push the Canadian government to help by sending rescue teams because we know there’s so many Canadians there too, aside from our parents, and their families must be worried sick like we are,” Rawla said.

For families still waiting, there’s little to do but search for information and find strength in each other.

“Community support, emotional support, are what one should seek at times like this,” Gaurav Subedi with the Nepal Cultural Society of B.C. said.

“But miracles do happen.”

stories.title: Music fans invade Bruce County village for weekend long music festival
stories.summary: A huge field on the edge of Lucknow is being taken over by music fans this week for the annual party known as, Music in the Fields.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A huge field on the edge of Lucknow is being taken over by music fans this week for the annual party known as, Music in the Fields.

“Year 18 for Music in the Fields, 2026. Mother nature is cooperating, and giving us some amazing weather. We’ve got over 1700 campers on site, right now. A few more are coming in today,” said Music in the Fields Marketing Manager, Cheryl Johnston.

Over 8000 people will take in Music in the Fields this weekend. What started as a country music festival in 2009, has added a full night of rock music, in recent years.

“People like to have that mix. So yeah, people got to bring their dancing shoes and be ready to go. There’s not going to be much downtime, and great feedback, so far. Koe Wetzel, he’s coming in tomorrow from Texas, as the Saturday headliner, And, we’ve got Finger Eleven tonight with Matthew Good, a great mix of music,” said Johnston.

For Finger Eleven, it’s their first time at Music in the Fields, first time in Lucknow for that matter, but they’re happy to add some rock, to a typically country music weekend.

“I love that we get to play music, to anybody that appreciates music the way we do. So, when it comes to Finger 11, you’re going to get all kinds of stuff. You’re going to get loud stuff, you’re going to get mellow stuff. And, I hope that it goes well tonight,” said Finger Eleven frontman, Scott Anderson.

While the sound crews and artists are professionals, what sets Music in the Fields apart from other music festivals, is that everyone else, working behind the scenes, is a volunteer.

The Lucknow Kinsmen bring together 300 volunteers each year, to pull this event off, and have raised over $2 million that stays in the local community, supporting hospitals, schools, and local charities. It keeps folks like Michelle Millar and her friend, Michelle Courtnage coming back, year after year.

“This is year number nine for us. We come back, because it’s super fun, clean, just really well organized, new bands every year. And, you know what, it’s 100% local,” said Millar.

Johnston says Music in the Fields has become an annual pilgrimage for thousands of Ontario music fans.

“It’s family reunions. It’s the last friend get together of the summer. You know, people are just talking about kids going away to university and school, so it’s their one last chance to get together, and enjoy the whole weekend,” said Johnston.

Finger Eleven hasn’t even hit the stage yet, but they say they’d already love to come back to Music in the Fields.

“For the most part, if you ask us, we’ll come play. We just love to play music, man,” said Finger Eleven guitarist, Rick Jackett.

Lucknow’s Music in the Fields | August 27-29, 2026

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives to gather for crisis meeting on Monday after departure of five MLAs
stories.summary: The Official Opposition won 44 seats two years ago but has since shrunk to just 31 MLAs
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
During the past provincial election, the B.C. Conservatives rose like a rocket from the ashes of a moribund party that hadn’t formed government in a century to come within a whisker of defeating the incumbent New Democrats.

But since winning 44 seats, three short of a majority, two years ago, the party has begun a self-immolation that picked up speed this month with six of its MLAs leaving to sit as Independents, citing the new leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay . That’s on top of four MLAs who left last year.

In all, the Official Opposition’s bench has shrunk to just 31 MLAs and the turmoil – five MLAs quit this past week – has forced a summer caucus meeting planned for Monday.

Ian Paton describes himself and the others who left the party this month as “slightly to the right of centre.”

“We’re not these deep dark-blue conservatives far to the right that are against vaccines and Maid and abortion and all that stuff.”

After Ms. Findlay assumed the leadership of the party in June, she declared that the B.C. Conservatives would pursue a vision of “faith, family and freedom.” She swiftly brought in a new executive and communications staff.

More centrist, socially progressive members of her party say she alienated them by making moves such as leaning into culture-war rhetoric and spreading fear that the New Democrats were “dismantling” the province by transferring vast swaths of land to First Nations.

Ms. Findlay was unavailable Friday for an interview on the tumult, but the party sent The Globe and Mail an unattributed statement in which it rejected the characterization that Conservatives under her leadership have been distracted by culture-war issues.

The statement accused the MLAs who left as preferring to spend their time engaging in nasty politics and said that those who say the party has moved too far right can’t point to any policy that has actually changed.

Mr. Paton and others say they have no confidence that Ms. Findlay, a former MP in Stephen Harper’s Conservative government, can create a credible alternative for voters despite numerous polls this year showing that NDP Premier David Eby’s support has ebbed substantially across the province.

Earlier this week, Ms. Findlay fired her director of operations without explanation. She was also forced to defend herself after an audio recording surfaced on social media of her appealing to caucus members, asking for one of them to give up their seat to allow her to win a by-election to join the legislature.

On the tape, she says she could give anyone who steps aside a senior role as a policy adviser, but in a statement Thursday she denied that she was enticing someone to leave office, which is a potential criminal offence.

“These were normal political discussions that respect the boundaries of the law and ethics,” her statement said.

The meeting Monday could decide the fate of the province’s Official Opposition as the fall session of the legislature approaches in October.

Azim Jiwani, a conservative strategist and former chief of staff to John Rustad who helped engineer the renewal of the B.C. Conservatives before the 2024 election, said it is too early to count the party out. He noted that it still enjoys a considerable provincial subsidy to help it function and still has a recognizable brand.

“Not all is lost,” he said.

He maintains that the recent spate of members leaving is because of becoming exhausted with the internal chaos, but that the Conservatives will find stability after a divisive leadership race.

And, Mr. Jiwani says, those decrying Ms. Findlay’s focus on culture-war issues are missing the fact that these topics are proven winners.

“In fact, the Conservative Party of British Columbia came within 400 votes of forming government on a campaign that was largely driven by highly salient cultural issues, which were resonant with swing voters and swing ridings and resulted in a very efficient vote,” he said.

Other insiders are not so sure.

Business leaders and political operatives who were hopeful that the party could capitalize on a strong spring performance in the legislature have mounted an effort to swing cash and clout away from the Conservatives toward a new party to challenge the New Democrats.

Their calculus rests on well-worn West Coast political wisdom: The party that can build a “big tent” of candidates united by their loyalty to lower taxes and less regulation has traditionally formed the provincial government.

Recently, dozens of conservatives met at a downtown White Spot, according to Global News, which filmed former provincial politicians and strategists entering the restaurant.

Elenore Sturko, who was booted from the party last fall after a falling out with Mr. Rustad, said she started to feel the tent pegs of the B.C. Conservatives unmooring shortly after their surprising election gains.

Ms. Sturko, an independent MLA and former Rmcp officer who is gay, recalled being at a caucus meeting during a mining conference and having the discussion sidetracked from policy solutions by a two-hour debate on Pink Shirt Day – the anti-bullying school campaign.

“I don’t think I said a word because my jaw was on the ground,” Ms. Sturko said in an interview this week. “Some people felt very strongly that they couldn’t [support it] because they said that they felt being forced to wear a pink shirt was bullying.

“Instead of having a debate about natural-resources policy, we were spending time talking about pink shirts, which, honestly, if you want to wear one, wear one. If you don’t want to, no one is forcing you to do that.”

Mr. Paton, who has served as an MLA for a riding south of Vancouver for nearly a decade, left the party to sit as an Independent last Monday and plans to soon start a new centre-right party with fellow MLA Peter Milobar. Mr. Milobar competed against Ms. Findlay for the Conservative leadership of the party, but he left earlier this month.

Mr. Milobar says he has heard from a “very strong number” of former colleagues in the party who are still pondering whether to jump ship to another nascent group.

“People have hard decisions to make,” he said.

stories.title: Calgary uses AI to determine the 50 highest-risk intersections for pedestrians
stories.summary: The list of the highest-risk intersections comes after the City of Calgary used AI to assess and assign a risk score to more than 17,000 intersections across the city.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
The City of Calgary has used artificial intelligence to determine the 50 riskiest intersections for pedestrians across the city, but it’s unclear what will be done to address the issue as just half are recommended for upgrades.

According to a report set to be presented at the city’s Community Development Committee meeting Tuesday, administration used the city’s AI platform to assess and assign a risk score to more than 17,000 intersections across Calgary.

Many of the locations don’t meet “conventional warrant” thresholds for upgrades like traffic signals, overhead flashers, or curb-bump outs, the report said, as that set of criteria is based on factors such as traffic volumes, pedestrian volumes, roadway geometry, and speed limits.

City administration compiled a list of the top 50 highest-risk pedestrian intersections identified by the AI platform that do not have existing traffic signals like rectangular rapid flashing beacons with risk scores ranging from 93.55 to 99.02.

The intersection of Martindale Boulevard and Martindale Gate N.E. topped the list, followed by Falshire Drive and Falton Drive N.E. with a score of 98.54.

Ward 5 Coun. Raj Dhaliwal told Global News he was surprised with the intersections that scored the highest risk ratings, with four of the intersections in the top 10 in his area.

“I was asking myself is there something missing from my assessment,” Dhaliwal said of the intersection in Martindale. “Every time I drive by there, I see less pedestrian traffic.”

Just 26 of the locations are recommended for pedestrian safety improvements which are estimated to cost approximately $6 million, the report said.

According to the report, administration could “proactively advance improvements” with additional funding rather than “waiting” for future traffic counts, collision history or studies to “justify intervention under traditional processes.”

Some on council have questions about how AI was used to determine those findings, including modelling, inputs and prompts.

“I’m all for data-driven decision making. This is empirical evidence that is telling me that these things need to be upgraded,” Dhaliwal said.

“But at the same time, I want to know why, how and what.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "But at the same time, I want to know why, how and what."

The report notes there “May be public scrutiny” around the city’s use of AI, but adds all the recommended improvements were reviewed and validated through professional engineering judgment and technical assessment.

The city’s use of AI is “innovative,” said Alex Gaio, an associate principal at Leading Mobility, with the sheer amount of data administration would need to comb through.

“We have a lot of data, the city updates its hotspot map every 10 minutes,” he said. “So the volume that we get is overwhelming for people to deal with, and we’re racing against risk.”

Last year, 15 people were killed on city streets and so far this year six people have died; another 283 incidents involving pedestrians resulted in injuries.

“If we really care about the safety of our residents, pedestrian safety, motor vehicle safety… then let’s put our money where our mouth is,” Dhaliwal said.

Although committee is not being asked to make a financial commitment Tuesday, city administration said it could incorporate the pedestrian safety upgrades into the next four-year budget.

If city council was to approve additional funding during budget talks in November, the report said design work could begin in 2027, with shovels in the ground in 2028.

“But at the same time, I want to know why, how and what.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "But at the same time, I want to know why, how and what."

The report notes there “May be public scrutiny” around the city’s use of AI, but adds all the recommended improvements were reviewed and validated through professional engineering judgment and technical assessment.
The city’s use of AI is “innovative,” said Alex Gaio, an associate principal at Leading Mobility, with the sheer amount of data administration would need to comb through.
“We have a lot of data, the city updates its hotspot map every 10 minutes,” he said. “So the volume that we get is overwhelming for people to deal with, and we’re racing against risk.”
Last year, 15 people were killed on city streets and so far this year six people have died; another 283 incidents involving pedestrians resulted in injuries.
“If we really care about the safety of our residents, pedestrian safety, motor vehicle safety… then let’s put our money where our mouth is,” Dhaliwal said.
Although committee is not being asked to make a financial commitment Tuesday, city administration said it could incorporate the pedestrian safety upgrades into the next four-year budget.

stories.title: B.C. NDP MLA and Indigenous activist Joan Phillip dies
stories.summary: The Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs says she died peacefully this afternoon, surrounded by her family
stories.content:
British Columbia legislator and Indigenous leader Joan Phillip has died, with Premier David Eby honouring her as an “epic fighter.”

The Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said in a statement on Friday that the NDP MLA died peacefully Friday afternoon, surrounded by her family, including “the love of her life,” husband Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, their children and grandchildren.

“Joan was a fearless warrior and inspirational leader, and we will miss her dearly,” the union said.

Phillip had been battling an illness for months, and the union’s post asked for donations to the B.C. Cancer Society in lieu of flowers.

The organization said in a previous post on Thursday that Phillip was in hospital “courageously fighting kidney infection and septic shock.”

Philip was first elected in Vancouver in a 2023 byelection, and won again in B.C.’s general election the following year.

Eby said B.C. had lost “a powerful and respected leader.”

“Our caucus and staff are grieving alongside her family and so many others who knew and loved her,” he said in a statement.

“Joan was an epic fighter who dedicated her life to making the world a better and fairer place. We’ll miss her so much. Rest in peace Joan.”

Attorney General Niki Sharma said it was an honour to witness the strength of the bond between Joan and Stewart Phillip.

Joan Phillip’s profile on the B.C. legislature website says the couple have five surviving children, 15 grandchildren and one great-grandchild.

“I will forever cherish every moment I shared with you. You lived with purpose, hope and love,” Sharma said in an online post.

“I will truly miss your presence. You taught me so much about life, history and what’s right.”

Phillip was first elected in Vancouver-Mount Pleasant, then Vancouver-Strathcona in 2024.

She became parliamentary secretary for community development and non-profits in November that year.

The B.C. NDP caucus called her a “respected Indigenous leader who has dedicated her life to fighting for justice, human rights and the environment.”

Her bonds with Eby and the NDP were tested this year when the government, with a one-seat majority, proposed a confidence vote on suspending the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, raising the threat of a provincial election call.

The law, known as Dripa, is designed to affirm the application of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in other B.C. legislation, but has become a flashpoint for critics.

The government backed off when Eby said Phillip told him she could not bring herself to vote for the suspension.

The NDP caucus said that before being elected in 2023, Phillip worked as a youth counsellor at Britannia Secondary School, as education and program director at the Aboriginal Friendship Centre, and as the lands manager for the Penticton Indian Band.

The caucus had announced in early December that Phillip was dealing with an illness that required additional testing.

Federal Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said on Friday: “We have lost a matriarch and a champion.”
