stories.title: 'Epic fighter': Tributes for B.C. Indigenous leader and MLA Joan Phillip, dead at 74
stories.summary: British Columbia legislator and Indigenous leader Joan Phillip has died, with Premier David Eby honouring her as an "epic fighter."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbia legislator and Indigenous leader Joan Phillip has died, with Premier David Eby honouring her as an “epic fighter.”

The Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs said in a statement on Friday that the NDP MLA died peacefully Friday afternoon, surrounded by her family, including “the love of her life,” husband Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, their children and grandchildren.

“Joan was a fearless warrior and inspirational leader, and we will miss her dearly,” the union said.

Phillip had been battling an illness for months, and the union’s post asked for donations to the B.C. Cancer Society in lieu of flowers.

The organization said in a previous post on Thursday that Phillip was in hospital “courageously fighting kidney infection and septic shock.”

Philip was first elected in Vancouver in a 2023 byelection, and won again in B.C.‘s general election the following year.

Eby said B.C. had lost “a powerful and respected leader.”

“Our caucus and staff are grieving alongside her family and so many others who knew and loved her,” he said in a statement.

“Joan was an epic fighter who dedicated her life to making the world a better and fairer place. We’ll miss her so much. Rest in peace Joan.”

Attorney General Niki Sharma said it was an honour to witness the strength of the bond between Joan and Stewart Phillip.

Joan Phillip’s profile on the B.C. legislature website says the couple have five surviving children, 15 grandchildren and one great-grandchild.

“I will forever cherish every moment I shared with you. You lived with purpose, hope and love,” Sharma said in an online post.

“I will truly miss your presence. You taught me so much about life, history and what’s right.”

Phillip was first elected in Vancouver-Mount Pleasant, then Vancouver-Strathcona in 2024.

She became parliamentary secretary for community development and non-profits in November that year.

The B.C. NDP caucus called her a “respected Indigenous leader who has dedicated her life to fighting for justice, human rights and the environment.”

Her bonds with Eby and the NDP were tested this year when the government, with a one-seat majority, proposed a confidence vote on suspending the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act, raising the threat of a provincial election call.

The law, known as Dripa, is designed to affirm the application of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples in other B.C. legislation, but has become a flashpoint for critics.

The government backed off when Eby said Phillip told him she could not bring herself to vote for the suspension.

The NDP caucus said that before being elected in 2023, Phillip worked as a youth counsellor at Britannia Secondary School, as education and program director at the Aboriginal Friendship Centre, and as the lands manager for the Penticton Indian Band.

The caucus had announced in early December that Phillip was dealing with an illness that required additional testing.

Federal Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said on Friday: “We have lost a matriarch and a champion.”

Emily Lowan, leader of the BC Green Party, said Phillip was a woman of “unparalleled courage and character who always stood for what’s right, no matter the consequences.”

“She leaves a hole as a leader and visionary that will be hard to fill,” said Lowan.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay, leader of the BC Conservative Party, said she was “deeply saddened” to hear of Phillip’s death.

“While we stood on different sides of the political aisle, I always respected Joan’s fierce dedication to her community, her lifelong advocacy and her unwavering leadership on Indigenous issues,” said Findlay. “She served the people of Vancouver with determination and conviction.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 28, 2026.

stories.title: CBC reverses policy against calling 9/11 a terrorist attack without attribution
stories.summary: CBC made the change after it was criticized by Canadian and U.S. officials.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The CBC has reversed its policy that prohibited reporters from referring to 9/11 as “terrorism” without direct attribution.

CBC made the change after it was criticized by Canadian and U.S. officials, including the U.S. ambassador to Canada and the FBI director.

In a blog post on Friday, Basem Boshra, CBC’s senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, wrote that a leaked memo about the policy “has caused significant concern, anger and hurt for many people who believe CBC News seeks to minimize or obscure the horror of that day and who was behind it.”

“That is the last thing we want to do,” said Boshra, who is the senior director of journalistic standards and public trust of CBC News.

Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture Marc Miller called the policy reversal “a welcome change to what was a piece of pedantic and foolish guidance that caused legitimate anger.”

The Conservative party’s shadow minister for culture, Rachael Thomas, had called on the CBC to apologize.

As National Post previously reported, the memo was sent to CBC staff ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 reminding reporters and editors of its “longstanding language guidance” on the 2001 attack, which killed almost 3,000 people, including at least 24 Canadians.

“Do not refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks,” the memo read.

In a post on social media, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree wrote that condemning the terrorist attack “is not merely a political position.” Canada has legally recognized 9/11 as a terrorist attack, he said.

“That legislation reflects Parliament’s own clear-eyed characterization of what happened that day: a deliberate, ideologically motivated terrorist attack on civilians,” Anandasangaree wrote.

“For nearly 25 years, Canada’s laws and policies have treated it as exactly that.”

In a pointed critique, FBI director Kash Patel referred to the language policy as a “bastardization of history.”

“Any agency in Canada that doesn’t publicly reject this bastardization of history, and an insult to the souls lost during our largest terrorist attack in US history will no longer have friend in this FBI… Not to mention our heroes that responded in the aftermath,” he wrote on X.

“The radical left (Canadian Broadcasting Company) is trying to rewrite history, but there is nothing controversial, complicated, or unclear about this,” the U.S. House Republicans wrote in a statement posted to X, adding, “9/11 was terrorism.”

CBC’s language guidance had instructed employees to “exercise extreme caution before using the words terrorist or terrorism” because they can be “highly contested” and could raise questions about the CBC’s “consistency and impartiality.”

“Terrorism generally implies attacks against unarmed civilians for political, religious or some other ideological reason,” the guidance reads. “But it’s a highly controversial term that can leave journalists taking sides in a conflict.” According to Boshra, the CBC has reviewed its language guidance and has “decided to adjust it to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism. We are doing so to remove what has unfortunately (and unintentionally) become an impediment to clarity and public understanding.”

Among those outraged following reports of CBC’s policy was Maureen Basnicki of Collingwood, Ont., whose husband, Ken Basnicki, was trapped on the 106th floor of the North Tower of the World Trade Center during the attack and died on Sept. 11, 2001.

“To know that this directive was sent, and at the management level, there’s not enough adjectives out there to describe my reaction. I was more than dismayed; I was angry,” Basnicki said.

“That is the last thing we want to do,” said Boshra, who is the senior director of journalistic standards and public trust of CBC News.

stories.title: Severe drought prompts water-restriction order on irrigation in B.C. interior
stories.summary: Conditions have cause record low flows in Bessette Creek in early July, threatening the local salmon population’s survival
stories.content:
A new water-restriction order has been placed on the Bessette Creek area in the southern Interior of British Columbia due to endangered chinook salmon being “at risk” as drought conditions persist.

A release from the B.C. Ministry of Land, Water and Resource Stewardship says ongoing severe drought conditions have cause record low flows in Bessette Creek in early July, threatening the local salmon population’s survival.

Bessette Creek, located about 480 kilometres northeast of Vancouver, has been described by provincial conservation officials as a “critical concern” for salmon conservation since low streamflows during spawning present a particularly high threat to the population.

The province says significant voluntary conservation efforts in the area have not provided the needed boost to water levels, prompting the ministry to issue the fish protection order that temporarily restricts water use for forage crops and certain mining and industrial purposes.

The ministry says 131 surface-water and groundwater license holders in the Bessette Creek watershed must stop using water for the irrigation of crops, harvesting, greenhouses, nurseries and well-drilling, effective Friday.

It also says the Ministry of Agriculture and Food is available to help producers with their questions or claims for those who suffer crop failures or income declines due to the drought.

stories.title: Ottawa rolls out $7.5B tariff support as Southwestern Ontario braces for fallout
stories.summary: The package includes expanded EI supports and provides new funding and financing for tariff-hit businesses.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
The package includes expanded EI supports and provides new funding and financing for tariff-hit businesses.

As Southwestern Ontario braces for the impact of escalating U.S. tariffs, the federal government is rolling out billions in support aimed at keeping businesses afloat and workers employed.

John Zerucelli, Canada’s secretary of state for labour, joined London MPs Peter Fragiskatos and Arielle Kayabaga at London-based Attica Manufacturing on Friday to outline measures designed to support workers and businesses amid the shifting Canada-U.S. trade relationship.

“This is what we’re fighting for, Canadian businesses, Canadian workers, and communities like London where we build things for other things,” Zerucelli said. “And, yes, Canada is going through a trade war, one that we did not choose and London and southern Ontario are on the front lines.”

Ottawa is introducing a $7.5-billion package of new and enhanced supports, including $3.5 billion for workers and employers, $2 billion through the Canada Strong Diversification Fund, $1.5 billion through the Regional Tariff Response Initiative and $500 million in liquidity support through the Business Development Bank of Canada.

“We recognize the challenge that is ahead of us,” Kayabaga said. “And these conversations, these investments that we’re making into workers, into businesses are the ones that are going to take us to the other side.”

The $3.5-billion Rapid Response Supports for workers and employers package includes extended Employment Insurance measures and training for workers affected by tariffs.

“We are removing the one-week waiting period for EI,” Zerucelli said. “Workers will not have to use their severance before receiving EI. And long-tenured workers who need it can receive up to 20 additional weeks of benefits. The goal is simple. If your job has been impacted by these tariffs, we will be here for you.”

While Fragiskatos said “nobody wants to see layoffs,” the government is preparing for the possibility.

“That’s why the government has moved to make employment insurance available more efficiently and much easier than before,” he said.

Support is also available for companies looking to buy equipment to become more competitive or find new markets, Fragiskatos said. Businesses must apply, with funding determined on a case-by-case basis.

Attica Manufacturing received $750,000 in federal funding through FedDev Ontario in May to modernize its high-precision metal component operations.

Owner Andy Mavrokefalos said the funding helped the company invest in the “latest machining technology, strengthen our capabilities, improve our competitiveness, and most importantly, continue building opportunities for our skilled workforce here in London.”

“These investments are not simply about purchasing machinery,” Mavrokefalos said. “They are investments in people, in productivity, in innovation, and in the long-term strength of Canadian manufacturing.”

The federal government will continue monitoring what businesses need as the trade dispute unfolds, Fragiskatos said.

“This is the introduction of federal support during a very tumultuous period,” he said.

stories.title: ‘We don’t know what is going on’: Family of Canadian couple missing in Nepal clinging to hope
stories.summary: Members of Canada's Nepali community are still waiting to hear from their loved ones two days after a landslide claimed hundreds of lives
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
For Seema Rawla the last few days have been filled with questions and pain. Her brother Sumit Rawla and her sister-in-law Shubhakshi Rawla were in the epicentre of the flash flooding along the Himalayan border on Wednesday preparing to take part in a mountain hike.

“He called us up at 7 a.m., he actually facetimed us,” she tells CityNews. “He was walking around, he was sitting at some small tea stall with his wife. He said that the weather was really nice here, he was so excited, he showed us the river which was so calm and he said he was just loving it here.”

That changed just after 8 a.m. local time when officials say a massive ice chunk broke free in the Himalayas leading to the flash flooding. Rawla’s brother and sister-in-law are now amongst the missing. The pair, from Vancouver, are permanent Canadian residents with Singaporean passports who travelled with a group of others from Canada.

“As of today we are aware of 32 Canadians, some of which are permanent resident, whose whereabouts have not yet been confirmed,” said Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand, who added that Global Affairs is aware of 866 Canadians who are in Nepal. “We have 24 hour emergency watch response centre based in Ottawa that is responding to calls.”

No Canadians were reportedly among the 121 foreign nationals who had been rescued on Friday , according to the Nepal Tourism Board.

Nepal’s disaster management authority said 1,924 people are listed as missing.

Anand also announced the federal government would contribute $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid toward organizations such as the Red Cross to deliver life-saving assistance to people on the ground.

Global Affairs Canada has deployed five consular officials to Kathmandu to support Canadians and work with local officials, and Anand said more can be sent if needed.

Rawla and Somali Raturi of Toronto, whose two friends Poonam Dilip-Kumar Thakkar and Himanshu Agar-Wal are also reported missing, say they welcome the relief funds but hope search efforts increase.

“All the Canadian families who were impacted, do not lose hope. Let’s raise our voice, let’s bring ourselves together to bring our families back,” said Raturi.

Families are being told to contact Global Affairs Canada but at this time its unknown yet if the team is on the ground and when these families will start to get answers.

Files from The Canadian Press and Associated Press were used in this report

stories.title: Harvard and MIT scholars head north as Mark Carney offers millions
stories.summary: Canada’s effort to lure top research talent contrasts with recent U.S. federal funding cuts
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Canada has awarded 64 global scholars with C$504 million ($362 million) in funding to relocate their work to Canadian universities and advance projects in areas such as health and artificial intelligence.

Some 48 of the researchers were poached from the US, including from elite institutions such as Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The other 16 researchers are coming from 12 other countries, including the UK, Germany, China and Japan.

“While certain countries are cutting research and turning their back on academic freedom, we’re doubling down on science and we’re doubling down on research,” Industry Minister Melanie Joly said in Vancouver on Thursday.

Canada’s effort to lure top research talent contrasts with recent U.S. federal funding cuts that, combined with tightening immigration policies and clashes between the Trump administration and top-tier universities, have led some scholars to look for opportunities elsewhere.

Joly noted that 23 of the research chairs are also Canadians returning home.

The announcement is part of an initiative Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government unveiled last year to boost Canadian universities, earmarking C$1.7 billion over 12 years to recruit more than 1,000 researchers. The bulk of that money — C$1 billion — was dedicated to attracting as many as 100 world-leading research chairs to schools across the country.

Robert Asselin, chief executive officer of U15 Canada, which represents the country’s leading research universities, said the government’s ability to attract these scholars reflects the strength of Canada’s post-secondary institutions. He also said policy changes in the US left scientists feeling less supported, helping Canada’s effort to attract them.

“That was absolutely a reason why they wanted to come to Canada. So we seized the opportunity and I’m really happy this happened,” Asselin said.

Among the new research chairs is Sara Seager, a renowned planetary scientist whom the University of Toronto already announced would be leaving MIT to return to her alma mater. Canada has also signed MIT professor James LeBeau, a materials scientist.

Brian Kuhlman, a researcher from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, whose work was referenced in connection with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, will be joining the University of British Columbia as a research chair.

Also heading to UBC is Curtis Huttenhower, a professor of computational biology and bioinformatics at Harvard whose research focuses on the intersection of microbes and human health.

The Canadian government also promised last year an accelerated immigration pathway for H-1B visa holders after the Trump administration decided to charge $100,000 for the visas. It has yet to roll out that program.

Other major world economies are also seeking to attract top scholars open to leaving the US. The European Union has also launched its own €500 million ($583 million) initiative to attract global researchers and scientists.

The new research chairs will receive funding over eight years to work on projects in priority fields set out by the Canadian government, including in health, advanced digital technologies and the environment.

“New chairs and their teams will advance transformational research projects that can be applied and/or commercialized by connecting with receptors in industry, government and society, while also developing the next generation of highly qualified personnel,” the government said about the initiative last year.

The government is set to announce the next round of chairs in the coming months.

stories.title: Manitoba to provide $100-million in tariff relief for local businesses
stories.summary: Tariff relief programs will complement and fill in gaps in the $7.5 billion in supports announced by the federal government on Tuesday
stories.author: Ian Bickis
stories.content:
Manitoba’s government has outlined more than $100 million in tariff supports to help local businesses deal with the fallout of Canada’s trade war with the United States.

Jobs Minister Jamie Moses says the measures include low-interest loans, wage subsidies and a four-month tax deferral.

He says the $50-million loan program is designed to help fill gaps in payroll and operating expenses and is on top of an existing $50-million loan program designed to help boost exports.

There’s also expanded loan guarantee programs for agriculture and a commitment to work directly with the province’s hard-hit honey producers to provide specific supports.

“We continue to work by listening to manufacturers, exporters, agricultural producers and Manitobans about the rising costs, and the access to markets around the world, and the uncertainty that the tariffs have caused,” said Moses.

He says the programs are to complement and fill in gaps in the $7.5 billion in tariff supports announced by the federal government on Tuesday.

Obby Khan, leader of Manitoba’s Opposition Progressive Conservatives, says the Ndp’s Friday afternoon announcement is “half-thought, half-baked” and doesn’t go far enough to help struggling businesses.

He says companies need more help like lower taxes and less regulation.

“Some of the things off the top of my head would be long-term relief, not a loan. How do we actually direct support for these businesses so that those businesses can weather this storm for however long it May be.”

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports last Saturday after trade talks fell apart. Canada has announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products starting Sept. 8.

stories.title: Ex-Blue Jay stars sweep doubleheader in multi-million-dollar tax battle against feds
stories.summary: Former Toronto Blue Jays all-stars Josh Donaldson and Russell Martin have swept a doubleheader court battle with the CRA.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Former Toronto Blue Jays all-stars Josh Donaldson and Russell Martin have swept a doubleheader court battle with the Canada Revenue Agency as an appeal court confirmed they do not owe taxes on millions of dollars of income.

On Friday, the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed a 2024 Tax Court decision that found that the Cra’s calculation of Donaldson and Martin’s taxable income during some of the years they played in Canada was “faulty.”

As a result, both players won’t have to pay additional taxes on millions of dollars of income, as claimed by the tax agency.

As first reported by National Post in 2023 , Donaldson and Martin’s cases raised a common issue that tax experts argued could have a chilling effect on Canadian sports teams’ ability to attract top international athletes: how non-resident top earners can protect their income and mitigate Canada’s higher income-tax rates.

In this case, the tax agency challenged how much income the players could deduct from their taxes using contributions to a form of pension plan called a Retirement Compensation Agreement (RCA).

RCAs are commonly used by high-earning athletes and top executives recruited by Canadian organizations. It defers income and tax payments, and isn’t subject to strict contribution limits like an Rrsp.

The taxpayer is allowed to contribute a “reasonable” amount to their retirement every year, but the CRA withholds half of it in a fund that cannot be invested.

When an RCA holder retires or loses their job, the pension account will begin paying out, at which point the money will be taxed, presumably when they are in a lower tax bracket. The CRA will then also refund the 50-per-cent portion of all contributions that it withheld.

The crux of the battle between CRA and the two former Blue Jays stars was a disagreement on how the players’ contributions should be deducted from their income tax while they played for Toronto.

At issue was that Russell and Donaldson spent 60 per cent of their time in the United States and only 40 per cent in Canada, with taxes payable split accordingly. The time spent in Canada was called “duty days.”

CRA argued that the retirement contributions should be deducted before the 60/40 American-Canadian split was calculated, meaning the players would end up paying more taxes on the Canadian portion.

The two baseball stars, represented by Davies lawyer Marie-France Dompierre, argued the opposite: that the contributions should only be deducted from the Canadian portion after the split.

The difference in taxable income was significant. For Donaldson, it was $2 million, whereas it topped $3.1 million for Russell.

Ultimately, both the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal sided with the players.

“In my view, the correct interpretation of the provisions of the (Income Tax Act) is the approach adopted by Russell Martin and Josh Donaldson and confirmed by the Tax Court,” wrote Federal Court of Appeal Judge Wyman W. Webb on behalf of the panel of three magistrates.

stories.title: Major redevelopment project at Yonge and St. Clair promises to set a high standard for urbanism
stories.summary: The Weston family’s Wittington Properties is advancing a project to bring three towers and a performing arts centre to the area
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
The intersection of Yonge Street and St. Clair Avenue is not one of Toronto‘s cultural hotbeds. The Weston family is planning to change that, and quickly.

The family’s Wittington Properties is advancing a major redevelopment project that would bring three new towers and a performing arts centre to the area. It involves top-tier designers, including Canadian Omar Gandhi Architects and the Pritzker Prize-winning Swiss architects Herzog and de Meuron.

The project, dubbed St. Clair Square, represents a rare attempt by one of Canada’s wealthiest families to alter the city’s geography. While it is unapologetically aimed at the top of the residential market, it promises to set a high standard for architecture and urbanism – and to give Toronto a substantial new public amenity.

The development will include 1.6 million square feet of new construction alongside the existing shopping complex and two office towers. Wittington expects to begin construction in 2027, building the entire complex at the same time.

In a recent meeting, Jay Cross, a prominent New York real estate executive who is leading the project for the Westons, cast it as an extension of Toronto’s midcentury ambition. “I remember when they dropped the needle on top of the CN Tower,” said Mr. Cross, who graduated from the University of Toronto’s engineering school in the 1970s. “That’s how I think of Toronto, as a place with the ability to do trendsetting projects.”

Today the district is a sleepy residential neighbourhood, its office blocks home to medical professionals as well as private offices for high-net worth individuals. One goes there to get a filling, not for a good time.

That could change. The development plan, while incomplete, promises to deliver some of the best new buildings the city has seen in decades.

In 2023, Wittington obtained planning permission for a project on this site with four towers; the new proposal includes only three, in addition to the cultural centre. Mr. Cross framed this as a better result for residents – who will enjoy more privacy. “We are thinking about the very long term,” he said.

New York’s Kohn Pedersen Fox is in charge of the urban design and two of the towers, 37 and 46 storeys tall, as well as the private amenity building, dubbed the Ravine Club. Herzog and de Meuron has designed a 24-storey tower that will include just 72 large condo apartments. These will occupy the space that is now parking lots and small retail buildings northeast of Yonge Street and St. Clair Avenue.

The flagship will be Mr. Gandhi’s building, which will include a roughly 300-seat performance hall, a café and potentially a new Toronto Public Library. This will replace Delisle Court, a small shopping mall on the west side of Yonge Street.

Mass timber will form a dramatic trapezoidal atrium – hefty wood beams wrapped in glass and then with a sculptural lattice, designed by Mr. Gandhi and Bruce Mau Design.

The hall could house chamber music or theatre performances; a flexible arrangement will deliver a flat floor for other events. The centre will be governed by an independent not-for profit.

The southern half of the building is envisioned, Mr. Cross said, as “a cultural centre,” its structure made partly of rammed earth. Wittington hopes for this to house a relocated branch of the Toronto Public Library, whose Deer Park branch occupies a significant but run-down building nearby. No agreement has been reached.

If realized, this will be the most beautiful public building Toronto has seen in at least a generation, with spatial verve and beautiful natural materials.

The urbanism will also do many things right. The plan calls for a large car-free public square, an L-shaped space designed by landscape architects Public Work. This will be surrounded by facades of hand-laid brick and small shops – which, Mr. Cross said, will be carefully chosen “to define the area,” and will be generally no more than 1,000 square feet each, about the size of those on a 19 th -century main street. Restaurants will fill the second floor.

Cars are shuffled into an underground concourse, where loading and back-of-house functions are all consolidated. A public park will go in on the north end of the block.

The other showpiece of the project is the tower by Herzog, perhaps best known for the Tate Modern in London and the Birds’ Nest stadium in Beijing. The Toronto tower proposes a rectangular base, dressed in travertine – the beige Italian limestone beloved of the Romans and of the modernist icon Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. Above that would rise a tower of two-storey apartments; its wavy form evokes Finnish architect Alvar Aalto and a 1920s proposal by Mies van der Rohe. For the average passerby, this will boil down to a highly refined and urbane block.

For this building, Mr. Cross said, Wittington conducted a private competition among four architects – three of whom, including Herzog, are winners of the Pritzker Prize, the profession’s top international honour.

This is unusual. Developers often prefer to work with familiar consultants, and the services of a firm like Herzog are not cheap. So why make this choice? “Great projects have to have great designers,” Mr. Cross said simply.

Mr. Cross was until recently a senior executive at Related Companies in New York. There, he led the development of the US$25-billion Hudson Yards project in Manhattan. That development, which includes office towers, apartments, retail and cultural facilities, received enormous criticism as an insular corporate enclave.

Mr. Cross identifies several lessons from the experience: the complex had too much luxury retail, a lack of neighbourhood-serving amenities and a drawn-out construction process. St. Clair Square, he said, will avoid those mistakes. “We want it to be a place to go for all Torontonians.”

Lofty rhetoric aside, this is largely a real-estate project. But its premise is that a well-resourced owner, thinking in decades, can provide deluxe housing and also be a good neighbour. Now Toronto will see how that recipe turns out.

stories.title: Pitching in: Four-time breast cancer survivor helps ease the financial burden of treatment
stories.summary: After noticing the financial hardship many women encountered while undergoing treatment, Donna Sheehan created the Breast Cancer Support Fund
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizer: Donna Sheehan

The pitch: Launching the Breast Cancer Support Fund

Shortly after Donna Sheehan was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2003, she began working with an organization that supported breast cancer patients and quickly noticed the financial hardship many women encountered.

“I realized that the most stressful part of their diagnosis was not the treatment, but the financial crisis,” she recalled.

That led her to create the Breast Cancer Support Fund , or Bcsf, a Toronto-based charity that provides financial assistance to women undergoing cancer treatment. The fund also works with partners in Ontario and parts of Atlantic Canada to offer a meal support program.

The fund receives referrals from social workers at cancer centres. Around 40 per cent of the patients it helps are single parents, many earning less than $25,000 annually. “We are looking for people who really don’t have resources to pay for basic necessities like food and shelter, utilities, medications, parking,” she said. The charity provides one-time payments of up to $2,000.

Since it started in 2011, the fund has helped around 700 women across Canada and provided $1-million in assistance.

The Bcsf relies on foundations and individual donations to cover its $280,000 annual budget. It’s launching a $25,000 fundraising campaign called Move for the Boob to encourage people to get active in their community and raise money for the fund.

Ms. Sheehan can still remember the first cancer patient the fund assisted; a 42-year-old woman in Oshawa, Ont. “She had absolutely no money and her new husband wasn’t supporting her,” she said.

Most of the women the fund helps are less than 50 and it has provided assistance to some in their 20s. Many were barely making ends meet before their diagnosis. “And sometimes cancer treatment can be more than a year if there’s reconstruction involved. So it’s a lot to take on.”

Ms. Sheehan, 72, has been diagnosed with breast cancer four times – in 2003, 2018, 2019 and 2020. Each time the cancer was caught early and she is doing well.

She has been asked whether her work on the charity gets depressing. “I said, ‘no, I’m inspired and I just feel honoured to be able to help people that truly need it’.”

stories.title: ‘Quite alarming’: E-scooter injuries surge among children at London hospital
stories.summary: The number of patients age 17 and under treated for e-scooter injuries jumped from 22 to 58 in one year.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
The number of patients age 17 and under treated for e-scooter injuries jumped from 22 to 58 in one year.

A London Health Sciences Centre Children’s Hospital doctor is calling the nearly 165 per cent rise in e-scooter-related injuries treated in the emergency department “quite alarming.”

Twenty-two youths age 17 and under were treated for e-scooter-related injuries at Children’s Hospital between April and June 2025 . During the same period this year, that number jumped to 58, said pediatric emergency medicine doctor Sheena Belisle.

The sharp increase prompted Belisle to urge parents and the broader community to be more cautious about the risks e-scooters pose to children.

“I think that we’ll continue to see a rise in e-scooter-related injuries if we don’t get the word out there about how dangerous they are for children,” she said. “We don’t have the summer statistics yet, but I do imagine that they’ll actually be higher than what we saw in the spring.”

Doctors are treating a wide range of injuries, from minor cuts and bruises to broken bones and concussions, Belisle said. They have also seen “potentially life-threatening” internal injuries and brain bleeds.

LHSC provided a breakdown of injuries among the 58 patients treated at Children’s Hospital between April and June.

Fourteen had head injuries, 17 had elbow or forearm injuries and nine had wrist or hand injuries, LHSC said in an emailed statement.

“(It) is very worrisome,” Belisle said.

Belisle believes e-scooter injuries among children will continue to rise.

Her key message to parents is that e-scooters are not toys and should not be ridden by children under 16.

She said there is a misconception that e-scooters are intended for children, pointing to a survey she conducted with medical students.

“A group of medical students from Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry, Western University , and I did a little bit of a survey of parents in the community to try and gage what parents know about e-scooters, and we did find that there’s a significant knowledge gap, and that people actually don’t know what the regulations are,” Belisle said.

Children’s Hospital is working with London police, Middlesex-London Health Unit, the City of London and Western University to develop a unified message about the risks of children riding e-scooters, Belisle said.

For those legally permitted to ride e-scooters, Belisle said wearing a helmet is paramount.

“Secondly, they’re to be ridden by single riders, so no double riding, and to be alert when you’re riding an e-scooter, so not to be distracted by phones or headphones,” she added.

stories.title: Sunny, warm weekend ahead
stories.summary: Friday is expected to bring comfortable conditions across the region, with sunshine returning after some early morning fog.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
It’s going to be a sunny, warm weekend, according to meteorologist Gary Archibald.

Friday saw seasonal highs of 22 to 23 C in and around London.

“Those daily maximums and minimums start to diminish a fraction of a degree each day,” he said.

“Yes, it is getting cooler as summer starts to wind down. We’re seeing the influence of northwesterly winds in the mid to upper levels of the atmosphere.”

There is a possibility for showers over the weekend in the region.

Here’s a full look at your forecast:

Friday night: Partly cloudy. Low 11 C.

Saturday: Mainly sunny. Wind becoming southwest 20 km/h in the morning. High 28 C, humidex 32 C. UV index 7 or high.

Saturday night: Cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers. Low 19 C.

Sunday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 27 C.

Monday: A mix of sun and cloud with a 40 per cent chance of showers. High 29 C.

stories.title: Video of alleged arson at Toronto MP’s home shows suspect pouring fuel on vehicles before fires set
stories.summary: Liberal MP Salma Zahid said that there were no damages to her home
stories.content:
Surveillance video released by police of a suspected arson at a Toronto MP’s home shows a lone suspect pouring fuel on five vehicles and setting two on fire before abandoning the lit-up gas can in the driveway.

Liberal MP Salma Zahid alleges her car and another vehicle were set on fire early Thursday outside her Scarborough home.

Police released the video today as they appealed for the public’s help identifying the suspect.

The footage shows a masked and hooded suspect emptying a red gas can on the front of five vehicles parked in the home’s driveway.

The suspect sets the first fire, but recoils as a burst of flames spreads to the can set down beside the car.

The burning can is then used to set fire to a second car before the suspect drops it in the driveway and runs out of view of the camera.

Zahid, the MP for Scarborough Centre-Don Valley East, has said both vehicles were destroyed but she is relieved everyone is safe and there was no damage to her home.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called the fire a “cowardly act of violence and intimidation.”

Editor’s note: The headline accompanying this story has been corrected.

stories.title: Edmonton-born father back in Canada after nine months in ICE custody
stories.summary: Wright, who moved to Houston in his youth, fought to remain in the U.S. to raise his children
stories.author: Dayne Patterson
stories.content:
A Edmonton-born man who lived most of his life in the United States is back in Canada, after losing a legal fight to remain south of the border to be with his two young sons.

Curtis Wright, 40, said he endured terrible conditions at different U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities in Texas after he was taken into custody 10 months ago.

Rather than self-deport to Canada, Wright said he fought to remain in the United States to raise the children he shares from a previous marriage.

“Can it be done from a different country? Sure, but that’s going to be holidays and summers,” Wright said in an interview from Kelowna, B.C.

“It drastically reduces my time and my ability to, you know, connect and be their father.”

Wright said he was returned to Canada from the South Texas ICE Processing Centre a little more than two weeks ago. His sons, ages eight and 11, remain in Texas.

Wright moved to Houston in his youth. He later got work in the oil and gas industry.

In November, while coming back from a work trip in Mexico speaking with oil companies and distributors, he was interviewed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, and an old conviction resurfaced.

When he was 17, he said, he was convicted of drug possession and ordered to do community service and serve probation. Xanax, an anti-anxiety medication, had been found in his truck, he added.

Wright said that when he returned from Mexico, immigration agents shackled and hauled him away in the back of a van.

He blames U.S. President Donald Trump’s heightened focus on deportation for why his life in the country hadn’t been an issue for nearly 30 years.

The whirlwind shift from unfettered freedom to being in federal custody was unbelievable, he said.

In the blaze of the Texas heat, he said, he ended up in freezing cold intake processing cells.

“The concrete that you’re sitting on and laying on is colder than the air itself,” he said.

Detainees were addressed by their dorm and bunk numbers rather than their names, he said.

The food was poor and the showers dirty and grimy.

“And some people would say that, ’Well, look where you are, maybe that’s what you should expect.’ And I say, well, we’re still humans.”

A spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said it rejects the claim that people housed at the South Texas ICE Processing Centre “are being subjected to inhumane conditions or that the facility is operating under unsafe or overcrowded conditions.”

“Individuals in ICE custody are provided appropriate meals and access to drinking water, hygiene facilities and recreation,” Sarah Loicano said in an emailed statement.

She said ICE has no tolerance for abuse, discrimination or misconduct against people in custody.

Wright said he was ordered to be sent back to Canada in February on a removal order, but he appealed. He later learned from his lawyer that his appeal might take months more.

He said he decided to give up the fight in July and his removal order finalized.

“I’d already been there for nine months and it was kind of time to just get out and go to Canada and kind of end this journey for everyone involved in my family,” he said.

Wright said he considers himself lucky to be sent back to Canada rather than another country.

Some people he befriended in detention told him stories of fleeing oppressive governments. One said he had been detained days after his daughter was born and hadn’t met her yet.

Immigration arrests in the United States dropped from January to May, but Trump’s administration still plans to remove one million people this fiscal year, compared with roughly 442,000 people last year.

“I’ve been removed for a mistake I made 22 years ago, when I was a 17-year-old kid in high school. And now two American children are going to be left without their father,” Wright said.

“I’m just one of thousands of others with similar stories.”

“So when people talk about how this just affects immigrants, it’s wrong. It affects many American families and children as well.”

For now, Wright is staying at his parents’ house in Kelowna with his fiancée, Kayla Thomsen, and their two-year-old daughter.

They plan to head to Edmonton so he can try to pick up a job with the same company he worked for in Texas.

Thomsen and the toddler travelled to B.C. to be with Wright when he arrived in Canada, first in Edmonton before moving west.

The first thing he did when he saw them was hug them, said Wright.

“That was number 1.”

stories.title: Harley-Davidson becomes unlikely flashpoint in Canada-U.S. trade war
stories.summary: Canadian planned tariffs on large US-origin motorcycles could test Trump’s reshoring agenda, turning Harley into a symbol before midterms.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Few brands symbolize American freedom and rebellion quite like Harley-Davidson.

The 123-year-old company is headquartered in Milwaukee and operates its largest U.S. manufacturing plant in York, Pennsylvania. Amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s global tariff campaign — aimed at reshoring production to American shores — Harley-Davidson announced in June that it would return production of some products from Thailand to U.S. facilities.

That announcement came before the U.S. administration announced the Section 301 and Section 338 tariffs, and before Ottawa unveiled its retaliation against those measures and earlier Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminum. If Canada implements duties on September 8, as planned, it would introduce a 50 per cent tariff on U.S.-origin motorcycle imports to Canada larger than 800cc with internal-combustion engines.

Ottawa said its list of tariffs was crafted to protect the “domestic market share for Canadian companies,” rather than to target politically sensitive products in U.S. battleground states ahead of November’s midterms, but affecting Harley motorcycles could have political implications in at least one swing district: Pennsylvania’s 10th, a highly competitive congressional seat.

While the Canadian tariff does not name Harley-Davidson, it is expected to cover many Harley models made in the United States. So while the company is being held up as evidence that Trump’s tariff strategy can bring manufacturing back to the United States, Canada’s 50 per cent tariff on motorcycles could test whether reshored factories can thrive when a major trading partner makes its products more expensive.

Canada accounted for roughly five per cent of Harley-Davidson’s global retail motorcycle sales last year, with 6,434 motorcycles sold north of the border. That means the tariff’s direct effect on the company May be limited — but its political symbolism could be larger.

“If production is reshored to the United States, then what form does it get reshored?” asked Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute. “How many jobs are you actually creating? What kinds of jobs are you creating?”

“If there is to an extent a certain reliance on Canadian parts … the fact that this product is tariffed and the fact that some inputs could be tariffed … could affect the prospect of reshoring it more extensively and creating jobs,” he said.

Harley said the move would return machining, powertrain assembly, painting and final assembly for its Revolution Max platform to U.S. facilities serving the North American market. Production is expected to begin as early as next year, and the company says the move will support “dozens of additional American manufacturing and union jobs.” It has not said how many net new jobs will be created.

“If you have production in a country where there’s very little U.S. value added, and then that production moves to the U.S., that will overall be a net gain for manufacturing in the U.S. for that specific product category,” said Jason Miller, a supply chain management professor at Michigan State University.

“But it May not be a net gain for overall jobs in the U.S. if that means less demand for that broader product, and therefore less employment in the distribution side,” he added.

“A lot of the manufacturing jobs that were lost were not necessarily because of offshoring to other countries, but because of technological changes,” Obregon said, noting that the advent of advanced robotics could mean that reshoring production means fewer jobs.

A 50 per cent tariff would likely reduce Harley-Davidson exports to Canada, Miller said. Exporters May lower their prices slightly, but not enough to offset the duty, meaning the total landed cost would still rise substantially, and import volumes would likely fall.

But Gary Hufbauer, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, said iconic brands such as Harley-Davidson are easy symbolic targets for foreign retaliation because they can absorb more of the tariff through their profit margins without immediately becoming unprofitable.

“Prices charged for iconic brands tend to have a large component of ‘economic rent,’” he said. “For this reason, the sellers can absorb a good part of the tariff and still make a decent profit.”

This means Canada can impose a high penalty for all to see, while Harley absorbs some of the tariff through its margins rather than passing along the full cost to buyers.

Miller does not expect the tariff’s effects to influence major business decisions — including production changes or layoffs — until early next year. The first effects are more likely to be commercial: companies accepting lower margins, reducing hours or postponing investments, even as the impact shows up quickly in balance sheets and export data.

The question is whether those effects will matter before the midterms.

In York, Pennsylvania, where Harley has its largest U.S. manufacturing plant, the House race is considered a toss-up between incumbent pro-tariff Republican Scott Perry and Democratic challenger Janelle Stelson.

“This is one of Democrats’ best pickup opportunities compared to other districts that are similar at the partisan level,” said Erin Covey, head of The Cook Political Report’s coverage of the U.S. House of Representatives.

“Perry is, by far, one of the most vulnerable Republicans in the country,” she added, noting that he “has been in lockstep with [the president]” on tariff policy.

Wisconsin presents a different political test. Harley-Davidson is headquartered in Milwaukee, but the company’s home district, the 6th Congressional District, is considered solidly Republican. Incumbent Glenn Grothman is also aided by a divided opposition, with independent candidate Mike Thurow and Democrat Brad Smith competing for votes that might otherwise consolidate behind a single challenger on the left.

“If people who are in the workforce make this link between tariffs and affordability … it could potentially impact their vote,” Obregon said.

And Harley-Davidson is a big brand capable of grabbing voters’ attention.

“Harley-Davidson is such an iconic American brand. It’s something that voters can maybe connect to more easily than if this were happening with a different company,” said Covey.

But Covey cautioned that Harley is unlikely to decide any race on its own. “I am not sure that in and of itself it is going to be a major issue in any of these races,” she said.

Miller also said the direct economic effects of the tariffs are unlikely to determine the midterms. The larger political effect, he said, May come from voters’ broader concerns about affordability and Trump’s decision to pick a fight with Canada.

stories.title: Edmonton-born father back in Canada after 9 months in U.S. immigration detention
stories.summary: A Edmonton-born man who lived most of his life in the United States is back in Canada, after losing a legal fight to remain south of the border to be with his two young sons. Curtis Wright, 40, said he endured terrible conditions at different U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities in Texas after […]
stories.author: Jessica Barile
stories.content:
A Edmonton-born man who lived most of his life in the United States is back in Canada, after losing a legal fight to remain south of the border to be with his two young sons.

Curtis Wright, 40, said he endured terrible conditions at different U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities in Texas after he was taken into custody10 months ago.

Rather than self-deport to Canada, Wright said he fought to remain in the United States to raise the children he shares from a previous marriage.

“Can it be done from a different country? Sure, but that’s going to be holidays and summers,” Wright said in an interview from Kelowna, B.C.

“It drastically reduces my time and my ability to, you know, connect and be their father.”

Wright said he was returned to Canada from the South Texas ICE Processing Centre a little more than two weeks ago. His sons, ages eight and 11, remain in Texas.

Wright moved to Houston in his youth. He later got work in the oil and gas industry.

In November, while coming back from a work trip in Mexico speaking with oil companies and distributors, he was interviewed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, and an old conviction resurfaced.

When he was 17, he said, he was convicted of drug possession and ordered to do community service and serve probation. Xanax,an anti-anxiety medication, had been found in his truck, he added.

Wright said that when he returned from Mexico, immigration agents shackled and hauled him away in the back of a van.

He blames U.S. President Donald Trump’s heightened focus on deportation for why his life in the country hadn’t been an issue for nearly 30 years.

The whirlwind shift from unfettered freedom to being in federal custody was unbelievable, he said.

In the blaze of the Texas heat, he said, he ended up in freezing cold intake processing cells.

“The concrete that you’re sitting on and laying on is colder than the air itself,” he said.

Detainees were addressed by their dorm and bunk numbers rather than their names, he said.

The food was poor and the showers dirty and grimy.

“And some people would say that, ‘Well, look where you are, maybe that’s what you should expect.’ And I say, well, we’re still humans.”

A spokesperson for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said it rejects the claim that people housed at the South Texas ICE Processing Centre “are being subjected to inhumane conditions or that the facility is operating under unsafe or overcrowded conditions.”

“Individuals in ICE custody are provided appropriate meals and access to drinking water, hygiene facilities and recreation,” Sarah Loicano said in an emailed statement.

She said ICE has no tolerance for abuse, discrimination or misconduct against people in custody.

Wright said he was ordered to be sent back to Canada in February on a removal order, but he appealed. He later learned from his lawyer that his appeal might take months more.

He said he decided to give up the fight in July and his removal order finalized.

“I’d already been there for nine months and it was kind of time to just get out and go to Canada and kind of end this journey for everyone involved in my family,” he said.

Wright said he considers himself lucky to be sent back to Canada rather than another country.

Some people he befriended in detention told him stories of fleeing oppressive governments. One said he had been detained days after his daughter was born and hadn’t met her yet.

Immigration arrests in the United States dropped from January to May, but Trump’s administration still plans to remove one million people this fiscal year, compared with roughly 442,000 people last year.

“I’ve been removed for a mistake I made 22 years ago, when I was a 17-year-old kid in high school. And now two American children are going to be left without their father,” Wright said.

“I’m just one of thousands of others with similar stories.”

“So when people talk about how this just affects immigrants, it’s wrong. It affects many American families and children as well.”

For now, Wright is staying at his parents’ house in Kelowna with his fiancée, Kayla Thomsen, and their two-year-old daughter.

They plan to head to Edmonton so he can try to pick up a job with the same company he worked for in Texas.

Thomsen and the toddler travelled to B.C. to be with Wright when he arrived in Canada, first in Edmonton before moving west.

The first thing he did when he saw them was hug them, said Wright.

“That was number 1.”

stories.title: Xanadu secures $195-million from Ottawa for quantum computing in Canada
stories.summary: Advanced photonics research, development and manufacturing facility will be built in Toronto, but rival warns much more support needed to keep domestic leaders from moving to U.S.
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
Xanadu Quantum Technologies Ltd. Xndu-T has secured $195-million in federal funding to support the building of an advanced photonics research, development and manufacturing facility in Toronto.

The Toronto-based quantum computer developer, which went public in March , is also negotiating for up to an equal amount of funding from the Ontario government. The project, located in a 158,000-square-foot facility on the site of a former Campbell’s soup plant in Etobicoke, is expected to cost $893-million.

While the federal government has provided financial support for Canada’s fertile quantum technologies sector for decades, Ottawa is under pressure to provide hundreds of millions more to keep domestic players from relocating abroad, a fate that has happened in other technology subsectors.

The stakes are high as the Canada-U.S. trade war worsens, which Evan Solomon, federal minister for artificial intelligence and digital innovation, alluded to as he announced the funding at the empty facility Friday.

“This is literally what it looks like” for Canadians to control their own destiny, he said of the funding. “We are going to take big swings and we’re going to build big. That’s what this moment requires.”

Several U.S. states including Illinois, Colorado and Maryland have been aggressively courting quantum companies from Canada and elsewhere with incentives to locate in their jurisdictions.

Christian Weedbrook: Seize the quantum future – or let the U.S. own it. Which way, Canada?

The U.S. government in May also agreed to invest a combined US$2-billion in nine quantum companies. One of the recipients, Australia’s Diraq Pty Ltd., opened a technology hub in Los Angeles this week. Another, D-Wave Quantum Inc., redomiciled to Delaware from Burnaby, B.C., in 2022 and later moved its headquarters to the U.S. D-Wave, a past recipient of Canadian government funding, was once majority-owned by Canadian pension fund PSP Investments.

Julien Camirand Lemyre, chief executive of Sherbrooke-based quantum computing developer Nord Quantique Inc., said that despite heavy public-sector investment in quantum infrastructure in the region east of Montreal, it might not be enough to keep his company here if government funding at home doesn’t keep up.

He said U.S. states are offering tens of millions of dollars in incentives just to open satellite offices in the U.S., and more if companies move some or all of their operations there. While he said the Canadian government has been supportive of the homegrown sector, “at the end of the day, money speaks. There is a strong pull from the U.S. to provide that capital to companies that are willing to set up a significant presence there. If the opportunity in Canada is no longer here, there’s a point where it doesn’t make sense for us to stay.”

He added Nord Quantique would “need sizable support in Canada for us not to move,” on the order of hundreds of millions of dollars. “Canada needs to act, it needs to act now, if we want to be competitive in that space, if we don’t want to repeat the story that we’re tired of hearing in Canada, about good companies leaving the country.”

When asked whether his government would make that level of further commitment to the sector, Mr. Solomon replied in an interview: “I just invested hundreds of millions of dollars today. Clearly we’re prepared to do it.” He added “We’re doing this because these are the best companies, we believe there is a real return for Canadians, and we’re trying to keep this stuff here.”

Mr. Solomon added the government could also consider taking equity stakes in domestic quantum companies through a new $500-million technology growth fund. Crown corporation Business Development Bank of Canada has also backed several Canadian quantum companies.

Canada was an early leader in the development of quantum computers, which unlike conventional systems don’t derive power from manipulating bits of information, but by tapping the peculiar properties of matter and light at microscopic scales.

There are several ways to leverage these effects in a quantum computer, and no clear winner has emerged yet. But if proponents are right, quantum computers will be vastly more powerful than the world’s most advanced supercomputers and able to do calculations beyond the reach of conventional systems. That could open new applications in fields such as material science, drug discovery and financial forecasting.

Quantum computers could also enable bad actors to pick the locks on cryptography algorithms that secure the world’s digital economy.

Canada had – and lost – its lead in AI. Can it avoid making the same mistake in the next emerging global technology race?

The Carney government has stressed that supporting its homegrown industry is of national importance. Three domestic companies – Xanadu, Nord Quantique and B.C.-based Photonic Inc. – have advanced to the second stage of a U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency competition challenging developers to show they can build a commercial-grade quantum computer by 2033.

Last December, Ottawa committed up to $23-million apiece to those three (plus a fourth company that isn’t in the competition) to match what Darpa has offered those that complete the first two stages. Companies that make it through a third and final leg could qualify for another US$300-million each in U.S. government funding.

Xanadu’s system performs calculations using packets of laser light connected by fibre optic networks. The method is different from other quantum computers whose chips need to be cooled to temperatures just above absolute zero (-273.15 C), to harness their quantum effects. Xanadu’s machines largely operate at room temperature.

Last year, Xanadu unveiled a chip capable of performing quantum error correction, a measure seen as essential for reaching reliable performance for practical uses. Continued efforts to correct errors and improve performance remain a key challenge for Xanadu and its rivals. Its system is also built via a modular approach, making it easier to network and scale up than other systems.

Xanadu has also developed open-source software called Penny Lane that has tens of thousands of active users across an array of quantum systems.

Xanadu CEO Christian Weedbrook said the company’s new facility is named Inception, after the film by his favourite movie director, Christopher Nolan. Mr. Weedbrook, a one-time film student, said Xanadu’s rapid advancement since its inception in 2016 “feels like we’re living in a dream.”

The operation will employ 275 people and serve as Xanadu’s global facility for manufacturing, packaging and assembling quantum computing components.

Mr. Weedbrook, who has committed to keep building Xanadu in Canada, said at the announcement, “I want the next generation of scientists and engineers to see Canada as a place where they can stay or come to build something very important.”

The government’s commitment is a repayable financing through its Strategic Response Fund, which previously provided $40-million to Xanadu in 2023.

stories.title: Aleksei Medvedev gets another shot at London Knights’ No. 1 job
stories.summary: The 18-year-old goalie says he’s coming off the best offseason of his life after losing the starting job last season.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The 18-year-old goalie says he’s coming off the best offseason of his life after losing the starting job last season.

Aleksei Medvedev needs to have a strong fall.

A dominant performance in net right away would reassure the London Knights brass, the players in front of him and fans that this will be the contending season everyone expects. Anything less from the Vancouver Canucks second rounder will hasten legitimate concern.

“I think I had the best offseason of my life,” the 18-year-old Russian goaltender said. “I’m coming in feeling really comfortable. I feel like you’re going to go through some adversity along the way. The best thing you can do is learn from it and I feel like I’ve picked up a ton of new things that work for me.

“I’ve done a lot of work in the summer and those things I picked up, I really developed and built on them.”

There were plenty of conversations throughout the summer about what happened last season and how to move on from it. Medvedev had a solid start but struggled as the Knights began to teeter and eventually surrendered the No. 1 job to American Sebastian Gatto, who is now at Dartmouth College.

The net is his to lose again, but he has to put up numbers closer to his rookie season with the 2025 Memorial Cup champions – 22-8-2 with a 2.79 goals-against average and .912 save percentage – than he did in the follow-up campaign, when he went 16-15-2-1 with a 3.26 GAA and .891 save percentage.

“Last year was a little bit of an eye-opener for him and a humbling experience,” London veteran goaltending coach Dave Rook said. “He put the time in and, conditioning-wise, he looks in great shape. It’s not a technical thing with Aleksei. He has all the compete and work ethic. He’s a class guy and as a personality and teammate, he’s great.

“A lot of his (work) is from the shoulders up. When things get settled down for us here (through the preseason), it’ll be a test.”

The Knights felt that once Gatto earned regular starts, Medvedev pushed too hard to regain his footing. The club re-emphasized the experience of his former crease partner Austin Elliott, who went from the pain of losing his starting job in Saskatoon to becoming nearly unbeatable in the London net.

“I feel really confident about our squad this year,” Medvedev, the 6-foot-3, 180-pounder, said. “Just getting to know the guys this year, I’m really excited. We have really good imports and overagers. That helps a lot. We also have a bunch of returning guys who have been through it and played the system.

“It will be interesting to see how we play this year and I’m betting it will be really fun.”

Rather than head overseas for the summer, Medvedev trained in Toronto and his parents visited for a month and a half. He stayed with them, enjoyed their company and spent time together in Ontario.

“You need to have a break away from (the game) for a bit,” Rook said. “He hadn’t had it for 2-3 years and for a kid his age, I don’t think people appreciate how important it is to be with your parents during the offseason. I feel like he’ll be better for going through what he did last year.

“You don’t lose the skill he has overnight.”

As exhibition games ramp up over the next few weeks, the focus will be on Medvedev’s progress and who will partner him to start the season. Three other goalies remain in camp: 18-year-old American newcomer Brian Cooke, 2025 fifth-rounder Charlie Weiss and 17-year-old Woodstock native Kobe Nadalin.

“Brian is older and coming in with expectations,” Rook said. “He’s a super-nice kid who wants to please and he’s got it from a technical standpoint. Weiss and Nadalin have done very well for themselves. Both are committed (to improve) and pushing for that second spot.”

These are the steps that will determine who gets the crease when the games matter most. Some years, it’s elementary and some turn into a surprise.

“You’re always building towards something,” Medvedev said. “You take these steps – camp, preseason, regular season – and want to use every day to your advantage. That’s my mindset – to have a purpose, keep working and see what happens in the long run.”

stories.title: Grain haulers loses its load on roundabout
stories.summary: Witnesses who came to the aid of the driver told CTV News he was shaken but not injured.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
A grain hauler carrying soy meal toppled over while negotiating the roundabout in Kilworth on Thursday afternoon.

Witnesses who came to the aid of the driver told CTV News he was shaken but not injured.

A portion of the roundabout was closed and westbound traffic on Glendon Drive was diverted through Kilworth.

A vacuum truck was brought in to help clean up the soy meal and a heavy tow crew was on site to upright the truck.

stories.title: London dad raises $128K on Queen’s Park walk for daughter’s surgery
stories.summary: The fundraiser is helping cover a roughly $493,000 U.S. surgery after the family says Ohip denied out-of-country coverage.
stories.author: Brian Williams
stories.content:
The fundraiser is helping cover a roughly $493,000 U.S. surgery after the family says Ohip denied out-of-country coverage.

A London father walking to Toronto in stages while pushing his daughter’s empty wheelchair has raised more than a quarter of the money needed for her potentially life-changing surgery in the U.S.

Joe Gesualdi launched Miles 4 a Miracle to raise money for his daughter Sydney, who developed craniocervical instability (CCI) following a 2023 car crash. The rare condition causes instability where the skull meets the upper spine, leaving the neck unable to properly support the head.

As of Friday morning, more than $128,000 had been raised toward the roughly $493,000 cost of the surgery.

Joe said the outpouring of support feels like “validation” for the cause and has given the family hope.

“Looking at that GoFundMe has given me hope that I am going to have a shot with the benefit and the generosity of the people to give Sydney a second shot at life at a surgery that is proven to give most people back a lot of functionality, and an almost complete return to full life, and that’s our hope for Sydney,” Joe said.

Joe is tackling the roughly 200-kilometre journey to Queen’s Park in stages because the family needs to return home to care for Sydney. He expected to reach Ancaster, about 15 kilometres outside Hamilton, ON Friday.

The fundraiser has “gone through the roof in the last four days,” tripling in donations, Joe said. He said many messages from supporters have shared a “consistent theme.”

“The shock that Ohip doesn’t cover these medically necessary services, and that there’s a feeling out there that the system is actually actively working against patients and not biasing in favor of patients,” he said.

Sydney requires cranio-cervical fusion surgery, which would fuse the base of her skull to the top of her spine. The procedure can be performed at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York.

Sydney has so far been denied out-of-country Ohip coverage. Joe is pushing the empty wheelchair toward Queen’s Park – where he expects to arrive Sept. 16 – while raising money and advocating for Ohip to cover the surgery.

Joe said the family has yet to receive an encouraging response from Ohip.

“It’s a big wall of silence, and they are not responsive,” he said. “Any time we reach out to Ohip, they send us the process that we need to follow to make an appeal, and it’s kind of strange because we’re already in an appeal.”

Decisions about out-of-country procedures are clinical decisions made by Ontario physicians, Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones, said in an emailed statement.

“To apply for funding, a request must be submitted to the ministry by a physician on behalf of the patient,” Barnes said. “While the ministry plays an integral role in health care, it does not direct individual patient care.”

Barnes said doctors are responsible for co-ordinating care for their patients.

“This includes determining the urgency of their patients’ need for health services and referrals to other appropriate health care providers and facilities, including referrals outside of province or country,” she said.

Sydney said she is trying to remain optimistic.

“As the months go by, and since we started my appeal with Ohip at the beginning of the year, I’ve just continued to deteriorate as the months go on and lose my functionality and my ability,” she said. “So it’s kind of a mixed bag, but I am very hopeful now.”

Joe said the family has been told the surgery could be available in Ontario and has asked for the names of surgeons who perform it, but has not received a response.

“So Ohip tells us that the surgery is available,” he said.

“We have asked them very simply tell us who they are, and we’ll go see them. And we’re happy to access the surgery here. Just tell us who the doctors are. (But), there’s been no change.”

Joe plans to hold a news conference at Queen’s Park when he arrives, which he expects will be Sept. 16.

stories.title: Halifax man accused of threatening the U.S. Consulate not ready to pursue bail
stories.summary: Halifax — The lawyer for a man accused of threatening to bomb the U.S. Consulate in Halifax earlier this month says his client is not ready to seek bail.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Halifax — The lawyer for a man accused of threatening to bomb the U.S. Consulate in Halifax earlier this month says his client is not ready to seek bail.

Ali Assakereh was arrested on Aug. 10 for allegedly placing a propane tank and flammable liquids in his car and parking it near the consulate, causing evacuations in a large section of downtown Halifax.

The 54-year-old is facing charges of mischief and uttering threats, as well as a charge for violating a section of the Criminal Code that prohibits threats against internationally protected people, including diplomats. The Crown said it considers the latter offence to be terrorist activity.

Lonny Queripel, Assakereh’s legal aid lawyer, told the court that the he has been working with the accused’s family on a bail plan, but it won’t be ready for some time.

He said Assakereh has agreed to remain in custody and the defence will inform the court if, and when, it is ready to pursue bail.

Assakereh, a balding man with a grey beard, appeared in person at Friday’s hearing wearing a grey sweater and grey sweatpants. He became emotional and appeared to cry at one point, holding his face in his hands before accepting a tissue from a sheriff. A translator relayed the proceedings to him in Farsi, the language mainly spoken in Iran.

It was the sixth adjournment of Assakereh’s bail hearing and the Crown has been opposing his release. In the meantime, Assakereh is scheduled back in court on Sept. 10 to enter a plea and inform the court of his choice of trial format.

Federal lawyer Lee-Ann Conrod said that the charge for threatening internationally protected people usually carries a maximum sentence of five years.

She said she had mistakenly told reporters earlier this month that the maximum was 14 years.

On Wednesday, Conrod notified the court that the prosecution plans to seek a longer sentence because it considers the alleged threat against diplomats to be terrorist activity, which can be punished by life in prison.

However, Conrod said the Crown does not plan to pursue the life sentence.

Police have confirmed they learned about the bomb threat on Aug. 9 and found the suspect’s vehicle parked near the consulate the next morning at 8:10 a.m. Assakereh was arrested 25 minutes later in the city’s west end, not far from his Halifax home.

By 2 p.m., an explosives expert determined the propane and liquids in Assakereh’s car posed no threat to public safety and all evacuation orders were lifted.

The alleged bomb threat came less than a week after two suspects were charged with shooting at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto in July — the second such incident at the building this year. A 19-year-old man and a 15-year-old boy are facing more than a dozen charges.

The consulate in Toronto was previously targeted on March 10, when two suspects allegedly fired multiple shots at the building. An 18-year-old and a 19-year-old are facing multiple charges.

No one was injured in either shooting.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 28, 2026.

Devin Stevens, The Canadian Press
