stories.title: Ottawa provides $5M to Nepal relief efforts as search continues for 32 Canadians
stories.summary: The federal government is providing $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal after a flash flood tore through the border region with China on Wednesday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The federal government announced Friday it is to provide $5 million in urgent aid to support Nepal as scores of Canadian families anxiously wait for news about their relatives missing after severe flash flooding in the region.

A flash flood Wednesday along the Himalayan border between Nepal and China, caused by a glacial collapse, killed nearly 600 people and left almost 2,500 missing.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said 32 Canadians and permanent residents are missing in the region.

No Canadians are among the 121 foreign nationals who the Nepal Tourism Board said had been rescued.

Entire villages have been wiped out in the region, with major roads, bridges, electricity systems and other critical infrastructure severely damaged. Officials said the loss of telecommunications has hindered efforts to account for victims.

Ottawa said its $5-million contribution is to go toward organizations such as the Red Cross to deliver life-saving assistance to people on the ground.

Anisha and Saumya Grover said no one has heard from their parents since the flash flooding.

Their 55-year-old father, Anil Grover, and 50-year-old mother, Samira Grover, were crossing the Nepal-Tibet border at the Gyirong Port when the flooding hit.

The couple from Markham, Ont., were to embark on a pilgrimage through Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists and others.

“It has been a nightmare of trying to get answers, trying get to updates, trying to locate them,” Anisha Grover said in a telephone interview, adding they have received little information from Global Affairs Canada.

The family is Hindu, but Anisha Grover said the more religious one is her mother, who is active in their local temple and the Isha Foundation, a non-profit spiritual organization.

“I think the part that really hurts is that our parents, they have done everything for us, and we really encouraged them to go on this trip and enjoy themselves,” the 25-year-old said.

Saumya Grover, 18, said it has been difficult not to imagine the worst. In looking for answers online about her parents’ whereabouts, she has come across disturbing images of casualties.

“Even the video of the flash flood itself hitting the immigration centre, it was really difficult to watch,” she said. “It just takes your mind to the worst circumstances and the worst possible outcome.”

Global Affairs has said it deployed five consular officials to Kathmandu to support Canadians and work with local officials. Anand said Friday more can be sent if needed.

“Nepal is facing a devastating humanitarian emergency with catastrophic damage,” Anand told a news conference.

She said Global Affairs is aware of 866 Canadians who are in Nepal.

Dhaval and Megha Shah, a couple from Port Moody, B.C., are also among the missing Canadians, said a relative.

Nikita Shah, Dhaval Shah’s cousin, said Thursday that the couple was on a spiritual journey in Nepal and family last heard from them Tuesday night.

Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Center for Integrated Mountain Development said an avalanche from a glacier likely caused the flooding.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 28, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

Daniela Germano, The Canadian Press

stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Ottawa — The federal government posted a deficit of $370 million for the April-to-June period of its 2026-27 fiscal year.
In its monthly fiscal monitor report, the Finance Department says the result compared with a deficit of $6.28 billion for the same period a year earlier.
The deficit came as revenue totalled $132.64 billion for the three-month period, up from $120.84 billion in the same period last year.

Program expenses excluding net actuarial losses amounted to $117.16 billion, up from $112.34 billion a year ago.
Public debt charges totalled $14.61 billion for the period, up from $13.77 billion.
Net actuarial losses were $1.25 billion, up from $1.01 billion a year ago.

stories.title: JJ Levine is having a moment
stories.summary: The Montreal photographer’s work on gender and sexuality is transgressive, irreverant and sometimes shocking – yet manages to be both timely and timeless
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee, Photography by JJ Levine
stories.content:
Jesus, Mary, and Joseph: the first queer family?

Such are the questions – transgressive, irreverent, maybe even a little shocking – provoked by the photography of JJ Levine.

The Montreal artist, whose portraiture toys with conventional ideas about gender and sexuality and familial bonds, is having a moment. His pieces have recently been acquired by major institutional collectors in Quebec and English Canada, while the National Gallery will feature his work in an upcoming show. Art fairs in New York and Toronto have been or will be wallpapered with Levines this year.

The artist is trans and his work has a particular relevance at a moment when trans people are under attack, after a period of progress and increased visibility.

But as the Biblical valence of some Levine images suggests, it is their timelessness, as much as their timeliness, that makes them stick in the viewer’s mind.

Far from being mere political statements, his best photographs engage in a deep art-historical conversation going back to medieval Siena and reaching forward to New York’s East Village in the 1980s. Immaculately composed (if not conceived), lushly coloured, and alternating between campy and austere, Levine’s work makes a surprising bid for immortality.

The camera is Levine’s first artistic love and primary implement. A Nan Goldin show at the Musée d’art contemporain was a formative youthful experience. In some ways it’s easiest to slot his work into the history of queer and outsider photography that Goldin represents, along with her contemporary and scene-mate Peter Hujar and later exemplars such as Catherine Opie.

Levine is clearly interested in overturning some of the photographic conventions, from Victorian family groupings to mugshots, that have been used in the past to define in-groups and outsiders. By posing himself and his friends with a classical, or carceral, stiffness, resolutely unsmiling, in temporally ambiguous settings, he places queer and trans subjects back in a tradition they have been excluded from. Looking at his tattooed, non-binary sitters recreating the starch-collared formality of black-and-white grandparents perched on the world’s mantelpieces prompts the question: What if these images were always the norm? And why weren’t they?

This is where Levine does battle with another fraught tradition in photography, the Diane Arbus mode. By shooting drag queens and pairs of male lovers alongside dwarfs, triplets, and other “freaks,” Arbus objectified her queer subjects – or so critics, including Susan Sontag, have argued. Others see deep compassion in her lens, but with Levine there is no question. He can be a tyrant behind the scenes, arranging the sitter’s clothes and limbs and posture just so. But where the viewer enters the equation, the subjects of Levine’s pictures possess undeniable power, gazing back as if to say, “What are you looking at?” These are not portraits for passive consumption, human curiosities to be studied or provide titillation. Levine’s people meet your eye, almost daring you to blink. (If Arbus photographed “them,” Levine photographs “us.”)

The severity of his sitter’s expressions serves a political purpose, returning agency to groups who have been stripped of it in the history of art. But again, the aesthetic echoes are just as interesting.

There is something painterly in Levine, despite his adoration of the camera – a meticulousness about colour and line that brings to mind great painters of the past as much as fellow photographers. The stylized brightness of his palette and starkness of his faces evoke Cézanne’s portraits, improbably.

The two artists also share an intimacy with their sitters that comes through on the canvas, or the print: among Cézanne’s favourite human subjects were his wife and himself, while Levine never photographs someone he doesn’t know, and has made some powerful self-portraits.

Family, both biological and chosen, is Levine’s great theme, which is surely why his work so heavily evokes medieval and Renaissance religious painting. A recent show of his at the downtown Montreal gallery Ellephant stunned me with its similarities to a 2024-2025 retrospective at the Metropolitan Museum in New York about the art of early modern Siena. The two collections could hardly have been more different in medium and historical background, but those 14th-century works in tempera on wood had an uncanny resemblance to Levine’s.

Both the photographer and the painter Duccio, say, depicted small, improbable family groupings who faced persecution and stare out at the viewer with almost eerie intensity, defiantly demanding acceptance or imploring belief.

After all, what is really more improbable: a parent, a sperm donor and their child; or a virgin mother, divine infant and, somewhere off scene, the immaculate donor Himself?

It is questions like these, sacrilegious as they May be, that give Levine’s work some of its charge, and why his photographs will have staying power beyond the urgency of their political moment.

stories.title: Woman, 73, dies after being stabbed in London, Ont., home invasion
stories.summary: Police allege a man broke into a London home on Saturday morning and then stabbed and assaulted a 73-year-old woman.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police in London, Ont., say a 73-year-old woman has died after she was stabbed during a weekend home invasion.

Police allege a man broke into a London home on Saturday morning and then stabbed and assaulted the woman.

Before he was arrested, police say the man allegedly threw broken glass at responding police, leaving one officer with minor injuries.

Police initially reported that the 73-year-old woman was sent to hospital with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.

In an update this morning, they say she has died in hospital.

A 40-year-old London man is facing a second-degree murder charge along with previous charges of break and enter, assaulting a police officer and obstruction.

Ontario Provincial Police say the body of a missing swimmer from Scarborough has been found.

The OPP said beachgoers found the body on Thursday, a day after the swimmer was reported missing.

Officers received reports the missing swimmer just after 1 p.m. on Wednesday.

The swimmer was last seen at the beach at Pinery Provincial Park near Grand Bend.

stories.title: Schulich students aim to tackle rise in e-scooter injuries among youth
stories.summary: Western University medical students are supporting an e-scooter youth injury prevention campaign to improve safety in London, Ont.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
paragraphs: A group of medical students at Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry has turned a school assignment into a passion project with hopes of preventing e-scooter injuries among youth in London, Ont.

As part of an experiential learning course in the second year of medical school, students were put into teams of eight to work on various long-term projects aimed at addressing problems related to the healthcare system.

Students working with paediatrics professors Dr. Sheena Belisle and Dr. Jennifer Kilgar have been focusing on e-scooter youth injury prevention. Long after the course wrapped in April, half the students in the group are still involved.

“I am incredibly proud of the students’ efforts during the school year and even more impressed that many of them have chosen to continue contributing over the summer months,” said Belisle, also a pediatric emergency physician at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), who came up with the topic of e-scooter safety.
“Their dedication and ongoing commitment are a reflection of their passion towards making a meaningful impact in our community.”
The decision wasn’t a difficult one for the students, however.
“It was never really a question,” said Nikita Burman, now starting her third year of medical school.
Burman and four others – Ethan Martin, Joseph Russell, Ojan Khosravifar and Eden Kemal – decided to keep working on the campaign, even after their class ended.
Belisle was moved to action by a rise in e-scooter-related visits to LHSC’s Victoria Hospital and Children’s Hospital emergency departments and overall concerns about child safety.
“I witness the impact of these injuries firsthand in the ED on a regular basis,” she said.
“The e-scooter injury prevention campaign is an important initiative as we continue to see a growing number of e-scooter-related injuries among children, both within our community and across Canada.”
Locally, LHSC reported that Children’s Hospital treated 58 e-scooter-related injuries between April and June of this year, compared to 22 in the same time the year prior.

Burman, who worked as a paediatric nurse before deciding to go to medical school, said injuries typical of e-scooter accidents include long bone fractures, head trauma and potentially life-threatening injuries to the torso.
“Often, intra-abdominal injuries happen when the person topples forward over the e-scooter and the handlebars go into their torso.”

This summer, the Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program published the results of a survey of paediatricians and paediatric subspecialists conducted between late 2025 and early 2026 asking about injuries associated with powered personal micromobility devices, or PPMDs (such as e-scooters, e-bikes and e-skateboards).
According to the results, there were 10 documented deaths, 12 ICU admissions and 26 hospitalizations lasting over two days related to those devices in the previous 12 months.
The overwhelming majority of incidents (where the specific device was reported) involved an e-scooter, at 86 per cent. Additionally, 42 per cent of all reported injuries involved kids aged 10 to 15.

Russell and Burman explained e-scooter injuries among youth stem from a range of factors, including being unfamiliar with how e-scooters operate, using an inappropriately sized e-scooter, tendency toward risk-taking behaviours, underdeveloped balance and coordination skills and lack of experience.
Russell said people are often unaware of the risks of e-scooters.

“Say mom gets a present for her 17-year-old son, who’s legally allowed to ride it with a helmet. Then his 14-year-old brother grabs the scooter and just zips off without a helmet, not recognizing the speed of the scooter and the safety risks.”
E-scooters are often marketed in a similar fashion to toys, with bright, colourful designs, Burman added.
“It encourages kids to use them.”

At the onset of the project, the students put together a survey to gauge the current level of knowledge within the community on the rules around e-scooter use, specifically focusing on two pieces of information: “you cannot ride an e-scooter if you’re under 16 years of age, period, and you have to wear a helmet if you’re under 18,” Burman said.
“As expected, we saw a lack of knowledge in regard to how to use e-scooters appropriately,” said Russell.

Of roughly 150 responses collected mostly from people in the ED as well as through responses to a QR code, only 42 per cent were even aware the province has rules and regulations surrounding e-scooter use.

Russell said 39 per cent of respondents correctly identified 16 as the minimum age for use and only 15 per cent knew riders under 18 are required to wear helmets. Nearly half of all respondents, 45 per cent, incorrectly believed e-scooters are permitted on sidewalks in London.

After determining the baseline level of awareness locally, the students developed an informational poster for public education – they plan to share it widely throughout the city and on social media. They hope it will contribute to a 10 per cent reduction in the number of e-scooter-related injuries in the Children’s Hospital Emergency Department by October.
“We don’t just pull that out of a hat. Based on the statistics and the results from other studies across Canada, 10 per cent seems very doable,” said Russell.

“If we’re seeing great success, we’d like to keep modifying our approach and figure out how to continue improving those numbers. We also want to work with the province and our municipality to inform and educate on policy decisions.”
Preventing injuries results in a healthier population and saves money by reducing the load on emergency departments, Martin added.
Left to right: Ethan Martin, Ojan Khosravifar and Nikita Burman presenting at a conference in Hamburg, Germany in June 2026. (Submitted)

Belisle’s project has already been well-received beyond Ontario, with Martin, Burman and Khosravifar presenting the project and its objectives at the International Conference of Emergency Medicine in Hamburg, Germany in June.
“We also learned about different cities that have also worked to improve e-scooter safety. Basically, we got homework for the way back,” Khosravifar laughed.

Similar projects have been conducted in Calgary and Toronto and in parts of the U.S. and Finland, Burman said. Calgary’s project, which she described as “a big inspiration,” also included a public education campaign.

“Information was shared on the City of Calgary’s social media channels and then researchers tracked injury incidents to see what impact it had. That was the paper that we read and built off,” she said. “We were inspired to start a similar campaign, but we are also looking to involve schools, community centers and arenas for wider dissemination.”
Khosravifar stressed there are still benefits to e-scooters, such as improving transportation access.
“But improving how they’re used and keeping people – especially younger people – safe has to be equally important.”
Burman summed it up simply: “The best-case scenario is to avoid the injury completely.”

stories.title: 7-in-10 Canadians support Carney’s decision to halt U.S. trade talks, new Abacus poll shows
stories.summary: Beyond the decision to suspend talks, 60% of Canadians approve of how Carney and the federal government have handled the negotiations.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Canada’s trade standoff with Donald Trump and the United States is entering a volatile new phase — but a large majority of Canadians say Prime Minister Mark Carney was right to walk away from negotiations rather than accept last‑minute terms from Washington, according to a sweeping new Abacus Data survey .

The poll, conducted Aug. 21–26 and based on just over 2,000 Canadian adults, finds 71 per cent believe the federal government made the right decision to suspend talks, even after respondents were explicitly reminded that doing so would mean higher tariffs and greater economic uncertainty. Only 17 per cent say Ottawa should have accepted the U.S. offer, while 12 per cent are unsure.

The results amount to a public endorsement of Carney’s decision to pull Canadian negotiators from Washington on Aug. 21, after the U.S. introduced what he called “unfair” and “uneconomic” changes that raised doubts about the reliability of any deal. The following day, 50 per cent U.S. tariffs took effect on roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs — 15, 25 and 50 per cent on $27.6 billion in U.S. imports — would take effect Sept. 8, alongside $7.5 billion in support for affected workers and businesses.

Support for suspending the talks crosses regional and partisan lines. Abacus data finds backing above 60 per cent in every region, including in Alberta, where support still sits at a majority‑level of 61 per cent — and reaches a high of 79 per cent in Quebec. Even 54 per cent of 2025 Conservative voters say walking away was the right call, despite the party’s criticism of Carney’s broader trade strategy.

Generational divides are sharper: support rises steadily with age, from 56 per cent among 18‑ to 29‑year‑olds to 85 per cent among Canadians 60 and older. Younger Canadians are not opposed, but they are more ambivalent — with more than one in four saying Ottawa should have taken the deal.

Beyond the decision to suspend talks, 60 per cent of Canadians approve of how Carney and the federal government have handled the negotiations overall. Only 18 per cent disapprove.

Approval is strongest in Québec, Ontario and British Columbia, and lowest in Alberta, where 48 per cent approve and 24 per cent disapprove.

The partisan split is more pronounced here: while Liberal, Bloc Québécois and NDP voters overwhelmingly approve of the government’s handling, Conservative voters are divided — 36 per cent approve, 38 per cent disapprove.

Despite strong support for Carney’s stance, Canadians are far less optimistic about what comes next.

Only 15 per cent expect a quick resolution that removes most tariffs. The most common expectation — held by 32 per cent — is that the dispute will drag on before an eventual agreement. But 40 per cent foresee a deeper rupture: either escalation with more tariffs (22 per cent) or a lasting breakdown in the relationship (18 per cent).

The pessimism extends to the future of the broader North American trade framework. After the U.S. declined to extend Cusma at its scheduled review earlier this summer, only 17 per cent of Canadians believe the agreement will ultimately be renewed or updated while maintaining a close trading relationship.

The partisan split is more pronounced here: while Liberal, Bloc Québécois and NDP voters overwhelmingly approve of the government’s handling, Conservative voters are divided — 36 per cent approve, 38 per cent disapprove.
Despite strong support for Carney’s stance, Canadians are far less optimistic about what comes next.

Only 15 per cent expect a quick resolution that removes most tariffs. The most common expectation — held by 32 per cent — is that the dispute will drag on before an eventual agreement. But 40 per cent foresee a deeper rupture: either escalation with more tariffs (22 per cent) or a lasting breakdown in the relationship (18 per cent).

The pessimism extends to the future of the broader North American trade framework. After the U.S. declined to extend Cusma at its scheduled review earlier this summer, only 17 per cent of Canadians believe the agreement will ultimately be renewed or updated while maintaining a close trading relationship.

stories.title: Neighbours ‘uneasy’ after woman, 73, dies from stabbing in home break-in
stories.summary: An elderly woman stabbed during a break-in at a south-end home a week ago has died in hospital, London police said on Friday, and a man is charged with second-degree murder.
stories.author: Jack Moulton, Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The woman and the accused did not know each other, London police say.

A 73-year-old woman stabbed during a break-in at a south-end London home a week ago has died in hospital, police said Friday, and a man is now charged with second-degree murder.

In an update Friday, London police said the elderly woman died in hospital following the Aug. 22 attack. Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, is charged with second-degree murder in addition to existing charges of aggravated assault, break and enter with intent, assaulting a peace officer with a weapon and obstructing a peace officer.

The court documents state the incident happened at 10 Raywood Ave. and the deceased woman is Lillian Leonard. The documents list Cornejo as having no fixed address.

Jerry Rozic, acting detective inspector of the London police criminal investigation division, said the incident was isolated and there is no further risk to the community.

“We know that this is a serious incident, it’s going to have an effect on the family and the community our thoughts are with the community,” he said.

Investigators are asking anyone with information about Cornejo, or anyone who May have interacted with him, to contact London police at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477).

Cornejo remains in custody and is expected to appear in London court Monday, police said.

The incident happened shortly after 6:10 a.m. last Saturday, when police said the woman was awakened by a loud noise and found a man entering her home in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road East.

Police said she was assaulted and stabbed before she was able to call 911. Multiple officers responded to the home, where the man “began throwing broken glass” at police.

One officer suffered minor injuries as police entered the home and arrested the suspect. Leonard was taken to hospital with serious injuries and later died. Property records show Leonard had owned the home since 1998 and became its sole owner in May 2025. While police had cleared the scene by Friday, glass still littered the property and damage could be seen near the door’s deadbolt. A knock at the door went unanswered. Neighbour Steve Walker was not home when the break-in happened and learned about it later when he saw the area taped off and police knocked on his door seeking information. “It’s really scary. I think she was an older woman living here by herself, and yeah, it’s horrible,” he said. “It’s a great neighbourhood . . . (it was) freaky when we found out.”

“It’s really scary. I think she was an older woman living here by herself, and yeah, it’s horrible,” he said. “It’s a great neighbourhood . . . (it was) freaky when we found out.”

Jeff Chapman, a neighbourhood resident of more than 30 years, described his household’s mood as “a little uneasy.” He has home security but said he is more concerned about some of his neighbours. “There is a fair number of single older women that live in this neighbourhood, and we bumped into one or two of them saying they’re quite uncomfortable,” he said. “There’s other people in the neighbourhood that are a little leery right now; concerned about their security.”

stories.title: Middlesex County invites local high school students to be “Warden for a Day”
stories.summary: Middlesex County is inviting local high school students to apply for their chance to be Warden for a Day on October 13, 2026.
stories.content:
Middlesex County (August 31, 2026): Do you want an inside look at local government? Middlesex County is inviting local high school students to apply for their chance to be Warden for a Day on October 13, 2026. The program offers a hands-on opportunity to experience municipal government in action and learn about the important role County Council plays in supporting Middlesex communities.

Students will join Warden Sue Clarke for a full day of leadership and learning at the County Administration Building. The day’s agenda will include a mock swearing-in ceremony, meetings with County staff, and a guided tour of the building, including the historic Middlesex County Gaol. This is your chance to learn about various departments including Forestry and Natural Heritage, Library Services, Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, and Economic Development and Tourism.

Apply now to join us on October 13 to discuss the challenges and rewards of municipal leadership and observe an official Middlesex County Council meeting. You’ll get a behind-the-scenes look at how decisions are made that shape services and support residents across the County.

Interested in applying? Submit a 60-second video OR a short essay answering these two questions:

What makes Middlesex County special to you?

If you were Warden for a day, what’s one thing you’d do to make a difference?

Submit your application: Warden for a Day Application

Complete the application by September 25, 2026.

The County of Middlesex extends its thanks to everyone for applying and showing enthusiasm for local government. Selected participants will hear back by September 28, 2026.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home offering exceptional lifestyle a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.

Media Contact: Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division @email

stories.title: Groovy, baby: Mike Myers turns Toronto’s Bloor–Yonge into a dance floor
stories.summary: The Scarborough‑born star, known for Wayne's World and Austin Powers, was filmed gliding, leaping and pirouetting across the concourse.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Toronto commuters got an unexpected dose of groovy energy this week when Canadian comedy icon Mike Myers posted an Instagram video of himself dancing through Bloor–Yonge station.

The Scarborough‑born star, known for Wayne’s World and Austin Powers, was filmed gliding, leaping and pirouetting across the concourse as a busker played keyboard nearby. Myers captioned the video “kinda chic to dance in the subway,” showing off a unique, albeit glamorous, dancing routine that he accompanied by donning a George Harrison T-shirt.

Most commuters barely reacted, walking past without realizing the man twirling beside them was one of Canada’s most famous comedic exports.

Online, though, the reaction was anything but subtle. Fans flooded the comments with Austin Powers references, GIFs and praise, calling the moment “simple and hilarious” and “comedic genius.” Even the TTC chimed in, writing, “Whatever this is, we approve.”

The video adds to a string of frequent sightings of Myers around Toronto, where he’s been spotted at restaurants and venues, such as Toronto Maple Leafs’ games, during visits home.

stories.title: Laurentian Bank reports $1.5-million net income in the third quarter as it works to complete sale
stories.summary: The Montreal-based bank says the result amounted to a loss of eight cents per diluted per share for the quarter
stories.content:
Laurentian Bank of Canada ( LB-T ) reported third-quarter net income of $1.5-million as it worked to complete its plan to be split in two and sold in a pivot to become a specialty commercial bank.

The Montreal-based bank says the result amounted to a loss of eight cents per diluted per share for the quarter ended July 31 compared with a profit of $37.5-million or 73 cents per diluted share a year earlier.

On an adjusted basis, Laurentian says it earned 51 cents per diluted share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted profit of 78 cents per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

Laurentian chief executive Éric Provost said the quarter reflected the work over the past several months to advance the bank’s transformation.

Last year, Laurentian announced a deal that will see Fairstone Bank buy it and its commercial operations for $1.9-billion, while its retail and small-and-medium-sized banking portfolios will be acquired by National Bank.

Laurentian expects to close the deal, which was approved by the federal finance minister in June, later this year.

stories.title: Morning fog advisory in London and region
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 11:50 AM | Last Updated: August 28
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 11:50 AM | Last Updated: August 28
Sunshine and temperatures of 23 C expected in the afternoon
Environment Canada has issued a fog advisory for the London region Friday morning.
The yellow-level advisory, which is the weather agency's lowest risk warning, covers London, Parkhill and Eastern Middlesex County.
Londoners May notice areas of dense fog and near-zero visibility, Environment Canada said on its website, adding that travel "will likely be hazardous in some locations."
The agency is recommending Londoners allow extra time to reach their destinations this morning.
Fog is expected to dissipate later this morning, revealing sunshine with a high of 23 C.
The sun is expected to continue into the weekend with highs of 27 C on both Saturday and Sunday.

stories.title: One divisive city council era. Two would-be comebacks. Will London voters care?
stories.summary: Two members of the so-called Fontana 8 voting bloc from nearly a generation ago are trying to win back their old seats in the fall civic election.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
In something of a blast from the past, two former London politicians who were part of an infamous voting bloc on city council are trying for comebacks in the fall civic election.

The question is, will the notoriety of the political past sink their hoped-for resurrection in the Oct. 26 vote?

Or, do voters have bigger issues on their minds – never mind enough recall to think back to an often-acrimonious era – for that to matter?

One of the two candidates says he’s unapologetic for his political record, and at least one prominent political observer says it’s not so clear past baggage will be a key factor for voters.

Among the 69 candidates running for election in London’s 14 ward council races are the two ex-politicians – Stephen Orser and Denise Brown – seeking their old seats back in Wards 4 and 11, respectively.

Orser and Brown were part of the so-called Fontana 8, a voting bloc of eight council members including then-mayor Joe Fontana between 2010 and 2014.

The spectre of a comeback has drawn the attention and ire of another former city councillor, Stephen Turner, who defeated Brown in 2014 and in a social media post said he hopes to see the former Fontana 8 members “swiftly” defeated at the ballot box.

“It’s disappointing to see Fontana 8 folks popping their heads back up for this election. That era was London politics at its worst,” he wrote.

With a voting majority on the 15-member council, the Fontana 8 dominated in its day – pushing through much of Fontana’s agenda.

Gord Hume, a former council member who bowed out of civic politics as the Fontana 8 era began, said the divide on that council occurred quickly and got bitter over the life of its term.

“(That) council certainly split very early in that term into a group of five, six who were more socially driven, and then seven or eight who were more business-driven coalesced around Fontana. There was a definite chasm on council,” said Hume, now a municipal consultant.

“The seven not in the bloc were increasingly frustrated because most of their ideas and motions and proposals were shot down. Not always for the best of reasons, but just because they could . . . and because of that, debate deteriorated.

“It was not civil in any way whatsoever, and a lot of people became embittered and that went out into the community,” Hume said.

Council’s standing committees, the first point of contact with politicians for all issues before they go to council for final decisions, were both chaired by and their memberships dominated by Fontana 8 members.

The acrimony boiled over after Fontana was criminally charged with fraud, breach of trust by a public official and uttering forged documents.

A first attempt at a council motion to ask Fontana to step aside was shot down before even being tabled.

A second go at it failed in an 8-5 vote, with Fontana sitting it out and once council member absent.

“That event caused a huge chasm in the community, and they (the public) lost confidence in the council. The public was angry . . . distaste for that council was palpable,” Hume said, noting many Londoners in 2014 were simply of a mood to vote councillors out.

Fontana would resign as mayor a few months ahead of the 2014 election, which brought a political sea change with an astounding 11 new members elected to council’s 15 seats – “a revolution,” as Hume put it.

Brown and Orser were booted from office. So was Paul Van Meerbergen, who was also part of the Fontana 8. He was subsequently elected in 2018 and has remained on council since as the Ward 10 representative.

Orser has run in every election as a candidate in Ward 4 since 2014, but Brown mounted her comeback bid last week, ON the last day for candidates to file their nomination papers for this fall’s contest.

For all the past drama, Hume notes it was more than a decade ago and says unless rival candidates or attentive voters raise it, it’s “history” that many Londoners either won’t remember or which could be overshadowed by other issues.

“Some of those views would have moderated in the (10-plus) years since, and everybody has the right to change their minds. Everybody has the right to get fresh thinking,” he said.

“I guess what would be interesting is, what are their platforms this time? What are they presenting as their vision for the city?”

Thursday, Orser told The Free Press he’s unapologetic. He takes credit for helping to form the bloc and said it contributed to achieving many of his goals for Ward 4, including bringing new highrise development to his district and cracking down on crime in the area.

“We organized a voting bloc for the purpose of pushing London forward,” he said, adding other councils have also had their own blocs. “It’s no different than any political party.”

Orser said hands-on experience is needed to handle “out of control” problems such as homelessness and open drug use, which he argues today’s council “has dropped the ball on.” He applauds Brown as “a hard working lady,” and similarly complimented fellow former councillor Roger Caranci, who left office in 2010 and is now seeking the Ward 1 council seat.

One of nine candidates vying for the Ward 4 seat, Orser said his priorities include cracking down on open drug use, establishing an incentive program for homeowners to build accessory dwellings for low-acuity homeless Londoners, and – as his election signs notably suggest – allowing backyard chickens.

“I made mistakes in the past. There’s no doubt about it. Nobody’s perfect. It’s the perfect ones you got to watch out for,” he said.

Brown hadn’t responded to a request for comment Thursday, but has told The Free Press she’d been thinking of running for several months. She is one of three Ward 11 candidates, including incumbent Skylar Franke and Harinder Kumar.

“There are so many issues that need to be addressed, and they have to be addressed efficiently,” she said on Aug. 21. “The homelessness, for example, the open drug use downtown, especially property taxes – how they keep on going up – and the spending and the roads and infrastructure.”

stories.title: Luxury London mansion listed for record-setting $5.5 million
stories.summary: A London home that sold for a record price of $5.3 million is up for sale again with an asking price of $5.5 million.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
A London home that sold for a local record price of $5.3 million four years ago is back on the market with an asking price of $5.5 million.

The property at 2-756 Riverside Dr., west of Wonderland Road in London’s Oakridge neighbourhood, previously sold at a record price for a publicly listed property in London in 2022.

Shahin Tabeshfard, the Century 21 broker of record for the sale, says the luxury housing market, which he describes as homes over $3 million, is stronger than it has ever been in the London area.

“People are getting more comfortable with this price point,” he said. “If you rewind about 10 years ago, it was very rare to see homes over $3 or $4 million switching hands.”

Tabeshfard said that the previous sale of the Riverside home still holds the record for a publicly listed sale in the city, meaning it would break its own record if sold for its asking price.

The London housing market previously experienced its worst start in five years from January to April, with March being the only month where home sales were higher than one year prior. The market did bounce back in May and June, with a slight increase in home sales compared to the same months in 2025, before dropping again in July.

Tabeshfard says that, for the luxury market, most are sold off the market, with sellers typically valuing confidentiality more than most people. So far this year, the luxury market is stable, with him even selling a $4-million home off the market just two weeks ago.

“The high-end home market in London is more active than the data might show, and this sale would be on par with market value,” he said.

Sitting on more than half an acre next to the Thames River, the Riverside Drive home was custom-built in 2014 and designed by Bradley Skinner of Skinner and Skinner Architects Inc. The home offers 7,664 square feet of total living space, including a heated exterior driveway and soundproof theatre room, among other features.

Tabeshfard says there’s been some aesthetic updating and maintenance since it changed hands back in 2022, but overall, the property has the same components. He confirmed that, since it was built, this will be just the second time it has changed hands.

Back in 2022, the property was originally listed at $5.5 million. Tabeshfard says the asking price is the same this time around, because he hasn’t seen a significant increase in the market but believes the house has not lost any value.

“We’re priced accurately for where the market sees it. Ultimately, the market will dictate the value. $5.5 million, we felt, is a good starting point to market the property for sale,” he said.

The house, Tabeshfard says, is a one-of-a-kind property in the London area, especially being built with concrete, steel and a glass curtain wall.

Tabeshfard says the current owner of the property has been building their dream home over the last few years and is near completion, which is why the home is changing hands again after just four years.

In 2022, the house sold after just three days on the market, but Tabeshfard does expect it to take a little longer this time around.

“(Friday) will be the third day on the market, and we’re not expecting it to sell by then,” he said. “Properties of this value, they don’t typically fly off the shelves. Last time we were lucky, where the buyer was ready to go right away.”

Sitting on more than half an acre next to the Thames River, the Riverside Drive home was custom-built in 2014 and designed by Bradley Skinner of Skinner and Skinner Architects Inc. The home offers 7,664 square feet of total living space, including a heated exterior driveway and soundproof theatre room, among other features.

Tabeshfard says there’s been some aesthetic updating and maintenance since it changed hands back in 2022, but overall, the property has the same components. He confirmed that, since it was built, this will be just the second time it has changed hands.

Back in 2022, the property was originally listed at $5.5 million. Tabeshfard says the asking price is the same this time around, because he hasn’t seen a significant increase in the market but believes the house has not lost any value.
“We’re priced accurately for where the market sees it. Ultimately, the market will dictate the value. $5.5 million, we felt, is a good starting point to market the property for sale,” he said.
The house, Tabeshfard says, is a one-of-a-kind property in the London area, especially being built with concrete, steel and a glass curtain wall.

Tabeshfard says the current owner of the property has been building their dream home over the last few years and is near completion, which is why the home is changing hands again after just four years.
In 2022, the house sold after just three days on the market, but Tabeshfard does expect it to take a little longer this time around.

“(Friday) will be the third day on the market, and we’re not expecting it to sell by then,” he said. “Properties of this value, they don’t typically fly off the shelves. Last time we were lucky, where the buyer was ready to go right away.”

stories.title: Watch: Pickup truck towing camper rolls over on Highway 401
stories.summary: Dramatic video submitted to CTV News shows the single-vehicle collision happened in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two people suffered minor injuries after a pickup truck towing a camper trailer rolled over on Ontario’s Highway 401 on Wednesday afternoon.

Dramatic video submitted to CTV News shows the single-vehicle collision happened in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401, just east of Kent Bridge Road in Chatham-Kent, at about 12:30 p.m.

Police said the pickup truck, which was hauling a camper trailer, lost control and entered the highway median before rolling over.

The driver and passenger were taken from the scene with minor injuries.

One eastbound lane of Highway 401 was closed for a short time while emergency crews worked at the scene.

Police thanked motorists who stopped to assist following the collision.

stories.title: Hot Stuff: It's hard turning an airport runway into a concert venue. But it's worth it
stories.summary: London International Airport as a concert venue? For the second straight year, yes. Part 13 of our series on people and things that make summer sizzle here
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
London International Airport as a concert venue? For the second straight year, yes. Part 13 of our series on people and things that make summer sizzle here

Got a suggestion for a Hot Stuff story about a person or thing that makes summer special in Southwestern Ontario? Email us at curiouslondon@postmedia.com or read our entire series so far right here .

A year ago, Rock the Runway turned the London International Airport into something it had never been before – an outdoor concert venue.

More than 25,000 people showed up on opening night of the inaugural two-day festival, the biggest concert in the city’s history.

But how did a commercial airport become the place to bring this massive concert to life?

Scott McFadzean, London International Airport’s chief executive officer, says the idea for a concert was born nearly two years ago. McFadzean says the airport is always looking into giving the community other reasons to come out, like Airshow London, beyond just getting on a commercial flight.

The idea for a music festival came about as a fix to a problem: London not having a large enough venue space to attract some major bands, though Rock the Park in Harris Park and Canada Life Place do attract some big-name performers.

“I kind of looked at the vast amount of open space we have here at the airport, and thought there could be potential to really take London’s music scene to the next level,” McFadzean said.

McFadzean soon reached out to Brad Jones, president of Jones Entertainment Group, and invited him to take a look at the grounds. He says the Jones family’s history with hosting Rock the Park seemed like a natural fit and the first place to start.

Jones says that when he first saw the airport grounds, he immediately could picture what the London airport was pitching to him. “We literally walked out on that runway, and I just sort of saw the vision,” Jones said.

But to make it come together, they needed the right act.

Jones says he gets calls every year from musicians’ agents asking if there are things he’s working on that are bigger in scale to host them. It just so happened that Noah Kahan’s agent mentioned he was playing in Louisville, Kentucky, in early September 2025 and wasn’t going to be making a trip to Toronto.

“When Noah Kahan was brought to us, one of the biggest stars in the world, we thought the runway was the right place,” Jones said.

But to host a concert on airport grounds is easier said than done.

McFadzean says the most important thing leading up to the concert was prioritizing aviation safety, because the airport would continue to operate on other runways while the concert was held.

He says the airport had to work closely with Transport Canada and NAV Canada throughout the process, not only to get the proper approvals, but to ensure they could keep surfaces for the airport active.

“We worked very closely with all the authorities and regulators, including both federal and municipal,” McFadzean said. “It was a great collaboration between everyone, including London police, EMS and fire. A great way to bring us together and prepare for various scenarios that can result from large crowds being in one location.”

The first edition of Rock the Runway drew 25,000 people for the first night to see Noah Kahan – which Jones says is the largest concert in Southwestern Ontario ever. About 10,000 showed up the second night to see American DJ Marshmello.

McFadzean believes that Rock the Runway is likely the first-ever concert to be held on active commercial airport grounds in the country.

Jones credits the timing of the festival with much of the success. He says hosting it in mid-September prevented them from competing with themselves and Rock the Park, and it has the advantage of London’s post-secondary students returning.

“You’ve got 40,000 or so students that attended Fanshawe and Western, and not a lot of them are in London in July,” he said. “You’ve got a whole new audience that’s coming back to London. So to capture that, that’s a big part of why we picked mid-September.”

The first year wasn’t without its lessons, however, with traffic and parking problems occurring throughout the festival and the need to bring in their own power to run the concert, Jones says.

The organization is capping attendance at 15,000 people for this year’s concert set for Sept. 17 and 18, a 40 per cent drop from last year’s record crowd. Limp Bizkit is the main headliner on a bill that also features Cypress Hill.

“We just want to get it perfect this year, so we’ve scaled it back,” Jones said. “Once we get everything perfect, then we will look at scaling it back up for future years.”

Jones says he doesn’t want to make any commitments that the festival will be around as long as Rock the Park, which has lasted more than two decades, but he does see it going for a number of years at this point.

“We certainly have an interest to continue to make the experience better every year,” he said.

rgoodison@postmedia.com

stories.title: Body of missing swimmer recovered at Pinery Provincial Park
stories.summary: The search remained underway Thursday, with two OPP vessels, the OPP Underwater Search and Recovery Unit and OPP Aviation Services.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say the body of a swimmer reported missing in Lake Huron at Pinery Provincial Park has been recovered.

Lambton County OPP said officers were called to the park shortly after 1 p.m. on Aug. 26 after receiving a report that a 28-year-old person from Scarborough had gone missing in the water.

Police said beachgoers located the swimmer’s body on Aug. 27.

OPP thanked several agencies and organizations that assisted in the search, including the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre, the Anishinabek Police Service, the Walpole Island Police Service and staff at Pinery Provincial Park.

No further details were released.

stories.title: Champagne touts deepening economic ties in visit with Indian counterpart
stories.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said he’s looking at ways to streamline payments between Canada and India as part of a broader effort to deepen ties with the world’s fast-growing major economy.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said he’s looking at ways to streamline payments between Canada and India as part of a broader effort to deepen ties with the world’s fast-growing major economy.

Champagne hosted Nirmala Sitharaman, India’s minister of finance and corporate affairs, in Toronto on Thursday where the two announced a new economic and financial dialogue between the nations. The pair also sat for a fireside chat at the Canadian Club Toronto in the afternoon.

Champagne told reporters the economies of the two countries are “uniquely complementary” and positioned Canada as a reliable supplier of food and energy for India.

“Canada can provide energy security and food security to India. And India can provide to Canada scale, talent, and technology,” he said.

Financial services was one of the primary areas where Champagne spoke about deepening co-operation with India.

He said Canada wants to facilitate easier payments between the two nations. That would help the families of the thousands of Indian students studying in Canada to save on fees and exchange costs when sending money internationally, he said.

Champagne also suggested Canada could be critical in supporting India’s high-tech ambitions, such as a rapid build-out of data centres for artificial intelligence.

“Critical minerals, energy, are going to be essential to the growth of India. And that’s what I think Canada can offer,” he said.

Canada has broadly been trying to position itself as a trusted supplier of key commodities as war and shifting trade flows upend the previous global order.

Asked whether Canada was ramping up its efforts to build out trade with India given the re-escalating trade war with the United States, Champagne said it was always Ottawa’s “plan A” to diversify Canadian trade.

Sitharaman said bilateral relations between countries are increasingly important in a period of geopolitical instability.

She credited prime ministers Mark Carney and Narendra Modi with bringing “fresh momentum” to the partnership.

“The economic and financial dialogue reflects this broad ambition to move beyond traditional trade and goods and services and build a deeper economic partnership, encompassing investment, finance, capital markets, and regulatory co-operation,” Sitharaman said.

Champagne joined Carney on a trip to India in late February — the first official visit by a Canadian prime minster since Justin Trudeau’s visit in 2018.

Modi is expected to visit Canada in the coming months.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said on Wednesday that he intends to lock down a trade agreement between Canada and India before the end of the year.

Canada and India are looking to more than double two-way trade between the nations to $70 billion by 2030.

Canadian investment in India was more than $110 billion in 2024. Champagne pointed out Thursday that Canadian pension plans are major investors in India’s infrastructure agenda.

Canada and India have worked to improve relations over the last year, after that relationship frayed over Canadian allegations that Indian government agents were involved in violence targeting Canadian citizens.

The allegations included involvement in the murder of a pro-Khalistan activist in British Columbia in 2023.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 27, 2026.

stories.title: It's Groundhog Day at London hospitals as rodents burrow, chew wires underground
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
Groundhogs drawn to good soil, plants and safety from predators, experts say
Amid an ongoing fraud investigation and costly infrastructure problems, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has a new – and much furrier – challenge on its hands: groundhogs.

In a memo sent to staff, which was reviewed by CBC News, the centre’s Support Services department said groundhogs have begun burrowing at multiple LHSC locations, such as Victoria Hospital, Children’s Hospital and University Hospital.
“Groundhogs have high potential to injure themselves and damage critical infrastructure at LHSC by burrowing through or chewing on systems like electrical networks,” the email said.
Evidence of groundhogs started popping up within the last two weeks, said LHSC’s director of facilities operations Chris Askew.

“We’ve had similar situations at a couple of our sites. It happens,” Askew said. “We have large sites so nature does tend to find locations of where they want to create their homes and sometimes it’s around our sites.”
Askew said his main concern with groundhogs on the property is the risk of them interacting with the plumbing and electrical systems that run underneath the LHSC grounds.
“If they were to come in contact or connect with them, that can have an impact on our operations. We want to make sure that doesn’t happen, and we also want to keep them safe at the same time.”
It’s not unusual for a groundhog to chew through a wire, according to Jared John Pineda, who works with Forest City Wildlife Removal.
“They chew through anything in their path,” Pineda said. “They might also confuse an electrical wire for a root because they probably don’t really know what an electrical wire is.”
The hospital is working with an external wildlife removal company to relocate the groundhogs with traps, Askew said.
“We are doing this for the safety of the groundhog as well as everybody else,” he said.
The memo sent to staff specifies Abell Pest Control is relocating the animals. The company was not available for an interview before publication.
While Askew did not specify the exact locations groundhogs were spotted, he said the animals tend to burrow in more isolated areas with less foot and vehicle traffic.

Pineda said he typically encounters groundhogs in large fields on the outskirts of the city or in residential backyards. There, they are often digging underneath homeowners’ porches, decks, sheds and gazebos, he said.
“It gives them a place to hide where they’re not being hunted by predators,” he explained.
Groundhogs are likely attracted to LHSC properties for the same reason, in addition to the soft soil and maintained greenery around the buildings, Pineda said.
“There’s a lot of shrubs and gardens that they have around the hospital. It gives them a nice little place to hang out and eat food,” he said.
Nearby construction at the intersection of Wellington and Commissioners May have also pushed groundhogs further into the Victoria and Children’s hospital grounds, Pineda added.
Both Pineda and Professional Wildlife Removal owner Patrick Blewett said they are receiving more groundhog-related calls in the city.
Blewett said it’s not necessarily that there are more groundhogs, but that the rodents are living differently.

“If the city grows and a lot of farmland around the city is now being developed into houses, the groundhogs aren’t actually going anywhere. They’re starting to live and adapt to the urban environment,” Blewett said. “When they used to just live in tunnels under the ground, a lot of them are now utilizing structures as protective spots.”

Blewett said it’s unlikely that burrowing groundhogs are capable of damaging the structural integrity of large-scale buildings at LHSC, but it is a risk for homeowners with groundhogs in their own backyards.
“If a groundhog is digging and creating tunnel systems, they’re excavating. Anywhere that dirt is displaced, then potentially all the surrounding dirt could start to cave in.”
Blewett and Pineda both advise reaching out to a reputable wildlife removal company if groundhogs are causing damage to property. Otherwise, they recommend enjoying them from afar.
“Just be respectful and observe it. They’re pretty mild creatures,” Blewett said. “They’re not interested in attacking. They’re just interested in doing their thing.”

stories.title: Londoners will be able to file noise complaints online starting next week
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
Service London portal replaces existing process using police non-emergency line
The London city councillor representing Old North and student-heavy neighborhoods near Western University is praising an upcoming change to the way residents make noise complaints.
Starting on Sept. 3, Londoners will be able to file noise complaints directly through the city’s online Service London portal, instead of through the London police non-emergency phone line.
The change will benefit both residents and London police, who will no longer have to triage complaints and forward them to city staff, said Sam Trosow, the councillor for Ward 6.
“Sometimes it’s very difficult to get through on the police non-emergency phone, depending on what their current demands are,” Trosow said.

“To have it initiate with the police seemed like a poor use of police resources, and it created a lot of frustration, so I’m very happy about this change because it’s something I’ve been talking to code enforcement and police about for a long time.”
Amanda Pfeffer, London’s director of municipal compliance, said the city had received feedback about the current process, and found the experience could be made “a little more seamless.”
“This way, residents will know that the report has been received immediately, and our noise and parking enforcement officers will be dispatched immediately upon receipt of those noise complaints.”

Trosow says he’s heard from some in his ward that voicemail messages left on the non-emergency line May not be returned, and responses May differ based on who answers the phone. He says some residents have reported being told to contact the city instead.
“I know that’s not what their policy is … but this is just what I’ve been hearing,” he said.

“All in all, I’ve been hearing a very frustrated and unhappy response from people who live in the near-campus neighbourhoods, particularly areas where you’re close to houses that might be considered party houses.”
Noise complaints that May be dangerous, including those that involve weapons, an altercation or a domestic situation, would still see police respond, Pfeffer said.

Londoners can already report other issues through the portal, including road and sidewalk problems, broken traffic lights and streetlights, needles, parking infractions, and lot and yard maintenance violations.
Starting Sept. 3, Pfeffer says Londoners can also use the portal to report noncompliance for nearly all bylaws investigated by municipal law enforcement officers.

stories.summary: The article Trudeau receives RCMP protection on trips: report (Aug. 21) begs the question does former prime minister Stephen Harper similarly receive RCMP protection when he sojourns in his dubious role heavily funded by the Republican Party as the chair of the International Democracy Union?
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
The article Trudeau receives RCMP protection on trips: report (Aug. 21) begs the question does former prime minister Stephen Harper similarly receive RCMP protection when he sojourns in his dubious role heavily funded by the Republican Party as the chair of the International Democracy Union?

For example when Harper appeared at a Mar-a-Lago gala in 2018? Or when Harper travelled to Budapest in 2023 seeking closer ties with the authoritarian autocratic Viktor Orban?

Michael Luce, London

We are witnessing the decline of the competitive spirit of America.

The demolishing of the standard of truth was the first indication of the American fear of losing competitiveness. Destruction and bullying came next.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is here to build a better country with positive values. Anyone with any sense at all will follow him.

Graeme MacLean, St. Thomas

When buyers in Ontario drive their new $50,000 EV into the garage of their new $1.5 million home, taxpayers, many of whom are working several jobs to make ends meet, must contribute to the $135,000 rebate to which these affluent buyers are entitled.

Bill Caldwell, London

stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
Update - London, ON (September 1, 2026) – The London Police Service continues to search for missing person Cole Rioux and has received additional information.

Cole is believed to be driving a 2001 Volkswagen Jetta with Ontario licence plate Avxm 279. The vehicle is described as missing the Volkswagen emblem on the front and May also be missing a muffler. A photo of the vehicle has been included.

Police and family remain concerned for his welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

Original - London, ON (August 28th, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 19-year-old Cole Rioux of London.

He is described as male, White, approximately 5’8”, 155lbs, slim build, with blue eyes, light brown buzz cut hair. He was last seen wearing a black T-shirt, with pink or green shorts, and operating a black Volkswagen Jetta.

He was reported missing yesterday and was last seen yesterday at approximately 3:40 a.m., in the area of High Street and Moore Street.

stories.title: Wellington Gateway enters final phase as Rapid Transit construction progresses
stories.summary: The Wellington Gateway project is entering its final phase of construction, with work beginning Monday, August 31, weather permitting, ON the
stories.content:
The Wellington Gateway project is entering its final phase of construction, with work beginning Monday, August 31, weather permitting, ON the remaining section of Wellington Road between Watson Street and south of Base Line Road East.

Phase 2B will complete the remaining major construction work needed to build out the Wellington Road Rapid Transit corridor. This includes widening the road, installing two centre-running transit lanes, building new transit stations, and replacing underground infrastructure.

This milestone comes as other sections of Wellington Gateway near completion. Phase 2B is the final phase of the project, with construction continuing through 2029 and some final restoration work carrying over into 2030.

Crews have begun mobilizing the Phase 2B area, including temporary road construction and traffic control setup.

Starting Monday, August 31, one lane in each direction will be closed between Frank Place and Wellington Court.

Enbridge Gas is also moving gas infrastructure to make room for the project. Drivers May see occasional lane closures while this work is underway.

Access to Victoria Hospital, local businesses and properties will be maintained throughout construction. Pedestrian access will remain available on at least one side of the road, and the City is continuing to coordinate with the hospital to maintain access for emergency services.

Drivers should follow posted signs and detour routes, use caution, allow extra travel time and plan ahead.

Wellington Road will remain open throughout construction, with at least one lane in each direction. Traffic will shift as crews move through different parts of the project.

Work in 2026 and 2027 will focus north of Whetter Avenue, with construction shifting south towards Base Line Road East by late 2027.

As Wellington Gateway moves into its final phase, other parts of London's Rapid Transit network are also taking shape.

This summer, crews have continued to make progress across the network.

Clark's Bridge is now widened and complete. The bridge between Grand Avenue and South Street now has two traffic lanes, dedicated transit lanes and a new multi use path for people walking and cycling. Asphalt, red transit lane markings and permanent pavement markings were completed this summer. Landscaping and other finishing work will continue through 2026.

Wellington Gateway Phase 3 is nearing completion. The road between Wilkins Street and Harlech Gate has been paved, centre-running transit lanes have been painted, and transit shelters and new traffic signals are in place. Remaining work includes final station work, landscaping, cleanup and restoration.

Wellington Gateway Phase 4 is also nearing completion. Underground infrastructure between Harlech Gate and the Wellington Commons entrance is complete. Crews are completing transit stations, permanent traffic signals, the multi use path, landscaping, surface asphalt, and red centre-running transit lanes.

Construction continues on Phase 2A of Wellington Gateway, from Wilkins Street to Base Line Road East. Crews are continuing work on underground infrastructure, road widening and other improvements needed to accommodate the new centre-running Rapid Transit lanes.

For the latest transit updates and detour information, visit the London Transit Commission website or follow @LTCLdnOnt on X.

London, ON (August 28, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 11-year-old Aadila Kochai, of London.

The missing person is described as a female, slim build, shoulder length red hair, and hazel eyes. She was last seen wearing black pants, a grey sweater, and blue flip-flops.

The missing person is believed to be in the area of Boullee St and Victoria St. She was reported missing on August 25, 2026.

stories.title: WOMAN STABBED DURING EARLY MORNING BREAK AND ENTER 26-83738
stories.summary: Suspect arrested, remains in custody London, Ont. (Aug. 24, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after police were called to a break and enter at a residence…
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: UPDATE – LONDON, ON (August 28, 2026 ) – The victim a 73-year-old woman of London, has died in hospital. Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section in collaboration with the Chief Coroner’s Office, continue to investigate.
The death has been deemed a homicide.
As a result of the investigation, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, has additionally been charged with second degree murder.
Investigators are asking anyone with information about the accused, or any interactions with him, to contact police.
The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court August 31, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .
LONDON, Ont. (Aug. 24, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after police were called to a break and enter at a residence in the south end of the city over the weekend.

On Saturday, August 22, 2026, at about 6:10 a.m., an elderly woman was woken by a loud noise and found a man entering the residence in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road East. The victim was assaulted and stabbed before she was able to call 911.

Multiple officers responded. As officers attended the residence the accused began throwing broken glass at police. One officer sustained minor injuries. Officers entered the residence, and arrested the suspect.
The victim was transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. The suspect was transported to hospital by paramedic services with minor injuries.
The suspect and victim were not known to each other.
As a result of the investigation, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, has been charged with the following offences:
Aggravated assault;
Break and enter with intent;
Assault a peace officer with a weapon; and
Obstruct peace officer.
The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court August 27, 2026, in relation to the charges.

stories.title: Expanding critical care where cardiology patients need it most
stories.summary: August 28, 2026
stories.content:
The addition of critical care Level 3 beds within the Coronary Care Unit supports patients and families, strengthens critical care capacity, and improves patient flow across London Health Sciences Centre

For patients arriving at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) with complex cardiac needs, care can move quickly from the Emergency Department or Catheterization Lab to the critical care unit for monitoring and ventilation, and then onto recovery in an inpatient unit. Now with the opening of three net new Level 3 beds in the Coronary Care Unit (CCU), LHSC is helping to smooth the care journey for cardiology-focused patients and their families.

The new beds, made possible through provincial funding from Ontario Health, add ventilated care capacity within the CCU at University Hospital. They are designed to support critically ill cardiac patients who previously May have required care in a traditional critical care unit before transitioning to a cardiology-focused unit as their condition improved.

"We didn't have the physical space needed to add beds within the critical care unit at University Hospital, so we started to look at what other centres were doing to support level 3 care for this patient population and found an example where they had incorporated advanced care within their CCU," says Rachel Rushton, Director, Cardiac Care at LHSC. "We were confident that a similar model could work here and the benefits that we've seen to-date have been threefold, with benefits to our patients and their families, to our CCU team members, and to our broader patient flow."

Benefits to our patients

With this new model, patients can be cared for by a cardiac-focused team from the most acute phase of their illness through recovery and, in many cases, discharge to home with appropriate supports in place. For patients and families, remaining within a familiar care environment and being supported by many of the same team members can bring comfort and confidence during a stressful and uncertain time.

"Being managed by a team that specializes in cardiac care in one location is important," says Dr. Daniel Durocher, Cardiologist and Critical Care physician at LHSC. "Ultimately, we can provide advanced critical care support for patients while keeping their care journey focused within a cardiac centre."

Benefits to our people

To make these new beds possible, CCU nurses who were already trained to care for Level 2 patients received additional education and hands-on preparation, including classroom learning, simulation labs and buddy shifts in the ICU. Clinical educators, respiratory therapy educators, Critical Care Outreach Team members, respiratory therapists, dietitians, physiotherapists and ICU nurse mentors have all helped support the transition.

That deep collaboration has also created new opportunities for staff development. Nurses working within cardiology can build from foundational skills to Level 2 and Level 3 care, supporting some of the hospital’s most complex cardiac patients, while also following patients through a broader portion of their recovery journey.

For CCU team members, that continuity has been especially meaningful. Rather than caring for patients only during one stage of illness, staff can see the progress patients make as they move from critical illness to recovery. The result is a less siloed experience for both patients and care teams, with a stronger sense of connection across the full inpatient journey.

Benefits to our capacity

The new beds also support improved patient flow across LHSC by adding critical care capacity for cardiac patients at University Hospital. By caring for appropriate ventilated cardiology patients within the CCU, the hospital can better preserve traditional critical care capacity for patients with other urgent needs, including medical and surgical critical care. The model helps better ensure patients receive the right care, in the right place, at the right time.

From a regional perspective, the Level 3 CCU beds strengthen access to advanced cardiac support at LHSC, a tertiary care centre that serves patients from London and across southwestern Ontario. The expansion helps advance the organization’s broader goal of increasing critical care capacity by leveraging existing space and expertise in a new way.
