stories.title: ‘Game on’ for AdaptAbilty network, co-founded by Western researchers
stories.summary: A new platform, AdaptAbility, provides information on local opportunities for sport and exercise for people with disabilities.
stories.author: Special
paragraphs: When her feet hit the water for her first coached swim, eight-year-old Hannah Burns thought, “this must be what flying feels like.”
“Swimming to me means freedom. No special equipment, no barriers. Just me and the water and how fast I can go,” she said.

Today, as a high-performance athlete and a swim coach, Burns wants to make sure other kids and families don’t have to rely on word-of-mouth, as she did, to find parasports opportunities that bring them joy.

“A lot of opportunities are out there but they need to be widely available and visible. Sport is so important for everyone’s developmental path whether you’re born with a disability or acquire one later in life. Sport challenges you and gives you a community in a deeper way.”

Burns is among several sports enthusiasts who – with St. Joseph’s Health Care London (St. Joseph’s) and Western University as catalysts and sustainers – have created a unique-in-Canada network of London-based groups and advocates involved in parasports and physical activity.
AdaptAbility London aims to build local support, connection and community through sport and exercise for people with a disability.
Its website, AdaptabilityLondon.CA , provides contact information for specific sports; is searchable by season, sport, venue and time; and is also a portal for volunteering and other resources.

Site visitors could learn, for example, that boccia takes place on Wednesdays, adaptive climbing monthly at The Junction, wheelchair basketball Thursday evenings, goalball on Fridays and fitness activities for people with physical and/or intellectual disabilities most weekdays at Hutton House.
Until now, that was information you might find – if you found it at all – by scouring the internet, scrolling through social media pages or by word-of-mouth.
“This is a one-stop shop in the London area,” said Stephanie Marrocco, research coordinator at St. Joseph’s Parkwood Institute.
Marrocco says the network is new but gaining momentum.
“Everyone is very passionate about what they do, so everyone wants to see their program succeed and grow.”

Network participants include athletes and adaptive sports organizations, along with co-founders Marrocco, Western kinesiology professor Laura Misener, Lawson Research Institute scientist Dalton Wolfe and Western psychology professor Dr. Blair Evans.

“Many of these groups don’t have any other way of getting connected so getting them together was the first big task. And then, because it’s their network and not ours, the next question we asked was, ‘what are your needs?’” said Misener, who is also Western’s Dr. Frank J. Hayden Endowed Research Chair in Sport and Social Impact.
We’re facilitators of the network, but we co-create the solutions with athletes, organizations and participants. It’s shared expertise, shared leadership,” added Wolfe.

For sport organizers, needs often include: resources to train, retain and sustain volunteer engagement; advertising and awareness; collective advocacy; finding fully accessible sports venues; and brainstorming sustainable funding models.
Participant needs include building social connections with peers and finding information on sports specific to their interests, preferred schedules and seasons.

Adam Purdy, a Canadian Paralympic swimmer, coach and Canadian Paralympic Committee member whose PhD studies focus on participation in accessible sports, says the network benefits everyone, from participants to high-performing competitors to the people who support them.
“Sport is what nourishes a culture. We need it for healthy communities and it should be accessible to all. Every body deserves to experience it.” – Adam Purdy, PhD candidate in kinesiology
There isn’t another network like this in Canada.

Calgary Adapted Hub powered by Jumpstart is similar to AdaptAbility London but is aimed at children and youth, not adults. ParaSport Ontario provides information about more than 30 sports accessible to people with disabilities but doesn’t sort by calendar or include sports specific to people with intellectual disabilities.
“We all have common needs, including the need for connection,” Misener said. “I sometimes think there’s a false dichotomy between high performance and participation.”
Misener believes in the importance of valuing self-determined physical activity and creating pathways for all these opportunities across the lifespan.
“If you want to do yoga twice a week, that’s great. And if you want to pursue a high-performance route, we need to make sure these opportunities are also available.”

stories.title: London library hunting for 125 missing high school yearbooks
stories.summary: The library is asking Londoners to donate yearbooks to help fill gaps in a collection dating back more than a century.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
The library is asking Londoners to donate yearbooks to help fill gaps in a collection dating back more than a century.

If you have an old high school yearbook lying around, chances are the London Public Library might want it.

A new campaign from the library is asking Londoners to donate their high school yearbooks for its collection at the Ivey Family London Room, the London-specific archive at Central Library, 251 Dundas St.

David Caloren, the library’s coordinator of central adult services and supervisor of the London Room, says the campaign is a way to fill gaps in the collection.

“Yearbooks are not something you can just buy from a vendor, you have to be connected to the school in some way to get them,” he said. “We’ve relied on people giving them to us because we can’t really seek them out that way.”

Caloren says the library has been building its yearbook collection for decades, starting in the 1960s, and has volumes from 34 different high schools in London and the surrounding area – some of which have since closed.

He estimates there are more than 750 unique yearbooks stored at the London Public Library, all donated by Londoners over the years.

“We’ve never had a program of actively collecting them, they come to us sort of haphazardly,” Caloren said.

Caloren says yearbooks are especially valuable to researchers and Londoners because of their hyperlocal subject matter, often showing what was happening in a community and trends in fashion, music and clubs.

“They tell a lot about what was important for that particular community at that particular time,” he said.

They are also a good source for finding old photos of famous Londoners from when they were younger, he joked.

Caloren says the oldest official yearbook in the collection is from London Central Secondary School in 1922.

But the library also has documents dating back to 1903 that he describes as “yearbook-adjacent” – small, student-produced booklets that were never formally issued as yearbooks.

The library is currently looking for around 125 yearbooks to fill gaps in the collection, he says, but most of what it needs is fairly recent.

“I’m really hoping those Gen Z kids have a look. We’re missing a lot of the 2010 yearbooks and that would be a great score for us if we could fill in our gaps for this century,” Caloren said.

Some of the oldest material the library needs is from De La Salle High School, which closed in the 1950s. The collection has only one yearbook from the school.

Londoners looking to donate their high school yearbooks can contact the London Room by email at research.request@lpl.CA or by phone at 519-661-5100 ext. 2410.

stories.title: Ingersoll Driver Charged in Thames Centre
stories.summary: The 23-year-old is facing impaired driving charges.
stories.content:
The 23-year-old is facing impaired driving charges.

Thames Centre - Someone from Ingersoll is facing charges in Thames Centre.

Middlesex OPP officers responded to reports of a suspicious vehicle at business on Hamilton Road shortly before 5:00 a.m. on Friday.

They pulled the vehicle over and charged the 23-year-old driver with operation while impaired and operation while impaired with a blood alcohol concentration over 80. He has a court date in London next month.

If you spot a drive that you believe could be impaired, the OPP say you should call police immediately.

stories.title: London's small, medium-sized businesses will be hit harder by new U.S. tariffs, warns expert
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 25, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 25
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 25, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 25
Some 700 London businesses exported $8B worth of goods to the U.S. in 2023: Ledc

New, steep tariffs imposed by the U.S. over the weekend will hit small and medium-sized businesses in the London area harder than previous levies, and the region’s economic picture will likely “get a whole lot worse” before it gets better, one economic expert says.

While previous tariffs announced by Donald Trump's administration were broad targeting sectors including auto, steel and aluminum, the 50 per cent levies that took effect Saturday affect billions of dollars worth of Canadian products from a range of industries, including alcohol, honey, hockey sticks and jewelry.

“All of those things involve small and medium-sized enterprises, or small and medium-sized enterprises who rely on some of the other producers,” said Mahmood Nanji, a policy fellow at Ivey Business School and former Ontario associate deputy finance minister.

“I think this will exacerbate London's, sort of, weaker economy. London has had one of the highest unemployment rates in Canada for the last six to nine months, and I think you're likely to see more layoffs. The uncertainty means that these businesses will not invest if they're going to expand their operations.”
For the London area, which has been dependent on the manufacturing sector, the tariffs have “had the impact, (and) it’s likely to get a whole lot worse,” he added.

Prime Minister Mark Carney suspended trade talks with the U.S. on Friday, accusing them of trying to introduce last-minute measures which could have restricted Canada’s ability to do deals with other countries and protect its culture.

As a result, new 50 per cent tariffs took effect Saturday on roughly $28 billion Cdn ($20 billion US) worth of Canadian goods, layering on top of existing sanctions. Carney has promised dollar-for-dollar reciprocal tariffs by Sept. 8.
Trump has since threatened a 50 per cent tariff on vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada effective Jan. 1, and on social media, threatened Canadian energy flowing through the United States.
"When the Americans go to the negotiation table first, with the right attitude toward our industries and a true partnership, of course we'll come to the negotiating table," Carney said Monday.
WATCH | Political scientist on Premier Ford's 'emotional' response to Trump:

According to the London Economic Development Corporation, some 700 businesses in London exported around $8 billion worth of goods to the U.S. in 2023, said Graham Henderson, CEO of the London Chamber of Commerce. Roughly 450 manufacturers employ about 20,000 people, he said.

“People hear tariffs and they tend to think of auto plants, but there’s businesses in London that manufacture here, they’ve built a market in the U.S., and suddenly there’s a 50 per cent tariff aimed directly at their product category,” Henderson said.

“This is not a blanket 50 per cent tariff on everything London exports. It covers $20 billion US of Canadian exports, and that is roughly five per cent of our annual exports to the United States,” he said.
While five per cent of Canadian exports sounds manageable, a London manufacturer whose product is inside that five per cent, "woke up Saturday with a 50 per cent problem,” Henderson added.
It’s a reality being faced by Melanie Pierce, owner of Seven Sisters Ritual Apothecary on Dundas Place.

The downtown business, which Pierce describes as a “house of authentic witchcraft and magic,” makes and sells several products that fall under the tariffs, including candles, essential oils, toilet waters and botanical herbs.

“I would say just over 80 per cent of our online clientele are American, so this is greatly going to affect our online sales, which are already greatly impacted, probably bringing them down to hardly anything at all,” Pierce said.
Like other local merchants selling south of the border, Seven Sisters has already had to contend with shifting regulations when it comes to shipping, including last year's
de minimis exemption which allowed goods under $800 to enter the U.S. duty-free.

“We have recently had to fill out a whole slew of extra paperwork to even be able to ship into the U.S., and it was such a headache I honestly couldn't even look at it for a while. I just wrapped my head around what that looked like and got that going again,” Pierce said.

Pierce hasn’t seen a clear drop in U.S. demand yet, but it’s still early days. Already concerned about trade volatility, she says work has been underway to add manufacturing capacity at a sister store in Massachusetts, but notes that's still months from completion.
In the meantime, she says she's looking to boost domestic sales and invest in local advertising away from social media to offset any tariff-related impacts.

stories.title: Dealer sentenced in London mother's fentanyl-tainted cocaine death
stories.summary: A judge said the dealer did not know the cocaine contained fentanyl, but his role still carried “devastating consequences.”
stories.author: Jane Sims
stories.content:
A judge said the dealer did not know the cocaine contained fentanyl, but his role still carried “devastating consequences.”

It was cocaine that everyone thought was clean – the street-drug dealer, his customer and his partner who died after ingesting it.

But the drugs that killed London mother Christina Bestward were part of what a judge described as “a troubling and increasingly common reality of the illicit drug trade: the contamination of street-level drugs with fentanyl.”

On Monday, Jordan Colley, 35, the drug dealer, was sentenced to a total of 42 months in prison for manslaughter in the death of Bestward, 41, and two years to be served concurrently for criminal negligence causing bodily harm to her partner, Daniel Gale, 39, ON May 12, 2023. Factoring in time already served, he has 35.5 months, or just under three years, left on his sentence.

“While fentanyl has attracted much of the recent public attention, cocaine remains a dangerous drug,” Superior Court Justice Marc Garson said. “The illicit drug trade operates in an environment where substances are frequently mixed, diluted, cut or contaminated. Users have little ability to know with confidence what they are consuming.”

“The facts of this case provide a stark illustration of that reality.”

Colley was convicted after a trial earlier this year in which Garson learned Colley didn’t know the cocaine he sold to Gale was contaminated with the highly potent opioid when he dropped it off at their Wyatt Street home.

Bestward and Gale had sent their young child to a relative’s home the night before so they could celebrate Bestward’s certification as a personal support worker. Gale was a cocaine addict, while Bestward was not a habitual drug user.

Gale had contacted Colley just after midnight to buy drugs and again early in the morning when the supply ran out. Colley delivered more drugs and Gale cooked them into crack. Both he and Bestward took a couple of tokes, and his last memory was walking into the living room before waking up in hospital.

The couple was found by their child after school. Gale was taken to hospital, but Bestward could not be revived.

While other drug dealers have been convicted of manslaughter throughout the province for supplying deadly drugs to clients, Colley was the first to be convicted of the serious charge stemming from a London police investigation.

As Garson pointed out in his decision, the opioid crisis has had a stranglehold on communities across the country, but its grip has been even tighter on London.

Garson referred to statistics filed by the Crown that formed a community impact statement presented in other fentanyl-related cases and that “paints a deep and troubling picture.”

“Fentanyl-related overdoses, illnesses, hospitalizations and deaths have increased dramatically over the last decade,” Garson said. “Young adults between the ages of 25 and 44 have borne a disproportionate share of that harm.”

“Behind every death is grief. Parents bury children. Children lose parents. Friends, co-workers and entire communities are left to bear the consequences.”

Local death rates have exceeded provincial averages. In the first quarter of 2020, there were an estimated 100 accidental deaths involving fentanyl. A year later, the number doubled. London is now approaching 300 deaths due to fentanyl annually.

“London has borne a disproportionate share of this crisis,” Garson said, noting that at one point London police were recording 2.7 fentanyl-related deaths every 2.7 days and police time spent responding to fentanyl calls rose 400 per cent.

Pressure has also been put on emergency departments, hospitals, paramedics and community agencies.

“Scarce public resources continue to absorb the burden of a preventable crisis that shows little signs of abating,” Garson said.

Contamination of the street drug supply is a constant threat. Fentanyl is 80 to 100 times more powerful than morphine and it takes only a few milligrams to be lethal.

“When fentanyl contaminates another illicit substance, users often consume it without knowing what they have purchased or ingested. What appears to be a routine drug transaction can quickly turn fatal,” Garson said.

The Crown had argued for a six-year prison sentence, while the defence suggested a two-year-less-a-day conditional sentence with three years of probation.

Colley, Garson noted, had a positive pre-sentence report. He has matured from an unstable childhood. While he has a criminal record, including convictions for drug trafficking, he has maintained steady employment and “made meaningful efforts to improve himself.”

He was described as “generous, kind-hearted, caring and someone who would not intentionally harm others.” He has wide support from family, friends and his employer, all of whom were in the courtroom to support him.

And he has deep remorse for what happened to Bestward and Gale.

Garson commended Colley for his turnaround, but said his thoughts were with the victims and their loved ones. “They have suffered a profound, tragic and entirely unnecessary loss.”

While no victim impact statements were filed, Garson said he knows “those consequences will endure long after these proceedings have concluded.”

The case was a reminder “that those who choose to traffic in illicit drugs participate in a dangerous enterprise with potentially catastrophic consequences.”

“Mr. Colley did not know the cocaine he trafficked contained fentanyl. It reduced, but did not erase his culpability,” Garson said.

“His decision and choice to participate in the illicit drug trade had devastating consequences and the sentence I have imposed reflects both realities.”

The Crown had argued for a six-year prison sentence, while the defence suggested a two-year-less-a-day conditional sentence with three years of probation.

Colley, Garson noted, had a positive pre-sentence report. He has matured from an unstable childhood. While he has a criminal record, including convictions for drug trafficking, he has maintained steady employment and “made meaningful efforts to improve himself.”

He was described as “generous, kind-hearted, caring and someone who would not intentionally harm others.” He has wide support from family, friends and his employer, all of whom were in the courtroom to support him.
And he has deep remorse for what happened to Bestward and Gale.
Garson commended Colley for his turnaround, but said his thoughts were with the victims and their loved ones. “They have suffered a profound, tragic and entirely unnecessary loss.”
While no victim impact statements were filed, Garson said he knows “those consequences will endure long after these proceedings have concluded.”
The case was a reminder “that those who choose to traffic in illicit drugs participate in a dangerous enterprise with potentially catastrophic consequences.”
“Mr. Colley did not know the cocaine he trafficked contained fentanyl. It reduced, but did not erase his culpability,” Garson said.
“His decision and choice to participate in the illicit drug trade had devastating consequences and the sentence I have imposed reflects both realities.”

stories.title: Western University’s free legal clinic moving closer to London courthouse
stories.summary: The clinic is expected to relocate to Fanshawe’s downtown campus in late December.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
The clinic is expected to relocate to Fanshawe’s downtown campus in late December.

Western University ’s legal clinic is moving downtown, with officials saying the new location will help bring free legal assistance to more low-income and marginalized people in London and Middlesex County.

Community Legal Services, a clinic operated by Western’s Faculty of Law, is expected to move into its new location on the fifth floor of Fanshawe College’s Howard W. Rundle Building on Dundas Street in late December.

The clinic will continue operating from the Josephine Spencer Niblett Law Building on Western’s campus while renovations are completed at the downtown location.

“This move marks a major milestone in strengthening community-based legal services to ensure people in London and region can access critical support that May otherwise be out of reach,” Western president Alan Shepard said.

The move will bring Community Legal Services closer to the London courthouse, which Western officials say will make legal assistance more accessible to potential clients.

“We’re pleased to have Western’s Community Legal Services clinic join us, strengthening the goals we’ve always had for our downtown campus – creating exceptional learning opportunities for students while contributing to the continued growth and vibrancy of the city’s core,” Fanshawe president Peter Devlin said.

Devlin and Shepard signed the lease for the new space Monday.

Community Legal Services gives law students hands-on experience assisting with cases involving criminal law, small claims of up to $50,000, tenant and housing disputes, provincial offences and family law.

Over the 2025-26 academic year, Western students took on more than 600 cases and consultations.

“A year in that support role showed me just how critical it is to ensure access to justice in London and the surrounding area, where many people can’t afford a lawyer,” said Ryan McCarthy, an articling student at the legal clinic. He began working as an administrative assistant for the clinic before applying to law school.

“I’ve seen how even a simple housing issue can snowball and affect people for the rest of their lives,” he said. “Our work helps clients and, in some cases, their children recover from the lasting effects of those experiences. With support from CLS, they can move on with their lives.”

stories.title: Trump’s 50% auto tariff threat rattles Southwestern Ontario manufacturers
stories.summary: Industry experts warn the threatened tariffs could devastate Canada’s auto sector while also disrupting U.S. production.
stories.author: Jonathan Juha
stories.content:
Industry experts warn the threatened tariffs could devastate Canada’s auto sector while also disrupting U.S. production.

Southwestern Ontario manufacturers reacted with surprise and disbelief Monday to U.S. President Donald Trump’s threat to slap 50-per-cent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts, with one calling it “a nuclear option” that could decimate the region’s auto parts industry while also inflicting pain south of the border.

Trump said he planned to impose the new tariffs starting Jan. 1, a move that comes after trade negotiations between the U.S. and Canada broke down Friday, resulting in 50-per-cent levies now being applied on about $28-billion worth of Canadian goods, ON top of sector-specific tariffs already applied to autos, steel and aluminum.

“On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Build in the U.S. and there are Zero Tariffs. Canada will be treated like a State no longer!

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with.”

For his part, Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Canada will retaliate with dollar-for-dollar tariffs of its own beginning Sept. 8.

Industry watchers said Monday the potential new tariffs would be devastating for Ontario’s auto belt, a key economic driver for the province that extends from Guelph, Cambridge and Woodstock in the east to Windsor in the west and includes four auto plants and dozens of parts makers along the Highway 401 corridor.

“That’s like a nuclear bomb kind of effect that would be bad for everyone,” said Ben Whitney, owner of Armo Tool Ltd. in London, a manufacturer of machinery used to make parts for the automotive, defence and food and beverage sectors, among others.

“There is no auto parts industry in Canada with that, but this would be extremely difficult for the entire automotive industry. This is a 50 per cent tariff in a sector that’s making six or seven (per cent) in profit margins, so something’s going to give.”

Flavio Volpe, president of Canada’s Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association, echoed that assessment, saying U.S. automakers would also suffer from such a move.

Can defence spending save Ontario's auto-parts sector?

London firms among manufacturers eyeing U.S. investment as tariffs bite

“The ‘importer of record’ pays the tariffs. A threatened U.S. tariff on Canadian auto parts will be paid by U.S. auto assembly,” he wrote on X, formerly Twitter.

“Without those specific parts, auto assembly throughout the U.S. would halt.”

Dave Johnson, general manager at London-based Ursa Manufacturing ULC, said the levies are so high it would take time to determine exactly how they would affect his company, which makes stampings and light assemblies for companies including General Motors Co. and Toyota Boshoku Corp.

“But if that is the case, quite potentially, all automotive in North America would stop moving,” he said.

“Whether it will occur or not is one thing, but it has the potential to bring the entire automotive industry to a halt . . . so let’s hope this is more bluster and bluff because it seems like a total shot in the dark that (Trump) is taking. The automotive companies, I would imagine, will have some sort of response to that.”

Currently, the Canadian auto sector faces a 25 per cent tariff on vehicles exported to the U.S., but that amount can be reduced based on the percentage of U.S. content in a vehicle.

It wasn’t immediately clear Monday whether the U.S. government would continue to apply that exemption to parts produced south of the border.

But even if it did, it would still represent an effective tariff rate of 25 per cent for automakers in Canada, said Greig Mordue, an associate professor at McMaster University’s Booth School of Engineering Practice and Technology.

Mordue, who questioned whether Trump “understands what he’s done,” given how intertwined the auto sector is, didn’t mince words when describing the potential impact of tariffs at that level on Canada’s industry.

“Frankly, an effective rate of 25 percent expedites the demise of the Canadian automotive manufacturing industry,” he said.

Mordue noted the move would put Japanese automakers Honda Motor Co., Ltd. and Toyota Motor Corporation, which so far have absorbed the cost of tariffs, in a difficult position. Unlike Ford Motor Co., General Motors Co. and Stellantis NV, Mordue said neither Honda nor Toyota has idle capacity to shift some production to the U.S.

And while the Japanese companies May have been willing to continue with a wait-and-see approach at current tariff levels, pending the results of the November midterm elections or a new administration in 2029, the potential new tariff levels change the equation, with Mordue pegging the financial hit for both manufacturers at about $10 billion.

“They would look at that and say, ‘We can’t put any new product or commit to new models at that level,’” he said.

“They like building cars in Canada. They’ve made a commitment to Canada, and they think that commitment is a long-term one to Canada . . . but they can’t look at their global operations and say Canada is going to absorb half of their profitability globally.”

jjuha@postmedia.com

With files from the Financial Post’s Gabriel Friedman

stories.title: London man charged after elderly woman stabbed in home break-in
stories.summary: The woman was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police say.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
paragraphs: The woman was taken to hospital with serious injuries, police say.
A London man faces aggravated assault and other charges after a woman was stabbed during a break-in at a south-end home over the weekend.
An elderly woman was woken by a loud noise around 6:10 a.m. Saturday and found a man entering the residence in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road East, police said in a Monday release .
The woman was assaulted and stabbed before she was able to call 911.
Multiple officers responded to the home, where police said the man “began throwing broken glass” at officers.
One officer sustained minor injuries, police said.
Officers entered the residence and arrested the suspect.
The woman was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.
The suspect was taken to hospital with minor injuries.
A 40-year-old London man is charged with aggravated assault, break and enter with intent, assaulting a peace officer with a weapon and obstructing a peace officer.
Police did not say whether the woman and the accused knew each other.
The man remains in custody and is expected to appear in London court Aug. 27 in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information about the incident is asked to call London police at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be submitted anonymously online to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers.
A 23-year-old man was charged with aggravated assault following an overnight stabbing that took place in downtown Windsor.
Police responded to reports of a disturbance around Wyandotte Street West and Pelissier Street just after 2:30 a.m. on Friday.
Upon arrival, officers found a 20-year-old man in an alleyway with stab wounds. He was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Police determined that the stabbing occurred during an altercation between two groups. K9 officer Link was deployed to assist with the investigation and found a knife hidden underneath a vehicle near the scene of the crime.
Officers quickly located and arrested the suspect near Pelissier Street and Elliott Street West.
With files from The Windsor Star
bbaleeiro@postmedia.com

stories.title: Western’s Community Legal Services moving to downtown London
stories.summary: Western University's Community Legal Services clinic for low-income Londoners is moving to the core - within Fanshawe College's downtown campus.
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
paragraphs: Community Legal Services (CLS), the legal clinic operated by the Faculty of Law at Western University, is moving downtown to a space within Fanshawe College’s Dundas Street campus. The new location will bolster the clinic’s role in providing free legal help to low-income and marginalized people across London, Ont. and Middlesex County.

Western President Alan Shepard and Fanshawe President Peter Devlin signed the lease on Aug. 24 at the clinic’s future home – the fifth floor of Fanshawe’s Howard W. Rundle Building at 137 Dundas St. in London, Ont. The location near the courthouse will reduce barriers to justice by placing legal assistance within easier reach of more potential clients.

“This move marks a major milestone in strengthening community-based legal services to ensure people in London and region can access critical support that May otherwise be out of reach,” Shepard said. “It also brings together two strong institutions in the downtown core, helping to realize our shared vision of a vibrant city. We’re deeply grateful for our partnership with Fanshawe College and for this new shared space.”

While renovations are completed, CLS will continue to operate from the Josephine Spencer Niblett Law Building on Western’s campus, with no interruption to services for existing clients. The clinic’s new location is expected to open by the end of December, in the downtown building n amed after Fanshawe’s long-serving president, Howard Rundle.
It opened in 2014 to support Fanshawe’s media and digital arts programs. Today, 264 students study at this downtown London, Ont. building.

“We’re pleased to have Western’s Community Legal Services clinic join us, strengthening the goals we’ve always had for our downtown campus – creating exceptional learning opportunities for students while contributing to the continued growth and vibrancy of the city’s core,” Devlin said.

London Mayor Josh Morgan welcomed CLS to its new space, thanking Fanshawe and Western for their commitment to London’s downtown.

“ This partnership between Western University and Fanshawe College is a powerful example of making better use of existing spaces while bringing students, faculty, learning, services and new energy into the core,” Morgan said.

“Our downtown is at its best when it is a place where people come to live, learn, work, create and connect. Initiatives like Western’s Community Legal Services help make that vision a reality by offering essential, barrier-free access to justice for vulnerable residents who might otherwise go without support. This partnership is a significant win for our downtown, and for the entire city of London.”

CLS combines community service with education, offering Western law students experiential learning where they can apply their knowledge and develop skills through real-world experience. As student caseworkers, they provide legal assistance under the supervision of a review counsel, a practicing lawyer who advises them on legal documents and strategy for trials or settlements. Students work in the clinic as part of their law program and others volunteer as mentors. Interns work in paid positions from May to August.

In 2025-26, students took on more than 600 cases and consultations. They assist their clients, including Western students, with a wide range of legal matters including criminal, provincial and municipal offences, small claims lawsuits up to $50,000 and housing disputes. Three days a week, they work from the London Courthouse, helping self-represented litigants navigate legal forms and meet deadlines critical for their case. Students also represent clients in family matters through the Court Assistance Program, funded through a two-year grant from the Law Foundation of Ontario .

After two years as a caseworker, Ryan McCarthy, BA’22, JD’26, is now an articling student with CLS. He got his start at the clinic as an administrative assistant, before he had even applied to law school.
“A year in that support role showed me just how critical it is to ensure access to justice in London and the surrounding area, where many people can’t afford a lawyer,” he said.
Who qualifies for legal help at Community Legal Services?
Who is eligible? Low-income residents of London and Middlesex County who meet financial eligibility requirements set by Legal Aid Ontario, and current Western University students.

Are services entirely free? Yes, representation and advice is provided by law students , under the supervision of experienced staff lawyers, at no cost. Clients May be responsible for expenses such as court filing fees or medical reports.
What types of cases are supported? Criminal law, small claims up to $50,000, tenant and housing disputes, provincial offences and family law.
How do you apply? Complete an intake form online or call 519-661-3352 to check eligibility and schedule an appointment.

Where is Community Legal Services located? In Western’s space on the fifth floor of the Fanshawe College downtown campus at 137 Dundas St. in London, Ont. Western students seeking legal services can also arrange to meet with student caseworkers on campus.

McCarthy encourages law students to volunteer time in the clinic, saying the experiential learning helps cultivate deeper empathy, reinforced by trauma-informed training from Western’s Student Experience team. He says working at CLS has heightened his own awareness of what clients are experiencing during their interactions with him.

“I want to accommodate people however I can, give them proper time and truly digest what they’re saying, even paying attention to the physical space to ensure they’re situated where they feel comfortable,” he said.

Some cases have honed McCarthy’s skill for managing the most distraught clients as they face potentially life-altering circumstances – imprisonment, crippling financial penalties or loss of access to their children or home.

“I’ve seen how even a simple housing issue can snowball and affect people for the rest of their lives,” he said. “Our work helps clients and, in some cases, their children recover from the lasting effects of those experiences. With support from CLS, they can move on with their lives.”

Community Legal Services has shaped the legal profession for more than five decades. The clinic came to life through the efforts of the late John Eberhard, BA’66, Llb’69. As a third-year Western Law student in 1968, he founded Western’s Student Defender Program, modelled on a student-run legal aid service at the University of British Columbia . By 1970, it evolved into the Student Legal Aid Services Society.

Funding from Legal Aid Ontario (LAO) allowed the clinic to hire its first full-time review counsel in 1977, when it became Community Legal Services with a broader mandate to serve low-income residents. Continued LAO funding ensures the clinic can operate, supported by additional funds from the Law Foundation of Ontario, and Western’s University Students Council and Faculty of Law.

Over the last four decades, generations of Western law students have gained the opportunity to experience law in practice. They also learn from the deeply personal circumstances of the clients they serve, says the dean of Western’s Faculty of Law, Mohamed Khimji.

“The enduring legacy of Community Legal Services can be seen in the network of socially minded lawyers it has trained and inspired, and in the expanded access to legal services for some of the community’s most vulnerable residents,” Khimji said.
For McCarthy, the experience at CLS has shaped his future ambitions. He aspires to help more Indigenous people and become an ally of Indigenous-led organizations.
“The clinic helped me realize I want to keep supporting equity-deserving groups, because access to justice can make a meaningful difference in our communities.”

stories.summary: Missing Person- 26-84498 FOR Immediate Release Missing Person – Seeking the public’s assistance Update - London, ON (August 24, 2026) – The previously reported missing 32-year-old male of London has been located and is safe. We would like to thank the public for sharing the info…
stories.author: - Aug
paragraphs: Update - London, ON (August 24, 2026) – The previously reported missing 32-year-old male of London has been located and is safe. We would like to thank the public for sharing the information.
We kindly ask that any photographs from prior publications of the missing person be removed.
London, ON (August, 24, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating a 32-year-old male, of London.

The missing person is described as a white male, 5 feet 8 inches tall, heavy build with short brown hair. The missing person was wearing a white and blue tie dye shirt with palm trees and basketball shorts.

The missing person was last seen on Monday, August 24, 2026, at approxi mately 1:30 p.m., in the area of Wharncliffe Road South and Tecumseh Avenue South. The missing person was reported missing on Monday, August 24, 2026, at 3:00 p.m.
Family and police are concerned for the missing person’s welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

stories.title: Leadership program inspires Schulich Dentistry students
stories.summary: Muntdr Madlol and Zahra Danaei chosen for American Dental Education Association Student Leaders for Social Change program
stories.author: Special
paragraphs: When Muntdr Madlol and Zahra Danaei arrived in Montreal for the opening of the 2026 American Dental Education Association (Adea) Student Leaders for Social Change program, they quickly realized they stood out. They were the only Canadians in the room.
“We were literally Team Canada,” Danaei said.

Selected through a competitive process, the Schulich Dentistry students recently completed the six-month program alongside peers from across North America. Through two in-person conferences and several virtual sessions, they explored some of dentistry’s biggest challenges, including access to care, ethics, patient advocacy and professional leadership.
“The program brought a bunch of like-minded students together,” said Madlol. “We were all hungry to learn from each other.”
Schulich Dentistry students Muntdr Madlol and Zahra Danaei (Submitted)

Although they entered the program with different experiences and aspirations, both Madlol and Danaei feel the program has given them a clearer vision of how they want to create change – lessons they’re already putting into practice.
“What is the problem? How do I want to fix it? What is the first step I can take? That’s the blueprint this program has given me,” Danaei said.
When Madlol, DDS Class of 2028, explains why he chose dentistry, he begins with his family.
He recalls the time his brother needed oral surgery. After hearing the cost, his mother left the clinic believing the procedure would not be possible.
To the family’s surprise, the dentist covered the entire cost of the procedure.
That simple act of compassion stayed with him and, ultimately, inspired him to pursue dentistry.

Since entering dental school, Madlol has become deeply involved in student leadership. He served as Class President and took on roles with the Federation of Canadian Dental Student Associations and the Student Professionalism and Ethics Association.
Madlol has also extended that leadership beyond dentistry, raising more than $24,000 for health-care workers by competing in an Ironman 70.3 wearing medical scrubs .

Through group exercises, the program helped Madlol connect his leadership experiences to patient education. With many patients turning to social media for health information, he sees an opportunity for dental professionals to help counter misinformation.

“We can’t regulate what circulates online about dentistry by remaining absent from it,” Madlol said. “Part of our responsibility as dental professionals is making sure patients have accurate information they can understand and use to make informed decisions about their care.”
Before participating in the Adea program, Danaei, DDS Class of 2027, associated leadership with holding prominent positions or prestigious titles.
“I didn’t really know what leadership could look like for me,” she said.

Through the program’s reflective exercises and conversations with other students and mentors, Danaei began to see leadership as something rooted in commitment, collaboration and a willingness to act on the issues that matter to her.

That perspective connected naturally with work she was already doing through the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario , creating educational case scenarios addressing ethics and conflicts between patients and dentists.

For Danaei, one area where she hopes to create change is improving care for patients with disabilities. She is now working with an instructor to give dental students more practical, hands-on experience in accessible care.
“A filling is a filling,” Danaei said. “It’s the communication that we have to adapt.”
Using her new definition of leadership, Danaei says she’ll continue advocating for care that responds to patients’ financial, cultural and accessibility needs.
“I want to make sure my patients are receiving equitable care.”

stories.title: Expert insight: Why are we so obsessed with true crime? It’s not just morbid curiosity
stories.summary: Western University's Michael Arntfield explains why true crime remains so popular, exploring the psychology behind the genre.
stories.author: Special
paragraphs: A couple of weeks ago, Netflix released The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare , a documentary revisiting the 2022 killings of four University of Idaho students – Ethan Chapin (20 years old), Kaylee Goncalves (21), Xana Kernodle (20) and Madison Mogen (21).

The case, which seemed closed when Bryan Kohberger pleaded guilty in 2025 and was sentenced to life in prison, isn’t actually closed. Kohberger has since petitioned the court to withdraw that plea , arguing coercion and bad legal advice. The victims’ families are ready and unafraid to face him in court again.

The three-part series, detailing the grisly mass slaying, is doing exceptionally well . In its first five days on the streamer, it had brought in 18.2 million views and outperformed other Netflix titles.
And this has revivified ongoing questions about why this type of programming is so alluring. What does it say about us as a society when lurid content like this is so central to our cultural milieu?

Although true crime feels current, it is the fourth iteration of the genre under one name or another since the mid-19th century. In terms of explaining its appeal, no one explanation suffices. It May be best understood as a system of complex processes, with each of the following mechanisms operating simultaneously at different levels: individual psychology, moral reasoning and social belonging.

Foremost among these is a phenomenon known as benign hedonic masochism . Masochistic behaviours, or enjoyment derived from self-suffering , can, in extreme forms, be pathological and even dangerous . But it’s the “benign” part that provides us the intellectual licence to enjoy content about murder and mayhem.
The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare trades on exactly this: dramatized crime-scene reconstruction and survivor interviews, all consumed from the safety of a couch.

Drawing on Paul Rozin’s pioneering theory of hedonic reversal , benign hedonic masochism describes a paradoxical psychological condition through which people acquire pleasure from simulated aversive experiences that generate fear, anxiety and emotional discomfort, all while remaining fundamentally safe.

The maladaptive and self-deprecating language that often surrounds true crime consumption, such as “binging,” “obsession,” “addiction” and being a true crime “junkie,” reflects a certain self-awareness of this reality.
More than just a voyeuristic exercise, true crime offers controlled encounters with uncertainty, danger and moral disorder, while simultaneously reassuring audiences of closure and finality.

In an era characterized by declining institutional trust and heightened perceptions of crime, the genre functions as an emotionally charged but socially acceptable means of indulging those same anxieties. Psychologists have a name for it: opponent-process theory .

The theory proposes that intense emotional experiences trigger a secondary, opposing emotional response. Dread, tension and even revulsion can give way to relief; anxiety to reassurance. With repeated exposure, the negative reaction May weaken while the positive after-effect, or the high, becomes more predictable and prolonged.
This is likely why true crime is especially prevalent on streaming and podcasting platforms that are built for continuous, immoderate consumption or “binging.”

One of the other recurring explanations for true crime’s enduring popularity has to do with who’s actually consuming it. Adult women, in particular, are consistently identified as the target demographic for cable and streaming true-crime series, and the pattern holds even more strongly in podcasting .
One explanation for that skew is that the genre serves a didactic function : it imparts factual and moral lessons.

Rather than consuming crime narratives solely for entertainment, audiences May be using them as informal lessons in vulnerability, risk and survival. They watch series and listen to podcasts about sadistic psychopaths like Ted Bundy and Richard Ramirez to know how to spot them, how to thwart a possible kidnapping and how to avoid becoming a victim in a way the women in those cases so often couldn’t.

Originally coined by communications professor George Gerbner as “mean world syndrome,” the theory holds that repeated exposure to mediated violence can cultivate heightened perceptions of danger, vulnerability and interpersonal threat. Audiences, in the grip of that same syndrome, May then use crime narratives to gradually build a repertoire of mental scripts regarding warning signs, predatory behaviour and situational risk.
In this respect, consuming true crime resembles a form of low-stakes threat simulation, allowing the rehearsal of responses to hazards they hope to never encounter in real life.
Whether these lessons are empirically valid or merely produce an exaggerated sense of danger remains subject to some debate .

There are certainly other theories, too, about the psychological undergirding of this current true-crime zeitgeist. Some researchers point to morbid curiosity . Others frame it as a form of boredom-induced sensation-seeking or what’s been called negative information seeking (an appetite for unsettling information for its own sake).

And in some cases, the fascination with male offenders in particular has been linked to a disordered erotic interest known as hybristophillia . But the one thing these theories tend to converge on is that true crime, in its current form, provides a sense of community.

The barriers to membership in this community are remarkably low. Listeners can move effortlessly from consumers to contributors through message boards, Facebook groups, TikTok communities and even their own DIY podcasts .

In contrast to traditional media, true crime invites collective interpretation: armchair sleuthing, theory-crowdsourcing, shared meaning-making. It fosters a participatory culture in which audiences do not merely follow cases; they also actively help retell them.

That the path to community, in an increasingly segmented and partisan reality, includes a road paved by serial killers and cold cases May say less about our fascination with death than it does about our enduring need to find one another through stories.
Michael Arntfield , Full Professor of Criminology & English Literature, Western University

The case, which seemed closed when Bryan Kohberger pleaded guilty in 2025 and was sentenced to life in prison, isn’t actually closed. Kohberger has since petitioned the court to withdraw that plea , arguing coercion and bad legal advice. The victims’ families are ready and unafraid to face him in court again.

The three-part series, detailing the grisly mass slaying, is doing exceptionally well . In its first five days on the streamer, it had brought in 18.2 million views and outperformed other Netflix titles.

And this has revivified ongoing questions about why this type of programming is so alluring. What does it say about us as a society when lurid content like this is so central to our cultural milieu?

Although true crime feels current, it is the fourth iteration of the genre under one name or another since the mid-19th century. In terms of explaining its appeal, no one explanation suffices. It May be best understood as a system of complex processes, with each of the following mechanisms operating simultaneously at different levels: individual psychology, moral reasoning and social belonging.

Foremost among these is a phenomenon known as benign hedonic masochism . Masochistic behaviours, or enjoyment derived from self-suffering , can, in extreme forms, be pathological and even dangerous . But it’s the “benign” part that provides us the intellectual licence to enjoy content about murder and mayhem.

The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare trades on exactly this: dramatized crime-scene reconstruction and survivor interviews, all consumed from the safety of a couch.

Drawing on Paul Rozin’s pioneering theory of hedonic reversal , benign hedonic masochism describes a paradoxical psychological condition through which people acquire pleasure from simulated aversive experiences that generate fear, anxiety and emotional discomfort, all while remaining fundamentally safe.

The maladaptive and self-deprecating language that often surrounds true crime consumption, such as “binging,” “obsession,” “addiction” and being a true crime “junkie,” reflects a certain self-awareness of this reality.

More than just a voyeuristic exercise, true crime offers controlled encounters with uncertainty, danger and moral disorder, while simultaneously reassuring audiences of closure and finality.

In an era characterized by declining institutional trust and heightened perceptions of crime, the genre functions as an emotionally charged but socially acceptable means of indulging those same anxieties. Psychologists have a name for it: opponent-process theory .

The theory proposes that intense emotional experiences trigger a secondary, opposing emotional response. Dread, tension and even revulsion can give way to relief; anxiety to reassurance. With repeated exposure, the negative reaction May weaken while the positive after-effect, or the high, becomes more predictable and prolonged.

This is likely why true crime is especially prevalent on streaming and podcasting platforms that are built for continuous, immoderate consumption or “binging.”

One of the other recurring explanations for true crime’s enduring popularity has to do with who’s actually consuming it. Adult women, in particular, are consistently identified as the target demographic for cable and streaming true-crime series, and the pattern holds even more strongly in podcasting .

One explanation for that skew is that the genre serves a didactic function : it imparts factual and moral lessons.

Rather than consuming crime narratives solely for entertainment, audiences May be using them as informal lessons in vulnerability, risk and survival. They watch series and listen to podcasts about sadistic psychopaths like Ted Bundy and Richard Ramirez to know how to spot them, how to thwart a possible kidnapping and how to avoid becoming a victim in a way the women in those cases so often couldn’t.

Originally coined by communications professor George Gerbner as “mean world syndrome,” the theory holds that repeated exposure to mediated violence can cultivate heightened perceptions of danger, vulnerability and interpersonal threat. Audiences, in the grip of that same syndrome, May then use crime narratives to gradually build a repertoire of mental scripts regarding warning signs, predatory behaviour and situational risk.

In this respect, consuming true crime resembles a form of low-stakes threat simulation, allowing the rehearsal of responses to hazards they hope to never encounter in real life.

Whether these lessons are empirically valid or merely produce an exaggerated sense of danger remains subject to some debate .

There are certainly other theories, too, about the psychological undergirding of this current true-crime zeitgeist. Some researchers point to morbid curiosity . Others frame it as a form of boredom-induced sensation-seeking or what’s been called negative information seeking (an appetite for unsettling information for its own sake).

And in some cases, the fascination with male offenders in particular has been linked to a disordered erotic interest known as hybristophillia . But the one thing these theories tend to converge on is that true crime, in its current form, provides a sense of community.

The barriers to membership in this community are remarkably low. Listeners can move effortlessly from consumers to contributors through message boards, Facebook groups, TikTok communities and even their own DIY podcasts .

In contrast to traditional media, true crime invites collective interpretation: armchair sleuthing, theory-crowdsourcing, shared meaning-making. It fosters a participatory culture in which audiences do not merely follow cases; they also actively help retell them.

That the path to community, in an increasingly segmented and partisan reality, includes a road paved by serial killers and cold cases May say less about our fascination with death than it does about our enduring need to find one another through stories.

Michael Arntfield , Full Professor of Criminology & English Literature, Western University

stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: LONDON, ON (August 21, 2026) – A London man is facing a number of charges after police located an unconscious driver in the east end of the city last night.

On Thursday, August 20, 2026, at approximately 8 p.m., an off-duty London police officer observed a vehicle stopped on Florence Street near Kellogg Lane. As the officer approached to check on the driver, the vehicle began moving and struck a nearby fence. As he approached the vehicle, a man was found unconscious behind the wheel. The officer called 9-1-1 and police and paramedic services attended.
The suspect male was arrested without incident.
A search resulted in the seizure of the following items:
254 grams of suspected cocaine, value: $25,400
Rifle and magazine
Small plastic bags
Quantity of Canadian currency
As a result of the investigation, James Beretta, 29, of London, has been charged with the following offences:
Occupy motor vehicle with firearm;
Careless storage of a firearm, weapon, prohibited device;
Possess restricted or prohibited firearm knowingly not holding a licence and registration certificate;
Possession of a prohibited or restricted weapon or prohibited device;
Impaired operation of a conveyance;
Possess loaded or unloaded regulated firearm;
Possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking.
The accused is scheduled to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: PROHIBITED DRIVER IN STOLEN VEHICLE FACING MULTIPLE CHARGES 26-80637
stories.summary: London man arrested London ON (August 21, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after members of the London Police Service Uniformed Divisio…
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: London ON (August 21, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after members of the London Police Service Uniformed Division responded to a report of a suspected impaired driver in the north end of the city last week.

A concerned citizen's call on August 13, 2026, led police to an unconscious male behind the wheel of a vehicle in the area of Arbour Glen Crescent and Kipps Lane. When officers positioned their cruisers to prevent the vehicle from leaving, the suspect awoke and attempted to drive away, striking one of the police cruisers. The suspect male was arrested after resisting officers.
There were no reported injuries.
A search yielded the following:
204 grams of suspected crystal methamphetamine
12 grams of suspected fentanyl
A scale
Small plastic baggies
Speed-measuring warning device

Through further investigation, police determined the suspect was wanted in relation to outstanding warrants, the vehicle had been reported stolen, the licence plates were not authorized for the vehicle, and the suspect had multiple court-imposed driving prohibitions.
As a result of the investigation, Robert Matthew Toms Roth, 42, of London, has been charged with the following offences:
Two counts of possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking;
Impaired operation of a conveyance;
Operation while prohibited;
Possession of property obtained by crime over $5,000;
Resist arrest;
Use plates not authorized for vehicle; and
Drive motor vehicle with speed-measuring warning device.
The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to re-appear in London court on August 24, 2026.

Anyone with information about this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent anonymously online to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Road closure on Sunningdale Road West
stories.summary: Sunningdale Road West between Wallingford Avenue and Robbie’s Way will be closed beginning Monday, August 24
stories.content:
Sunningdale Road West between Wallingford Avenue and Robbie’s Way will be closed beginning Monday, August 24. This closure will be in place until Friday, September 4 while crews install a new culvert.

This work is part of the City’s Sunningdale Road Widening project. As this area of the city continues to develop, upgrades are needed to keep up with increasing traffic and to improve infrastructure.

A culvert is a structure that allows water to pass under or around infrastructure, such as a road or railroad. Culverts help prevent flooding, minimize erosion, and maintain roads in good condition longer.

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area. Through traffic will be detoured around the closure using Wonderland Road North, Fanshawe Park Road West, and Richmond Street. Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Local access will be maintained along Sunningdale Road for residents and businesses.

Residents can access the Wallingford Avenue area using Sunningdale Road from the west. Access to Meadowlands Way, Village Walk Boulevard, Robbie’s Way and local businesses will be maintained on Sunningdale Road from the east.

After this culvert is completed, work will then shift to widening Medway Creek bridge along Sunningdale Road beginning this fall. More information will be shared when this construction is confirmed to begin.

The Sunningdale Road Widening project includes reconstructing the roadway between Wonderland Road North and Richmond Street , upgrading underground infrastructure, adding sidewalks, and constructing cycling improvements. Work is beginning this year, and improvements will continue until early 2028.

stories.title: Temporary road closure on Western Road between Windermere Road and Ambleside Drive
stories.summary: Western Road between Windermere Road and Ambleside Drive will be closed beginning Monday, August 24 until Friday, August 28.
stories.content:
Western Road between Windermere Road and Ambleside Drive will be closed beginning Monday, August 24 until Friday, August 28.

This temporary closure is needed to complete a watermain connection at a private development in the area.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules.

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area. Please follow the detour signage. Drivers will be detoured around the closure using Richmond Street nearby. Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Access to University Hospital will be maintained.

People traveling in the area should also note that the City’s Western Road/Philip Aziz Avenue Corridor and Intersection Improvements project is also under construction nearby, and Philip Aziz Avenue at Western Road remains closed.

stories.title: Aerospace meets IT: Fanshawe repositions Norton Wolf School for the future of defence innovation
stories.summary: Fanshawe College is strengthening its role in Canada’s aerospace and defence economy with the ren
stories.content:
Fanshawe College is strengthening its role in Canada’s aerospace and defence economy with the renaming of the Norton Wolf School of Aviation and Aerospace Technology to the Norton Wolf School of Aerospace, Information and Defence Technologies.

The new name follows an academic realignment that brings aviation programs together with Fanshawe’s School of Information Technology. This integration reflects the accelerating convergence of aerospace, digital systems and national security – and the growing demand for graduates who can work across disciplines.

Stephen Patterson, Dean of the Faculty of Science, Trades, Technology and Design, says the change marks a strategic shift that aligns with federal priorities and responds to rapid technological transformation across the sector.

“Today’s aerospace industry extends far beyond aircraft,” says Patterson. “Innovation increasingly happens where aerospace, information technology and defence intersect. Our new School of Aerospace, Information and Defence Technologies reflects that reality and positions our students to thrive in a rapidly evolving economy. By bringing these disciplines together, we’re preparing graduates with the technical expertise and adaptability employers are looking for today—and the capabilities they’ll need for the industries of tomorrow.”

Fanshawe first renamed its School of Aviation in 2016 in honour of the late Norton Wolf, an avid pilot and prominent philanthropist whose family foundation has made lasting contributions to London’s arts, medical and educational communities. At the time, the School focused primarily on aircraft maintenance and repair. In 2021, the College updated the name to reflect the expanded programming in aviation and aerospace manufacturing, fleet services, administration and commercial flight.

The latest renaming builds on that legacy while positioning Fanshawe to meet the needs of an industry increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, data analytics, autonomous and remotely piloted systems and low-Earth orbit technologies.

Listen to Stephen Patterson's interview on CBC's Afternoon Drive.

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.CA

stories.title: Eight Western projects awarded Canada Foundation for Innovation funding to support cutting-edge research
stories.summary: Western's first 4D imaging system for organoid research is one of eight Western research projects that received Canada Foundation for Innovation funding
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
paragraphs: Western University researchers have received more than $1.5 million from the Canada Foundation for Innovation (CFI) to fund advanced technologies in eight projects that address solutions Canadians need for environmental, economic and health challenges. Among the projects receiving funding is a 4D imaging system for organoid research – not only the first of its kind in London, Ont., but the only one like it in Southwestern Ontario.

The funding comes through the John R. Evans Leaders Fund (Jelf), a core CFI stream that provides up to 40 per cent of the costs for labs and equipment to ensure universities recruit and retain top researchers.

Van Lu, a member of the physiology and pharmacology department at Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, received more than $322,000 for the 4D imaging system. The high-tech microscope and camera system to be housed at Western can image complex biological systems in extraordinary detail, offering researchers unprecedented insight into how tissues develop and disease unfolds.

Lu worked with fellow Schulich Medicine & Dentistry professors Dean Betts and Dr. Julio Martinez-Trujillo to give researchers across disciplines access to this cutting-edge technology. The 4D imaging system is expected to accelerate discoveries in cancer, reproductive health, bowel disease, neuroscience and precision medicine.
“We wanted to take the lead on bringing this equipment to Western, so a wide range of organoid researchers can benefit,” Lu said.

Lu, Betts and Martinez-Trujillo collaborate in a research group that studies simplified versions of human organs, known as organoids . These miniature organs, grown in a lab based on human tissues, measure about one millimetre in diameter at most. Though small, the 3D models form all the basic components an organ needs to start developing outside of a living organism.
Using organoids instead of animal models in preclinical studies improves the likelihood of successful treatments that can be moved into clinical trials.

“It’s precision medicine. We can generate many different organoids based on a sample of tissue, test a range of therapeutics or drugs and determine which treatment a person responds to best,” Lu said.

Lu’s organoid research is revealing more about conditions such as colon cancer and inflammatory bowel disease by focusing on gastrointestinal tract development and how it senses nutrients. Betts aims to improve in vitro fertilization outcomes by examining how human stem cell-derived embryo models develop. Martinez-Trujillo is studying how brain stem cells form the earliest stages of neural connections in organoids to better understand neurodevelopmental diseases.

Schulich Medicine & Dentistry professors (L to R) Dean Betts, Van Lu and Dr. Julio Martinez-Trujillo put their efforts together to successfully apply for Canada Foundation for Innovation funding that will bring a high-tech 4D imaging system to Western, enabling advancements in a wide range of organoid research programs in London, Ont. and beyond. (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

The new 4D imaging system will allow researchers to simultaneously examine hundreds of organoids as they develop over the course of weeks or months, instead of analyzing only three-dimensional static images. The system will significantly improve the team’s ability to accurately model living systems by revealing how cells respond to their environment, how they communicate and how diseases begin and progress.

“The advantage is its capacity to capture 3D images over a long period of time, which is necessary because organoids take several weeks to develop,” Lu said. “We can see in real time where the cells we’ve labelled have moved, how many more appear and how they change when we apply a certain treatment.”

The system includes an incubator to keep the cells growing. Robotics are used to image tissue samples around the clock, while AI built into the system tracks cell changes as they occur. The automation of numerous processes eliminates tedious, repetitive tasks humans can’t do, while allowing multiple researchers to use the system at the same time. The infrastructure will expand Western’s research impact in biotherapeutics, neuroscience and developmental biology.

Though the 4D imaging system will be installed at Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, it will be available to researchers across Western and its affiliated institutes, bringing together diverse organoid research programs and positioning Western as a hub for organoid research in London, Ont.

“It took a lot of research and development to establish organoids. Now, we’re taking the next step – making organoid models more widely available to researchers,” Lu said. “That could spark new therapies, allow them to be tested relatively quickly and deepen our understanding of the fundamental biology behind cell development.”

Western University researchers have received more than $1.5 million from the Canada Foundation for Innovation (CFI) to fund advanced technologies in eight projects that address solutions Canadians need for environmental, economic and health challenges. Among the projects receiving funding is a 4D imaging system for organoid research – not only the first of its kind in London, Ont., but the only one like it in Southwestern Ontario.

The funding comes through the John R. Evans Leaders Fund (Jelf), a core CFI stream that provides up to 40 per cent of the costs for labs and equipment to ensure universities recruit and retain top researchers.

Van Lu, a member of the physiology and pharmacology department at Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, received more than $322,000 for the 4D imaging system. The high-tech microscope and camera system to be housed at Western can image complex biological systems in extraordinary detail, offering researchers unprecedented insight into how tissues develop and disease unfolds.

Lu worked with fellow Schulich Medicine & Dentistry professors Dean Betts and Dr. Julio Martinez-Trujillo to give researchers across disciplines access to this cutting-edge technology. The 4D imaging system is expected to accelerate discoveries in cancer, reproductive health, bowel disease, neuroscience and precision medicine.

“We wanted to take the lead on bringing this equipment to Western, so a wide range of organoid researchers can benefit,” Lu said.

Lu, Betts and Martinez-Trujillo collaborate in a research group that studies simplified versions of human organs, known as organoids . These miniature organs, grown in a lab based on human tissues, measure about one millimetre in diameter at most. Though small, the 3D models form all the basic components an organ needs to start developing outside of a living organism.

Using organoids instead of animal models in preclinical studies improves the likelihood of successful treatments that can be moved into clinical trials.

“It’s precision medicine. We can generate many different organoids based on a sample of tissue, test a range of therapeutics or drugs and determine which treatment a person responds to best,” Lu said.

Lu’s organoid research is revealing more about conditions such as colon cancer and inflammatory bowel disease by focusing on gastrointestinal tract development and how it senses nutrients. Betts aims to improve in vitro fertilization outcomes by examining how human stem cell-derived embryo models develop. Martinez-Trujillo is studying how brain stem cells form the earliest stages of neural connections in organoids to better understand neurodevelopmental diseases.

stories.title: Middlesex County Brings Local Priorities to the Forefront at 2026 AMO Conference
stories.summary: Middlesex County concluded a productive 2026 AMO conference discussing local priorities, shared regional perspectives, and advocating for initiatives that support strong communities.
stories.content:
Middlesex County (August 20, 2026) – Middlesex County concluded a productive 2026 AMO Conference discussing local priorities, shared regional perspectives, and advocating for initiatives that support strong communities.

County representatives brought local priorities directly to provincial decision-makers through a series of delegation meetings focused on topics such as employment and industrial lands, community safety, high-speed internet infrastructure, long-term care, municipal fleet vehicles, and privacy protection.

They discussed investments to support employment and industrial growth, opportunities to accelerate rural broadband expansion, strategies to address increasing demand for modern long-term care services, and measures to streamline administrative and regulatory processes for municipalities. The discussions reinforced the importance of collaboration between all levels of government to advance solutions to regional challenges and opportunities.

The conference was also an opportunity to learn about emerging municipal issues, share best practices, and collaborate on solutions that support the needs of residents, businesses and local municipalities.

“The AMO Conference provided a valuable opportunity to engage directly with provincial representatives and municipal colleagues from across Ontario," said Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke. "The conversations and relationships built through these meetings help ensure Middlesex County's priorities are understood and considered as we continue working to support our communities.”

The insights gained at the conference will help inform Middlesex County's ongoing advocacy efforts and strategic planning activities. The County will continue working with municipal, provincial, and community partners to address shared challenges and support residents across the region.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.
