stories.title: SEEKING PUBLIC ASSISTANCE IN ONGOING LHSC FRAUD INVESTIGATION 24-93680
stories.summary: Police Seek Public Assistance IN Ongoing LHSC Fraud Investigation Dedicated tip line established London, ON (August 20, 2026) – Investigators are asking anyone with information to come forward in an ongoing i…
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: LONDON, ON (August 20, 2026) – Investigators are asking anyone with information to come forward in an ongoing investigation into alleged historical financial practices at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

The investigation, launched by the London Police Service in October 2024 following concerns brought forward by LHSC, is being conducted as a joint investigation with Ontario Provincial Police investigators from the Serious Fraud Office due to its complexity and the specialized resources required.
A dedicated tip line has been established to support the investigation and encourage members of the public to come forward.

“We remain fully committed to this investigation and value the continued partnership with the Ontario Provincial Police and the Serious Fraud Office ,” said Detective Superintendent Sean Travis of the London Police Service Criminal Investigation Division. “Shared expertise and investigative collaboration are essential in advancing this complex file. We also encourage anyone with information to come forward, as even the smallest detail may assist investigators.”

“Information from the public can be critical in complex fraud investigations,” said Detective Superintendent Jennifer Spurrell, Serious Fraud Office, Ontario Provincial Police. “We encourage anyone who may have information to come forward, no matter how minor it may seem. Even small details can play an important role in advancing the investigation.”

Anyone with information related to this investigation is asked to call the dedicated tip line at 1-844-677-9413, the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

LONDON, ON (August 20, 2026) – Investigators are asking anyone with information to come forward in an ongoing investigation into alleged historical financial practices at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

The investigation, launched by the London Police Service in October 2024 following concerns brought forward by LHSC, is being conducted as a joint investigation with Ontario Provincial Police investigators from the Serious Fraud Office due to its complexity and the specialized resources required.

A dedicated tip line has been established to support the investigation and encourage members of the public to come forward.

“We remain fully committed to this investigation and value the continued partnership with the Ontario Provincial Police and the Serious Fraud Office ,” said Detective Superintendent Sean Travis of the London Police Service Criminal Investigation Division. “Shared expertise and investigative collaboration are essential in advancing this complex file. We also encourage anyone with information to come forward, as even the smallest detail may assist investigators.”

“Information from the public can be critical in complex fraud investigations,” said Detective Superintendent Jennifer Spurrell, Serious Fraud Office, Ontario Provincial Police. “We encourage anyone who may have information to come forward, no matter how minor it may seem. Even small details can play an important role in advancing the investigation.”

On Tuesday, August 18, 2026, at approximately 12:40 p.m., officers responded to a hotel in the city’s east end in relation to checking the welfare of an occupant.
While inside the hotel room, officers observed a quantity of drugs and Canadian currency.
A man and a woman were arrested, and the following items were seized:
101 grams of suspected fentanyl, value: $8,080
Approximately $2,000 in Canadian currency
The investigation was reassigned to members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section (POIS)

As a result of the investigation, Robert Degrace, 29, and Laurie Elizabeth Young, 37, both of London, have been jointly charged with possession of a Schedule I substance for the purpose of trafficking.

Both accused remain in custody. Robert Degrace is scheduled to appear in London court August 21, 2026, in relation to the charge. Laurie Elizabeth Young is scheduled to appear in London court August 24, 2026, in relation to the charge.

stories.summary: Stabbing Investigation London man wanted London, ON (August 20, 2026) – A London man is wanted in connection with a stabbing that left another man with life-threatening injuries. On August 16, 2026, shortly before 4 a.m., London police…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (August 20, 2026) – A London man is wanted in connection with a stabbing that left another man with life-threatening injuries.

On August 16, 2026, shortly before 4 a.m., London police responded to a reported stabbing in the 400-block of Dundas Street. Officers located an adult male suffering from injuries, including multiple stab wounds. He was transported to hospital by paramedic services with life-threatening injuries.

The investigation was reassigned to members of the LPS Major Crime Section.

Video surveillance was obtained, and investigators identified a suspect male.

As a result of the investigation, Tyler James Lyttle, 40, of London, has not been located, and as a result, has been charged by way of warrant of arrest in relation to the following offences:

· Aggravated assault, and

· Fail to comply with probation order

A photograph of the suspect is being shared, in the hope that members of the public can assist police in locating him. Members of the public are reminded not to approach the suspect, and to call 9-1-1 if seen.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Overnight road closures on York Street, Florence Street, and Rectory Street
stories.summary: Temporary overnight road closures will begin Sunday, August 23 until the morning of Wednesday, August 26 on York and Florence St
stories.content:
Temporary overnight road closures will begin Sunday, August 23 until the morning of Wednesday, August 26 on York and Florence Streets between Lyle Street and Egerton Street, as well as at the Rectory Street intersection.

These overnight closures from 7:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. are to allow for road paving and new traffic lines as part of the York and Florence Street Arterial Road Rehabilitation Project.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules.

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area overnight and in the early morning.

Please follow the detour signage. Drivers will be detoured north around the closure using Adelaide Street, Dundas Street and Egerton Street, or south using Adelaide Street, Hamilton Road and Egerton Street.

Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Businesses will remain accessible.

stories.content:
For many years riders have asked us for real time information and trip planning through an app. We have partnered with Transit App for a one year pilot to offer our riders full access to all the benefits the app offers. Transit App has always been an option for London Transit riders however additional features previously protected behind a paywall are now available to everyone, these include:

Access to all transit routes in London

Trip planning with an extended number of trips available to choose from

Customization of the app for look and function including personalized walk times

Learn how to download the app as well as how to use it .

Already paid for the enhanced (Royale) package for the year? You can request a refund by contacting Transit App’s Customer Service at info@transitapp.com

London Transit’s realtime.londontransit.CA remains available and a great option for our riders.

Please contact us if you have any questions.

Plan your trip and find the best route to your destination using Google Maps.

Find a quick overview of significant detours and stop closures.

Whether you have lived in London for years or are new to the city, this section will provide you with all the information you need to use London Transit efficiently.

Find out exactly where your bus is so you can better plan your trip and schedule your day.

stories.title: Western scholars help shape landmark Supreme Court decision on intimate partner violence
stories.summary: Introduction of new tort of intimate partner violence influenced heavily by research from Western’s Tort Law Research Group
stories.author: Lauren daSilva
paragraphs: Research from Western University law professors was instrumental in a landmark Supreme Court of Canada decision creating a new civil wrong for intimate partner violence. Several of Western’s Tort Law Research Group (Tlrg) scholars were cited in the Supreme Court of Canada’s landmark decision in Ahluwalia v Ahluwalia, 2026 SCC 16 .

A tort is a distinct civil wrong for which individuals can sue. The Supreme Court’s latest decision creates a new avenue for civil claims based on intimate partner violence. Previously, victims were limited to claims based on existing torts of assault, battery or infliction of emotional distress, which did not necessarily capture the cumulative harms caused by patterns of coercive control.
“I think it’s important the court recognized the social reality and highly gendered nature of intimate partner violence,” said Western law professor Erika Chamberlain, co-director of Tlrg.

Plaintiffs can now bring civil claims that better reflect how a partner’s controlling behaviour affected their ability to make fundamental decisions about their own lives, and May receive greater compensation as a result.

The case that landed before the Supreme Court arose from a divorce proceeding in which a woman disclosed years of abuse by her husband. Along with incidents of physical violence, the evidence included conduct designed to demean, isolate and control, including financial threats, psychological manipulation and behaviour that undermined the woman’s dignity and equality within the relationship.

Legal experts were split on whether the case showed the need for a new tort to capture the specific realities of intimate partner violence. The trial judge concluded intimate partner abuse often consists of a sustained pattern of behaviour and recognized a new tort of family violence to reflect that reality.
Members of Western’s Tort Law Research Group. (L to R) Professors Erika Chamberlain, Jason Neyers, Manish Oza, Joanna Langille, Zoe Sinel and Stephen Pitel. (Submitted)
The Court of Appeal for Ontario disagreed and found that existing torts sufficiently captured the harm. The case was then appealed to the Supreme Court.

In the majority decision written by Justice Nicholas Kasirer , the Supreme Court cited more authors from Western Law than from any other law school, referring to articles and book chapters on tort law theory by professors Andrew Botterell, Stephen Pitel and the late Gerald Fridman. Also, the court referenced leading tort texts co-written by Tlrg members and co-edited by Pitel and Chamberlain.

The ruling further cited a family law casebook co-authored by professor Claire Houston and a collection co-edited by professor Melanie Randall. Both the majority and dissenting opinions referred to Fridman’s scholarship on common law methodology and the creation of new torts – a central issue in the case.
“Western Law has a very strong and diverse group of tort scholars,” Chamberlain said. “It’s great to see so much of our work helping the court navigate such a landmark case.”

Members of Western’s Tlrg have since written about the case for a special issue of the periodical Canadian Cases on the Law of Torts. Chamberlain’s commentary, When the Facts Cry Out for a Remedy: Ahluwalia’s Framework for Recognizing New Torts, examines the idea that a new tort May be justified where the defendant commits a wrong that infringes the plaintiff’s interests and where existing law does not provide an adequate remedy.
Chamberlain suggests the decision reflects a greater willingness by courts to recognize new torts than has traditionally been the case.

“I tend to be cautious about creating new labels for wrongful conduct when existing law May already cover the field, but in this case, I think the majority has identified a legitimate gap in the law,” Chamberlain said.

A second commentary by Pitel and Randall, The New Tort of Intimate Partner Violence: Definitional Difficulties , examines the scope and terminology of the new tort. The third commentary, Everything Old is New Again: Corrective Justice and Rights in Ahluwalia v. Ahluwalia by Botterell, Jason Neyers and Zoë Sinel examines the court’s understanding of corrective justice.
Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities .

“I tend to be cautious about creating new labels for wrongful conduct when existing law May already cover the field, but in this case, I think the majority has identified a legitimate gap in the law,” Chamberlain said.

A second commentary by Pitel and Randall, The New Tort of Intimate Partner Violence: Definitional Difficulties , examines the scope and terminology of the new tort. The third commentary, Everything Old is New Again: Corrective Justice and Rights in Ahluwalia v. Ahluwalia by Botterell, Jason Neyers and Zoë Sinel examines the court’s understanding of corrective justice.

stories.title: City advances key priorities at AMO Conference in Ottawa
stories.summary: A City of London delegation met with provincial ministers and officials during the 2026 Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) Confer
stories.content:
A City of London delegation met with provincial ministers and officials during the 2026 Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) Conference in Ottawa to advance key priorities for London and Southwestern Ontario, focused on strengthening public safety, supporting housing and homelessness services, and advancing regional transportation and economic growth.

London was represented by Mayor Josh Morgan, as well as Councillors Steve Lehman, Corrine Rahman, Susan Stevenson and Anna Hopkins, who was re-elected to the AMO Board of Directors, continuing London’s representation at the provincial municipal table. Council members were accompanied by representatives from London Hydro and Fanshawe College, as well as senior City staff.

“London and cities across Ontario are facing significant challenges that require real province-wide planning and coordinated action if we’re going to turn the corner,” said Mayor Josh Morgan. From homelessness and public safety to transportation and economic growth, none of these issues can be solved by one level of government alone. That’s why AMO is an important opportunity to be at the table with provincial ministers and officials to drive investments, partnerships and policies that can make a difference for residents. We came to Ottawa alongside our municipal colleagues with a clear set of priorities, and we’ll keep pushing to turn these conversations into action for London and Southwestern Ontario.”

Among the key priorities discussed by the City of London and provincial representatives were:

Having the province take over ownership and maintenance of Highbury Avenue and supporting more reliable and frequent passenger rail service through High Performance Rail in Southwestern Ontario. These priorities were discussed with the Ministry of Transportation as part of a joint delegation with the City of St. Thomas and Elgin County.

Additional operating support for Highly Supportive Housing with the Ministry of Health.

Increased support for homelessness prevention with the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing.

Provincial support to advance the new London Emergency Services Campus with the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Support for the Aerospace Innovation Corridor at London International Airport with the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade.

“AMO provides a valuable forum to build relationships and advance projects that respond to some of the most significant pressures facing our community,” said City Manager Sandra Datars Bere. “We appreciated the productive discussions and will continue working with provincial partners on next steps.”

The City will build on these discussions by working with provincial ministries and regional partners to identify next steps and move these priorities toward implementation.

stories.title: Makerspaces at Western thrive under student leadership
stories.summary: An engineering student helped expand the makerspaces at Western and 3D printing, creating new opportunities for innovation at Morrissette Entrepreneurship
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
paragraphs: Troy Leishman became a student leader at Western University through moxie, resilience and a quest that led to a timely coincidence. The chain of events opened more doors for the entire campus community to bring ideas to life with specialized tools and technology in the makerspaces in the Ronald D. Schmeichel Building for Entrepreneurship and Innovation .

Before arriving at Western, Leishman had already co-founded a 3D printing and prototyping company, grown it to a team of six, operated a retail storefront and taken on contracts with companies like Nestlé and Ford. He later wound down the company and enrolled in mechatronic systems engineering at Western. The reputation of the faculty drew him in, though his interest in the discipline stems from its applications beyond engineering.
Troy Leishman, Western engineering student and president of 3D Western (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

“I’ve always wanted to be an entrepreneur, not necessarily an engineer,” Leishman said. “But being able to understand all the mechanical, electrical and software aspects of a technical business is invaluable when you’re leading a team.”

By his second year, Leishman stepped into leadership as president of 3D Western, a club for enthusiasts of 3D printing, the technology that creates three-dimensional physical objects from digital files. While eager to design and build, members were often frustrated by limited access to printers and disappointing results from home machines. That set Leishman on a mission.
“I wanted to make 3D printing free and available to all students, not just engineering, to benefit Western as a whole,” he said.

Leishman’s instinct for social impact goes back to his high school days during the pandemic. He used his home 3D printer to produce face shields for 10 health-care organizations, financing the donation with his own fundraising. His efforts – recognized by MP Peter Fragiskatos in the London North Centre Honour Roll – laid the groundwork for more service-oriented enterprise.

Leishman’s ambition to source industrial printers that all Western students could access led him to K3D Technology in Montreal. The company was upgrading its equipment and willing to donate 24 industrial 3D printers. The catch was that he had nowhere to house them.

The search for a space brought him to the Schmeichel Building, an innovation hub for students and founders to explore entrepreneurial thinking, build prototypes and start new ventures . There, leaders from Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship were undertaking their own ambitious plans.
This slideshow requires JavaScript.

“We’d set up two makerspaces intending for them to eventually be student-run creativity incubators for all Western students,” said Eric Morse, executive director of Morrissette Entrepreneurship. “We were ready to think through how to get the right students leading them, and then Troy came to us. The timing was amazing.”

Leishman’s self-starting initiative was in motion. He drove a rented truck to Montreal and brought the printers back to London, Ont. He had more conversations at Morrissette about the possibilities and mobilized a team of students from 3D Western. The momentum didn’t stop with the 3D printers.

The students set up operating procedures for running each makerspace as an open-access workshop. They handled day-to-day operations, with Morrissette coordinating supporting projects such as the installation of the ventilation needed to safely run 24 additional 3D printers.

By the end of Leishman’s third year, the team had grown to about 50 students working to get both makerspaces fully operational by the start of the Fall 2026 term. The team also built and tested a new 3D Western website , a gateway to the makerspaces where students can submit 3D printing requests, book equipment and discover training, mentorship and events.
Kendra Green, an entrepreneur-in-residence at Morrissette, supported the team while giving Leishman room to grow as a leader.
“I wanted to make sure he had the runway to accomplish what he wanted to,” Green said.

With that backing, plans reached the leading edge. Now the team is developing a fully automated, AI-enabled 3D print farm. The system is designed to review submitted designs, provide instant design feedback to help students learn, optimize files and then route jobs to available printers. The process would dramatically expand access to 3D printing while reducing material waste and wait time.

Leishman recognized that high-tech alone wouldn’t draw students in – it would take a welcoming culture to make them feel comfortable using the makerspaces. His team focused on supporting students from all faculties, regardless of prior building experience. Last year, the club ran twice-weekly workshops that helped students earn certification on certain machines or simply discover what’s available.

The club also led trial open-hours days, when the makerspaces were open to walk-in traffic. Twenty students signed up to be makerspace supervisors who helped users safely explore the tools. Some came back to develop projects they’d started.

“We saw students light up with even more ideas once they got involved. The biggest potential of the maker spaces isn’t just the tools and m aterials , it’s the culture where everyone can feel inspired and lead their own ideas with the support of the community that forms in them.” – Troy Leishman, Western engineering s tudent and president of 3D Western

The mission Leishman set for 3D Western, to make 3D printing free and accessible to all students, expanded with its evolution from a hobbyist club to a partner of Morrissette Entrepreneurship. The student organization now leads both the Sabourin Family Foundation Makerspace and the digital makerspace in the Schmeichel Building.
“The students continually amaze me,” Green said. “They’re working diligently in all areas including marketing, development and onboarding the next group of makerspace supervisors.”

Students can apply to be a makerspace supervisor , a volunteer role where they help users work with tools and technology, share their existing skills and learn from other makers. As they assume a key role in operating and growing the makerspaces, they’ll build technical, teaching and leadership skills.

Surrounded by tools in the Sabourin Family Foundation Makerspace, engineering student Troy Leishman has helped build a culture of creativity, collaboration and innovation that welcomes students from every faculty to Western’s makerspaces. (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

“It’s an incredible opportunity for students to take ownership of the spaces,” Leishman said. “In leading a small team, I’ve been learning life lessons about how culture works, navigating systems and showing appreciation for the people around you.”
Morse credits Leishman’s success as a student leader to his technical aptitude and teaching skill, combined with an ability to motivate and rally others behind shared purpose.

“Troy really cares about two things – student learning and community building – and it shows,” Morse said. “He’s already put together a succession plan for the next 3D Western president to ensure a seamless transition and long-term success ,” he said.
Morse hopes the makerspaces will become an essential part of the student experience at Western, not just an extracurricular option, where cross-disciplinary innovation thrives.
“We’d like students from every faculty to build prototypes for a business, but if we are able to spark creativity in students who wouldn’t otherwise have had the opportunity, that’s a win for us.”

stories.content:
Troy Leishman became a student leader at Western University through moxie, resilience and a quest that led to a timely coincidence. The chain of events opened more doors for the entire campus community to bring ideas to life with specialized tools and technology in the makerspaces in the Ronald D. Schmeichel Building for Entrepreneurship and Innovation .

Before arriving at Western, Leishman had already co-founded a 3D printing and prototyping company, grown it to a team of six, operated a retail storefront and taken on contracts with companies like Nestlé and Ford. He later wound down the company and enrolled in mechatronic systems engineering at Western. The reputation of the faculty drew him in, though his interest in the discipline stems from its applications beyond engineering.

Troy Leishman, Western engineering student and president of 3D Western (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

“I’ve always wanted to be an entrepreneur, not necessarily an engineer,” Leishman said. “But being able to understand all the mechanical, electrical and software aspects of a technical business is invaluable when you’re leading a team.”

By his second year, Leishman stepped into leadership as president of 3D Western, a club for enthusiasts of 3D printing, the technology that creates three-dimensional physical objects from digital files. While eager to design and build, members were often frustrated by limited access to printers and disappointing results from home machines. That set Leishman on a mission.

“I wanted to make 3D printing free and available to all students, not just engineering, to benefit Western as a whole,” he said.

Leishman’s instinct for social impact goes back to his high school days during the pandemic. He used his home 3D printer to produce face shields for 10 health-care organizations, financing the donation with his own fundraising. His efforts – recognized by MP Peter Fragiskatos in the London North Centre Honour Roll – laid the groundwork for more service-oriented enterprise.

Leishman’s ambition to source industrial printers that all Western students could access led him to K3D Technology in Montreal. The company was upgrading its equipment and willing to donate 24 industrial 3D printers. The catch was that he had nowhere to house them.

The search for a space brought him to the Schmeichel Building, an innovation hub for students and founders to explore entrepreneurial thinking, build prototypes and start new ventures . There, leaders from Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship were undertaking their own ambitious plans.

This slideshow requires JavaScript.

“We’d set up two makerspaces intending for them to eventually be student-run creativity incubators for all Western students,” said Eric Morse, executive director of Morrissette Entrepreneurship. “We were ready to think through how to get the right students leading them, and then Troy came to us. The timing was amazing.”

Leishman’s self-starting initiative was in motion. He drove a rented truck to Montreal and brought the printers back to London, Ont. He had more conversations at Morrissette about the possibilities and mobilized a team of students from 3D Western. The momentum didn’t stop with the 3D printers.

The students set up operating procedures for running each makerspace as an open-access workshop. They handled day-to-day operations, with Morrissette coordinating supporting projects such as the installation of the ventilation needed to safely run 24 additional 3D printers.

By the end of Leishman’s third year, the team had grown to about 50 students working to get both makerspaces fully operational by the start of the Fall 2026 term. The team also built and tested a new 3D Western website , a gateway to the makerspaces where students can submit 3D printing requests, book equipment and discover training, mentorship and events.

Kendra Green, an entrepreneur-in-residence at Morrissette, supported the team while giving Leishman room to grow as a leader.

“I wanted to make sure he had the runway to accomplish what he wanted to,” Green said.

With that backing, plans reached the leading edge. Now the team is developing a fully automated, AI-enabled 3D print farm. The system is designed to review submitted designs, provide instant design feedback to help students learn, optimize files and then route jobs to available printers. The process would dramatically expand access to 3D printing while reducing material waste and wait time.

Leishman recognized that high-tech alone wouldn’t draw students in – it would take a welcoming culture to make them feel comfortable using the makerspaces. His team focused on supporting students from all faculties, regardless of prior building experience. Last year, the club ran twice-weekly workshops that helped students earn certification on certain machines or simply discover what’s available.

The club also led trial open-hours days, when the makerspaces were open to walk-in traffic. Twenty students signed up to be makerspace supervisors who helped users safely explore the tools. Some came back to develop projects they’d started.

“We saw students light up with even more ideas once they got involved. The biggest potential of the maker spaces isn’t just the tools and m aterials , it’s the culture where everyone can feel inspired and lead their own ideas with the support of the community that forms in them.” – Troy Leishman, Western engineering s tudent and president of 3D Western

The mission Leishman set for 3D Western, to make 3D printing free and accessible to all students, expanded with its evolution from a hobbyist club to a partner of Morrissette Entrepreneurship. The student organization now leads both the Sabourin Family Foundation Makerspace and the digital makerspace in the Schmeichel Building.

“The students continually amaze me,” Green said. “They’re working diligently in all areas including marketing, development and onboarding the next group of makerspace supervisors.”

Students can apply to be a makerspace supervisor , a volunteer role where they help users work with tools and technology, share their existing skills and learn from other makers. As they assume a key role in operating and growing the makerspaces, they’ll build technical, teaching and leadership skills.

Surrounded by tools in the Sabourin Family Foundation Makerspace, engineering student Troy Leishman has helped build a culture of creativity, collaboration and innovation that welcomes students from every faculty to Western’s makerspaces. (Colleen MacDonald/Western News)

“It’s an incredible opportunity for students to take ownership of the spaces,” Leishman said. “In leading a small team, I’ve been learning life lessons about how culture works, navigating systems and showing appreciation for the people around you.”

Morse credits Leishman’s success as a student leader to his technical aptitude and teaching skill, combined with an ability to motivate and rally others behind shared purpose.

“Troy really cares about two things – student learning and community building – and it shows,” Morse said. “He’s already put together a succession plan for the next 3D Western president to ensure a seamless transition and long-term success ,” he said.

Morse hopes the makerspaces will become an essential part of the student experience at Western, not just an extracurricular option, where cross-disciplinary innovation thrives.

“We’d like students from every faculty to build prototypes for a business, but if we are able to spark creativity in students who wouldn’t otherwise have had the opportunity, that’s a win for us.”

stories.title: $100 buys just enough to fill 2 small bags: A look at grocery-item inflation in Canada
stories.summary: Grocery store inflation has now outpaced the rise in the overall consumer price index in Canada for 18 straight months.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax – Whenever Halifax shopper Mary Coady goes to the grocery store, at best food prices appear to be unchanged.

“They are definitely staying the same, or going up, but they are not going down,” said Coady. “I am not feeling a drop in prices, not at all.”

According to Statistics Canada , food inflation dropped to 3.1 per cent in July, down from 3.9 per cent the previous month.

Chicken and fresh vegetables saw a slower rise in prices. Cereal products and vegetables have gone down in price while fresh fruit, most notably berries and melons, are now more expensive.

Grocery store inflation has now outpaced the rise in the overall consumer price index in Canada for 18 straight months.

“We are still seeing pressure on grocery prices and food,” said Signal49 Research’s chief economist Pedro Antunes. “The inflation pressures on households, is still problematic for many households in Canada.”

The high cost of food continues to contribute to an ongoing affordability crisis in Canada.

“I feel for a lot of people, families in particular,” Coady. “And people on fixed incomes and seniors.”

CTV News went shopping to examine first-hand how costly some items are, including breakfast cereals, berries, pasta, bananas, and bread. The total price was $99.67, which amounted to barely enough to fill two small grocery bags.

Things have become so expensive that shopper Brennan Dempsey is getting creative, as he tries to save money.

“I have not really noticed them,” said Dempsey when asked if he seen any cheaper prices in the grocery store.

Dempsey said as food costs climb, it has dramatically changed his buying habits.

“I have been going to Walmart because I noticed it is a bit cheaper and when I go to Costco, I try to buy in bulk and then try to freeze things, and I now do a lot of googling of what can be frozen, and for how long,” said Dempsey, who added, when prices drop slightly, it is often not noticed.

The high cost of food has also forced him to shop around for the best deals, be selective, and only buy the essential items he needs.

stories.title: In photos: Western helps host international rowing championship
stories.summary: Student-athletes from more than 20 countries, including 34 rowers from Canada, competed on Fanshawe Lake in 2026 Fisu World University Rowing Championships.
stories.author: Western Communications
paragraphs: The Western Mustangs rowing teams shared their training ground at Fanshawe Lake from Aug. 13 to 15 as London, Ont. played host to the 2026 Fisu World University Rowing Championships . It marked the first time the international competition for university-level rowing was hosted in North America.
“It was just unbelievable to see everyone work together to make this a true international event,” said Mustangs men’s rowing team head coach Dan Bechard.

More than 300 student-athletes from over 20 countries took part, including six current or former Mustangs. Italy finished atop the leader board with four gold medals, two silver and five bronze. Aidan Hembruff, BSc’26, and Oliver Baker, an environmental science student, were part of the bronze medal-winning Canadian men’s four crew .

“Bringing home the bronze makes me feel so proud to have represented Canada, as well as Western, ON the international stage. This is my first international medal and to achieve that on a home course is incredible meaningful,” said Hembruff.
Baker and Hembruff have rowed together the last three years as Mustangs.

“It was one of the hardest and most exciting races of my career. We executed a lot of the fundamentals that we learned this summer and went out as fast as we could. At the starting gate, I smiled a bit knowing that this was my home course and a bit of familiarity that settled the nerves,” Baker told Rowing Canada.

stories.summary: Assault Investigation 26-81156 Assault Investigation London man arrested London, ON (August 18, 2026) – A London man was arrested after an assault in the downtown core over the weekend. On Saturday, August 15, 2026, at approximately 12:50 a.m., a man was standing in line outside…
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: LONDON, ON (August 18, 2026) – A London man was arrested after an assault in the downtown core over the weekend.
On Saturday, August 15, 2026, at approximately 12:50 a.m., a man was standing in line outside an establishment in the area of Richmond and John streets when he was approached by a male.
The victim was assaulted by the suspect male and police were contacted.
Emergency services attended, and the victim was transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.
A description of the suspect male was provided to police. Video surveillance footage was also obtained, and at approximately 1 a.m., officers located and arrested the suspect nearby.
The victim and suspect were not known to each other.
As a result of the investigation, Deionte Lord, 29, of London, has been charged with one count of assault causing bodily harm.
The accused has an upcoming court date of September 16, 2026, in relation to the charge.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Candidate nomination period closes August 21 for London’s 2026 municipal election
stories.summary: Anyone planning to run for Mayor, City Councillor or School Board Trustee in London’s 2026 municipal election must file their nomination no l
stories.content:
Anyone planning to run for Mayor, City Councillor or School Board Trustee in London’s 2026 municipal election must file their nomination no later than 2 p.m. on Friday, August 21, 2026.

Nominations must be filed in person at the Elections Office, located on the first floor of City Hall, 300 Dufferin Avenue. Electronic submissions are not accepted.

Individuals filing a nomination must provide:

A completed Nomination Form

Signatures from 25 eligible voters supporting the nomination for Mayor and City Councillor candidates

A completed Declaration of Qualifications

Current identification

The required nomination fee of $200 for Mayor or $100 for City Councillor and School Board Trustee

Candidates are also required to swear an oath at the Elections Office.

No later than 2 p.m. on Friday, August 21, is also the deadline for registered candidates to withdraw their nomination. Withdrawals must be submitted in writing and filed in person.

The City Clerk will review and certify nominations following the deadline. The certified list of candidates will be posted at London.CA/elections .

London’s 2026 municipal election will take place on Monday, October 26, 2026, with voting available from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Advance voting will also be available at polling stations across London on:

Thursday, October 1, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Saturday, October 3, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

Monday, October 5 through Saturday, October 10, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. each day

For more information about becoming a candidate, voting dates and election requirements, visit London.CA/elections or email elections@London.CA .

stories.summary: Break AND Enter 26-81393 Break AND Enter Investigation Two Londoners facing charges London, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section have laid charges following an attempted break and enter involving a firearm over the w…
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: LONDON, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section have laid charges following an attempted break and enter involving a firearm over the weekend.

On Saturday, August 15, 2026, shortly before 7 p.m., members of the London Police Service responded to a residence on Lovett Street after receiving reports of an attempted break-in involving an armed suspect.

Two individuals attended the residence and attempted to break into the home while two adult occupants were inside. During the incident, threats were made toward the occupants and a firearm was pointed at one of the victims. A window of the residence was also damaged during the incident.
The victims contacted 9-1-1 and remained inside the residence while officers responded.

Members of the Uniformed Division and Emergency Response Unit attended the area. Within minutes, officers located and arrested a male suspect on Chesley Avenue. During the arrest, officers recovered an imitation firearm and approximately 500 Nabilone pills.
A second suspect was located a short time later in the backyard of a residence on Dame Street and was arrested without incident.
The accused and victims were known to each other. There were no reported injuries.
As a result of the investigation, Daniel Francis Edward MacDonald, 43, of London, has been charged with:
Break and enter with intent;
Pointing a firearm;
Two counts of possession of a firearm contrary to a prohibition order;
Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm; and
Possession of a Schedule II substance.
Julie Marshall, 23, of London, has been charged with:
Break and enter with intent.
Both accused remain in custody and are scheduled to reappear in London court on August 18, 2026, in relation to the charges.

The London Police Service would like to remind residents that if they witness suspicious, threatening or criminal activity, they should contact police immediately. Timely reporting can play a critical role in protecting public safety and assisting investigations.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Study finds advanced genetic testing opens new treatment options for nearly one in three cancer patients
stories.summary: August 17, 2026 A new study from London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) shows that expanded genetic testing can help match cancer patients to more personalized treatment options…
stories.content:
Media Release August 17, 2026

A new study from London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri) shows that expanded genetic testing can help match cancer patients to more personalized treatment options, with nearly one in three found to be eligible for therapies not typically used for their specific type of cancer based on the unique DNA of their tumour.

When someone is diagnosed with cancer, physicians run tests to learn more about the tumour. Currently, standard of care testing looks at a small number of genes linked closely to the type of cancer the patient has. This prospective study, published in The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics , looked at whether next generation sequencing, which includes testing for genes linked with numerous types of cancer, could help improve care.

The study examined 554 patients with a wide range of cancers, including gastrointestinal, lung, head and neck, breast, gynecologic, genitourinary, brain and nervous system, sarcoma, skin, and cancers of unknown origin. Patients treated at London Health Sciences Centre’s (LHSC) Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre underwent advanced DNA testing that analyzes hundreds of cancer-related genes at the same time. This approach uncovered genetic changes that standard testing often misses, enabling access to therapies and clinical trials that would otherwise be unavailable and offering new hope for patients with limited treatment choices.

“This study is one of the first to show, in real-world settings, that broader testing can find important changes in a tumour’s DNA and help identify alternative treatment options,” says Dr. Bekim Sadikovic, PhD, Scientist at Lhscri and Head of the Verspeeten Clinical Genome Centre. “In almost one in three patients we tested, we found changes in their DNA that would make them eligible for different therapies that May be more effective than the standard of care.”

Many patients with advanced cancer eventually run out of standard treatment options. The results of this study give physicians evidence to support access to off‑label and compassionate‑use treatments, helping connect patients to therapies most likely to benefit them based on advanced genetic testing.

“Accessing off‑label drugs, which are treatments approved for one use but not another, is often challenging. However, when there is strong evidence that a specific therapy is likely to work for an individual patient, it can help open the door to access and has the potential to transform cancer care,” says Dr. Sadikovic, senior author and co-principal investigator of the study.

The research found that 79 per cent of patients had a clinically relevant genetic variant, meaning researchers found a mutation that would respond to a specific therapy. Twenty-eight per cent of participants in the study became eligible for new treatment options including clinical trials, off-label therapies, and compassionate access programs that were previously unavailable to them.

“I meet with patients every day whose only remaining options are compassionate access to a specific drug or enrollment in a clinical trial,” says Dr. Stephen Welch, Scientist at Lhscri and Medical Oncologist at LHSC. “This kind of evidence helps us make more informed decisions, so patients are not asked to endure treatments that are unlikely to help and instead are guided toward options with real potential.”

The research team also found the results could have broader benefits to the Ontario health-care system.

Fourteen-and-a-half per cent of patients gained access to treatment options deemed safer by oncologists, potentially reducing treatment-related morbidity.

For 12.5 per cent of patients, genomic testing helped identify effective treatments earlier, reducing the need for later use of more costly publicly funded cancer drugs.

For 17.3 per cent of patients, the order in which treatments were given was adjusted, helping ensure they received the most appropriate therapy at the most effective time.

The research team is continuing this prospective study and collecting more information about the impact of this expanded genetic testing on patient outcomes and the larger health-care system.

“Our team is building real-life evidence that this genomic testing is making a difference in the lives of patients with cancer and has a true positive impact on our health-care system. It’s the future of precision medicine and the future of cancer care that we are really excited about,” says Dr. Welch.

The study was conducted through the Verspeeten Clinical Genome Centre and supported by a donation to London Health Sciences Foundation by the late Archie and Irene Verspeeten. Thanks to this transformational gift in 2020, the Verspeeten Clinical Genome Centre was established as the first of its kind in Canada, enabling state-of-the-art genetic diagnostics, personalized treatment options, better care and improved patient outcomes.

stories.title: Serious Motor Vehicle Collision 26-81112
stories.summary: Update - London, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Road Safety Section continue to investigate a serious motor vehicle collision from over the weekend.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
UPDATE - LONDON, ON (August 17, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Road Safety Section continue to investigate a serious motor vehicle collision from over the weekend.

A female passenger of one of the vehicles was transported to hospital by paramedic services with life-threatening injuries and has since succumbed to those injuries.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area on August 14, 2026, between 9:20 and 9:40 p.m. and may have witnessed the collision, or who has dashcam, residential or business surveillance footage, to contact the London Police Service or Crime Stoppers.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent anonymously online to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers.

LONDON, ON (August 14, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Road Safety Section are investigating a motor vehicle collision that occurred in the city’s east end late this evening.

On Friday, August 14, 2026, at approximately 9:30 p.m., emergency crews responded to a serious motor vehicle collision on Veterans Memorial Pkwy at Bradley Ave involving multiple motor vehicles.

All vehicles involved remained on scene.

Four individuals involved in the collision were transported to hospital with serious life-threatening injuries.

The intersection is temporarily closed, including Veterans Memorial Pkwy’s exit at highway 401 (From Wilton Grove to Hamilton Road) for accident reconstruction.

The investigation has now been taken over by the LPS Road Safety Section and remains ongoing.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 9:00 p.m. – 9:30 p.m. and may have witnessed the collision, or who have dashcam, residential, or business surveillance footage, to please contact us.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: After 42 years of trying, Canada loses another bid to deport alleged top Mafia boss in Toronto
stories.summary: Jimmy DeMaria was convicted of second-degree murder in 1982 and released ten years later. He was first ordered deported in 1984.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Jimmy DeMaria was convicted of second-degree murder in 1982 and released ten years later. He was first ordered deported in 1984, while still in prison

On the 42nd anniversary of Ottawa trying to deport a man who police named as Toronto’s top Mafia boss, the government has again failed to prove he should be deported back to Italy.

Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.

Access articles from across Canada with one account.

Enjoy additional articles per month.

The Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) rejected arguments that Vincenzo DeMaria, better known as Jimmy DeMaria, has been a member of the shadowy and powerful ’Ndrangheta, which is the proper name of the Mafia formed in Italy’s southern region of Calabria, and that he engaged in Mafia activities, including money laundering.

If the Canada Border Services Agency (Cbsa) had succeeded, it could have led to DeMaria being deported from Canada.

The government’s latest effort ended in failure with a decision by the Irb’s appeal division quietly released in July after a year of hearings, arguments and deliberation.

DeMaria and the Canadian government have been fighting a monumental legal and bureaucratic war on many fronts over whether he is a Mafia boss and the related question of whether he can remain in Canada.

So far, the war has tilted decidedly in DeMaria’s favour.

Now 72 years old, DeMaria has lived in Canada for all but the first nine months of his life, after he was born in Siderno, Italy, and came to Canada in 1955 with his parents.

Although he has lived here, he never became a Canadian citizen. His eligibility for citizenship ended in 1981 when he shot dead a man who owed him money. DeMaria was convicted of second-degree murder in 1982. He was released on full parole ten years later, but as a convicted murderer he remains on parole for the rest of his life.

He was first ordered out of Canada in 1984, while still in prison. He successfully defeated that deportation — and every other attempt to remove him since.

At immigration tribunals, parole hearings, and in court, DeMaria has mounted well-resourced and successful challenges, rebutting various allegations of involvement in organized crime. By disputing, denying, and delaying, he has remained with his wife and children in Canada.

His latest battle began last summer.

The minister of public safety appealed a 2023 decision by the IRB that the government had not proven that DeMaria is or was a member of the Mafia.

As is typical of DeMaria’s battles, the latest hearing was long and complicated; it stretched over 10 days of hearings in the summer and fall of 2025, followed by lengthy written submission from both Cbsa officials and DeMaria’s team of lawyers.

Documentation filed in the case was so lengthy — more than 20,000 pages — that the Irb’s computer system kept crashing at the hearing when more than one of the huge files was opened at the same time.

“There is a long history of administrative hearings and judicial reviews in this case,” IRB member Benjamin Dolin said in a stroke of understatement in his written decision.

At past immigration proceedings, police named DeMaria as an influential member of the ’Ndrangheta, but conceded their inability to prove it beyond reasonable doubt in criminal court. An officer from Peel Regional Police said DeMaria was the “top guy in Toronto” for the ’Ndrangheta.

In 2018, the IRB declared him inadmissible in Canada for having a “high-ranking position within this organization, which engages in criminal activities, including weapons smuggling, drug trafficking and counterfeit products.” DeMaria appealed that decision to the Federal Court and won a new hearing.

The new proceeding in 2023 came to a different conclusion, finding no viable evidence of DeMaria’s link to the Mafia, writing: “The Panel finds the Minister’s evidence to be no more than unfounded suspicions based on flimsy and circumstantial evidence.”

It was then the government’s turn to appeal that decision, which sparked the latest IRB hearing, that featured new controversies.

At the hearing, Cbsa entered transcripts of wiretaps that secretly recorded conversations of alleged mafiosi visiting Canada from Italy in 2019. As first reported by National Post , Italian police used spyware to surreptitiously force the visitors’ own cellphones to record and transmit their conversations, regardless of whether the phone was in use or not.

The IRB heard from a police officer from Italy, called by Cbsa as a witness, who said the visitors, one of whom was a relative of DeMaria’s, came to Canada to meet with Angelo and Cosimo Figliomeni, alleged to be senior mob figures, to investigate the murder of a mobster in Italy. The Italian officer testified that the visitors talked about DeMaria.

DeMaria’s lawyers argued the wiretaps were illegal, unconstitutional, and unreliable, calling it “foreign interference.” A lawyer for Cbsa then said they would no longer rely on the wiretaps to make their case.

The government alleged that DeMaria used the family’s cash services business to launder mob money.

DeMaria testified at the hearing, denying any link to the Mafia and involvement in organized crime. He denied any criminality by the family’s money business, saying he left the family’s cheque cashing business years earlier, and none of the transactions questioned by authorities had been linked to him or to the mob.

In his written decision, Dolin said the government’s evidence of DeMaria’s involvement in money laundering amounted to “nothing more than speculation.”

In my view, the Minister’s case amounts to no more than conjecture and speculation

Dolin rejected the government’s contention that the murder DeMaria was convicted of was related to the ’Ndrangheta in DeMaria’s capacity as a mob enforcer.

Dolin also said evidence heard at the hearing of DeMaria interacting with men suspected of alleged Mafia involvement, including Cosimo and Rocco Remo Commisso, the Figliomeni brothers, and Carmine Verduci, was not evidence that DeMaria was a mobster himself. DeMaria told the hearing the few interactions mentioned were mostly social occasions at ethnic community events.

He also rejected the government’s evidence that various underworld snitches or other gangsters caught on wiretaps alluded to DeMaria as being involved in the mob. Dolin characterized it variously as unreliable or untrustworthy.

“The Respondent is a convicted murderer who came to Canada as an infant from an Italian province associated with the ‘Ndrangheta,” Dolin wrote in his conclusion. The government’s case against DeMaria, he wrote, does not amount to evidence that he is a mobster or criminally involved in the mob.

“In my view, the Minister’s case amounts to no more than conjecture and speculation.” He dismissed the government’s appeal, and confirmed that DeMaria was not deemed inadmissible to Canada.

A request for comment from DeMaria’s immigration lawyer was not responded to prior to publication deadline.

stories.title: Temporary road closures for culvert replacements on Wellington Road South
stories.summary: The City of London will be undertaking culvert replacements this summer and into the fall which will mean temporary road closures as the work
stories.content:
The City of London will be undertaking culvert replacements this summer and into the fall which will mean temporary road closures as the work gets underway. This work is being done primarily on Wellington Road South.

The culvert replacement program will take place at the following locations and dates:

{'text': 'Wellington Rd South – between Harry White Drive and Fisher Lane - August 17 to August 28', 'html': 'Wellington Rd South – between Harry White Drive and Fisher Lane - August 17 to August 28'}

{'text': 'Wellington Road/Glanworth Drive - east/west section of Glanworth Drive to August 17 – August 28', 'html': 'Wellington Road/Glanworth Drive - east/west section of Glanworth Drive to August 17 – August 28'}

What is a culvert?

A culvert is a structure that allows water to pass under or around infrastructure, such as a road or railroad. Culverts help prevent flooding, minimize erosion, and maintain roads in good condition longer.

Why is this happening now?

Repairs and replacement in the near term are required to ensure structural integrity, address safety hazards, protect infrastructure from damage due to stream water fluctuation and precipitation runoff, prevent upstream flooding, and ensure compliance with environmental standards.

Transportation impacts

Drivers are advised to expect traffic delays if traveling in this area. Please follow the detour signage. Drivers should give themselves some extra time when traveling, use navigation apps to plan routes, and leave a little earlier to get to where they need to go.

Above: A map showing the project areas for the culvert replacements on Wellington Road.

You can learn more on Renew London .

stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (August 14, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Patrol Operations Investigative Section have arrested a London man after recovering two stolen vehicles and determining he was operating both while prohibited from driving. On August 2, 2026, an off-duty London police officer observed a man known to police driving a white Dodge Ram displaying an Ontario licence plate at a gas station on Hamilton Road. Investigators confirmed the suspect was a prohibited driver, that the licence plate was not registered to the vehicle and believed cloned plates were being used. Police attended the suspect male’s place of work in the south end of the city on August 13, 2026, where they located the Dodge Ram and confirmed it had been previously reported stolen. The suspect was arrested without incident. Investigators determined the suspect had arrived at work operating a 2013 Harley-Davidson motorcycle that had also been reported stolen two days earlier. As a result of the investigation, Richard Kyle Newstead, 45, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

stories.title: Middlesex County advocating for local priorities at 2026 AMO Conference
stories.summary: Middlesex County representatives are bringing local priorities directly to provincial leaders at the the 2026 Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) Conference.
stories.content:
Middlesex County (August 13, 2026) – Middlesex County representatives are attending the 2026 Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO) Conference from August 16 to 19 to bring local priorities directly to provincial leaders, connect with municipal partners from across Ontario, and advocate for priorities that matter to residents.

The annual AMO Conference brings together municipal officials, senior staff, provincial representatives, and organizations from across Ontario to exchange ideas, discuss shared challenges, and advance solutions that support strong and sustainable communities.

Throughout the conference, Middlesex County representatives will participate in meetings and discussions focused on priorities that support residents, businesses, and local municipalities. Meeting with provincial officials will highlight topics such as employment and industrial lands, community safety, high-speed internet infrastructure, long-term care, municipal fleet vehicles, and privacy protection.

"The AMO Conference is an important opportunity to bring the voice of Middlesex County directly to provincial decision-makers and municipal partners," said Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke. “These conversations help us build momentum on initiatives that will benefit our communities now and into the future."

The County's participation reflects its commitment to advocating for local needs while working collaboratively with municipal and provincial partners to address shared opportunities.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 88,000 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community. Media Contact: Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division @email

stories.title: Children’s Hospital performs first in Ontario paediatric spinal surgery using new robotic spine platform
stories.summary: August 13, 2026
stories.content:
Children's Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has achieved a major milestone in surgical innovation, becoming the first hospital in Ontario to use the Medtronic Mazor robotic spine platform for a paediatric scoliosis correction.

Mazor features software that allows surgeons to upload their patients’ imaging in order to plan their procedures ahead of time and then

action them in the operating room (OR). The system has three arms: a robotic arm that assists with the procedure, one that performs CT scans and another that takes X-rays, giving care teams access to the latest imaging right in the OR.

Fourteen-year-old Paige Hillman first started complaining about back pain last summer. Not long after, her mother Melissa spotted the telltale signs of scoliosis, a condition she also has.

“I could see the curve in Paige’s back. It was like her whole body was curving to the spine, even her shoulders,” Melissa says. “You could see it when she was walking and when she was wearing tighter clothes.”

Given her first-hand knowledge of how painful a scoliosis spinal malformation can be, Melissa didn’t want the same fate for her daughter.

“As I get older, I’m in more pain than I used to be with a lot of pain in my lower back and up in my neck area,” Melissa says. “I just didn’t want her to feel like that. I wanted her to grow up and have fun.”

Melissa called their family physician in Windsor, who then referred Paige to Children’s Hospital.

Dr. Patrick Thornley, Paediatric Orthopaedic Surgeon, and his colleagues worked with Paige and her family to come up with a plan to address her scoliosis. Knowing the Hillmans were open to surgical intervention, they asked if they would be interested in having the robotic Mazor platform used during Paige’s procedure. Up until that point, the system had only been used on adults at LHSC.

After conversations with the care team, the Hillmans said yes and in March 2026 Paige became the first paediatric patient in the province to undergo a scoliosis correction using Mazor.

Using images of Paige’s spine taken during low-dose radiation CT scans, Dr. Thornley and the care team used the Mazor planning software to map out Paige’s entire procedure ahead of time and design the surgical plan.

That plan was then uploaded directly onto the robotic platform in the operating room (OR) where they took X-rays to confirm Paige’s positioning, all of which enabled real-time visualization that supported Dr. Thornley through the procedure.

Dr. Thornley opted to use the robot to place the most challenging screws in Paige’s spine, reducing the time it would usually take to accomplish that task from roughly 20 minutes manually down to about three. The actual spinal correction took a little less than four hours to complete, with Paige’s dedicated care team spending about eight hours in total with her in the OR.

The procedure was a success resulting in a near-perfect result with Paige even gaining a couple of inches in height thanks to the spine correction. She was able to go home to Windsor after just a few days in hospital and returned to school after roughly four weeks, instead of the expected six.

Most importantly, her quality of life has greatly improved.

“My back would hurt most of the time before the surgery and even more when I would lie down,” Paige says. “Now it barely hurts. It’s really nice.”

As for how it makes her feel to know her surgery was the first such case in Ontario, Paige doesn’t hold back.

“It feels amazing. Sometimes I like to brag to my friends about it,” she says with a chuckle.

"Performing the corrective surgery now rather than when Paige reached adulthood will greatly reduce her chances of further issues and ensure she’ll have a much healthier spine moving forward,” says Dr. Thornley.

“The risk of progressive deformity has been removed by this surgery,” he says. “It’s everything we could hope for at least in the early stages.”

“I feel proud of Paige as a patient, I think she’s done a great job.”

Paige’s positive experience is a testament to Children’s Hospital’s commitment to innovation and investment in the latest technologies. Both the University Hospital as well as the Victoria Hospital and Children’s Hospital sites now operate their own Mazor robotic platforms, and to date, surgeons across LHSC have performed 10 to 15 procedures using the platform, across a range of patient ages and conditions. The costs associated with both robotic platforms are supported through provincial funding.

Robotic‑assisted surgery is transforming operating rooms worldwide, but uptake across Canada remains varied. LHSC has long been a leader in the field, recognizing the potential for improving patient care.

“The strength of Mazor and other spine robotic platforms, will ultimately be that we're going to see increased accuracy, increased safety, better outcomes, and safer, faster surgeries for kids and adults,” says Dr. Thornley. “That's the whole point of why we want to use it.”

stories.title: Lifelong Friends Donate $2.4 Million to Advance Cancer Care—and Encourage Others to Give Back
stories.summary: August 13, 2026
stories.content:
London, Ont. — What began as a friendship has grown into a shared dedication to helping others. Today, that dedication is reflected in an extraordinary $2.4-million gift from the Combe and MacMaster families to expand access to specialized cancer treatment at the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

Their desire to support better cancer care was inspired by seeing how the disease has touched their friends and loved ones. Long-time supporters of London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf), Ken and his wife, Barb, have been giving back to LHSC and the community it serves for more than 20 years. As previous owner and long-time leader of MacMaster Chevrolet Cadillac Buick GMC, a family-owned and operated dealership, Ken has long been committed to supporting the communities his business serves.

"I took it in my heart to help people if I could," says Ken. "If we can eliminate some suffering or grief for families, then it'll be worth it." Together, they saw an opportunity to make a meaningful difference by helping ensure patients have access to the latest cancer treatments in the area.

"I wanted to see this advanced way of treating people brought to London," says Craig. "Our physicians already have the expertise, but this helps ensure they have the tools to match. If we can help give patients even greater peace of mind during one of the most difficult times in their lives, that's worth investing in."

Their gift will support the purchase of LHSC's second Varian Ethos therapy system, an AI-driven linear accelerator and the introduction of the AlignRT radiation therapy and HyperSight imaging system across the hospital's fleet of linear accelerators (LINACs). Donor-funded upgrades to medical technology are crucial to helping LHSC deliver faster, more precise and personalized radiation therapy while expanding capacity to meet the needs of a growing number of patients.

Linear accelerators are used to treat many types of cancer, including prostate, bladder and lung cancers, as well as some blood cancers. Together, these software upgrades will enhance the precision and efficiency of radiation treatment in London, helping clinicians deliver even more accurate, personalized radiation treatment while improving each patient’s experience.

AlignRT allows continuous monitoring of a patient's position throughout treatment, helping clinicians maintain accuracy during radiation delivery. For many patients, it can also eliminate the need for the small permanent tattoos traditionally used to guide treatment—a lasting reminder of one of life's most difficult chapters. Hypersight gives a sharper, faster picture of the patient on the machine for clearer visualization of the tumour and nearby organs.

LHSC provides radiation treatment to approximately 300 patients each day across 9 linear accelerators (LINACs). As patient demand continues to grow, the hospital is working to expand access to new advanced technology, with donor support playing a critical role in completing specialized software upgrades for its linear accelerators (LINACs). Craig and Ken's gift is a significant step toward that goal. They hope it will inspire others to help complete the remaining upgrades so more patients can benefit from this technology. Donations of every size will help bring these innovations to more treatment rooms, improving care for people with cancer across the region.

Thanks to Ken and Craig's generosity, these innovations will help clinicians deliver faster, more personalized radiation treatment by allowing them to adapt treatment plans in real time, improve precision and better protect healthy tissue. The technology is designed to target tumours with exceptional accuracy while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue—similar to treating only the yolk of an egg without affecting the white or shell.

"This remarkable gift will help ensure our patients continue to benefit from some of the most advanced radiation technologies available," says Dr. Michael Ott, department head of oncology at LHSC. "By giving our clinical teams greater precision and flexibility in how we plan and deliver treatment, this investment will enhance the care experience for thousands of patients in the years ahead. We are deeply grateful to the Combe and MacMaster families for helping shape the future of cancer care in our region."

As longtime supporters of London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf), the two friends believe investing in local health care strengthens the entire community. They hope their gift will encourage others to help fund the remaining funding needed to upgrade LHSC's linear accelerators.

"Craig and Ken's generosity is already changing what's possible for cancer patients in our community," says John H. MacFarlane, president and CEO of Lhsf. "Donor support helps make innovations like these possible, ensuring more patients across Southwestern Ontario can benefit from the latest developments in cancer care."

It is estimated that over two in five Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime, a reality the Combes and MacMasters hope will inspire others to give back. While their gift will help shape the future of cancer care, they believe every donation can make a meaningful difference. Together, gifts of every size help bring new advancements to LHSC and ensure more patients can receive the care they need.

Donations of every size will help bring these innovations to more treatment rooms, improving care for people with cancer across the region.

Thanks to Ken and Craig's generosity, these innovations will help clinicians deliver faster, more personalized radiation treatment by allowing them to adapt treatment plans in real time, improve precision and better protect healthy tissue. The technology is designed to target tumours with exceptional accuracy while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissue—similar to treating only the yolk of an egg without affecting the white or shell.

"This remarkable gift will help ensure our patients continue to benefit from some of the most advanced radiation technologies available," says Dr. Michael Ott, department head of oncology at LHSC. "By giving our clinical teams greater precision and flexibility in how we plan and deliver treatment, this investment will enhance the care experience for thousands of patients in the years ahead. We are deeply grateful to the Combe and MacMaster families for helping shape the future of cancer care in our region."

As longtime supporters of London Health Sciences Foundation (Lhsf), the two friends believe investing in local health care strengthens the entire community. They hope their gift will encourage others to help fund the remaining funding needed to upgrade LHSC's linear accelerators.

"Craig and Ken's generosity is already changing what's possible for cancer patients in our community," says John H. MacFarlane, president and CEO of Lhsf. "Donor support helps make innovations like these possible, ensuring more patients across Southwestern Ontario can benefit from the latest developments in cancer care."

It is estimated that over two in five Canadians will be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime, a reality the Combes and MacMasters hope will inspire others to give back. While their gift will help shape the future of cancer care, they believe every donation can make a meaningful difference. Together, gifts of every size help bring new advancements to LHSC and ensure more patients can receive the care they need.
