stories.title: Teen who killed grandmother in random attack still relishes violence despite apology, court hears
stories.summary: His apparent deficit in remorse for killing Eleanor Doney was highlighted by Crown prosecutors at his sentencing hearing.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
His apparent deficit in remorse for killing a stranger in broad daylight was highlighted by Crown prosecutors at his sentencing hearing

During his months in custody since stabbing an 83-year-old woman to death in a frenzy of unprovoked violence outside her Ontario home, the teenager killer was involved in a fight after which he declared he “hasn’t felt this alive” since he committed his murder.

Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.

Access articles from across Canada with one account.

Enjoy additional articles per month.

His apparent deficit in remorse while relishing violence was highlighted by Crown prosecutors at his sentencing hearing on Tuesday.

Eleanor Doney, whom many friends and family called Ellie, was raking leaves outside her home in Pickering, just east of Toronto, ON May 29, 2025, when she was attacked by a 14-year-old boy dressed in a black shiny trench coat, a black COVID-style mask, black gloves, overly large dress shoes and carrying a briefcase.

Because of his young age, the identity of the killer is protected by law and cannot be published. In April, he pleaded guilty to first-degree murder.

In court Tuesday, the boy stood up inside the prisoner’s box and slowly unfolded a sheet of paper he pulled from the dark suit jacket he wore over a white shirt and addressed Justice Lisa Wannamaker.

He apologized to court and said people learn from knowledge.

“I’ve learned from this,” he said, asking that the murder not define who he is.

The bizarreness of the encounter and the viciousness of the attack were captured on a neighbour’s doorbell camera. The boy is seen stopping and talking with Doney for a couple of minutes before pulling a knife from his briefcase and repeatedly stabbing her as she tried to retreat into her house.

He then continued walking down the street. A community warning was issued until the boy was identified to police by school administrators and arrested that night at his home.

At his sentencing hearing, both the Crown and the boy’s defence lawyer jointly asked for the maximum sentence allowable under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, which is a 10-year sentence, split between six years in custody and four years of conditional supervision in the community, under an intensive rehabilitative custody and supervision order. Such an order is for enhanced rehabilitative programming for youth with serious mental health issues who committed serious crimes.

The two lawyers differed, however, ON whether the year he has already been in custody waiting for his sentencing should be deducted from his sentence to be served.

Crown prosecutor Tammi D’Eri said the Crown had planned to ask court to have the boy tried and sentenced as an adult, but various psychological reports suggested they would not meet a new Supreme Court of Canada requirement of first proving a young offender had an adult-like maturity at the time of the offence.

Mental health problems and psychosocial deficits of the boy meant that hurdle likely could not be met, although he had suitable written and verbal skills and interactions with teachers and others.

“This was a completely unprovoked, random, extremely violent attack on an innocent woman cleaning up her yard on a spring day,” D’Eri said at the hearing which was packed by Doney’s family and friends, the boy’s parents and siblings, and journalists.

This was a completely unprovoked, random, extremely violent attack on an innocent woman

“This brutal attack occurred in Ms. Doney’s yard in the middle of the afternoon, a place where she was entitled to feel safe and likely did feel safe.”

D’Eri said the boy’s sentence must promote a sense of responsibility in him and acknowledge the harm done to the victims and the community.

She said it was “highly concerning” the boy displayed little insight into his violence and was inconsistent in his explanation for it. She said he continues to show persistent preoccupation with violence and serial killers.

He has also been the subject of several behavioural incident reports from the facility where he is incarcerated, she said, including an altercation with another resident which staff broke up.

After the incident, court heard, the boy said he “hasn’t felt this alive” since he murdered Doney.

This, D’Eri said, supports the Crown’s position that his risk of re-offending continues and that a lengthy sentence is necessary to try to address underlying issues, and that his time already served should not be deducted from his sentence to lengthen this process.

The Crown also asked for a lifetime weapons ban and an order to take his DNA for the government’s DNA bank.

Erin Dann, the boy’s lawyer, agreed her client committed a horrific, pre-meditated murder causing deep and lasting hurt to many people.

She asked that the boy be granted a year’s credit from his time already spent in custody. She said it would increase the likelihood he remains in a youth facility until his conditional release, which she said would aid his rehabilitation. Young offenders can typically remain in a youth facility until the age of 20. If he serves the extra year requested by the Crown, he will turn 21 before release and might be transferred to an adult prison.

By the time his sentence is complete, Dann said, it will be 2035 and his sentence period will account for more than 41 per cent of his life: “This is a considerable sentence for someone so young,” she said.

Her client has “high needs” for mental health treatment and psychosocial assistance for his rehabilitation and that five years in custody is a long time for someone his age, Dann said.

She said he has a “good capacity for rehabilitation.” He was assessed at a low to moderate risk to violently reoffend and that dropped to “likely low if his mental health is properly attended to and monitored.”

Dann said psychological assessments suggested his serial killer obsession and a lack of remorse and empathy likely stemmed from mental health problems and are not fixed attitudes.

“Because these risk factors relate to mental health concerns, there’s real potential here for rehabilitation and reintegration if properly addressed,” Dann said, and the youth facility, where he is engaged with the treatment programming, is the best place to meet that need.

Court earlier heard of the boy’s dark fixations .

Police seized two cell phones and a computer from his home that uncovered his vast online activity and intense interest in murder, serial killers, psychopathy and an obsession with a fictional serial killer from a Japanese comic book called Yoshikage Kira, as well as the real-life serial killer Ted Bundy.

It was the characteristics of the cartoon character that apparently influenced his unusual dress for a 14-year-old on the day of Doney’s murder.

On Tuesday, the boy sat quietly and mostly still in court listening to the detailed discussion of his history, behaviour, difficult upbringing, and mental health.

Court also heard that on the day before the stabbing, school officials had caught the boy with a knife and suspended him for five days. During two medical assessments prepared for the boy’s court appearances prior to his guilty plea, he told psychologists he had a fluctuating “urge to kill” in the weeks leading up to his attack.

There were 18 victim impact statements given to the judge.

The victim’s husband, Bruce Doney, said he and his wife had been together for 63 years and he misses her greatly and is looking forward to seeing her again in heaven, as both are devout Christians.

“I used to enjoy working in the garden with my wife with the flowers stretched over a couple of ponds and the songs of birds which returned to the birdhouse. Now it’s like a little bird has flown into a closed window and was killed. I can only put it now in a place where it rests, is buried and marked. I’ll never forget that little bird that I spent 63 years with,” Bruce Doney told court.

He requires a wheelchair and has significant vision loss, and his wife was his primary caregiver. He has since sold the home where Doney was killed.

He said he has forgiven his wife’s killer but still feared that if he is released from custody, because of his mental state, he would hurt someone else. “I wish the best for him,” he wrote, but also hopes the teen receives the treatment needed to prevent him committing other crimes in the future.

Brian Kirwin, Doney’s son-in-law, called the boy’s attack “cowardly” and “calculated.”

“By the heinous act committed it not only shattered Eleanor’s life but so many Eleanor had deeply impacted. This was all taken away in an instant for the utter senselessness of nothing short of cold-blooded murder…. The fear/worry/terror that was caused lasted, and still lasts, to this day. Safety and peace were stolen, not just from us who knew Eleanor but to all of our community and beyond. What is left is anxiety, stress, pain, hurt and fear.”

Jeff Doney said the violence that ended his mother’s life makes grief harder to cope with.

“The emotional impact of losing my mother has been profound and life-altering. Her death was sudden, violent, and hard to understand. She was attacked in front of her own home — a place where she should have felt safe and protected. The fact that her life was taken by a young offender is something I still struggle to make sense of,” he told court. “My mother was a sweet, gentle person whom everyone loved. She had a strong Christian faith that guided the way she lived her life. Helping others wasn’t just something she did — it was who she was.”

Judy Kirwin, Doney’s daughter, said her mother was her mentor and closest friend and support. “The loving relationship I enjoyed with my Mom was abruptly torn from me. I was violently robbed. His apparent deficit in remorse while relishing violence was highlighted by Crown prosecutors at his sentencing hearing on Tuesday.

Eleanor Doney, whom many friends and family called Ellie, was raking leaves outside her home in Pickering, just east of Toronto, ON May 29, 2025, when she was attacked by a 14-year-old boy dressed in a black shiny trench coat, a black COVID-style mask, black gloves, overly large dress shoes and carrying a briefcase.
Because of his young age, the identity of the killer is protected by law and cannot be published. In April, he pleaded guilty to first-degree murder.
In court Tuesday, the boy stood up inside the prisoner’s box and slowly unfolded a sheet of paper he pulled from the dark suit jacket he wore over a white shirt and addressed Justice Lisa Wannamaker.
He apologized to court and said people learn from knowledge.
“I’ve learned from this,” he said, asking that the murder not define who he is.

The bizarreness of the encounter and the viciousness of the attack were captured on a neighbour’s doorbell camera. The boy is seen stopping and talking with Doney for a couple of minutes before pulling a knife from his briefcase and repeatedly stabbing her as she tried to retreat into her house.
He then continued walking down the street. A community warning was issued until the boy was identified to police by school administrators and arrested that night at his home.

At his sentencing hearing, both the Crown and the boy’s defence lawyer jointly asked for the maximum sentence allowable under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, which is a 10-year sentence, split between six years in custody and four years of conditional supervision in the community, under an intensive rehabilitative custody and supervision order. Such an order is for enhanced rehabilitative programming for youth with serious mental health issues who committed serious crimes.
The two lawyers differed, however, ON whether the year he has already been in custody waiting for his sentencing should be deducted from his sentence to be served.

Crown prosecutor Tammi D’Eri said the Crown had planned to ask court to have the boy tried and sentenced as an adult, but various psychological reports suggested they would not meet a new Supreme Court of Canada requirement of first proving a young offender had an adult-like maturity at the time of the offence.
Mental health problems and psychosocial deficits of the boy meant that hurdle likely could not be met, although he had suitable written and verbal skills and interactions with teachers and others.

“This was a completely unprovoked, random, extremely violent attack on an innocent woman cleaning up her yard on a spring day,” D’Eri said at the hearing which was packed by Doney’s family and friends, the boy’s parents and siblings, and journalists.
This was a completely unprovoked, random, extremely violent attack on an innocent woman
“This brutal attack occurred in Ms. Doney’s yard in the middle of the afternoon, a place where she was entitled to feel safe and likely did feel safe.”
D’Eri said the boy’s sentence must promote a sense of responsibility in him and acknowledge the harm done to the victims and the community.

She said it was “highly concerning” the boy displayed little insight into his violence and was inconsistent in his explanation for it. She said he continues to show persistent preoccupation with violence and serial killers.
He has also been the subject of several behavioural incident reports from the facility where he is incarcerated, she said, including an altercation with another resident which staff broke up.
After the incident, court heard, the boy said he “hasn’t felt this alive” since he murdered Doney.

This, D’Eri said, supports the Crown’s position that his risk of re-offending continues and that a lengthy sentence is necessary to try to address underlying issues, and that his time already served should not be deducted from his sentence to lengthen this process.
The Crown also asked for a lifetime weapons ban and an order to take his DNA for the government’s DNA bank.
Erin Dann, the boy’s lawyer, agreed her client committed a horrific, pre-meditated murder causing deep and lasting hurt to many people.

stories.title: Middlesex County Warden’s Statement on 2026 Warden's Charity Golf Tournament
stories.summary: On July 14, 2026, Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke issued the following statement regarding the total proceeds of the 2026 Warden’s Charity Golf Tournament.
stories.content:
Middlesex County: On July 14, 2026, Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke issued the following statement regarding the total proceeds of the 2026 Warden’s Charity Golf Tournament.

“I’m proud to share with you today that the 2026 Warden’s Charity Golf Tournament raised a net total of $36,550.61 in support of three great community groups: Four Counties Heath Services Foundation, Strathroy Middlesex General Hospital Foundation, and the Optimist Club of Kerwood-Adelaide-Metcalfe. The funds raised will help our local hospitals get the equipment they need to continue providing high quality healthcare and help the Optimist Club continue to be a positive presence in our community. Thank you to everyone who had a role in making this year’s tournament a success. To the sponsors who generously contributed, the golfers who braved the morning rain, and the County staff who brought us all together. It’s encouraging to see what we can accomplish when we come together and unite for a common cause. The record amount that we raised highlights the spirit and generosity of the place we call home." Thank you again for helping make a difference in our community.

Media Contact: Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division @email

stories.title: Middlesex County ratifies new collective agreement with Cupe 101.5
stories.summary: Middlesex County (July 10, 2026) – Middlesex County Council has ratified a new collective agreement with Cupe 101.5.
paragraphs: Middlesex County (July 10, 2026) – Middlesex County Council has ratified a new collective agreement with Cupe 101.5.

The collective agreement is for the term of January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2029. It provides wage increases of 3.95% in the first year, 3.55% in the second year and 3.25% in the third and final year. Other provisions include enhancements to employee vacation leave and improved health and wellness benefits.

“Our employees are essential to everything we do. The expertise, dedication, and professionalism they bring every day are the foundation of the programs and services we provide to residents across the County. This collective agreement reflects a commitment to supporting our employees and delivering excellent outcomes for the community,” said Paul Shipway, Middlesex County CAO. “I’d like to thank everyone on both sides of the table for their collaborative efforts in reaching an agreement.”

“Cupe 101.5 wants to thank the employer, Board, Bargaining Committees and the members for all their hard work in Bargaining and we are excited that this has been ratified by both Union and Employer. We look forward to the next four years working together,” said Cupe 101 President, Steve Holland.

Cupe Local 101.5 represents full-time and part-time, permanent and temporary employees who provide a broad range of frontline and operational services across Middlesex County. These employees perform vital work across many areas of the organization, including roads, finance, administration, human services, planning, and information technology.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.

stories.content:
Middlesex County (July 10, 2026) – Middlesex County Council has ratified a new collective agreement with Cupe 101.5.

The collective agreement is for the term of January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2029. It provides wage increases of 3.95% in the first year, 3.55% in the second year and 3.25% in the third and final year. Other provisions include enhancements to employee vacation leave and improved health and wellness benefits.

“Our employees are essential to everything we do. The expertise, dedication, and professionalism they bring every day are the foundation of the programs and services we provide to residents across the County. This collective agreement reflects a commitment to supporting our employees and delivering excellent outcomes for the community,” said Paul Shipway, Middlesex County CAO. “I’d like to thank everyone on both sides of the table for their collaborative efforts in reaching an agreement.”

“Cupe 101.5 wants to thank the employer, Board, Bargaining Committees and the members for all their hard work in Bargaining and we are excited that this has been ratified by both Union and Employer. We look forward to the next four years working together,” said Cupe 101 President, Steve Holland.

Cupe Local 101.5 represents full-time and part-time, permanent and temporary employees who provide a broad range of frontline and operational services across Middlesex County. These employees perform vital work across many areas of the organization, including roads, finance, administration, human services, planning, and information technology.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.

stories.title: The 'King' sent to U.S. prison for 20 years for running cocaine and meth smuggling into Canada
stories.summary: Guramrit Sidhu, of Brampton, could have faced a life sentence but his sentence was lower for pleading guilty and not fighting the charges.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Guramrit Sidhu, of Brampton, Ont., could have faced a life sentence as a maximum penalty, but his sentence was lower for pleading guilty rather than fighting the charges at a trial

For years an Ontario man was called “King” while orchestrating truckloads of cocaine and meth worth tens of millions of dollars to be smuggled from the United States into Canada, but at his sentencing in Los Angeles, Thursday, court heard of his struggles as an immigrant and of his “working-class life in Canada.”

Enjoy the latest local, national and international news.

Access articles from across Canada with one account.

Enjoy additional articles per month.

Guramrit Sidhu, 63, of Brampton, Ont., who led a vast cross-border drug smuggling network of long-haul commercial truckers was given the minimum allowable sentence of 20 years in prison.

Sidhu was arrested in Canada in 2024 as the lead defendant in a sprawling international investigation.

He signed a plea agreement with the U.S. government in February, pleading guilty to one count of engaging in a continuing criminal enterprise, admitting his management-level involvement in the network that smuggled large loads of meth and cocaine for distribution in Canada between 2020 and 2023.

Prosecutors told U.S. District Judge John Kronstadt that Sidhu’s operation was energetic and active — in just a one-month period in 2022, he arranged eight drug loads, totalling about 523 kilograms of meth and 347 kilograms of cocaine, which were seized by law enforcement. Prosecutors estimated the wholesale value of just that month’s tally was about US$16 million.

Sidhu’s lawyer, Vitaly Sigal, argued Sidhu’s age and life struggles should merit a lower sentence.

“He will, in other words, grow old and increasingly infirm in federal custody,” Sigal told court.

“Sidhu acknowledges that his participation in a drug-trafficking enterprise was a serious offense, and he accepts full responsibility for his conduct. He does not seek to minimize, excuse, or justify what he did,” Sigal told the judge. “At the same time, the offense was non-violent. It involved no weapons, no force or threats of force, and no identifiable victim.”

Court heard that Sidhu was born in India and immigrated to Canada with his parents and siblings in 1974 when he was 11.

Sidhu’s childhood was marred by his father’s alcoholism and violence. His father was “nice when he did not drink,” but usually drank a forty-ounce bottle of liquor nightly, “making kind moments rare.”

Sidhu said he had a rough transition to life in Canada as the only Sikh family in his Ontario neighbourhood and his inability to speak English. He said he was picked on at school, got into fights nearly every day and left school early to work.

In 1986, he met his future wife. She was in an arranged marriage at the time but filed for divorce. After her divorce she and Sidhu married in a union that created rifts within the families. They moved to a home in Brampton, Ont., where they raised two children while he worked as a commercial truck driver and at a foundry, maintaining “a working-class life in Canada,” Sigal told court.

Sidhu said he slid into criminality through his own substance abuse, including heavy drinking since he was a teenager, daily heroin use from 2004 until 2011, and using fentanyl each day from 2016 to 2019, court heard. He said his family helped him quit.

Court heard Sidhu has health problems and takes medication for diabetes and high cholesterol and for opiate withdrawal.

Seven of Sidhu’s family members wrote to the judge saying they maintain their support for him despite his mistakes and urged the judge to consider Sidhu’s contributions as a good family man.

“It’s important to me that he knows he has a positive environment to return home to and the entire family is committed to doing whatever we can to help rehabilitate him and help him assimilate back into life,” his daughter wrote in a letter to the judge.

In return for Sidhu’s guilty plea, U.S. prosecutors agreed to not seek a sentence longer than 20 years and not to oppose a prisoner transfer request for Sidhu to serve the last half of his sentence in Canada.

Sidhu caught a break by being considered to have no criminal history by the U.S. court despite him having a previous conviction in Canada. In 2011, he was convicted of kidnapping and sentenced to more than nine years’ imprisonment, but U.S. sentencing guidelines do not consider foreign convictions.

Prosecutors agreed a 20-year sentence was sufficient.

“This sentence reflects the serious nature and circumstances of the offense, the history and characteristics of the defendant, and the need to protect the public from further crimes of defendant,” Assistant United States Attorney Kelly Larocque told court.

Sidhu was given credit for his nine months in custody in Canada in 2024 while he faced extradition to California for trial. Sigal entered as an exhibit a certificate from the Ontario Ministry of the Solicitor General confirming Sidhu’s time in the Maplehurst Correctional Complex, a maximum-security jail in Milton, Ont., sarcastically called the “Milton Hilton,” by inmates.

Prosecutors said that after buying bulk quantities of cocaine and meth in the Los Angeles area, that originally came from Mexico, Sidhu arranged for the drugs to be hauled into Canada hidden aboard commercial tractor-trailers for further distribution.

In text messages, “water” was code for meth and “girls” for cocaine; “Lisa” meant Los Angeles. They used the unique serial number on bank notes to confirm identities of those exchanging the drugs as an underworld form of two-factor authentication.

The trucks shuttled drugs across the border, using the Detroit-Windsor tunnel, the Peace Bridge in Niagara, and the Blue Water Bridge connecting Michigan to Sarnia.

Sidhu did not know that one of the men he was working with had become an informant for the FBI. He trusted the snitch because he had worked with Sidhu before he became a cooperating witness.

The informant was the key to a sweeping joint investigation, led by the FBI, against several cross-border smuggling networks that was called Operation Dead Hand.

Sidhu was named as one of the top-level targets when two lengthy indictments were unsealed in Los Angeles. Among the other Canadians named in the indictments is a man with a notorious last name: Roberto Scoppa, brother of two leaders in a faction of the Montreal Mafia who were killed in 2019 during a mob war. Scoppa is still fighting extradition to the United States.

Sidhu is the eighth person arrested in the operation to plead guilty.

stories.title: Scotiabank Scholars Pitch Fair breaks down post-secondary barriers for students from marginalized communities
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

Forty Thames Valley District School Board students will showcase their creativity, research and leadership skills while getting a hands-on look at campus life during the Scotiabank Scholars Pitch Fair on Friday, July 10, from 10 to 11:30 a.m. at Huron University.

The Pitch Fair serves as the culminating event of the week-long Scotiabank Scholars Summer Camp for grade 11 and 12 students. Scholars experience university life on campus as they research, create and present original projects inspired by real-world issues related to water, with help from the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority. From environmental sustainability to artistic and social interpretations, each presentation reflects the unique interests and perspectives of its creator.

The Scotiabank Scholars program is a unique partnership between Huron University, Scotiabank and the Thames Valley District School Board. The program is designed to break down barriers to post-secondary education and highlight post-secondary pathways through hands on-campus experiences and firsthand exposure to university life.

The program supports students from communities that have historically faced barriers to post-secondary participation, including low-income, minoritized, Indigenous, newcomer and first-generation students.

"As a TVDSB employee, we aim to build each student’s tomorrow, and the Scotiabank Scholars program does this in such a profound way," said Sarah Hoy, a TVDSB educator and co-creator of the program alongside fellow educator Robert Gillespie. "Students have the opportunity to earn their English credit through an innovative approach to education, teaching them to redefine what’s possible. They finish the course with a greater sense of self, community, and global stewardship."

"What always stands out is the partnerships. Thames Valley, Huron University, Scotiabank, Upper Thames River Conservation Authority – everyone works together for the sole purpose of supporting these students," said Robert. "Every aspect is all about the students."

Following the presentations, participants and guests will gather for a closing ceremony.

Media are welcome to attend the Pitch Fair and speak with participating students about their projects, experiences and future aspirations.

Date: Friday, July 10, 2026

Time: 10:00 a.m. – 11:30 a.m.

Location: Huron University Burnlea Hall Dining Room 1349 Western Rd, London, ON

stories.title: New Urban Arts program gives emerging artists a canvas for career growth
stories.summary: Fanshawe’s Corporate Training Solutions (CTS) has developed a new
stories.content:
Fanshawe’s Corporate Training Solutions (CTS) has developed a new Urban Arts micro-credential program to equip emerging artists with the skills, experience and industry knowledge needed to participate in the growing field of outdoor art.

The program, developed in collaboration with St. Thomas-based Andrew Gunn Consulting and young & free press, will launch at the College’s St. Thomas/Elgin Regional Campus in September 2026.

“Urban art is creating new opportunities for artists, communities and local economies across the region,” says Heather Carey, senior manager of Fanshawe’s CTS. “By working closely with industry partners, we’ve developed a unique learning experience that will help emerging artists build their portfolios, expand their professional networks and gain valuable real-world experience.”

The program curriculum, delivered in approximately 120 hours over a four-week period, emphasizes artistic development, safety certifications, project planning, business and marketing fundamentals, portfolio development and the tools and techniques used in large-scale outdoor art projects. Students will learn how to design, plan, execute and manage urban art installations responsibly, professionally and sustainably.

A significant portion of the program will focus on mural design and painting. Students will have opportunities to apply their learning through hands-on projects, including adding a mural on a dedicated practice wall recently installed by the City of St. Thomas Parks and Recreation Department.

Andrew Gunn, president of Andrew Gunn Consulting, says his team has been working with the St. Thomas Economic Development Corporation and Railway City Tourism for several years to add murals and other outdoor artwork in the community.

"We have seen tremendous interest from emerging artists who want to learn more about this art form," says Gunn. "We're excited to support Fanshawe in bringing this program to the region. St. Thomas is the perfect setting. Over the past six years, the city has transformed into a community bursting with artwork."

For more information, or to apply to join the inaugural intake, please visit the program page .

About Corporate Training Solutions:

Fanshawe’s Corporate Training Solutions (CTS) develops and delivers responsive, industry-informed training that helps individuals, businesses and organizations build skills and achieve their goals. Through customized training, professional development, micro-credentials and continuing education opportunities, CTS provides flexible learning solutions that respond to evolving workforce and community needs.

About Andrew Gunn Consulting and young & free press:

Andrew Gunn Consulting focuses on assembling funding for community projects in cities, towns and rural areas in southwestern Ontario. The company concentrates on city-building and youth engagement, accelerating economic and cultural development by facilitating innovative projects and collaboration. Details are shared through the media platform young & free press , which is driven by university, college and high school students from the region. Youth are kept front and centre in project development through the ‘Students Build Cities’ program run in collaboration with Thames Valley District School Board. Learn more at www.andrewgunnconsulting.CA

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.CA

stories.title: Canadian choices to elevate your Canada Day barbecue
stories.summary: As Canadians prepare to fire up the grill this Canada Day, there’s an opportunity to think beyond
stories.content:
As Canadians prepare to fire up the grill this Canada Day, there’s an opportunity to think beyond the usual backyard menu and create meals that are both budget-friendly and support local producers.

With food prices still a concern for many households, a great barbecue doesn’t have to centre on premium cuts of meat. Choosing local ingredients and exploring more affordable options can deliver great flavour, stretch grocery dollars and support Canadian farmers at the same time.

Troy Spicer is a professor and program coordinator of Fanshawe’s Professional Butchery Techniques program and the Cook Apprentice program. Spicer is available to speak to how home cooks can rethink their Canada Day menus and get the most out of the grill.

Key discussion areas include:

Why lower-cost cuts and alternative proteins can deliver excellent results on the barbecue;

Where to shop, from local butchers to grocery store sales, to maximize value;

Simple tips for better results to improve flavour and reduce the risk of overcooking.

“Canada Day is the perfect moment to celebrate what we produce here at home,” Spicer says. “You don’t need the most expensive cut of meat to create a memorable meal. With the right approach, you can cook something that is affordable, delicious and supports local Canadian producers.”

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.CA

stories.title: TVDSB students join Team Ontario at international business competition in Atlanta
stories.summary: Six ambitious students from Sir Frederick Banting Secondary School and London Central Secondary School recently competed against more than 20,000 students from around the world as members of Team Ontario at the Deca International Career Development Conference (Icdc) business competition in Atlanta, GA.
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
Six ambitious students from Sir Frederick Banting Secondary School and London Central Secondary School recently competed against more than 20,000 students from around the world as members of Team Ontario at the Deca International Career Development Conference (Icdc) business competition in Atlanta, GA.

Deca Inc. is a career and technical studentorganization that prepares emerging leaders and entrepreneurs for careers in marketing, finance, hospitality and management in high schools and colleges around the globe. The Icdc brings together thousands of high school students, teacher-advisors, business professionals and alumni for several days of competition to attain 21st century skills in the areas of collaboration, communication, critical thinking and creativity.

After an intense week of training and competition, the students each earned a Certificate of Achievement from Deca Inc., scoring at least 70% with rigorous standards in their respective events during the competition. They also met new friends from around the globe while gaining valuable academic, professional and life experiences.

Congratulations to all TVDSB competitors – we look forward to another great year of Deca in 2026-2027!

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: After making 54 donations, Elizabeth Peloza reflects on receiving the gift of life
stories.summary: As a regular donor at Canadian Blood Services, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has given the gift of life to others. She now knows firsthand what it also means to receive.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
As a regular donor at Canadian Blood Services, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has given the gift of life to others.

She now knows firsthand what it also means to receive.

Peloza is sharing her experiences during chemotherapy treatments in a CTV News series called ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’

On the morning of April 29, she recorded a brief video inside the London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) explaining that she would require a blood transfusion while being treated for pneumonia.

“My doctor asked if I had ever received a blood transfusion. I need to receive one because my hemoglobin levels are low,” she said into her phone.

Peloza then reflected on the significance of the moment.

“I’ve been honored to have been 54 times a Canadian Blood Services donor. This is my first transfusion. So humbly, thank you to those who donate,” she said.

The blood transfusion helped save her life and maintain her schedule chemotherapy treatments.

A month and a half later, she visited the Canadian Blood Services donation centre at 820 Wharncliffe Rd. S. in recognition of National Blood Donor Week.

Her chemotherapy treatments prevent Peloza from donating, but she held her donor ID card in her hand, proudly glancing at the large 50 printed on its face — knowing fully what it represents.

“When summer vacation comes, people go out of the town, [they] reprioritize things, and the donations drop, but the demand stays the same. So, it’s really important to schedule those appointments,” she explained.

“Canadian Blood Services needs to welcome over a million new donors by 2030, and the reason is the need for blood is increasing by 10 per cent, and plasma by 50 per cent,” explained Marisa Gatfield, community development manager at Canadian Blood Services.

National Blood Donor Week runs from June 8 to 14.

“It’s actually moving to have the councillor here right now,” said David House, who spoke with Peloza while making his weekly plasma donation. “It’s very nice to know it’s going to help real people.”

“The need for blood is constant, and you never know when you’re going to need it, or someone that you know May need blood or a blood product,” Gatfield said. “I’m grateful for Elizabeth being here and sharing her journey with others, and inspiring others to step-up and become a donor.”

A few years ago, blood plasma donations also saved Peloza’s son.

“I was donating then, and along the way my son had become ill with GBS (Guillain-Barré syndrome) and for that, the only cure is human plasma donation,” she explained. “So, we were already gifted that his life was saved with blood products.”

“We did a donor drive after that to get more awareness, and I became really meticulous about donating,” Peloza recalled.

But now it’s her inability to continue repaying the gift of life that saved her son that makes visiting the donation centre tough for the mom of three.

“I miss it. It’s an opportunity I can’t take right now and it’s going to be years until I can take that again,” Peloza says. “So, I really want to make this a public call for all those donations I would be doing weekly. I need people to step in to help fill my seat, and the seats of those who want to donate — but can’t.

Booking an appointment to make a donation can be done online , by calling 1-888-2-Donate, or on the GiveBlood app.

content_blocks.text: As a regular donor at Canadian Blood Services, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has given the gift of life to others.
She now knows firsthand what it also means to receive.
Peloza is sharing her experiences during chemotherapy treatments in a CTV News series called ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’
On the morning of April 29, she recorded a brief video inside the London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) explaining that she would require a blood transfusion while being treated for pneumonia.
“My doctor asked if I had ever received a blood transfusion. I need to receive one because my hemoglobin levels are low,” she said into her phone.
Peloza then reflected on the significance of the moment.
“I’ve been honored to have been 54 times a Canadian Blood Services donor. This is my first transfusion. So humbly, thank you to those who donate,” she said.
The blood transfusion helped save her life and maintain her schedule chemotherapy treatments.

content_blocks.alt: Elizabeth Peloza - London
content_blocks.caption: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is seen at the Canadian Blood Services donation centre in London, Ont. (Daryl Newcombe/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: A month and a half later, she visited the Canadian Blood Services donation centre at 820 Wharncliffe Rd. S. in recognition of National Blood Donor Week.
Her chemotherapy treatments prevent Peloza from donating, but she held her donor ID card in her hand, proudly glancing at the large 50 printed on its face — knowing fully what it represents.

“When summer vacation comes, people go out of the town, [they] reprioritize things, and the donations drop, but the demand stays the same. So, it’s really important to schedule those appointments,” she explained.

“Canadian Blood Services needs to welcome over a million new donors by 2030, and the reason is the need for blood is increasing by 10 per cent, and plasma by 50 per cent,” explained Marisa Gatfield, community development manager at Canadian Blood Services.
National Blood Donor Week runs from June 8 to 14.
“It’s actually moving to have the councillor here right now,” said David House, who spoke with Peloza while making his weekly plasma donation. “It’s very nice to know it’s going to help real people.”

“The need for blood is constant, and you never know when you’re going to need it, or someone that you know May need blood or a blood product,” Gatfield said. “I’m grateful for Elizabeth being here and sharing her journey with others, and inspiring others to step-up and become a donor.”

stories.title: North Middlesex student becomes first in TVDSB to qualify for Ontario’s Focused Apprenticeship Skills Training (Fast) program
stories.summary: The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) is proud to celebrate Larkin MacLean, a Grade 12 student at North Middlesex District High School, who was the first student in the board to qualify for the Ontario government’s Focused Apprenticeship Skills Training (Fast) program.
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) is proud to celebrate Larkin MacLean, a Grade 12 student at North Middlesex District High School, who was the first student in the board to qualify for the Ontario government’s Focused Apprenticeship Skills Training (Fast) program.

Through her co-operative education placement at CSN High Street Auto Body in Strathroy, Larkin gained valuable, real-world experience in the industry and was formally registered as an apprentice while still in high school.

In addition to qualifying for the Fast program, Larkin was recently awarded the Skilled Trades Bursary, which is presented to a senior student who demonstrates exceptional performance in a co-operative education placement and intends to pursue a career in the skilled trades. She also received the McTavish Award, which honours students who have overcome significant personal challenges to achieve academic success.

Larkin’s accomplishments reflect years of dedication to the automotive trade — a passion sparked early in life through her connection to her grandfather’s autobody business. When Larkin was in Grade 9, her late mother, Crystal MacLean, was also inspired by her daughter help launch the school’s Ticket to the Trades event, which recently celebrated its fourth year.

More details about the Focused Apprenticeship Skills Training (Fast) program are available in a Ontario Government’s news release.

stories.title: Canadian social media ban raises questions about implementation, impact and enforcement
stories.summary: Yesterday, the federal government introduced legislation to restrict social media use among Canad
stories.content:
Yesterday, the federal government introduced legislation to restrict social media use among Canadians under 16, with questions emerging about how a ban could be enforced, how effective it May be, and what it could mean for families and social media platforms.

Garrett Gaudet is a professor and program coordinator of the Business - Entrepreneurship and Management program at Fanshawe’s Woodstock/Oxford Regional Campus. Gaudet is available to provide insight into how similar policies have been implemented elsewhere, what challenges Canada May face and how families can prepare.

Topics for interviews include:

How a youth social media ban could be implemented, including age verification and platform accountability;

How this legislation reflects a broader global trend toward stricter online safety measures for youth;

Why enforcement May be challenging, particularly for a generation that has grown up online;

What success could look like in terms of reducing harms and improving youth well-being;

Practical tips for families to manage social media use and support healthy online habits.

“The success of a social media ban will depend on how well it is implemented and supported,” Gaudet says. “Reducing access is one piece of this complex puzzle. Education, community involvement and engagement from the provincial and federal government will also be important.”

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.CA

stories.title: A.B. Lucas Secondary School raises $2 million for cancer research
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

Last Friday, A.B. Lucas Secondary School held its annual Relay for Life fundraiser benefitting the Canadian Cancer Society, pushing the school past an incredible milestone: $2 million raised as a school community over the past 19 years.

Over 650 students and staff canvassed and organized fundraising events throughout the spring, collectively raising an outstanding $168,206.79 and exceeding their fundraising goal for the year.

A.B. Lucas is the top school in Canada in Relay for Life fundraising, and the first and only school nationwide to reach $2 million raised. The school has a strong legacy of philanthropy and community outreach, teaching students the value of empathy, leadership and social responsibility.

Students led a variety of fundraising activities to meet their ambitious goal, including dances, bingo and ping pong tournaments.

Grade 12 student leads Brooke, Lexi and Lily were recently interviewed by CBC London about this incredible milestone.

“It’s indescribable,” said Lily King of the school’s achievement. “If it can help one family have an easier go at their journey with cancer, that’s all that matters.”

“As always, the Lucas community came through in just an incredible way,” said Lexi Webster. “I think what is truly the most impactful about this event is we get to see the impact that young people are willing to make on the world around them, for the people they love and for people they don’t event know.”

“I’ve always loved getting involved in my community,” said Brooke Rhiger. “It’s such a big feat for our school. I knew it was something I wanted to get involved in and help with, because it’s such an incredible cause.”

The school is already looking forward to next year’s fundraiser. “We’re starting to prepare our younger grades, so they can follow in our footsteps like we followed in the seniors’ footsteps before us,” said Lily. She shared her advice for younger students joining the cause: “Always stay true to why you’re doing this.”

For media opportunities, please email communications@TVDSB.CA .

Listen on CBC London

stories.title: Trucking industry safety, training standards in focus amid growing concerns
stories.summary: As concerns grow around commercial truck training and licensing standards in Ontario, a Fanshawe
stories.content:
As concerns grow around commercial truck training and licensing standards in Ontario, a Fanshawe expert is available to share what prospective drivers, employers and the public should know when evaluating training quality, safety practices and career pathways.

Heather Carey, senior manager of Fanshawe’s Corporate Training Solutions, can speak about the current trucking landscape and offer practical guidance for those considering a career in commercial driving, as well as for employers looking to recruit or train drivers.

Topics for interviews include:

Why quality training matters for road safety and career success;

What to look for in a reputable training program;

Warning signs to watch for, such as programs promising quick results or guaranteed jobs without strong standards;

What to look for in an employer, including safety culture, mentorship and working conditions;

Funding programs that support driver training and fleet upskilling.

“Choosing the right training program and employer can have a significant impact on both safety and career outcomes in the trucking industry,” Carey says. “It is important that prospective drivers take the time to understand what quality training looks like and seek out organizations that prioritize safety, experience and ongoing development.”

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.CA

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Elizabeth Peloza discovers how a Look Good Feel Better workshop supports cancer patients
stories.summary: Since undergoing breast cancer surgery last December, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has been sharing her healthcare journey during chemotherapy in a CTV News series titled ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Since undergoing breast cancer surgery last December, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has been sharing her healthcare journey during chemotherapy in a CTV News series titled ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’

Previous rounds of chemo triggered hair loss, then a recent change to her medications caused her eyebrows and eyelashes to fall out.

Peloza turned to the Look Good Feel Better (Lgfb) workshop for cancer patients offered inside the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

“Makeup’s never been a strong suit for me,” she admitted. “So, when the many visual changes started happening to me, I was definitely out of my depth about how to address them. So, I signed up for the Look Good Feel Better workshop.”

Look Good Feel Better is Canada’s only national charitable program dedicated to helping people manage the appearance-related impacts of cancer and its treatment.

Volunteers offer free workshops that teach cancer patients of all ages and genders about skincare, makeup and hair loss including an eyebrow-mapping technique.

“We offer a free hair and cosmetic workshop for patients with cancer, and we help them with the appearance-related side effects,” Cottell explained.

But the impact of the workshop extends well beyond makeup techniques.

“When participants come in, they’re very quiet and shy. They’re not talking a whole lot [because] they don’t know other women who have cancer,” Cottell explained. “After two hours, it’s truly magical what happens in that room. The women are all talking, sharing different stories, and they all leave with a smile on their face.”

Peloza understands.

“You just feel so terrible inside, and sometimes you let that reflect on your outside,” she said about the side effects of her chemo treatments.

As Cottell applied makeup to Peloza’s face, her instructions included many words of kindness and compassion.

“You have such beautiful blue eyes,” she told Peloza while rubbing a disposable makeup sponge into an eyeshadow compact.

Cottell then warned against reusable makeup brushes during chemotherapy because they can harbour bacteria.

Later while applying blush on Peloza’s cheek, she offered this instruction, “I want you to smile. So that’s the best part of putting that [blush] on your cheek. You get to smile into the mirror.”

She also asked Peloza about her moisturizing routine to address the extremely dry skin brought on by chemotherapy.

“It’s wonderful to see the transformation in people,” Cottell said while examining Peloza’s drawn-in eyebrows. “And it does give them confidence. If you’re not feeling well one day, just a quick lipstick, blush and eyebrows get you out the door and you feel really good.”

At the end, Peloza smiled as she gazed in a mirror at the results of her makeup workshop.

She spoke candidly to Cottell, “I’ll probably start to care more once I can actually go back out in public. I’ve been kind of isolating after the pneumonia and hospitalized for a week.”

Earlier Cottell had explained that the workshops are an opportunity for cancer patients to speak with others who know firsthand what they’re going through.

Cottell is herself a cancer survivor.

“I personally have had cancer, and I can tell you that all of the other women that have gone through this program helped me when I had mine,” she said.

“As you go through treatment and so many things change, you might isolate more because you don’t feel as confident in yourself,” Peloza explained. “You don’t bother to [apply makeup] like you used to. So, it’s getting that back and being reminded that you are still you - and you are still beautiful.”

Cottell hopes more cancer patients will try the workshop saying, “We really would like to get the word out because so many patients don’t know about it.”

National skincare and makeup brands donate the products given to each workshop participant, and they include shades for all skin tones.

Lgfb also offers special online workshops for teens with cancer.

Details about the program and upcoming workshops (in-person or online) can be found on the Look Good Feel Better website .
paragraphs: Since undergoing breast cancer surgery last December, Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has been sharing her healthcare journey during chemotherapy in a CTV News series titled ‘Healing in the Public Eye.’
Previous rounds of chemo triggered hair loss, then a recent change to her medications caused her eyebrows and eyelashes to fall out.
Peloza turned to the Look Good Feel Better (Lgfb) workshop for cancer patients offered inside the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC).

“Makeup’s never been a strong suit for me,” she admitted. “So, when the many visual changes started happening to me, I was definitely out of my depth about how to address them. So, I signed up for the Look Good Feel Better workshop.”
Look Good Feel Better is Canada’s only national charitable program dedicated to helping people manage the appearance-related impacts of cancer and its treatment.
Volunteers offer free workshops that teach cancer patients of all ages and genders about skincare, makeup and hair loss including an eyebrow-mapping technique.
“We offer a free hair and cosmetic workshop for patients with cancer, and we help them with the appearance-related side effects,” Cottell explained.
But the impact of the workshop extends well beyond makeup techniques.

“When participants come in, they’re very quiet and shy. They’re not talking a whole lot [because] they don’t know other women who have cancer,” Cottell explained. “After two hours, it’s truly magical what happens in that room. The women are all talking, sharing different stories, and they all leave with a smile on their face.”
Peloza understands.
“You just feel so terrible inside, and sometimes you let that reflect on your outside,” she said about the side effects of her chemo treatments.
As Cottell applied makeup to Peloza’s face, her instructions included many words of kindness and compassion.
“You have such beautiful blue eyes,” she told Peloza while rubbing a disposable makeup sponge into an eyeshadow compact.
Cottell then warned against reusable makeup brushes during chemotherapy because they can harbour bacteria.
Later while applying blush on Peloza’s cheek, she offered this instruction, “I want you to smile. So that’s the best part of putting that [blush] on your cheek. You get to smile into the mirror.”
She also asked Peloza about her moisturizing routine to address the extremely dry skin brought on by chemotherapy.

“It’s wonderful to see the transformation in people,” Cottell said while examining Peloza’s drawn-in eyebrows. “And it does give them confidence. If you’re not feeling well one day, just a quick lipstick, blush and eyebrows get you out the door and you feel really good.”
At the end, Peloza smiled as she gazed in a mirror at the results of her makeup workshop.
She spoke candidly to Cottell, “I’ll probably start to care more once I can actually go back out in public. I’ve been kind of isolating after the pneumonia and hospitalized for a week.”
Earlier Cottell had explained that the workshops are an opportunity for cancer patients to speak with others who know firsthand what they’re going through.
Cottell is herself a cancer survivor.
“I personally have had cancer, and I can tell you that all of the other women that have gone through this program helped me when I had mine,” she said.

“As you go through treatment and so many things change, you might isolate more because you don’t feel as confident in yourself,” Peloza explained. “You don’t bother to [apply makeup] like you used to. So, it’s getting that back and being reminded that you are still you - and you are still beautiful.”
Cottell hopes more cancer patients will try the workshop saying, “We really would like to get the word out because so many patients don’t know about it.”
National skincare and makeup brands donate the products given to each workshop participant, and they include shades for all skin tones.
Lgfb also offers special online workshops for teens with cancer.
Details about the program and upcoming workshops (in-person or online) can be found on the Look Good Feel Better website .

stories.title: Community bike riding event returns to London
stories.summary: The Forest City Slow Roll takes place on June 6, with cyclist of all level ride through London neighborhoods. ...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
The Forest City Slow Roll takes place on June 6, with cyclist of all level ride through London neighborhoods.

This year’s London Cycle Link ride will go through six different neighborhoods, including two new additions: old south and SoHo Laura Galvis Daza said the organizer of the event.

“Our mission is to celebrate the bicycle,” Galvis Daza said. “To encourage active transportation and pedestrian-first and cycling infrastructure in London.”

The ride will also showcase major biking projects along Central Ave, Colborne, Ridout Street, and the newly opened Victoria Street Bridge, Galvis Daza said. As well to enjoy the historical infrastructures the city has to offer.

“Streets are meant for people. It’s pedestrians, cyclists, motorists, all abilities young and old, and we need to continue finding ways to share our streets” she said.

The idea for the slow roll began in 2022, when the Forest City Cycling Challenge approached London Cycle Link after seeing similar events in other cities and proposed a partnership.

London Cycle Link is a charitable organization that helps Londoners ride more. It was established in 2013, then launched a community bike repair shop in 2017, and added an education program in 2021. They advocate for safer streets at all levels of government and nurture a thriving cycling culture in London, Galvis Daza said.

“It’s a lot of work setting up an event like this, especially in downtown London. It took about seven months to organize,” said Galvis Daza.

The event runs from 1 p.m. to 6 p.m., with the ride starting at 3 p.m. on Dundas Street between Ridout and Talbot Street. Riders are encouraged to dress up. Food trucks, prizes, and activities will be available before and after for all those who register online.

Due to the amount of work involved, there is no rain date. Organizers say the event will proceed in all weather, with tents available if needed.

Currently there’s more than 300 participants with a capacity of 500 riders. Registration is free online for those interested.

Galvis Daza also thanked all sponsors, volunteers, vendors, and riders for making the event possible.

stories.title: Thames Valley students step up to the plate for Girls at Bat All Star Series
stories.summary: 700 female identifying students from across the Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) will come together at Labatt Memorial Park on Thursday, June 11 for the second annual Girls at Bat All Star Series, a celebration of confidence, connection and inclusion through sport.
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
700 female identifying students from across the Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) will come together at Labatt Memorial Park on Thursday, June 11 for the second annual Girls at Bat All Star Series, a celebration of confidence, connection and inclusion through sport.

Girls at Bat is an introductory level baseball program supported by the Jays Care Foundation, designed to increase participation and retention of female identifying youth in sport by breaking down barriers. The program creates spaces that center female identifying voices, empower leadership and provide opportunities to learn and play sport with a resilient and inclusive community.

Participation in the Girls at Bat program across TVDSB has more than doubled since last year, with over 1,000 students from 30 schools participating.

Students will take part in two sessions throughout the day, rotating through baseball skill-building activities in the outfield and a carnival area with lawn games, activities with the London Public Library and Western Engineering, a DJ, and more.

The event highlights TVDSB’s commitment to creating inclusive, supportive environments where all students can thrive, both on and off the field.

Learn more by visiting the Girls at Bat All Star Series website.

Media are welcome to attend. Students and staff will be available for media opportunities. For more information and to arrange interviews, please contact communications@TVDSB.CA.

stories.title: 12 people displaced after townhouse fire
stories.summary: *This story was updated on June 4, 2026 Twelve people have been displaced as a result of this week's fire at a...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
*This story was updated on June 4, 2026

Twelve people have been displaced as a result of this week’s fire at a north London townhouse complex, firefighters said.

The blaze damaged three units from the complex on Silverbrook Drive, but could have been worse if not for working smoke detectors, the London Fire Department (LFD) said in a post on social media.

Fire crews responded to multiple 911 calls early Wednesday morning, firefighters said. When they arrived around 1 a.m., firefighters saw multiple units flames and smoke pouring out of mutltiple unites in the back of one of the homes.

“Firefighters acted quickly to knock down the fire and successfully limit the extension to the adjacent units,” London Fire Department said in a post on X.

No civilians were reported injured, but one firefighter sustained minor injuries, LFD. The cause of the fire has not been determined but is under investigation, firefighters said.

“Today’s townhouse fire serves as an important reminder of the critical role working smoke detectors play in protecting lives,” they said in the post on X. “Early warning smoke detectors provides valuable time to escape – this is especially important in multi-unit dwellings were fire and smoke can quickly affect neighbouring units.”

Initially the damages were estimated to be over $1 million dollars, but since the initial statement the estimate has decreased to $800,000.

stories.title: ‘When the sun is shining, it’s very busy’; How beautiful weather effects golf courses
stories.summary: Weather can make or break a golfer's day on the course. With the warmer weather London golf courses' time shee...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Weather can make or break a golfer’s day on the course. With the warmer weather London golf courses’ time sheets are filling up.

“I’m thankful, since winter was so cold it’s very nice to have this sun” said Jean whose been golfing for eight years.

“It’s beautiful out here, it was a slow start only on my seventh round this year, but great weather no humidity” said Jeff Van Geel a golfer for 42 years.

“Its very good weather considering the start of the season, but it’s very good” said Jeff’s wife Sylvie who has been golfing with him for 11 years.

Bitter cold winds and rain in the early spring always hurts the club house at the start of golf season, but it builds up the eagerness of the golfers to get out there.

“You never want a damp April because you’ll see a little dip in sales, but it builds the hunger for everyone once the weather turns” said Rob Vincent the professional supervisor at Fanshawe Golf Course.

Owners have been very lucky this year with how the weather is treating the golf courses. Even when it’s bad, diehard fans come out to fill up those spots.

“We have quite a few passholders between the two sites that are going to play rain or shine” Vincent said “But the diehards will play when it’s 2 C and raining.”

He added that golf as a whole has been growing in popularity at a rapid rate. After COVID-19 people who would normally play a couple times per week now come up to five times, and the dedicated golfers who were four times are coming almost everyday. Vincent has been with the city for 20 years watching the growth of golf first hand.

“When we were reopening the world all you could do was get gas, get groceries and play golf, there were no soccer leagues, couldn’t play tennis, and all the gyms were closed” Vincent stated. “2022 was a good year, I expected for numbers to go down, but it was the opposite. I think people saw how great the game is and they stuck around.”

Vincent has been golfing for nearly 35 years. He said golf relaxing for his mind, gets him away from screens, and meeting with your friends.

stories.title: ‘Most powerful protest, is love’: Fanshawe reveals new permanent pride symbol
stories.summary: Fanshawe revealed the newly painted sidewalk in commemoration of Pride Month and commitment for a safe communi...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Fanshawe revealed the newly painted sidewalk in commemoration of Pride Month and commitment for a safe community.

“ This sidewalk is a reminder that we are walking on ground that is shaped by courage” said Joseph Pazzano, Executive Director of Student Wellbeing. It was revealed at the London campus’ annual flag raising ceremony on June 1.

“The sidewalk is near the flag poles at the London campus, and the regional campuses will have a framed pride flag to symbolize our strong commitment for the community” said Xieling Zhang the Centre for Edi’s Consultant at Fanshawe.

“We’re not just focusing on one campus but trying all the regional campuses.”

The ceremonies have taken place on June 1 and June 2 with London and Simcoe on the 1st, and St. Thomas and Woodstock on the 2nd.

“I t’s a way for Fanshawe College to display that visible symbol and also a commitment to creating really safe , affirming and inclusive spaces for all students and employees” said Zhang.

The progress pride flag is the symbol of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, the flag has changed a lot over the years adding colours for the trans, intersex, black, indigenous, and people of colour communities.

“N ot only represents the strength and history that the que er commun ity has, but it s howcases the communit y that comes together regardless of gender, sex, love, all of that is more of those family vibes that the queer community brings together” said Veronica Royale a drag queen in London.

Royale has been performing as a drag queen in London for seven years, appearing in shows that support local charities such as Y.O.U. and St. Leonard’s. Through these performances, she helps raise funds for community organizations while also bringing greater visibility to drag culture and the broader queer community.

June 1 marks the start of pride month for the 2SLGBTQIA+ community that celebrates the pride and contributions of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community.

“ This sidewalk is a reminder that we are walking on ground that is shaped by courage” said Joseph Pazzano, Executive Director of Student Wellbeing. It was revealed at the London campus’ annual flag raising ceremony on June 1.

“The sidewalk is near the flag poles at the London campus, and the regional campuses will have a framed pride flag to symbolize our strong commitment for the community” said Xieling Zhang the Centre for Edi’s Consultant at Fanshawe.
“We’re not just focusing on one campus but trying all the regional campuses.”
The ceremonies have taken place on June 1 and June 2 with London and Simcoe on the 1st, and St. Thomas and Woodstock on the 2nd.
“I t’s a way for Fanshawe College to display that visible symbol and also a commitment to creating really safe , affirming and inclusive spaces for all students and employees” said Zhang.

The progress pride flag is the symbol of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, the flag has changed a lot over the years adding colours for the trans, intersex, black, indigenous, and people of colour communities.

Royale has been performing as a drag queen in London for seven years, appearing in shows that support local charities such as Y.O.U. and St. Leonard’s. stories.title: TVDSB student earns Platinum Award at national science fair for asteroid detection innovation
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

Grade 7 student Siddharth Patel from Clara Brenton Public School is being celebrated nationally after earning one of the top honours at the Canada-Wide Science Fair (Cwsf).

Siddharth received the Platinum Award for Discovery (Junior Division) at the 2026 Cwsf in Edmonton, AB, for his project Automating Asteroid Detection Criteria to Strengthen Citizen Science for Planetary Defense .

Siddharth developed a custom computer algorithm that helps streamline the process of detecting asteroids in telescope images, improving the accuracy and reliability of citizen science efforts in planetary defence.

His national win builds on earlier success this year, when he earned gold and other special awards at the Thames Valley Science and Engineering Fair and advanced to represent the region at the Cwsf. The event is Canada’s largest annual youth Stem competition, bringing together top young innovators from across the country.

Siddharth’s passion for space science is well established. In 2025, he discovered two provisional asteroids through a Nasa-affiliated citizen science initiative and has since been featured on CTV News and CBC Radio for his work and insights.

stories.title: TVDSB Special Education Advisory Committee seeks nominations for membership
stories.summary: General News
stories.author: Thames Valley District School Board
stories.content:
General News

Board Meetings and Agendas

Board Meeting Highlights

The Thames Valley District School Board invites local associations or organizations of parents that operate locally within the jurisdiction of the Board to apply to serve on its Special Education Advisory Committee (Seac) for the period of November 15, 2026, to November 14, 2030.

The Committee will include up to 12 representatives selected from the nominations.

The local associations/organizations must be affiliated with associations or organizations that:

are incorporated;

operate throughout Ontario;

further the interests and well-being of one or more groups of exceptional children or adults; and,

do not represent professional educators.

Organizations with an interest in special education that do not fully meet the above criteria May apply as an additional member.

Visit the Seac page on our website to learn more and apply. Applications must be received by 4:00 p.m. September 18, 2026.

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza describes hospitalization that threatened chemotherapy treatments
stories.summary: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is opening up about a recent health scare that jeopardized her chemotherapy treatments following breast cancer surgery.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Coun. Elizabeth Peloza is opening up about a recent health scare that jeopardized her chemotherapy treatments following breast cancer surgery.

Since March, Peloza has been sharing her healthcare journey in a CTV News series called ‘Healing in the Public Eye’ but was recently forced to take a break from filming.

“I’m well enough now to do a public update and catch everybody up,” she says while sitting in her living room. “I ended up coming down with pneumonia, and then a secondary infection that my family doctor said was sepsis. I ended up being hospitalized for a week,” she explained.

Peloza had previously discussed her concerns about chemotherapy temporarily suppressing her immune system, and while hosting a community meeting on April 17 admitted to CTV News, “It has not been a good couple days.”

She now reflects on the days that followed her community meeting.

“I knew I wasn’t feeling well,” she said. “We started to notice that I was losing my voice, and then the coughing and fatigue set in. It was obviously escalating very quickly.”

A high fever convinced her to visit the emergency department.

Peloza is grateful her 20-year-old son had recently returned home from university.

“You always hope that your kids, because you’ve raised them, will step-up when it’s time,” she said.

He has a driver’s license and drove her to the hospital.

“I’m sure he was terrified as well. [I was] trying to put on a brave face for my kid even as my body was telling me, I think we’re dying. It was absolutely terrifying. I’m lucky he drives,” she said.

A pair of short cellphone videos Peloza recorded at the hospital shed light on the situation.

“Halfway through chemotherapy treatments and unfortunately celebrating that accomplishment in the emergency department,” she said while laying in a hospital bed.

In the second video she’s holding onto an IV cart, “My doctor asked if I had ever received a blood transfusion.”

She would receive a transfusion and eventually return home to continue her recovery.

But Peloza was disheartened to learn that the ordeal left her too weakened to receive her next scheduled round of chemotherapy.

“Devastated,” she admitted. “For me, this is dose-dense treatment for cancer because the cancer could potentially be aggressive. They took out the tumours, but you’re always worried about free floating cells somewhere hiding in your body.”

Dose-dense chemotherapy is a strategy where medications are administered more frequently than in standard schedules to maximize the impact on tumour cells and reduce the time cancer cells have to regrow.

“My chemo’s on an every-other-week schedule to make sure that they find it and kill it,” she said. “But in the back of my mind, I know every delay is potentially making it less effective.”

The mother of three admits to struggling with the possibility of losing the progress made during the previous two months of chemotherapy.

“If we’re being honest, I was crying in the shower because it muffles [the sound] a little bit,” Peloza said. “I do have my children at home, but regardless of their age, they’re still your kids and you’re still the parent. I was just taking that time to emotionally process it.”

She now wants to share the lesson she learned during those difficult days.

“Wherever you’re at, it’s okay. Hopefully tomorrow will be a better day. It might not be, but eventually you will hit the low in the valley and things will improve,” she said.

Peloza eventually received the positive news she needed to get out of her valley.

Her doctor cleared to resume chemotherapy treatments a week ago.

“I was able to start chemo treatments again last Friday, which was great. So now that’s five of eight rounds done,” she said.

Peloza is sharing her experiences during chemotherapy to raise awareness about the importance of early detection, spotlight local resources for cancer patients, and to let others know what to expect if they begin chemotherapy treatments.

Her chemotherapy is expected to conclude in late June.

stories.title: London house fire is under investigation after $500k in damage
stories.summary: Crews responded at about 1:30 a.m. Friday to the 300 block of Grey Street for a structure fire. Firefighters e...
stories.author: Daniel Thuss
stories.content:
Crews responded at about 1:30 a.m. Friday to the 300 block of Grey Street for a structure fire.

Firefighters encountered heavy smoke and flames on arrival.

Crews initially launched an offensive attack but were pulled back by command due to structural instability. Firefighters then switched to a defensive aerial attack.

This incident comes four days after a former church caught fire, that took place down the road on Wellington Street near Grey Street.

All crews have been cleared from the scene. No injuries were reported. Damage is estimated at more than $500,000.
